[13] In the three small uppermost lakes the sediment volume was estimated on the basis of coring and survey on site. The interface between organic sediment (gyttja, clay gyttja or gyttja clay) and the underlying mineral soil (till, sand, silt or clay) was interpreted to indicate lake isolation. The thickness of the lake sediment bed was determined at seven sites in Lake Valkea-Kotinen (1), 35 sites in Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and 48 sites in Lake Ekojärvi (3). In the largest lowland lakes, Kuohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5), echo sounding was used to estimate the volume of the lake sediment bed with survey transects of 15 and 31 km, respectively. In these transects the proportion of accumulation bottom was measured. This proportion and the total lake area were used to estimate the accumulation area, which was multiplied with the average thickness to obtain the sediment volume. For the analysis of sediment density and C content, a sediment core was collected from each lake. The cores extended from the surface of the sediment bed to the depth of lake isolation. In the laboratory the cores were opened and their stratigraphy determined. The cores were divided into samples and a total of 104 samples were analyzed. The sample treatment and laboratory methods are thoroughly described by Pajunen et al. [2000]. The amount of total dry matter is based on sediment volume and average density and the amount of C on the amount of total dry matter and average C content. The average C store (g C m⁻²) was divided by the age of the lake to obtain the average Holocene accumulation rates (g C m⁻² yr⁻¹). [14] The gross sedimentation rate was measured only in the uppermost lake as part of a long-term monitoring program [cf. Keskitalo and Salonen, 1994]. Sedimenting material was collected with three acrylic plastic tubes (length 45 cm, diameter 5 cm) placed below the epilimnion at a depth of 4 m. During the ice-free period, material settled in the tubes was removed every 2 weeks, dried, weighed and analyzed for C content with a high-temperature combustion method [Salonen, 1979]. For annual estimates of gross sedimentation we used the results from the under ice measurements, conducted in 1995 and 1996 with exactly the same methods as during the open water period but using a 3 week collection period. In addition to C, the Fe content of the gross sedimentation was measured during one open water season (in 2000) with a Varian AAS (Varian Inc. Palo Alto, Calif., United States). [15] The samples for TOC and DIC analyses of the water column were taken at 0.2–05 m depth in rivers and at 1 m depth in the lakes. The sampling frequency in the rivers was primarily once a month during the open water season (May–November) and once in winter (early April). The uppermost lake (Valkea-Kotinen) was sampled 24 times during the both years. The other lakes in the chain were sampled 1–4 times in 1997 and four times in 1998 (late winter, spring, summer, and autumnal mixing). For the missing data for spring 1997 in Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and Kukkia (5), and for winter, spring and autumn 1997 in Kuohijärvi (4) the values for the corresponding season of 1998 were used. [16] The TOC concentration of the water was analyzed with a Shimadzu TOC-500 analyzer (Shimadzu Corp. Kyoto, Japan). For some occasions (about half of the river samples), water color values (platinum reference) were available instead of TOC. However, TOC was linearly related to water color in the samples taken from the study rivers and the lakes, and the missing TOC values were estimated with the regression equation: TOC [mg C L⁻¹] = 0.0408 * water color [mg Pt L⁻¹] + 5.29 (r² = 0.84, P < 0.05, n = 110). The DIC concentrations were estimated from the measured alkalinity values with the regression equation DIC [μmol L⁻¹] = 0.996 * Alkalinity [μeq L⁻¹] + 19.3, r² = 0.95, n = 874, obtained from measurements in randomly selected Finnish soft water lakes with similar range of alkalinity [Rantakari and Kortelainen, 2008]. Temperature and oxygen concentration in the water column of the lakes was measured with YSI 55 (Yellow Springs Instruments) combined probe (accuracy ±0.3°C, ±0.3 mg O₂ L⁻¹). [17] The discharge from each subcatchment was estimated using measured daily runoff data for the years 1997 and 1998 (Finnish Environment Institute, OIVA service on environment and geographic information, 17 March 2010) from the rivers Mustajoki and Haarajoki, both situated less than 30 km from the study sites and having land use characteristics very similar to the study lakes, assuming that the discharge from each subcatchment was related to its area. The TOC and DIC input and output were calculated by multiplying the monthly discharge (the sum of measured daily values) at the inflows and outflows with the TOC and DIC concentration during the respective period in the rivers between the lakes. [18] Emissions of CO\(_2\) from the lakes were calculated using the equation by Cole and Caraco [1998], in which the CO\(_2\) saturation in the surface water was compared with the equilibrium value. The CO\(_2\) concentrations were calculated from the available open water DIC and pH results of each lakes, with correction for water temperature [Stumm and Morgan, 1970; Butler, 1982; Kling et al., 1992]. Partial pressure of CO\(_2\) (\(p\)CO\(_2\)) was calculated from the CO\(_2\) concentrations, using Henry’s law constants corrected for temperature and atmospheric pressure [Plummer and Busenberg, 1982]. The equilibrium CO\(_2\) concentration in the lake water was calculated using the elevation of the lake and Henry’s law constants, assuming an atmospheric mixing ratio of 361 ppm by volume (ppmv) for 1996 and an annual increase of 1.5 ppmv y\(^{-1}\) by Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change [2001], equaling the values measured in Finland [e.g., Kulmala et al., 2000]. The piston velocity of CO\(_2\) was obtained by first determining the piston velocity of SF\(_6\), using the empirical relationship between the piston velocity of SF\(_6\) normalized to a Schmidt number of 600 and the wind speed at a height of 10 m [Cole and Caraco, 1998] and then calculating the Schmidt number for CO\(_2\), using empirical third-order polynomial fits to temperature [Jähne et al., 1987]. The wind speed was assumed to be 3 m s\(^{-1}\), which is the average long-term open water period wind speed for inland measurement stations in Finland [Leinonen, 2000]. All the equations for calculations of the CO\(_2\) emissions are presented by Rantakari and Kortelainen [2005]. Additional data for the range of CO\(_2\) emissions from the lakes, estimated for the year 2000 (annual precipitation 634 mm, summer precipitation 266 mm) on the basis of four measurements in three of the lakes, are also presented in the Table 6. The emissions of CH\(_4\) from some of the study lakes were minor compared to CO\(_2\) efflux and have been presented elsewhere [Kankaala et al., 2005, 2006; Bergström et al., 2007]. The measured atmospheric deposition of C in the area was 1 g C m\(^{-2}\) yr\(^{-1}\) [Kortelainen et al., 2006a]. [19] The annual production of phytoplankton in Lake Valkea-Kotinen (1) was measured weekly during the open water season in situ using the \(^{14}\)C method [Keskitalo and Salonen, 1994]. Since the incubation time was 24 h, the measurements resulted in net primary productivity values (NPP). For the other lakes, the range of NPP of phytoplankton was estimated using data obtained in previous measurements in neighboring lakes [Ilmavirta and Kotimaa, 1974; Arvola 1983, 1984; Arvola et al., 1999], with the same types of trophic status and chemical and physical properties as in the study lakes. The areas covered by different macrophyte species were mapped in 1997–2000. The macrophyte C pool was estimated as a seasonal maximum biomass (g dry weight (DW) m\(^{-2}\)) converted to C by a factor 0.38 [Duarte, 1992], obtained from the data for stands of the dominant species in the three uppermost lakes [Keskitalo and Heitto, 1996; Kankaala et al., 2003, 2005]. The NPP of macrophytes was estimated to be twofold the seasonal maximum biomass of all the stands [Westlake, 1982]. [20] We also made a regional, landscape-scale estimate of CO\(_2\) emissions and sediment net C accumulation of all the lakes in the cumulative catchment area of the lake chain. The results of the five lakes studied were upscaled for the respective lake size classes (area <0.1, 0.1–1, 1–10 and 10–50 km\(^2\)) throughout the area. The areal results (g C m\(^{-2}\)) of the largest size class were also applied to the size class 1–10 km, because none of the lakes in the chain studied belonged to that size class. [21] The statistical relationships between the different variables in the data set were calculated as Pearson’s linear correlations (Pearson’s r). The variables with skewed distributions were first log-transformed to approach normality. The analyses were done with PASW (SPSS) Statistics 17.0 software. 3. Results 3.1. Carbon Pools [22] In all the lakes, >98% of C was in the sediments (Table 4). The proportion of organic matter (Table 4) in the sediments decreased, while the density of the lake sediment bed increased downstream of the lake chain. In Lake Valkea-Kotinen (1), the average sediment density was 0.056 g cm\(^{-3}\), in Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) 0.14 g cm\(^{-3}\), in Lakes Ekojärvi (3) and Kuohijärvi (4) about 0.25 g cm\(^{-3}\) and in Lake Kukkia (5) 0.35 g cm\(^{-3}\). In the uppermost lake, the average thickness of the sediment bed (computed for the entire lake area) was 1.6 m, while in the succeeding three lakes the bed was around 2 m thick and in the lowermost lake only 1.2 m thick. [23] The water column TOC, including phytoplankton, constituted 95% of the lake water C pool in Lake Valkea-Kotinen (1) (Table 4). The proportion of TOC decreased along the lake chain to 68% in Kuohijärvi (4) and to 67% in Kukkia (5) while the proportion of DIC increased from 5% in Valkea-Kotinen to 33% in Kukkia. Accordingly, the annual maximum biomass of littoral macrophytes during late summer varied from 13% to 4% of the total C pool in the first three lakes, but in the larger lowland lakes the percentage of macrophytes was almost insignificant (Table 4). [24] The areal sediment C store correlated positively with the proportion of peatlands in the catchment and lake water TOC and Fe concentrations but negatively with lake area and the ratio between lake area to catchment area (LA/CA) (Table 7). The TOC concentration of the water correlated negatively with the size of the lakes and with LA/CA, and positively with the proportion of peatlands in the catchment. 3.2. Carbon Fluxes [25] The annual TOC loads into the lakes increased by 40–210% in the wet year 1998 compared with the dry year 1997 (Figure 2). The increased runoff in 1998 (average runoff in 1998 and 1997 was 9.03 L s⁻¹ km⁻² and 5.04 L s⁻¹ km⁻², respectively) was the main determinant for the higher loads, whereas the higher concentrations of TOC in river water in summer 1998 (average 14.7 mg C L⁻¹) compared with those in 1997 (average 10.8 mg C L⁻¹) played a minor role. During the wet year TOC inflow was higher than outflow in all the lakes, but during the dry year in the two uppermost lakes TOC loss by outflow exceeded that coming by inflow. The DIC loads were also higher in the wet year but the DIC/TOC ratios were higher in the dry year in all the lakes (average in the dry year 0.22 and in the wet year 0.14). [26] The annual input of C by the net production of macrophytes was always small compared with the C input to the lake by runoff. The net production of macrophytes was lower than the estimated net primary production by phytoplankton in each lake (Table 6). With the exception of the uppermost headwater lake during the dry year, C input from the catchment exceeded the autochthonously produced C in the lakes (Figure 4). [27] The high summer precipitation generally increased the C fluxes in the lakes (Figure 2 and Table 6). Hydrological import and export of TOC dominated the carbon fluxes especially in the two small drainage lakes with small LA/CA ratios (Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and Ekojärvi (3)) in the middle of the chain (Table 6 and Figure 4). Atmospheric emissions were highest in the three uppermost lakes during the wet year (79–86 g C m⁻² a⁻¹). However, throughout the lake chain, the efflux of CO₂ into the atmosphere was not significantly correlated with the TOC input (Table 7). [28] In the uppermost headwater lake (Valkea-Kotinen (1)) the average long-term sediment deposition rate was 0.14 mm yr⁻¹ while in the small drainage lakes (Alinen Rautjärvi (2), Ekojärvi (3)) and in the large Kuohijärvi (4) the average deposition rate was higher, about 0.20 mm yr⁻¹. In Lake Kukkia (5) the average long-term deposition rate was the lowest, 0.12 mm yr⁻¹. In the uppermost lake the gross sedimentation rate of C was 7, eightfold compared with the average long-term accumulation rate in the sediment. The short-term gross sedimentation rates of C and Fe were positively correlated in the uppermost lake (Figure 3a). Throughout the lake chain the long-term net sedimentation of C was also positively correlated with Fe and TOC concentrations of the water column (Figure 3b). The proportion of net sedimentation was low in the lake C budgets; in the uppermost lake it was 3–5% of the annual C output and in the other lakes the proportion was 1–2% (Figure 4). [29] On the landscape scale, the small lakes (area <1 km²) were important in the net accumulation of carbon in the sediments, since they were responsible for 56% of the net C accumulation in all the lakes although they formed only 14% of the entire lake area (Table 8). On the other hand, the large lowland lakes (size class 10–50 km²) played a more important role in the CO₂ emissions. In the dry year, the emissions from these lakes made up 60% of the total C effluxes from all lakes in the area, and during the wet year the proportion was 47%. 4. Discussion [30] In the typical boreal lake chain C fluxes were dominated by the input of allochthonous organic matter from the catchment, especially in small drainage lakes with low LA/CA ratio (Figure 4). Although the sediments formed the most important carbon pool (>98%) in the lakes of all size classes, the average Holocene net accumulation rate of C was very small compared with that evaded as CO₂ to atmosphere. This indicates effective mineralization of the organic C within the lake chain. On the landscape scale, small lakes played more important role in long-term C accumulation in the sediments than the large ones, which were more important as emitters of atmospheric CO₂. As hypothesized, the hydrological conditions were important drivers of C transfer from the catchment and along the lake chain, since during the rainy year the transport of C from the catchments was remarkably enhanced, compared with the dry year (Table 6 and Figure 4). Influence of Lake Size, Position, and Catchment Characteristics [31] In the uppermost lake the mean long-term accumulation rate of C in the sediment was only about 13–14% of the recent annual gross sedimentation rate, indicating that the bulk of the organic C produced in the lake and received from the catchment is mineralized in sediment respiration. In a time series of varved sediments from a lake in Sweden, Gälman et al. [2008] observed that 20% of the annually deposited C in the sediment was lost within 5 years, after which the C loss rate decreased. Sobek et al. [2009] showed that C burial efficiency in lake sediments is negatively related to oxygen exposure time. In our study lakes, the lowest areal pools of C in the sediment were found in the two largest lakes (Table 4), in which the water column is oxic throughout the year. [32] In our study the sediment C pool estimates represent average accumulation during the whole Holocene period, which presumably underestimates the recent net accumulation rates; increasing human impact in the catchments generally results in increasing accumulation rates [e.g., Einsele et al., 2001]. In our study lakes, the human impact has been modest in the two uppermost lakes and more intensive in the catchments of the large lakes. Agriculture in the catchment promotes erosion, leading to increased mass accumulation rates, but to lower organic matter content [Kortelainen et al., 2004], as also found in the studied lake chain. The proportion of TOC in the lake water C pool decreased along the lake chain, while the proportion of DIC increased indicating mineralization of allochthonous C within the lake chain. This is also attributable to the increasing proportion of agriculture in the catchments. The proportion of DIC in the lake water total C is typically greater in lakes surrounded by agricultural land than in lakes in forested or peatland-rich areas [Oh and Raymond, 2006; Rantakari and Kortelainen, 2008]. [33] We found that the lake water Fe content was a very good predictor for the pool and long-term accumulation rate of C in the sediment. Although we used mean chemical composition of the lake water during the recent 20 years, the differences in the analyzed Fe contents of the lake waters (Table 2) presumably do not reflect only the recent Fe leaching from the catchment. [35] Upstream lakes decrease the quantity of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in streams [Larson et al., 2007] and lakes [e.g., Kortelainen, 1993; Rantakari et al., 2004] and also decrease riverine TOC loads [e.g., Mattsson et al., 2005]. In our study, the proportion of lakes in the catchments did not affect the in-lake TOC concentrations, but decreased both the TOC inflow and the outflow (Table 7). In our study lakes the TOC concentrations correlated negatively with the lake area and the LA/CA ratio, but positively with the proportion of peatlands in the catchments; the latter has been shown in several studies in the Boreal Zone [e.g., Kortelainen, 1993]. [36] The size of the lake also affects the emissions as the annual evasion of CO₂ increases toward the smaller size classes. In 177 randomly selected lakes in Finland the average value of CO₂ emissions varied from 37 g C m⁻² in the largest lakes (between 10 and 100 km²) to 102 g C m⁻² in the smallest lakes (<0.1 km²) [Kortelainen et al., 2006b]. The two middlemost lakes in our lake chain showed emission of the same range, while the emissions of both the uppermost and the lowest lakes were lower than the average size class values in the study by Kortelainen et al. [2006b]. [37] The partition and the actual values of different C pools and fluxes in the three smallest lakes of the chain mostly agreed with the ones reported from the small, boreal, humic Lake Friksjön [Sobek et al., 2006], with the most noticeable difference being the smaller role of macrophytes in our lakes. The areal sediment C pool in Lake Friksjön was lower than that in our small lakes, but remarkably higher than that of the two large lakes in our study. The C pools of large lakes also differed from Lake Friksjön in having higher proportions of DIC in the water column. Our results on the riverine C influx as the major regulator of the lake chain C budget might represent various vegetation zones and soils, since Finlay et al. [2010] had similar results in the hard water lake chain. Although inorganic C accounted for the highest proportion of the C budget in the hard water lake chain and the total C sedimentation was higher, the bulk density of the sediments as well as the total C content were similar in both studies. On the landscape scale, our study emphasizes not only the role of small lakes (<1 km²) in C accumulation in the sediments, as also observed by Kortelainen et al. [2004], but also the role of large lakes (>10 km²) as intensive sites of organic C mineralization and emitters as atmospheric CO₂. 4.2. Influence of Hydrological Conditions [38] The hydrology was an important driver of C transfer from the catchment and along the lake chain, since during the rainy year the transport of C from the catchments was remarkably enhanced, compared with the dry year. This situation was comparable to tundra ponds, where the hydrological pathways acted as biogeochemical pathways for C during periods of high runoff [Macrae et al., 2004]. In addition to the rapid transport of C out of the catchments, the TOC concentrations in the lakes were also higher in the rainy year, the pattern which was shown in Lake Valkeakotinen by Arvola et al. [2010]. The C budgets of the lakes were negative in the dry year (1997), presumably indicating losses of C that had been formerly accumulated in the lakes. During the wet year, the three lakes along the chain acted as sinks of C, probably replacing the lake water C pool that had been decreasing during the preceding dry year. The output of C in the uppermost lake clearly dominated over the input, as was also noted in a small nearby lake by Arvola et al. [1990]. This may have been due to the difficulties in determining the amount of the C input from the catchment in the small lakes, and especially in lakes without inlets. Thus, our presumption of groundwater being an insignificant source of C may also have been wrong in Lake Valkeakotinen, since a strong groundwater signature in aquatic \( pCO_2 \) has been found in many lakes and streams in Sweden [Humborg et al., 2010]. [39] During the rainy year, the CO₂ emissions were higher than during the dry year in the three smallest upstream lakes. Rantakari and Kortelainen [2005] also found a close connection between annual CO₂ emission and precipitation in large Finnish lakes, and suggested that during periods of high precipitation more organic C produced in the terrestrial ecosystem is transported to the lakes and decomposed. They also emphasized the importance of the weather conditions of the previous autumn contributing to the delay between heavy rainfall in the autumn and increasing CO₂ concentrations in the large lakes in winter. This may have influenced our largest study lakes, Kuhohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5), which have long residence times and large water volume. In these two lakes, the CO₂ emissions were higher during the dry year. On the other hand, the water temperatures of all the study lakes were higher during the dry year (Table 3), which may also have impacted the CO₂ fluxes to the atmosphere. Kosten et al. [2010] found that the \( pCO_2 \) closely followed the temperature in 82 South American lakes with wide ranges in DOC concentrations, suggesting an increase in temperature-dependent mineralization of DOC and larger lacustrine CO₂ emissions due to climate warming. The in-lake processes presumably had greater influence on the C fluxes in the large lakes of our study, while in the small drainage lakes with small LA/CA ratios, the allochthonous matter dominated. In the river input to all our lakes the DIC/TOC ratios were higher in the dry year. Thus the higher increase in concentrations of inorganic compared with organic C during the dry year was a characteristic of the allochthonous input. Not all the CO₂ in the lake results from the in-lake processes, since part of the DIC transported from the catchment is emitted directly from the lake to the atmosphere [Ojala et al., 2011]. Overall, the retention of C in the study lakes ((sedimentation + atmospheric emission)/C input) was more efficient in the dry year. This was presumably related to the longer hydraulic residence time during the dry year, providing longer time periods for sedimentation as well as for the biogeochemical and physical mineralization processes. [40] The increasing frequency of heavy precipitation events and wet/dry periods may further strengthen the variability in timing and magnitude of C loads [e.g., Hongve et al., 2004; Erlandsson et al., 2008]. Naden et al. [2010] showed that the future projection (for years 2071–2100) for the Mustajoki River, situated close the study area, includes a 7% increase in annual mean DOC concentrations and a 16% increase in annual mean DOC load. Our results emphasize the role of terrestrial signals and underline climate as the major driver of ecosystem C balances. Peatland C sequestration rates are highly sensitive even to minor climatic fluctuations [Yu et al., 2003], with wet periods correlating rapidly with peat accumulation. Similarly, the soil organic C pool in Nordic forest soils increases with both mean annual temperature and mean annual precipitation [Callesen et al., 2003]. There will presumably be variation in the response of lakes to climatic drivers, depending on the characteristics of the lakes (e.g., size, morphology and LA/CA ratios) as well as on the properties of their catchments. 5. Conclusions [41] Boreal lakes are important conduits of terrestrially fixed C to the atmosphere. Over the long-term and on the landscape scale, they are also important sinks of C. The sediments of the uppermost headwater lakes are important storages of organic C, and in our boreal lakes Fe played an important role in C accumulation. [42] The lakes in the chain may play different roles in C transport, processing and storage. In the upstream lakes with low LA/CA ratios, the C budget is strongly controlled by TOC inflow and outflow. In the large lowland lakes the partition can be different between the components of the C budget: while the impact of riverine transport is lower, the emissions to the atmosphere play greater role in the C budget. [43] We have also shown that freshwater C budgets, including all major pools and fluxes, show highly variable patterns during dry and wet years. In our study, precipitation was an important driver for C balance in all these boreal lakes. Changing climate can thus greatly modify the role of lakes in landscape C balances. [44] Acknowledgments. Carbon pools and fluxes in a chain of five boreal lakes: A dry and wet year comparison E. Einola,1 M. Rantakari,2 P. Kankaala,3 P. Kortelainen,2 A. Ojala,4 H. Pajunen,5 S. Mäkelä,1 and L. Arvola1 Received 23 December 2010; revised 6 May 2011; accepted 18 May 2011; published 27 July 2011. [1] Lakes play an important role in catchment carbon (C) balances. However, the role of lakes in landscape C cycling in changing climate is highly uncertain. We studied C pools in a chain of five boreal lakes and compared the C fluxes during a wet and a dry year. The included pools were dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and total organic carbon (TOC) in lake water, as well as C pools in littoral macrophytes and lake sediments. The estimated C fluxes consisted of hydrological input and output of DIC and TOC, emission of carbon dioxide (CO2) to the atmosphere, DIC incorporated as organic carbon in primary production of phytoplankton and littoral macrophytes, and sedimentation of C. The riverine input of C into the lakes increased remarkably (40–210%) in the year with high precipitation. Simultaneously, there was a clear increase in the flux of CO2 to the atmosphere from the three small uppermost lakes, whereas in two large lowland lakes the CO2 fluxes were higher during the warm dry year. On the landscape scale, the role of small lakes (area <1 km2) was emphasized in net C accumulation, whereas the large lowland lakes released more CO2 to the atmosphere. In parallel, the concentration of TOC in the water column decreased downstream the lake chain whereas DIC increased. The largest pool of C (>98%) in all the lakes was in the sediment. Sediment C store, calculated relative to the lake area, was positively correlated with lake water TOC (r2 = 0.93, P < 0.05) and Fe (r2 = 0.96, P < 0.05) concentrations. Lake water Fe content was also a good predictor for the long-term accumulation (r2 = 0.99, P < 0.01), as well as gross sedimentation rate of organic carbon (r2 = 0.48, P < 0.01). Citation: Einola, E., M. Rantakari, P. Kankaala, P. Kortelainen, A. Ojala, H. Pajunen, S. Mäkelä, and L. Arvola (2011), Carbon pools and fluxes in a chain of five boreal lakes: A dry and wet year comparison, J. Geophys. Res., 116, G03009, doi:10.1029/2010JG001636. 1. Introduction [2] Although freshwater lakes and rivers cover a small area of the earth’s surface, their role in regional carbon (C) budgets and also in global C cycling is much more pronounced than expected only by their area. Rivers and lakes transport, mineralize and accumulate significant amounts of terrestrially fixed C and exchange inorganic C between water-air interfaces [e.g., del Giorgio and Peters, 1994; Kortelainen et al., 2004; Cole et al., 2007; Downing, 2010]. [3] The riverine transport of organic carbon plays an important role in functioning of boreal lakes; e.g., in humic lakes, common in the Boreal Zone, terrestrial carbon input can be much higher than in-lake production [Sarvala et al., 1981; Arvola et al., 1990; Jonsson et al., 2001]. As a consequence, the majority of lakes and rivers are net heterotrophic, i.e., the biological C mineralization exceeds primary production [Alin and Johnson, 2007; Tranvik et al., 2009]. Moreover, the recent trend of increasing concentrations of colored organic substances in many northern lakes and rivers [e.g., Monteith et al., 2007; Lepistö et al., 2008] may further strengthen heterotrophy in these freshwater ecosystems because of decreasing light availability for primary producers. [4] In the Boreal Zone, the concentration of total organic carbon (TOC) in lakes and the export of TOC from catchments are strongly related to the coverage of peatlands [Kortelainen, 1993; Kortelainen et al., 2006a] and coniferous forests in the catchment area [Mattsson et al., 2003; Humborg et al., 2004]. Most (>80%) of the organic matter exported from the catchments is in dissolved form [Wetzel, 2001]. A small proportion of the dissolved organic matter (DOM) may aggregate with metals (amorphous iron and aluminum) [Jonsson, 1997] and/or flocculate with bacteria [von Wachenfeldt et al., 2009], contributing to C accumulation in bottom sediments. In small boreal headwater streams as well as large rivers flowing to the Figure 1. Map of the study area showing the study lakes, the rivers connecting them, and the vegetation type and land use of each study lake. Thick arrows indicate the main inlets of rivers running to and from the study lakes. Baltic Sea, the proportion of particulate organic carbon (POC) of TOC is <5% [Kortelainen et al., 2006a; Mattsson et al., 2005]. The contribution of living material is low especially in running waters, where bacteria, algae, protozoa and larger zooplankton may comprise only about 1% of the TOC [Arvola and Nurmesniemi, 2000]. [5] Most lakes in the Boreal Zone are connected by streams as chains that can differ considerably in their morphology and physical and chemical characteristics. The residence time of water in each basin, defined by the catchment setting and lake morphology, together with the average annual runoff, may be crucial for biogeochemical processing of the organic matter [cf. Algesten et al., 2004], i.e., for microbial decomposition in the water column and in the sediment as well as ultraviolet (UV) irradiance-induced breakdown in the uppermost water layer [Vähätalo et al., 2000; Jonsson et al., 2001]. As a consequence, the residence time influences the quantity and quality of organic matter flowing downstream, and the proportion of organic C released as carbon dioxide (CO_2) and methane (CH_4), or stored in the bottom sediments. Mattsson et al. [2005] showed that proportion of lake area in the upper catchment significantly reduced TOC transport by the large Finnish rivers to the coast. Thus, upstream lakes may be intensive sites for DOM processing, which decreases the export of C downstream [Rasmussen et al., 1989; Kortelainen, 1993; Larson et al., 2007]. [6] Climate change scenarios predict increasing precipitation and temperature for many areas in the Boreal Zone, resulting in major changes in seasonal runoff patterns in northern catchments [e.g., Andréasson et al., 2004], including increasing frequency of extreme weather conditions and thus also extremes in hydrology [e.g., Christensen and Christensen, 2003]. Since hydrology is a major driver of the variability of water C concentrations on the catchment scale [e.g., Erlandsson et al., 2008], the interannual variations in C budgets of individual lakes may be considerable [Arvola et al., 1990]. Although carbon budgets for single lakes [e.g., Arvola et al., 1990; Sobek et al., 2006] and also for a chain of hard-water lakes [Finlay et al., 2010] have been studied, C budgets for a chain of boreal lakes in climatically different years have remained unknown. [7] The aim of our study was to (1) estimate C pools (store in the sediment and in the water column and biomass of primary producers) in a chain of five boreal lakes consisting of one small headwater lake, two small drainage lakes, and two large downstream lakes and to (2) compare C fluxes (net primary production, inflow, outflow, sedimentation, and atmospheric efflux) between a dry and a rainy year within this Table 1. Material and Methods [8] The five study lakes (areal range 0.036–44 km2), situated in the southern Boreal Zone in Finland were numbered by their order in the chain: (1) Valkea-Kotinen, (2) Alinen Rautjärvi, (3) Ekojärvi, (4) Kuohijärvi, and (5) Kukkia (Figure 1). The area deglaciated about 11,500 years ago [Pajunen, 2004]. The uppermost and the smallest lake, Valkea-Kotinen (1), was isolated immediately after deglaciation, while the other lakes were submerged by waters of the ancient Baltic Sea. Since the postglacial land uplift was more rapid than the rise of sea level, the land area expanded and new lakes became isolated. Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) was isolated about 11,400 years ago, Lake Ekojärvi (3) about 9800 years ago and the largest lakes, Kuohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5) about 9700 years ago [Pajunen, 2004]. [9] The Precambrian bedrock in the area consists of veined gneiss with granodiorite occurring around Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and close to Lake Kuohijärvi (4). The soil is mostly moraine but there is gravel and sand around Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and the river draining it, while clay areas partly surround lakes Kuohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5). Coniferous forests with Norway Spruce (Picea abies [L.] H. Karst.) and Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris L.) cover 65–80% and peatlands less than 20% of the catchment areas of each lake (Figure 1). Except for the first lake of the chain, Valkea-Kotinen, which is situated in a nature reserve area, the human impact on the catchments has been quite intense, because of a >150 year long history of forestry and related activities, including draining of wetlands. Some agriculture is also practiced, predominantly in the lowland areas, but the proportion of agricultural land in the catchment does not exceed 5% around any of the studied lakes. The local names suggest that historically the local people have utilized lake iron (e.g., Alinen Rautjärvi = Lower Iron Lake). The lakes vary in their morphological characteristics (Table 1), and the lake area to catchment area ratio (LA/CA) is significantly higher in the two largest lowland lakes than in the first three lakes in the chain. The concentrations of TOC, total phosphorus, total nitrogen and chlorophyll \( a \) are higher in the small upstream lakes than in the largest lowland lakes (Table 2). In the uppermost lake, Valkea-Kotinen (1), the hypolimnion is anoxic during winter and summer stratification. In Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and Ekojärvi (3), the hypolimnetic anoxia during the stratification periods is occasional, whereas in Kuohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5) the entire water column is oxic throughout the year. The larger lakes are covered by ice usually from late November to late April and the smaller ones from late October or early November to early May. [10] The annual long-term (1987–2007) average precipitation in the area is 632 mm (Finnish Meteorological Institute). The highest runoff peaks are generally observed in spring after snowmelt. The runoff can also peak during autumn, when precipitation is generally higher than in summer and the evapotranspiration is small. However, high runoffs can also occur during summer, as in 1998, if the precipitation is high and the antecedent soil conditions are wet. [11] The annual precipitation during 1997 was 5% lower and during 1998 22% higher than the average (Table 3), with the most distinguishable difference in the precipitation patterns observed in summer: in 1997 the summer precipitation was 10% lower than the long-term average, while in 1998 it was 70% higher than the average. The differences in precipitation were reflected in the water residence time of the lakes. There was also a difference of almost 2°C between the daily average air temperatures during the two summers (Table 3). [13] In the three small uppermost lakes the sediment volume was estimated on the basis of coring and survey on site. The interface between organic sediment (gyttja, clay gyttja or gyttja clay) and the underlying mineral soil (till, sand, silt or clay) was interpreted to indicate lake isolation. The thickness of the lake sediment bed was determined at seven sites in Lake Valkea-Kotinen (1), 35 sites in Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and 48 sites in Lake Ekojärvi (3). In the largest lowland lakes, Kuohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5), echo sounding was used to estimate the volume of the lake sediment bed with survey transects of 15 and 31 km, respectively. In these transects the proportion of accumulation bottom was measured. This proportion and the total lake area were used to estimate the accumulation area, which was multiplied with the average thickness to obtain the sediment volume. For the analysis of sediment density and C content, a sediment core was collected from each lake. The cores extended from the surface of the sediment bed to the depth of lake isolation. In the laboratory the cores were opened and their stratigraphy determined. The cores were divided into samples and a total of 104 samples were analyzed. The sample treatment and laboratory methods are thoroughly described by Pajunen et al. [2000]. The amount of total dry matter is based on sediment volume and average density and the amount of C on the amount of total dry matter and average C content. The average C store (g C m⁻²) was divided by the age of the lake to obtain the average Holocene accumulation rates (g C m⁻² yr⁻¹). [14] The gross sedimentation rate was measured only in the uppermost lake as part of a long-term monitoring program [cf. Keskitalo and Salonen, 1994]. Sedimenting material was collected with three acrylic plastic tubes (length 45 cm, diameter 5 cm) placed below the epilimnion at a depth of 4 m. During the ice-free period, material settled in the tubes was removed every 2 weeks, dried, weighed and analyzed for C content with a high-temperature combustion method [Salonen, 1979]. For annual estimates of gross sedimentation we used the results from the under ice measurements, conducted in 1995 and 1996 with exactly the same methods as during the open water period but using a 3 week collection period. In addition to C, the Fe content of the gross sedimentation was measured during one open water season (in 2000) with a Varian AAS (Varian Inc. Palo Alto, Calif., United States). [15] The samples for TOC and DIC analyses of the water column were taken at 0.2–05 m depth in rivers and at 1 m depth in the lakes. The sampling frequency in the rivers was primarily once a month during the open water season (May–November) and once in winter (early April). The uppermost lake (Valkea-Kotinen) was sampled 24 times during the both years. The other lakes in the chain were sampled 1–4 times in 1997 and four times in 1998 (late winter, spring, summer, and autumnal mixing). For the missing data for spring 1997 in Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and Kukkia (5), and for winter, spring and autumn 1997 in Kuohijärvi (4) the values for the corresponding season of 1998 were used. [16] The TOC concentration of the water was analyzed with a Shimadzu TOC-500 analyzer (Shimadzu Corp. Kyoto, Japan). For some occasions (about half of the river samples), water color values (platinum reference) were available instead of TOC. However, TOC was linearly related to water color in the samples taken from the study rivers and the lakes, and the missing TOC values were estimated with the regression equation: TOC [mg C L⁻¹] = 0.0408 * water color [mg Pt L⁻¹] + 5.29 (r² = 0.84, P < 0.05, n = 110). The DIC concentrations were estimated from the measured alkalinity values with the regression equation DIC [μmol L⁻¹] = 0.996 * Alkalinity [μeq L⁻¹] + 19.3, r² = 0.95, n = 874, obtained from measurements in randomly selected Finnish soft water lakes with similar range of alkalinity [Rantakari and Kortelainen, 2008]. Temperature and oxygen concentration in the water column of the lakes was measured with YSI 55 (Yellow Springs Instruments) combined probe (accuracy ±0.3°C, ±0.3 mg O₂ L⁻¹). [17] The discharge from each subcatchment was estimated using measured daily runoff data for the years 1997 and 1998 (Finnish Environment Institute, OIVA service on environment and geographic information, 17 March 2010) from the rivers Mustajoki and Haarajoki, both situated less than 30 km from the study sites and having land use characteristics very similar to the study lakes, assuming that the discharge from each subcatchment was related to its area. The TOC and DIC input and output were calculated by multiplying the monthly discharge (the sum of measured daily values) at the inflows and outflows with the TOC and DIC concentration during the respective period in the rivers between the lakes. For the uppermost lake in the chain, the input of TOC and DIC from the catchment was estimated using the values of small brooks having similar catchments with no upstream lakes. We assumed that the input of C by groundwater was insignificant to the C fluxes in this flat landscape. [18] Emissions of CO\(_2\) from the lakes were calculated using the equation by Cole and Caraco [1998], in which the CO\(_2\) saturation in the surface water was compared with the equilibrium value. The CO\(_2\) concentrations were calculated from the available open water DIC and pH results of each lakes, with correction for water temperature [Stumm and Morgan, 1970; Butler, 1982; Kling et al., 1992]. Partial pressure of CO\(_2\) (\(p\)CO\(_2\)) was calculated from the CO\(_2\) concentrations, using Henry’s law constants corrected for temperature and atmospheric pressure [Plummer and Busenberg, 1982]. The equilibrium CO\(_2\) concentration in the lake water was calculated using the elevation of the lake and Henry’s law constants, assuming an atmospheric mixing ratio of 361 ppm by volume (ppmv) for 1996 and an annual increase of 1.5 ppmv y\(^{-1}\) by Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change [2001], equaling the values measured in Finland [e.g., Kulmala et al., 2000]. The piston velocity of CO\(_2\) was obtained by first determining the piston velocity of SF\(_6\), using the empirical relationship between the piston velocity of SF\(_6\) normalized to a Schmidt number of 600 and the wind speed at a height of 10 m [Cole and Caraco, 1998] and then calculating the Schmidt number for CO\(_2\), using empirical third-order polynomial fits to temperature [Jähne et al., 1987]. The wind speed was assumed to be 3 m s\(^{-1}\), which is the average long-term open water period wind speed for inland measurement stations in Finland [Leinonen, 2000]. All the equations for calculations of the CO\(_2\) emissions are presented by Rantakari and Kortelainen [2005]. Additional data for the range of CO\(_2\) emissions from the lakes, estimated for the year 2000 (annual precipitation 634 mm, summer precipitation 266 mm) on the basis of four measurements in three of the lakes, are also presented in the Table 6. The emissions of CH\(_4\) from some of the study lakes were minor compared to CO\(_2\) efflux and have been presented elsewhere [Kankaala et al., 2005, 2006; Bergström et al., 2007]. The measured atmospheric deposition of C in the area was 1 g C m\(^{-2}\) yr\(^{-1}\) [Kortelainen et al., 2006a]. [19] The annual production of phytoplankton in Lake Valkea-Kotinen (1) was measured weekly during the open water season in situ using the \(^{14}\)C method [Keskitalo and Salonen, 1994]. Since the incubation time was 24 h, the measurements resulted in net primary productivity values (NPP). For the other lakes, the range of NPP of phytoplankton was estimated using data obtained in previous measurements in neighboring lakes [Ilmavirta and Kotimaa, 1974; Arvola 1983, 1984; Arvola et al., 1999], with the same types of trophic status and chemical and physical properties as in the study lakes. The areas covered by different macrophyte species were mapped in 1997–2000. The macrophyte C pool was estimated as a seasonal maximum biomass (g dry weight (DW) m\(^{-2}\)) converted to C by a factor 0.38 [Duarte, 1992], obtained from the data for stands of the dominant species in the three uppermost lakes [Keskitalo and Heitto, 1996; Kankaala et al., 2003, 2005]. The NPP of macrophytes was estimated to be twofold the seasonal maximum biomass of all the stands [Westlake, 1982]. [20] We also made a regional, landscape-scale estimate of CO\(_2\) emissions and sediment net C accumulation of all the lakes in the cumulative catchment area of the lake chain. The results of the five lakes studied were upscaled for the respective lake size classes (area <0.1, 0.1–1, 1–10 and 10–50 km\(^2\)) throughout the area. The areal results (g C m\(^{-2}\)) of the largest size class were also applied to the size class 1–10 km, because none of the lakes in the chain studied belonged to that size class. [21] The statistical relationships between the different variables in the data set were calculated as Pearson’s linear correlations (Pearson’s r). The variables with skewed distributions were first log-transformed to approach normality. The analyses were done with PASW (SPSS) Statistics 17.0 software. 3. Results 3.1. Carbon Pools [22] In all the lakes, >98% of C was in the sediments (Table 4). The proportion of organic matter (Table 4) in the sediments decreased, while the density of the lake sediment bed increased downstream of the lake chain. In Lake Valkea-Kotinen (1), the average sediment density was 0.056 g cm\(^{-3}\), in Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) 0.14 g cm\(^{-3}\), in Lakes Ekojärvi (3) and Kuohijärvi (4) about 0.25 g cm\(^{-3}\) and in Lake Kukkia (5) 0.35 g cm\(^{-3}\). In the uppermost lake, the average thickness of the sediment bed (computed for the entire lake area) was 1.6 m, while in the succeeding three lakes the bed was around 2 m thick and in the lowermost lake only 1.2 m thick. [23] The water column TOC, including phytoplankton, constituted 95% of the lake water C pool in Lake Valkea-Kotinen (1) (Table 4). The proportion of TOC decreased along the lake chain to 68% in Kuohijärvi (4) and to 67% in Kukkia (5) while the proportion of DIC increased from 5% in Valkea-Kotinen to 33% in Kukkia. Accordingly, the annual maximum biomass of littoral macrophytes during late summer varied from 13% to 4% of the total C pool in the first three lakes, but in the larger lowland lakes the percentage of macrophytes was almost insignificant (Table 4). [24] The areal sediment C store correlated positively with the proportion of peatlands in the catchment and lake water TOC and Fe concentrations but negatively with lake area and the ratio between lake area to catchment area (LA/CA) (Table 7). The TOC concentration of the water correlated negatively with the size of the lakes and with LA/CA, and positively with the proportion of peatlands in the catchment. 3.2. Carbon Fluxes [25] The annual TOC loads into the lakes increased by 40–210% in the wet year 1998 compared with the dry year 1997 (Figure 2). The increased runoff in 1998 (average runoff in 1998 and 1997 was 9.03 L s⁻¹ km⁻² and 5.04 L s⁻¹ km⁻², respectively) was the main determinant for the higher loads, whereas the higher concentrations of TOC in river water in summer 1998 (average 14.7 mg C L⁻¹) compared with those in 1997 (average 10.8 mg C L⁻¹) played a minor role. During the wet year TOC inflow was higher than outflow in all the lakes, but during the dry year in the two uppermost lakes TOC loss by outflow exceeded that coming by inflow. The DIC loads were also higher in the wet year but the DIC/TOC ratios were higher in the dry year in all the lakes (average in the dry year 0.22 and in the wet year 0.14). [26] The annual input of C by the net production of macrophytes was always small compared with the C input to the lake by runoff. The net production of macrophytes was lower than the estimated net primary production by phytoplankton in each lake (Table 6). With the exception of the uppermost headwater lake during the dry year, C input from the catchment exceeded the autochthonously produced C in the lakes (Figure 4). [27] The high summer precipitation generally increased the C fluxes in the lakes (Figure 2 and Table 6). Hydrological import and export of TOC dominated the carbon fluxes especially in the two small drainage lakes with small LA/CA ratios (Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and Ekojärvi (3)) in the middle of the chain (Table 6 and Figure 4). Atmospheric emissions were highest in the three uppermost lakes during the wet year (79–86 g C m⁻² a⁻¹). However, throughout the lake chain, the efflux of CO₂ into the atmosphere was not significantly correlated with the TOC input (Table 7). [28] In the uppermost headwater lake (Valkea-Kotinen (1)) the average long-term sediment deposition rate was 0.14 mm yr⁻¹ while in the small drainage lakes (Alinen Rautjärvi (2), Ekojärvi (3)) and in the large Kuohijärvi (4) the average deposition rate was higher, about 0.20 mm yr⁻¹. In Lake Kukkia (5) the average long-term deposition rate was the lowest, 0.12 mm yr⁻¹. In the uppermost lake the gross sedimentation rate of C was 7, eightfold compared with the average long-term accumulation rate in the sediment. The short-term gross sedimentation rates of C and Fe were positively correlated in the uppermost lake (Figure 3a). Throughout the lake chain the long-term net sedimentation of C was also positively correlated with Fe and TOC concentrations of the water column (Figure 3b). The proportion of net sedimentation was low in the lake C budgets; in the uppermost lake it was 3–5% of the annual C output and in the other lakes the proportion was 1–2% (Figure 4). [29] On the landscape scale, the small lakes (area <1 km²) were important in the net accumulation of carbon in the sediments, since they were responsible for 56% of the net C accumulation in all the lakes although they formed only 14% of the entire lake area (Table 8). On the other hand, the large lowland lakes (size class 10–50 km²) played a more important role in the CO₂ emissions. In the dry year, the emissions from these lakes made up 60% of the total C effluxes from all lakes in the area, and during the wet year the proportion was 47%. 4. Discussion [30] In the typical boreal lake chain C fluxes were dominated by the input of allochthonous organic matter from the catchment, especially in small drainage lakes with low LA/CA ratio (Figure 4). Although the sediments formed the most important carbon pool (>98%) in the lakes of all size classes, the average Holocene net accumulation rate of C was very small compared with that evaded as CO₂ to atmosphere. This indicates effective mineralization of the organic C within the lake chain. On the landscape scale, small lakes played more important role in long-term C accumulation in the sediments than the large ones, which were more important as emitters of atmospheric CO₂. As hypothesized, the hydrological conditions were important drivers of C transfer from the catchment and along the lake chain, since during the rainy year the transport of C from the catchments was remarkably enhanced, compared with the dry year (Table 6 and Figure 4). Influence of Lake Size, Position, and Catchment Characteristics [31] In the uppermost lake the mean long-term accumulation rate of C in the sediment was only about 13–14% of the recent annual gross sedimentation rate, indicating that the bulk of the organic C produced in the lake and received from the catchment is mineralized in sediment respiration. In a time series of varved sediments from a lake in Sweden, Gälman et al. [2008] observed that 20% of the annually deposited C in the sediment was lost within 5 years, after which the C loss rate decreased. Sobek et al. [2009] showed that C burial efficiency in lake sediments is negatively related to oxygen exposure time. In our study lakes, the lowest areal pools of C in the sediment were found in the two largest lakes (Table 4), in which the water column is oxic throughout the year. [32] In our study the sediment C pool estimates represent average accumulation during the whole Holocene period, which presumably underestimates the recent net accumulation rates; increasing human impact in the catchments generally results in increasing accumulation rates [e.g., Einsele et al., 2001]. In our study lakes, the human impact has been modest in the two uppermost lakes and more intensive in the catchments of the large lakes. Agriculture in the catchment promotes erosion, leading to increased mass accumulation rates, but to lower organic matter content [Kortelainen et al., 2004], as also found in the studied lake chain. The proportion of TOC in the lake water C pool decreased along the lake chain, while the proportion of DIC increased indicating mineralization of allochthonous C within the lake chain. This is also attributable to the increasing proportion of agriculture in the catchments. The proportion of DIC in the lake water total C is typically greater in lakes surrounded by agricultural land than in lakes in forested or peatland-rich areas [Oh and Raymond, 2006; Rantakari and Kortelainen, 2008]. [33] We found that the lake water Fe content was a very good predictor for the pool and long-term accumulation rate of C in the sediment. Although we used mean chemical composition of the lake water during the recent 20 years, the differences in the analyzed Fe contents of the lake waters (Table 2) presumably do not reflect only the recent Fe leaching from the catchment. The riverine inflow and outflow remarkably influenced the annual C budget of the two middlemost, relatively small drainage lakes with large catchments generating short residence times of only a few months. [35] Upstream lakes decrease the quantity of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in streams [Larson et al., 2007] and lakes [e.g., Kortelainen, 1993; Rantakari et al., 2004] and also decrease riverine TOC loads [e.g., Mattsson et al., 2005]. In our study, the proportion of lakes in the catchments did not affect the in-lake TOC concentrations, but decreased both the TOC inflow and the outflow (Table 7). In our study lakes the TOC concentrations correlated negatively with the lake area and the LA/CA ratio, but positively with the proportion of peatlands in the catchments; the latter has been shown in several studies in the Boreal Zone [e.g., Kortelainen, 1993]. [36] The size of the lake also affects the emissions as the annual evasion of CO₂ increases toward the smaller size classes. In 177 randomly selected lakes in Finland the average value of CO₂ emissions varied from 37 g C m⁻² in the largest lakes (between 10 and 100 km²) to 102 g C m⁻² in the smallest lakes (<0.1 km²) [Kortelainen et al., 2006b]. The two middlemost lakes in our lake chain showed emission of the same range, while the emissions of both the uppermost and the lowest lakes were lower than the average size class values in the study by Kortelainen et al. [2006b]. [37] The partition and the actual values of different C pools and fluxes in the three smallest lakes of the chain mostly agreed with the ones reported from the small, boreal, humic Lake Friksjön [Sobek et al., 2006], with the most noticeable difference being the smaller role of macrophytes in our lakes. The areal sediment C pool in Lake Friksjön was lower than that in our small lakes, but remarkably higher than that of the two large lakes in our study. The C pools of large lakes also differed from Lake Friksjön in having higher proportions of DIC in the water column. Our results on the riverine C influx as the major regulator of the lake chain C budget might represent various vegetation zones and soils, since Finlay et al. [2010] had similar results in the hard water lake chain. Although inorganic C accounted for the highest proportion of the C budget in the hard water lake chain and the total C sedimentation was higher, the bulk density of the sediments as well as the total C content were similar in both studies. On the landscape scale, our study emphasizes not only the role of small lakes (<1 km²) in C accumulation in the sediments, as also observed by Kortelainen et al. [2004], but also the role of large lakes (>10 km²) as intensive sites of organic C mineralization and emitters as atmospheric CO₂. 4.2. Influence of Hydrological Conditions [38] The hydrology was an important driver of C transfer from the catchment and along the lake chain, since during the rainy year the transport of C from the catchments was remarkably enhanced, compared with the dry year. This situation was comparable to tundra ponds, where the hydrological pathways acted as biogeochemical pathways for C during periods of high runoff [Macrae et al., 2004]. In addition to the rapid transport of C out of the catchments, the TOC concentrations in the lakes were also higher in the rainy year, the pattern which was shown in Lake Valkeakotinen by Arvola et al. [2010]. The C budgets of the lakes were negative in the dry year (1997), presumably indicating losses of C that had been formerly accumulated in the lakes. During the wet year, the three lakes along the chain acted as sinks of C, probably replacing the lake water C pool that had been decreasing during the preceding dry year. The output of C in the uppermost lake clearly dominated over the input, as was also noted in a small nearby lake by Arvola et al. [1990]. This may have been due to the difficulties in determining the amount of the C input from the catchment in the small lakes, and especially in lakes without inlets. Thus, our presumption of groundwater being an insignificant source of C may also have been wrong in Lake Valkeakotinen, since a strong groundwater signature in aquatic \( pCO_2 \) has been found in many lakes and streams in Sweden [Humborg et al., 2010]. [39] During the rainy year, the CO₂ emissions were higher than during the dry year in the three smallest upstream lakes. Rantakari and Kortelainen [2005] also found a close connection between annual CO₂ emission and precipitation in large Finnish lakes, and suggested that during periods of high precipitation more organic C produced in the terrestrial ecosystem is transported to the lakes and decomposed. They also emphasized the importance of the weather conditions of the previous autumn contributing to the delay between heavy rainfall in the autumn and increasing CO₂ concentrations in the large lakes in winter. This may have influenced our largest study lakes, Kuhohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5), which have long residence times and large water volume. In these two lakes, the CO₂ emissions were higher during the dry year. On the other hand, the water temperatures of all the study lakes were higher during the dry year (Table 3), which may also have impacted the CO₂ fluxes to the atmosphere. Kosten et al. [2010] found that the \( pCO_2 \) closely followed the temperature in 82 South American lakes with wide ranges in DOC concentrations, suggesting an increase in temperature-dependent mineralization of DOC and larger lacustrine CO₂ emissions due to climate warming. The in-lake processes presumably had greater influence on the C fluxes in the large lakes of our study, while in the small drainage lakes with small LA/CA ratios, the allochthonous matter dominated. In the river input to all our lakes the DIC/TOC ratios were higher in the dry year. Thus the higher increase in concentrations of inorganic compared with organic C during the dry year was a characteristic of the allochthonous input. Not all the CO₂ in the lake results from the in-lake processes, since part of the DIC transported from the catchment is emitted directly from the lake to the atmosphere [Ojala et al., 2011]. Overall, the retention of C in the study lakes ((sedimentation + atmospheric emission)/C input) was more efficient in the dry year. This was presumably related to the longer hydraulic residence time during the dry year, providing longer time periods for sedimentation as well as for the biogeochemical and physical mineralization processes. [40] The increasing frequency of heavy precipitation events and wet/dry periods may further strengthen the variability in timing and magnitude of C loads [e.g., Hongve et al., 2004; Erlandsson et al., 2008]. Naden et al. [2010] showed that the future projection (for years 2071–2100) for the Mustajoki River, situated close the study area, includes a 7% increase in annual mean DOC concentrations and a 16% increase in annual mean DOC load. Our results emphasize the role of terrestrial signals and underline climate as the major driver of ecosystem C balances. Peatland C sequestration rates are highly sensitive even to minor climatic fluctuations [Yu et al., 2003], with wet periods correlating rapidly with peat accumulation. Similarly, the soil organic C pool in Nordic forest soils increases with both mean annual temperature and mean annual precipitation [Callesen et al., 2003]. There will presumably be variation in the response of lakes to climatic drivers, depending on the characteristics of the lakes (e.g., size, morphology and LA/CA ratios) as well as on the properties of their catchments. 5. Conclusions [41] Boreal lakes are important conduits of terrestrially fixed C to the atmosphere. Over the long-term and on the landscape scale, they are also important sinks of C. The sediments of the uppermost headwater lakes are important storages of organic C, and in our boreal lakes Fe played an important role in C accumulation. [42] The lakes in the chain may play different roles in C transport, processing and storage. In the upstream lakes with low LA/CA ratios, the C budget is strongly controlled by TOC inflow and outflow. In the large lowland lakes the partition can be different between the components of the C budget: while the impact of riverine transport is lower, the emissions to the atmosphere play greater role in the C budget. [43] We have also shown that freshwater C budgets, including all major pools and fluxes, show highly variable patterns during dry and wet years. In our study, precipitation was an important driver for C balance in all these boreal lakes. Changing climate can thus greatly modify the role of lakes in landscape C balances. [44] Acknowledgments. Characterizing ponds in a watershed simulation and evaluating their influence on streamflow in a Mississippi watershed

Lindsey M. W. Yasarera, Ronald L. Bingnera and Henrique G. Momm b

aUnited States Department of Agriculture-Agricultural Research Service, National Sedimentation Laboratory, Oxford, Mississippi, USA; bDepartment of Geosciences, Middle Tennessee State University, Murfreesboro, Tennessee, USA

ABSTRACT
Small water bodies, such as ponds and wetlands, are common landscape features, but often are not simulated within a watershed modeling framework. The wetland modeling tool, AgWET, uses a GIS framework to characterize the features of ponds and wetlands so that they can be incorporated into watershed simulations using the Annualized Agricultural Non-Point Source (AnnAGNPS) pollution model. AgWET was used to characterize farm ponds on the Goodwin Creek Experimental Watershed in northwest Mississippi and AnnAGNPS simulated watershed hydrology. Monthly streamflow was validated at four watershed gauges with Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency values between 0.91 and 0.94. Ponds influenced watershed hydrology at various scales, with a decrease in average streamflow by 4% at the watershed outlet, 8% at the sub-watershed scale, and an average of 56% immediately downstream of the ponds. AgWET can be used to simulate ponds in watershed assessments for improved results and evaluation of future scenarios.

ARTICLE HISTORY
Received 12 September 2017
Accepted 6 November 2017

EDITOR
R. Woods

ASSOCIATE EDITOR
X. Fang

KEYWORDS
AnnAGNPS; Mississippi; ponds; simulation; hydrology

Introduction

From farm ponds to prairie potholes, constructed wetlands to playa lakes, small water bodies (SWBs) are predominant features in many landscapes. Estimates of pond numbers in the United States (US) range from 2.6 to 9 million (Smith et al. 2002, Renwick et al. 2005). In the US the density of SWBs is highest in central Mississippi, Florida, and throughout the Southern Great Plains (Renwick et al. 2005). These SWBs influence hydrological connectivity and trap water, sediment, and nutrients from the landscape, which can lead to a decrease in peak flow during large events, reduced downstream sediment transport, and reduction of watershed nutrient loads (Verstraeten and Poesen 2000, Downing et al. 2008). For example, small impoundments in Alabama have been estimated to store a water volume of 6.01 km³, which reduces statewide annual runoff by 8.1% (Chaney et al. 2012). A study of sediment accumulation in small ponds in Pennsylvania found that organic matter sequestration is elevated in ponds connected to headwater streams and area-specific sediment accumulation rates are inversely related to pond size (Brainard and Fairchild 2012). Another study in Texas found that downstream reservoir sedimentation decreased an average of 55% as ponds in the upstream watershed have increased in number (Berg et al. 2016). These studies highlight that small ponds may have an important influence on local and regional hydrological processes and should be considered in future research.

However, SWBs are often ignored in watershed assessment and modeling efforts for several reasons: (1) SWBs are typically underrepresented or not represented in water body databases (Smith et al. 2002); (2) the size of SWBs may be smaller than the resolution of land-use datasets and therefore undetectable in geospatial datasets; (3) SWBs may be erased when small depressions are filled during standard digital topographic processing (Garbrecht and Martz 1996, Chang 2012); or (4) SWBs may be assumed to have an inconsequential influence or are challenging to parameterize within a modeling framework (Downing 2010, Berg et al. 2016). Tools that can geospatially characterize SWBs and integrate them into a watershed model are necessary to improve SWB representation in regional models. The Annualized Agricultural Non-Point Source (AnnAGNPS) pollution model has an integrated topographic toolset, TOPAGNPS, which includes the GIS-based wetland component, AgWET. AgWET is able to identify and parameterize constructed wetlands anywhere within the stream network of a watershed system based on topographic and user-defined criteria for use by AnnAGNPS in hydrological

</page>

<page number="2">

assessments (Momm et al. 2016). While AgWET was originally designed for wetlands, we hypothesize that the tool should also be able to represent and simulate other SWBs that are connected to the surface hydrology network in the landscape, such as farm ponds.

To test the functionality of AgWET for simulating farm ponds and to assess the influence of farm ponds on watershed hydrology, the AnnAGNPS model was used to simulate the Goodwin Creek Experimental Watershed (GCEW) from 1982 to 1991 and the tool, AgWET, was used to parameterize the ponds for use with AnnAGNPS within the watershed. The main objectives were to: (1) evaluate the ability of AgWET to identify and parameterize ponds using a one-meter spatial resolution LiDAR-generated raster grid; (2) evaluate the ability of AnnAGNPS to simulate the hydrological cycle including ponds; and (3) determine the local and watershed-scale influences of the ponds on peak discharge and streamflow.

Methods

Study area and model parameterization

The Goodwin Creek Experimental Watershed (GCEW) is located within the bluff hills region in Panola County, Mississippi, and consists of a 2132 ha drainage area with highly erodible soils and high rainfall (1358 mm/year) (Kuhnle et al. 2008). In the early 1980s, when data collection began in the watershed, land use was evenly distributed between forest/timber, pasture/idle, and cultivated land. However, cultivated land has declined from 26% in 1982 to 12% in 1989, then to 6% in 2004 (Kuhnle et al. 2008). Most cultivated land has been replaced by forest or suburban land use, with any remaining cropland located on the alluvium soils near the main stream channel. Upland soils are predominantly silty and easily eroded without surface cover. Sediment yields from the watershed have been estimated at 13.2 tons/ha per year, with suspended sediment concentrations reaching thousands of parts per million during runoff events in late winter and spring (Kuhnle et al. 1989, 2008).

The watershed has been studied intensely since 1981 when runoff data collection began at 14 stations with supercritical flow structures designed and installed by the Vicksburg District of the US Army Corps of Engineers. These structures allow for grade control, flow measurement, and sediment measurement stations. Flumes were designed with a longitudinal slope of 0.04 and V-shaped; the design maintains supercritical flows across a range of flow rates and prohibits sediment deposition on the bottom structure (Kuhnle et al. 2008). Currently, the most complete and quality controlled dataset is available from 1982 to 1991; therefore, this time period was used in this study. The GCEW has also been designated as a Conservation Effects Assessment Project (CEAP) benchmark watershed since 2005. Land-use and land-management data were available in the watershed during the study period 1982–1991 in both tabular and spatial form and were used to parameterize the model (Fig. 1). Soil land use came from the Soil Survey Geographic (SSURGO) Database (Natural Resources Conservation Service, 2016). The precipitation and temperature daily record was generated from 30 gauges located in and around the watershed and cells were assigned to stations based on Thiessen polygons created from the 30 gauge locations. Raingauges were co-located with flume structures, with additional stations located throughout the watershed. All topographic processing was done using a 1-m resolution digital elevation model (DEM) derived from LiDAR and hydrologically

corrected to retain flow connection with ponds, and allow flow under culverts and bridges. LiDAR data were collected between 19 February 2009 and 2 August 2010 as part of the US Corps of Engineers Delta Phase 1 2009 LiDAR dataset.

AGNPS

AGNPS is a system of modeling components that include both topographic tools (TOPAGNPS) as well as a watershed modeling framework (AnnAGNPS). AnnAGNPS is the watershed-scale modeling tool designed to simulate the impacts of agricultural practices on nonpoint source pollution by estimating loads of water, sediment, and nutrients at various locations. Used with AnnAGNPS is the topographic analysis tool, TOPAGNPS, to delineate the watershed boundaries and subdivide it into sub-catchments (referred to as cells) and concentrated flow paths (referred to as reaches) (Garbrecht and Martz 1997). Other optional topographic components include modules to define wetland/ponds (AgWET; Momm et al. 2016), buffers (AgBUF; Momm et al. 2014), and potential ephemeral gullies (PEG; Momm et al. 2012). Runoff is estimated with a modified Soil Conservation Service curve number (CN) method (USDA Soil Conservation Service 1985) and Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) technology to estimate sheet and rill erosion and to simulate land cover and management conditions (Renard et al. 1997). The Hydro-geomorphic Universal Soil Loss Equation (HUSLE) estimates sediment delivery (Theurer and Clarke 1991) and sediment transport capacity of the flow paths is determined using the Bagnold equation (Bagnold 1966).

By varying user-provided parameters in TOPAGNPS the watershed can be divided into smaller drainage areas (i.e. cells) that represent homogeneous conditions of weather, soil type, and farming management (Momm et al. 2017). Cells are then assigned soils, management, and a weather station based on a spatial join between cell feature class and respective feature classes for soils, management, and weather station defined polygons. Input databases to define soil characteristics, land-management types, management schedules, climate, and wetlands/ponds can be built either using the AnnAGNPS Input Editor or by manually building individual data section as comma separated values in ASCII file format.

Representing small water bodies in AGNPS

AgWET: topographic component
The AgWET feature was used to characterize ponds and generate the input database for AnnAGNPS to simulate these features within the watershed. Currently, AgWET only considers ponds located on concentrated flow paths (i.e. reaches) and includes a barrier structure that intersects the reach perpendicular to flow. Known or proposed barriers can be placed in AgWET using a digitized line or point. Using a barrier line allows the user to control the length of the barrier in addition to the height (as determined from the DEM), while using points the user has to provide the barrier height and the software determines the length. A detailed description of the AgWET GIS functionality can be found in Momm et al. (2016).

The locations and approximate areas of the ponds were determined using aerial imagery from 1985 and 1996, as these were the best available images to determine pond sizes and locations. The 1996 image provided the best resolution for determining pond sizes and was used to compare to AgWET-generated ponds. However, the 1985 image was used to cross-check pond locations, and expert knowledge of watershed conditions helped to determine ponds that were constructed after 1992 and therefore should be excluded from the analysis. The height of the dam or barrier was determined using a LiDAR-based 1-m DEM. Barriers were digitized as lines and points, and both were used as inputs to AgWET to characterize pond dimensions and spatial extent based on the DEM. The lines were found to best represent pond areas (see Fig. 2). Inflow into ponds was estimated as flow exiting the upstream reach (es) and outflow from the pond was added to the reach in which the pond was located. In the current version of AgWET ponds can only be associated with a reach and not as a water body in a cell. However, many of the ponds in GCEW were located in uplands areas in the watershed. To simulate as many ponds as possible, the critical source area (CSA) and maximum source length (MSCL) were modified during the cell and reach network generation to improve pond placement on a generated reach. The final values used were CSA = 1.2 ha and MSCL = 25 m.

AnnAGNPS: process representation
An additional capability within the AnnAGNPS model is simulating the physical and chemical processes occurring in the wetlands or SWBs. While the AnnAGNPS model includes an estimate of potential nitrogen processing in simulated wetlands and ponds, such results are not shown here as the hydrological aspect is the focus of this study. A mass balance approach is used to track water through the wetland/pond systems within AnnAGNPS. The hydrology mass balance is governed by the equation:

\[
V_i = V_{(i-1)} + Q_{\text{inflow}} - Q_{\text{outflow}} + P - \text{ET} - I
\] (1)
