Diel vertical migrations of zooplankton in a shallow, fishless pond: a possible avoidance-response cascade induced by notonectids JOHN J. GILBERT and STEPHANIE E. HAMPTON Department of Biological Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, U.S.A. Dedication: This paper is dedicated to the memory of Thomas M. Frost, 1950–2000 SUMMARY 1. Day (noon) and night (midnight) vertical distributions of zooplankton and phytoplankton in the water column (1.5 m) of a Vermont pond were determined on two consecutive days from 470 mL water samples taken at three depths (0.1, 0.5 and 1.0 m) at three sites. There was little variation across depths in temperature, dissolved oxygen concentration and phytoplankton. All individuals of each zooplankton species (a small copepod, Tropocyclops extensus and six rotifers) were counted. 2. A three-way ANOVA on the zooplankton data showed no effect of date or time of day on the abundance of any species. Significant diel shifts in vertical distribution (depth × time-of-day interactions) were found for T. extensus (nauplii, as well as copepodites and adults) and Polyarthra remata, but not for Hexarthra mira, Keratella cochlearis, Anuraeopsis fissa, Ascomorpha ovalis and Plationus patulus. Tropocyclops extensus showed a pronounced, typical diel vertical migration, avoiding the surface and occurring most abundantly near the bottom during the day. Polyarthra remata showed an equally pronounced, reverse diel vertical migration, avoiding the bottom and being most abundant near the surface during the day. 3. The diurnal descent of Tropocyclops is interpreted as an avoidance response to Buenoa macrotibialis, a notonectid which feeds on this copepod at the surface during the day but not at night. The diurnal ascent of Polyarthra is thought to be an avoidance response to Tropocyclops, which strongly suppresses this rotifer in field enclosures and laboratory vessels. Thus, these out-of-phase migrations may be coupled and represent a behavioural cascade initiated by Buenoa. 4. At night, Tropocyclops and Polyarthra both were uniformly distributed across depths. This is believed to reflect the absence of appreciable depth-related variation in temperature, algal food resources (biovolume of cryptomonads and chrysophyte flagellates) and predation risk at this time. 5. The five rotifer species that did not exhibit diel vertical migrations may be less susceptible to Tropocyclops predation than Polyarthra. Keywords: diel vertical migrations, notonectids, Polyarthra, rotifers, Tropocyclops Introduction The zooplankton community of a small, shallow and fishless pond in Vermont (Johnson Pond) is dominated by small taxa – rotifers and the cyclopoid copepod Tropocyclops extensus (Kiefer). The exclusion of larger crustacean taxa from this ecosystem may be primarily because of size-selective predation by notonectids, several species of which are common in the open water and littoral zones (Buenoa macrotibialis Hungerford and Notonecta lunata Hungerford). Notonectids generally prefer large over small zooplankton prey (Gilbert & Burns, 1999; J.J. Gilbert & R.J. Shiel, unpublished), and they can consume very large numbers of planktonic crustaceans throughout their life or as early instars (McArdle & Lawton, 1979; Scott & Murdoch, 1983; Murdoch & Scott, 1984; Reynolds & Geddes, 1984; Cooper, Smith & Bence, 1985; Gilbert & Burns, 1999). While Tropocyclops extensus is small (adult body length of c. 0.5 mm), its abundance in Johnson Pond appears to be controlled by B. macrotibialis, all stages of which occur in the open water both day and night. Enclosure experiments showed that both instars II and IV of this small notonectid significantly reduced Tropocyclops populations (Hampton, Gilbert & Burns, 2000), and feeding experiments conducted in the laboratory and the field demonstrated that instars II to VI readily ate Tropocyclops copepodites and adults (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished). Preliminary observations suggested the possibility that the coexistence of Tropocyclops with Buenoa in Johnson Pond might be facilitated by an avoidance response of Tropocyclops to Buenoa. Semi-quantitative zooplankton samples taken near the surface during the day and night in the summer of 1998 indicated that Tropocyclops was much more abundant there at night. A diurnal migration away from the surface could decrease the susceptibility of Tropocyclops to predation by Buenoa if Buenoa occurred near the surface and fed on Tropocyclops primarily during the day. Buenoa macrotibialis does in fact live near the surface (J.J. Gilbert & S.E. Hampton, unpublished), just as other notonectids do (Gittelman & Bergtrom, 1977; Streams, 1992). Also, B. macrotibialis requires light to feed on Tropocyclops (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished). This observation is consistent with previous studies showing that notonectids feed on other small crustaceans most effectively during the day when they can be visually detected, but can feed efficiently at night on larger prey which create disturbances detectable by mechanoreception (Cooper, 1983; Streams, 1982). The preliminary zooplankton samples from the surface of Johnson Pond also suggested that the vertical distribution of the rotifer Polyarthra remata (Skorikov) was different from that of Tropocyclops. This rotifer was more abundant at the surface during the day than at night, indicating that it might be avoiding Tropocyclops. Tropocyclops is reported to be primarily herbivorous and to have very low ingestion rates on small rotifers such as Polyarthra (DeMott & Watson, 1991; Adrian & Frost, 1992). However, there is evidence that Tropocyclops can strongly suppress P. remata in Johnson Pond. When instar IV Buenoa are present in enclosures, populations of this rotifer rapidly increase as Tropocyclops populations decrease (Hampton et al., 2000). Also, populations of P. remata in laboratory cultures rapidly decline when Tropocyclops is present (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished). The purpose of the present study is to conduct a detailed analysis of the day and night vertical distributions of the zooplankton in Johnson Pond. We believe that the zooplankton community in this shallow system may show pronounced vertical differentiation as a result of interspecific behavioural interactions. Specifically, we test the hypotheses that T. extensus exhibits a typical diel vertical migration, perhaps to avoid Buenoa, and that P. remata, and possibly other rotifers, display a reverse diel vertical migration, perhaps to avoid Tropocyclops. Methods Johnson Pond is a small (c. 0.1 × 0.05 km), shallow (maximum depth c. 2 m), privately owned and well-protected ecosystem in Norwich, Vermont, U.S.A. While there are no fish in the pond, there are insects which may prey on open-water zooplankton – larvae of Chaoborus americanus and C. flavicans, the notonectid B. macrotibialis and several larger notonectids of the genus Notonecta, especially N. lunata. Buenoa is abundant in open water day and night; Notonecta occurs primarily in the littoral zone during the day but moves into open water at night. The study was conducted at noon and midnight on both 31 August and 1 September 1998. Three permanent stations where water depth was about 1.5 m were marked with buoys to which a boat could be attached. Profiles of water temperature and dissolved oxygen concentration, from the surface to 1.5 m at 0.5 m intervals, were taken at the central station with a YSI model 57 meter. Separate water samples for zooplankton and phytoplankton were collected at 0.1, 0.5 and 1.0 m at each of the three sites with a custom-made 470 mL (18.5 cm × 6.5 cm dia.) Van Dorn trap and released into a bucket. For zooplankton, the entire 470 mL sample was filtered through 25 μm mesh and the retained organisms were preserved in acid Lugol’s solution. For phytoplankton, a 100 mL sub-sample of unfiltered water was preserved in acid Lugol’s solution. Phytoplankton species, genera or groups of taxa were enumerated using the Utermöhl procedure. Cell volumes of taxa were estimated from cell measurements and assumptions of particular geometric shapes. All individuals of each zooplankton species in each sample were enumerated. For Tropocyclops, nauplii were counted separately from copepodites and adults. The effects of date, depth and time of day on the abundance of each species or developmental stage were determined by three-way ANOVA (JMP, SAS Institute, Cary, NC, U.S.A.). Data that were not normally distributed or heteroscedastic (Polyarthra, Keratella, Anuraeopsis, Ascomorpha) were square-root transformed to meet the assumptions of ANOVA. The data for Plationus were very heteroscedastic, because of extremely patchy distribution, and were not stabilized by square-root transformation; logarithmic transformation equalized variance but did not normalize the data (\( P = 0.0027 \), Shapiro–Wilks test). To allow for the non-independence of the separate ANOVAs, the acceptable significance level (\( \alpha = 0.05 \)) was adjusted to \( P = 0.00639 \) with the Dunn–Sidák formula. The purpose of the ANOVA was to detect diel vertical migrations, which would be indicated by significant depth × time-of-day interactions. Significant time-of-day effects were not predicted; all taxa were expected to remain in the water column and to be sampled with similar efficiency, at mid-day and midnight. Also, no significant date effects were predicted, as diel patterns of depth distribution were expected to be similar on the two consecutive days as long as weather conditions were similar. Results On both dates the weather was calm and sunny with intermittent clouds. Profiles of temperature and dissolved oxygen concentration are shown in Fig. 1. In general, there was very little variation in temperature across depths, times of day and dates. All values were between 20 and 23 °C. During the day, temperatures were slightly higher near the surface and on the second date. At night, all temperatures were between 21 and 22 °C. During the day, oxygen concentrations were uniformly high (8–11 ppm) across depths, but showed an increase with depth on both dates. This probably reflects photosynthesis of submerged macrophytes, especially Chara. At night, oxygen concentrations decreased with depth on both dates, with ![Profiles of water temperature and dissolved oxygen in Johnson Pond at noon and midnight on 31 August and 1 September 1998.](page_1012_180_728_1042.png) Fig. 1 Profiles of water temperature and dissolved oxygen in Johnson Pond at noon and midnight on 31 August and 1 September 1998. surface values being considerably higher (9–10 ppm) than those at 1.5 m (4–7 ppm). This pattern probably was because of respiration of benthic macrophytes and continual exchange of oxygen near the surface. Day and night vertical distributions of the abundance of phytoplankton taxa, averaged across dates, are shown in Table 1. Only several taxa exhibited pronounced diel shifts in abundance or depth distribution. Sphaerocystis and Anabaena were much more abundant at night, suggesting that they were deeper than 1 m during the day and migrated upwards at night. During the day several groups of flagellates were about twice as abundant at the surface than at 1 m – both size categories of chrysophyte flagellates, Mallomonas, Rhodomonas and Gymnodinium. This may reflect diurnal migrations to the surface to maximize light availability. During the day Dinobryon was somewhat less abundant at the surface than at 1 m and was primarily at the surface at night. The vertical distribution of phytoplankton food available to the zooplankton was estimated by calculating the volumes of algal taxa considered likely to be eaten by most zooplankton species – cryptomonads and chrysophyte flagellates. The data (Fig. 2) show that the total biovolume of these cells was quite similar across depths and times of day, varying only between 2.2 and 4.7 × 10\(^5\) µm\(^3\) mL\(^{-1}\). At 0.1 m, mean biovolumes were almost twice as high during the day (\(4.5 \times 10^5 \mu\mathrm{m}^3 \ \mathrm{mL}^{-1}\)) than at night (\(2.4 \times 10^5 \mu\mathrm{m}^3 \ \mathrm{mL}^{-1}\)). Again, this pattern is consistent with diurnal migrations to the surface to maximize light availability. Day and night vertical distributions of *Tropocyclops* and the six rotifer species are presented in Fig. 3. The results of the ANOVAs testing for effects of date, depth and time of day on abundance are shown in Table 2. There was no significant effect of date or time of day for any species. Only *Tropocyclops* and *P. remata* showed pronounced, and statistically significant, diel shifts in depth distribution. In both of these species, the effect of depth and the depth \(\times\) time-of-day interaction were highly significant. *Tropocyclops* nauplii and stages C1–6 both showed the same pattern of migration, avoiding the surface during the day and being more or less uniformly distributed across depths at night. *Polyarthra* showed the exact reverse pattern of distribution, being most abundant near the surface and avoiding the deeper water during the day, and being quite uniformly distributed across depths Fig. 2 Vertical distributions of cryptomonads and chrysophyte flagellates, expressed as biovolumes, in Johnson Pond at noon (open bars) and midnight (closed bars) on 31 August [1] and 1 September [2] 1998. Discussion The results clearly show striking diel vertical migrations of T. extensus and P. remata over two consecutive days in Johnson Pond (Fig. 3). Tropocyclops displays a typical migration, avoiding the surface and occurring at greatest abundance near the bottom during the day. Polyarthra, on the other hand, exhibits a reverse migration, avoiding the bottom and moving to the surface during the day. The results of these two migrations is a marked spatial segregation of the two species during the day (Fig. 4). Typical diel migrations, such as that of T. extensus, are exhibited by a variety of freshwater zooplankton, and have been particularly well analysed in Daphnia, copepods and Chaoborus larvae (Hutchinson, 1967; Lampert & Sommer, 1997). These migrations with a diurnal descent increase fitness by decreasing encounters with visually feeding predators, notably fish, during the day, and they can be rapidly induced by the presence of the predator, or a kairomone released by the predator (Lampert, 1993; Lampert & Sommer, 1997; De Meester et al., 1999). While there are no fish in Johnson Pond, Tropocyclops is subject to predation by notonectids, probably especially B. macrotibialis. Buenoa is common in the open water during the day and probably is more zooplanktivorous than larger notonectids, such as Notonecta, which likely prefer insect prey, at least as later instars (Streams, 1974, 1992; Giller, 1986). Buenoa macrotibialis does in fact readily eat Tropocyclops copepodites and adults (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished) and can dramatically suppress Tropocyclops populations in field enclosures (Hampton et al., 2000). In addition, like zooplanktivorous fish, B. macrotibialis uses vision to feed on Tropocyclops, eating it in the light but not in the dark (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished). The typical diel migration of Tropocyclops in Johnson Pond may be an avoidance response to Buenoa. Migrating away from the surface during the day should decrease visual detection by surface-dwelling notonectids. There is, in fact, some evidence that crustacean zooplankton may avoid the surface during the day to escape predation by notonectids. Herwig & Schindler (1996) reported that the experimental removal of Notonecta and other surface-dwelling insects from a fishless pond caused Daphnia to move higher in the water column during the day. Nesbitt, ![Bar graph showing daytime (noon) vertical distributions of P. remata and T. extensus (all stages) averaged over two dates, with percent maximum abundance on the y-axis and depth (m) on the x-axis.](page_1012_1342_484_484.png) Fig. 4 Daytime (noon) vertical distributions of P. remata and T. extensus (all stages) averaged over two dates (see Fig. 3) and expressed as percent maximum abundance. Riessen & Ramcharan (1996) found that the addition of Notonecta to enclosures with Chaoborus induced Daphnia to move lower in the water column during the day. Finally, Dodson (1988) demonstrated in the laboratory that a Notonecta kairomone induced sinking in large species of Daphnia. The diurnal descent of Tropocyclops in Johnson Pond cannot be an avoidance response to Chaoborus. Tropocyclops is eaten by C. flavicans (M.C. Diéguez, unpublished) and probably C. americanus, but these predators remain at or near the bottom during the day and enter the water column only at night (M.C. Dieguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished). Thus, during daylight hours Tropocyclops is most abundant nearest the bottom and Chaoborus. The uniform distribution of Tropocyclops across depths at night (Fig. 3) may be because of the fact that temperature, food availability and predation risk at that time were similar across depths. Water temperatures at night varied only from 21 to 22 °C (Fig. 1). Oxygen concentrations at night did decrease with depth but probably were not sufficiently low at 1.0 m (6 ppm, Fig. 1) to be restrictive. Also, potential algal food for Tropocyclops, as estimated from the biovolume of cryptomonads and chrysophyte flagellates, was quite uniform across depths, especially at night (Fig. 2). Thus, the strategy of many crustacean zooplankton exhibiting typical diel vertical migrations to move up in the water column at night where food is more abundant and temperatures are higher should not apply to Tropocyclops in Johnson Pond. Regarding nocturnal predation, the risk near the surface from Buenoa and Notonecta should be very low. Buenoa is unable to feed effectively on this copepod in the dark or even in full moonlight (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished), and the larger-sized Notonecta should be less able to feed on small zooplankton like Tropocyclops than Buenoa. Chaoborus americanus and C. flavicans certainly prey on Tropocyclops when they are in the water column at night (M.C. Diéguez, unpublished), but their abundance may be similar across depths. Even if these predators were more abundant near the bottom, Tropocyclops may be unable to orient away from them at night. The reverse diel migration of P. remata in Johnson Pond may be an avoidance response to Tropocyclops. During the day when Tropocyclops is most abundant near the bottom, Polyarthra avoids the bottom and is most abundant near the surface (Figs 3 & 4). While T. extensus has been reported to be primarily herbivorous and to have very low feeding rates on small rotifers such as Polyarthra (DeMott & Watson, 1991; Adrian & Frost, 1992), it strongly suppresses P. remata in Johnson Pond. Enclosure experiments showed that population sizes of Polyarthra greatly increased when instar IV Buenoa was present and reduced abundances of Tropocyclops (Hampton et al., 2000). Furthermore, P. remata populations cultured in the laboratory on cryptomonad food grow rapidly in the absence of Tropocyclops but are dramatically suppressed in the presence of Tropocyclops (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished). The mechanism by which Tropocyclops inhibits P. remata appears to be direct and to be primarily predation (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished). While Polyarthra has an impressive escape response, in which it tumbles many body lengths at about one hundred times its normal swimming speed (Gilbert, 1985), it can be very susceptible to copepod predation (see below). In addition, Tropocyclops could mechanically interfere with Polyarthra. When encountering Polyarthra it could induce escape responses and thereby lead to a considerable expenditure of energy and reduction in feeding time. The diurnal ascent of P. remata is unlikely to be an avoidance response to Chaoborus. While all larval instars of Chaoborus probably readily eat rotifers (Moore & Gilbert, 1987; Moore, 1988; Swift, 1992; Lüning-Krizean, 1997; Wissel & Benndorf, 1998), the later ones select larger, crustacean prey (Moore, 1988; Swift, 1992; Lüning-Krizean, 1997). Polyarthra was consumed by C. punctipennis (Moore & Gilbert, 1987; Moore, 1988), but apparently not at all by C. flavicans (Lüning-Krizean 1997). At any rate, as the Chaoborus in Johnson Pond occur only at or near the bottom sediments during daytime, P. remata would not have to move very far up the water column to avoid this predator. The occurrence of P. remata at the surface of Johnson Pond during the day could make it susceptible to predation by Buenoa. However, even the smallest instars of Buenoa (I and II) cannot eat this rotifer (M.C. Diéguez, unpublished), probably because it is too small (<120 μm) to be visually detected or captured. Early instars of Anisops wakefieldi only ate rotifers larger than 150 μm (Gilbert & Burns, 1999). Therefore, concentration of P. remata at the surface during the day does not put this rotifer at risk from predation by Buenoa. Polyarthra remata in Johnson Pond, just like Tropocyclops, was uniformly distributed across depths at night (Fig. 3). Again, as with Tropocyclops, this probably reflects the fact that there was little variation across depths in temperature, food availability and predation risk. Polyarthra feeds primarily on flagellated cells (Pourriot, 1965; Bogdan & Gilbert, 1984, 1987); therefore, the estimate of similar food availability across depths at night, based on cryptomonads and chrysophyte flagellates (Fig. 2), probably applies to P. remata as well as to Tropocyclops. As Tropocyclops may be the primary predator of P. remata and is uniformly distributed across depths at night, predation risk to P. remata at night should be similar across depths. Thus, at night P. remata has no spatial refuge from Tropocyclops. It is noteworthy that P. remata was the only rotifer in Johnson Pond to exhibit a diel vertical migration. All other species either were similarly abundant across depths both mid-day and midnight (H. mira, K. cochlearis, A. fissa, As. ovalis) or else were found primarily near the bottom at both times of day (Pl. patulus). Perhaps P. remata is the only rotifer to migrate because it is the most susceptible to predation by Tropocyclops. Despite its escape response, Polyarthra generally is readily eaten, and often selected, by calanoid and cyclopoid copepods (Brandl & Fernando, 1978; Gilbert & Williamson, 1978; Karabin, 1978; Williamson & Gilbert, 1980; Williamson, 1984; Stemberger, 1985; Nero & Sprules, 1986; Williamson & Butler, 1986; Roche, 1990a,b; Adrian, 1991; Paul & Schindler, 1994; Couch, Gilbert & Burns, 1999). This probably is because of its soft body wall and the often limited effectiveness of its escape response against copepod predators. Reasons why the other rotifer species in Johnson Pond might be less susceptible than P. remata to Tropocyclops are not entirely clear. Hexarthra mira also has a soft body wall, but it is almost certainly too large (c. 200 μm) for Tropocyclops to eat. In addition, Hexarthra, like Polyarthra, has an escape response. This response is effective against the predatory rotifer Asplanchna (Sarma, 1993; Iyer & Rao, 1996; Hampton & Starkweather, 1998), and may also be against copepods. Keratella cochlearis is about the same size as P. remata (c. 130 μm, with spines, and 110 μm, respectively), but it has a tough, rigid lorica with anterior and posterior spines which may make it difficult for Tropocyclops to ingest. Several investigators have shown that other copepods have lower feeding rates on K. cochlearis than similarly sized rotifers with softer body walls (Gilbert & Williamson, 1978; Karabin, 1978; Williamson & Butler, 1986; Williamson, 1987; Roche, 1990a,b). Anuraeopsis fissa definitely is small enough (c. 80 μm) to be eaten by Tropocyclops, but it also may have a lorica rigid enough to deter ingestion. However, this species was one of several small rotifers eaten by Boeckella triarticulata and B. hamata (Couch et al., 1999). There appears to be no information on the ability of copepods to prey on Ascomorpha ovalis. This rotifer was very uncommon – mean abundances varied between 2 and 8 individuals L⁻¹ (Fig. 3) – and may have been avoided for this reason. Alternatively, it may be unpalatable. Its congener A. ecaudis is avoided by Diacyclops thomasi, possibly because the mucus house it produces is repellent (Stemberger, 1985, 1987). Mucus production appears to require light (Stemberger, 1987), and hence may depend on the symbiotic algal cells or plastids present in the wall of its stomach (de Beauchamp, 1932, 1965). Ascomorpha ovalis does not produce a mucus house, but it does similarly harbor symbiotic algal cells and possibly plastids (de Beauchamp, 1932, 1965); thus, it may also produce a distasteful mucus. Plationus patulus is a benthic species associated with sediment and aquatic vegetation (Koste, 1978; Koste & Shiel, 1987), and in the laboratory it usually attaches to substrata via a mucus thread (Hampton & Gilbert, 2001). Therefore, its greater abundance near the bottom in Johnson Pond at both mid-day and midnight, and its failure to exhibit a diel migration, was expected. While P. patulus consequently coexists with Tropocyclops near the bottom of the water column during the day, it probably is well defended against it by its size (c. 200 μm) and rigid lorica. There have been many reports of diel vertical migrations in rotifers (Ruttner, 1905; Pennak, 1944; Dumont, 1972; Fairchild et al., 1977; Miracle, 1977; Pivoda, 1977; Cruz-Pizarro, 1978; Magnien & Gilbert, 1983; Carillo, Cruz-Pizarro & Morales-Baquero, 1989; Williamson, 1993; González, 1998; Gilbert & Burns, 2001). However, clear reverse migrations, such as the one displayed by P. remata in Johnson Pond, have been documented only by Dumont (1972), Williamson (1993) and González (1998). In these three cases, the ecological significance of the migration also appears to be avoidance of predation by, or interference from, crustaceans exhibiting typical migrations. In the Dumont study, Asplanchna priodonta migrated out-of-phase with Bosmina spp. and Cyclops vicinus. In the Williamson study, As. ovalis, K. cochlearis and P. vulgaris reduced spatial overlap with Mesocyclops edax. In González’s study, a diurnal ascent of Polyarthra sp. occurred in enclosures without but not with Chaoborus, perhaps to rise above the more dense population of Daphnia pulicaria in the former. In conclusion, the present study in Johnson Pond demonstrates that a zooplankton community may exhibit pronounced vertical differentiation even in a very shallow (1.5 m) water column with little vertical stratification in temperature, dissolved oxygen concentration or phytoplankton. The pronounced diurnal segregation of T. extensus and P. remata may reflect a cascade of strong interspecific behavioural interactions dependent upon the presence of the notonectid Buenoa. In this hypothesized scheme, Tropocyclops migrates towards the bottom to avoid predation by Buenoa near the surface, while Polyarthra, in turn, migrates to the surface to avoid Tropocyclops. The stimuli for these migrations may be kairomones from Buenoa and Tropocyclops, respectively, and are currently under investigation. The migrations should greatly reduce the intensity of interactions between Buenoa and Tropocyclops, and between Tropocyclops and Polyarthra, and therefore promote the coexistence of Tropocyclops and Polyarthra with Buenoa in the ecosystem. Diel vertical migrations of zooplankton in a shallow, fishless pond: a possible avoidance-response cascade induced by notonectids JOHN J. GILBERT and STEPHANIE E. HAMPTON Department of Biological Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, U.S.A. Dedication: This paper is dedicated to the memory of Thomas M. Frost, 1950–2000 SUMMARY 1. Day (noon) and night (midnight) vertical distributions of zooplankton and phytoplankton in the water column (1.5 m) of a Vermont pond were determined on two consecutive days from 470 mL water samples taken at three depths (0.1, 0.5 and 1.0 m) at three sites. There was little variation across depths in temperature, dissolved oxygen concentration and phytoplankton. All individuals of each zooplankton species (a small copepod, Tropocyclops extensus and six rotifers) were counted. 2. A three-way ANOVA on the zooplankton data showed no effect of date or time of day on the abundance of any species. Significant diel shifts in vertical distribution (depth × time-of-day interactions) were found for T. extensus (nauplii, as well as copepodites and adults) and Polyarthra remata, but not for Hexarthra mira, Keratella cochlearis, Anuraeopsis fissa, Ascomorpha ovalis and Plationus patulus. Tropocyclops extensus showed a pronounced, typical diel vertical migration, avoiding the surface and occurring most abundantly near the bottom during the day. Polyarthra remata showed an equally pronounced, reverse diel vertical migration, avoiding the bottom and being most abundant near the surface during the day. 3. The diurnal descent of Tropocyclops is interpreted as an avoidance response to Buenoa macrotibialis, a notonectid which feeds on this copepod at the surface during the day but not at night. The diurnal ascent of Polyarthra is thought to be an avoidance response to Tropocyclops, which strongly suppresses this rotifer in field enclosures and laboratory vessels. Thus, these out-of-phase migrations may be coupled and represent a behavioural cascade initiated by Buenoa. 4. At night, Tropocyclops and Polyarthra both were uniformly distributed across depths. This is believed to reflect the absence of appreciable depth-related variation in temperature, algal food resources (biovolume of cryptomonads and chrysophyte flagellates) and predation risk at this time. 5. The five rotifer species that did not exhibit diel vertical migrations may be less susceptible to Tropocyclops predation than Polyarthra. Keywords: diel vertical migrations, notonectids, Polyarthra, rotifers, Tropocyclops Introduction The zooplankton community of a small, shallow and fishless pond in Vermont (Johnson Pond) is dominated by small taxa – rotifers and the cyclopoid copepod Tropocyclops extensus (Kiefer). The exclusion of larger crustacean taxa from this ecosystem may be primarily because of size-selective predation by notonectids, several species of which are common in the open water and littoral zones (Buenoa macrotibialis Hungerford and Notonecta lunata Hungerford). Notonectids generally prefer large over small zooplankton prey (Gilbert & Burns, 1999; J.J. Gilbert & R.J. Shiel, unpublished), and they can consume very large numbers of planktonic crustaceans throughout their life or as early instars (McArdle & Lawton, 1979; Scott & Murdoch, 1983; Murdoch & Scott, 1984; Reynolds & Geddes, 1984; Cooper, Smith & Bence, 1985; Gilbert & Burns, 1999). While Tropocyclops extensus is small (adult body length of c. 0.5 mm), its abundance in Johnson Pond appears to be controlled by B. macrotibialis, all stages of which occur in the open water both day and night. Enclosure experiments showed that both instars II and IV of this small notonectid significantly reduced Tropocyclops populations (Hampton, Gilbert & Burns, 2000), and feeding experiments conducted in the laboratory and the field demonstrated that instars II to VI readily ate Tropocyclops copepodites and adults (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished). Preliminary observations suggested the possibility that the coexistence of Tropocyclops with Buenoa in Johnson Pond might be facilitated by an avoidance response of Tropocyclops to Buenoa. Semi-quantitative zooplankton samples taken near the surface during the day and night in the summer of 1998 indicated that Tropocyclops was much more abundant there at night. A diurnal migration away from the surface could decrease the susceptibility of Tropocyclops to predation by Buenoa if Buenoa occurred near the surface and fed on Tropocyclops primarily during the day. Buenoa macrotibialis does in fact live near the surface (J.J. Gilbert & S.E. Hampton, unpublished), just as other notonectids do (Gittelman & Bergtrom, 1977; Streams, 1992). Also, B. macrotibialis requires light to feed on Tropocyclops (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished). This observation is consistent with previous studies showing that notonectids feed on other small crustaceans most effectively during the day when they can be visually detected, but can feed efficiently at night on larger prey which create disturbances detectable by mechanoreception (Cooper, 1983; Streams, 1982). The preliminary zooplankton samples from the surface of Johnson Pond also suggested that the vertical distribution of the rotifer Polyarthra remata (Skorikov) was different from that of Tropocyclops. This rotifer was more abundant at the surface during the day than at night, indicating that it might be avoiding Tropocyclops. Tropocyclops is reported to be primarily herbivorous and to have very low ingestion rates on small rotifers such as Polyarthra (DeMott & Watson, 1991; Adrian & Frost, 1992). However, there is evidence that Tropocyclops can strongly suppress P. remata in Johnson Pond. When instar IV Buenoa are present in enclosures, populations of this rotifer rapidly increase as Tropocyclops populations decrease (Hampton et al., 2000). Also, populations of P. remata in laboratory cultures rapidly decline when Tropocyclops is present (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished). The purpose of the present study is to conduct a detailed analysis of the day and night vertical distributions of the zooplankton in Johnson Pond. We believe that the zooplankton community in this shallow system may show pronounced vertical differentiation as a result of interspecific behavioural interactions. Specifically, we test the hypotheses that T. extensus exhibits a typical diel vertical migration, perhaps to avoid Buenoa, and that P. remata, and possibly other rotifers, display a reverse diel vertical migration, perhaps to avoid Tropocyclops. Methods Johnson Pond is a small (c. 0.1 × 0.05 km), shallow (maximum depth c. 2 m), privately owned and well-protected ecosystem in Norwich, Vermont, U.S.A. While there are no fish in the pond, there are insects which may prey on open-water zooplankton – larvae of Chaoborus americanus and C. flavicans, the notonectid B. macrotibialis and several larger notonectids of the genus Notonecta, especially N. lunata. Buenoa is abundant in open water day and night; Notonecta occurs primarily in the littoral zone during the day but moves into open water at night. The study was conducted at noon and midnight on both 31 August and 1 September 1998. Three permanent stations where water depth was about 1.5 m were marked with buoys to which a boat could be attached. Profiles of water temperature and dissolved oxygen concentration, from the surface to 1.5 m at 0.5 m intervals, were taken at the central station with a YSI model 57 meter. Separate water samples for zooplankton and phytoplankton were collected at 0.1, 0.5 and 1.0 m at each of the three sites with a custom-made 470 mL (18.5 cm × 6.5 cm dia.) Van Dorn trap and released into a bucket. For zooplankton, the entire 470 mL sample was filtered through 25 μm mesh and the retained organisms were preserved in acid Lugol’s solution. For phytoplankton, a 100 mL sub-sample of unfiltered water was preserved in acid Lugol’s solution. Phytoplankton species, genera or groups of taxa were enumerated using the Utermöhl procedure. Cell volumes of taxa were estimated from cell measurements and assumptions of particular geometric shapes. All individuals of each zooplankton species in each sample were enumerated. For Tropocyclops, nauplii were counted separately from copepodites and adults. The effects of date, depth and time of day on the abundance of each species or developmental stage were determined by three-way ANOVA (JMP, SAS Institute, Cary, NC, U.S.A.). Data that were not normally distributed or heteroscedastic (Polyarthra, Keratella, Anuraeopsis, Ascomorpha) were square-root transformed to meet the assumptions of ANOVA. The data for Plationus were very heteroscedastic, because of extremely patchy distribution, and were not stabilized by square-root transformation; logarithmic transformation equalized variance but did not normalize the data (\( P = 0.0027 \), Shapiro–Wilks test). To allow for the non-independence of the separate ANOVAs, the acceptable significance level (\( \alpha = 0.05 \)) was adjusted to \( P = 0.00639 \) with the Dunn–Sidák formula. The purpose of the ANOVA was to detect diel vertical migrations, which would be indicated by significant depth × time-of-day interactions. Significant time-of-day effects were not predicted; all taxa were expected to remain in the water column and to be sampled with similar efficiency, at mid-day and midnight. Also, no significant date effects were predicted, as diel patterns of depth distribution were expected to be similar on the two consecutive days as long as weather conditions were similar. Results On both dates the weather was calm and sunny with intermittent clouds. Profiles of temperature and dissolved oxygen concentration are shown in Fig. 1. In general, there was very little variation in temperature across depths, times of day and dates. All values were between 20 and 23 °C. During the day, temperatures were slightly higher near the surface and on the second date. At night, all temperatures were between 21 and 22 °C. During the day, oxygen concentrations were uniformly high (8–11 ppm) across depths, but showed an increase with depth on both dates. This probably reflects photosynthesis of submerged macrophytes, especially Chara. This pattern probably was because of respiration of benthic macrophytes and continual exchange of oxygen near the surface. Day and night vertical distributions of the abundance of phytoplankton taxa, averaged across dates, are shown in Table 1. Only several taxa exhibited pronounced diel shifts in abundance or depth distribution. Sphaerocystis and Anabaena were much more abundant at night, suggesting that they were deeper than 1 m during the day and migrated upwards at night. During the day several groups of flagellates were about twice as abundant at the surface than at 1 m – both size categories of chrysophyte flagellates, Mallomonas, Rhodomonas and Gymnodinium. This may reflect diurnal migrations to the surface to maximize light availability. During the day Dinobryon was somewhat less abundant at the surface than at 1 m and was primarily at the surface at night. The vertical distribution of phytoplankton food available to the zooplankton was estimated by calculating the volumes of algal taxa considered likely to be eaten by most zooplankton species – cryptomonads and chrysophyte flagellates. The data (Fig. 2) show that the total biovolume of these cells was quite similar across depths and times of day, varying only between 2.2 and 4.7 × 10\(^5\) µm\(^3\) mL\(^{-1}\). At 0.1 m, mean biovolumes were almost twice as high during the day (\(4.5 \times 10^5 \mu\mathrm{m}^3 \ \mathrm{mL}^{-1}\)) than at night (\(2.4 \times 10^5 \mu\mathrm{m}^3 \ \mathrm{mL}^{-1}\)). Again, this pattern is consistent with diurnal migrations to the surface to maximize light availability. Day and night vertical distributions of *Tropocyclops* and the six rotifer species are presented in Fig. 3. The results of the ANOVAs testing for effects of date, depth and time of day on abundance are shown in Table 2. There was no significant effect of date or time of day for any species. Only *Tropocyclops* and *P. remata* showed pronounced, and statistically significant, diel shifts in depth distribution. In both of these species, the effect of depth and the depth \(\times\) time-of-day interaction were highly significant. *Tropocyclops* nauplii and stages C1–6 both showed the same pattern of migration, avoiding the surface during the day and being more or less uniformly distributed across depths at night. *Polyarthra* showed the exact reverse pattern of distribution, being most abundant near the surface and avoiding the deeper water during the day, and being quite uniformly distributed across depths Fig. 2 Vertical distributions of cryptomonads and chrysophyte flagellates, expressed as biovolumes, in Johnson Pond at noon (open bars) and midnight (closed bars) on 31 August [1] and 1 September [2] 1998. Discussion The results clearly show striking diel vertical migrations of T. extensus and P. remata over two consecutive days in Johnson Pond (Fig. 3). Tropocyclops displays a typical migration, avoiding the surface and occurring at greatest abundance near the bottom during the day. Polyarthra, on the other hand, exhibits a reverse migration, avoiding the bottom and moving to the surface during the day. The results of these two migrations is a marked spatial segregation of the two species during the day (Fig. 4). Typical diel migrations, such as that of T. extensus, are exhibited by a variety of freshwater zooplankton, and have been particularly well analysed in Daphnia, copepods and Chaoborus larvae (Hutchinson, 1967; Lampert & Sommer, 1997). These migrations with a diurnal descent increase fitness by decreasing encounters with visually feeding predators, notably fish, during the day, and they can be rapidly induced by the presence of the predator, or a kairomone released by the predator (Lampert, 1993; Lampert & Sommer, 1997; De Meester et al., 1999). While there are no fish in Johnson Pond, Tropocyclops is subject to predation by notonectids, probably especially B. macrotibialis. Buenoa is common in the open water during the day and probably is more zooplanktivorous than larger notonectids, such as Notonecta, which likely prefer insect prey, at least as later instars (Streams, 1974, 1992; Giller, 1986). Buenoa macrotibialis does in fact readily eat Tropocyclops copepodites and adults (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished) and can dramatically suppress Tropocyclops populations in field enclosures (Hampton et al., 2000). In addition, like zooplanktivorous fish, B. macrotibialis uses vision to feed on Tropocyclops, eating it in the light but not in the dark (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished). The typical diel migration of Tropocyclops in Johnson Pond may be an avoidance response to Buenoa. Migrating away from the surface during the day should decrease visual detection by surface-dwelling notonectids. There is, in fact, some evidence that crustacean zooplankton may avoid the surface during the day to escape predation by notonectids. Herwig & Schindler (1996) reported that the experimental removal of Notonecta and other surface-dwelling insects from a fishless pond caused Daphnia to move higher in the water column during the day. Nesbitt, ![Bar graph showing daytime (noon) vertical distributions of P. remata and T. extensus (all stages) averaged over two dates, with percent maximum abundance on the y-axis and depth (m) on the x-axis.](page_1012_1342_484_484.png) Fig. 4 Daytime (noon) vertical distributions of P. remata and T. extensus (all stages) averaged over two dates (see Fig. 3) and expressed as percent maximum abundance. Riessen & Ramcharan (1996) found that the addition of Notonecta to enclosures with Chaoborus induced Daphnia to move lower in the water column during the day. Finally, Dodson (1988) demonstrated in the laboratory that a Notonecta kairomone induced sinking in large species of Daphnia. The diurnal descent of Tropocyclops in Johnson Pond cannot be an avoidance response to Chaoborus. Tropocyclops is eaten by C. flavicans (M.C. Diéguez, unpublished) and probably C. americanus, but these predators remain at or near the bottom during the day and enter the water column only at night (M.C. Dieguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished). Thus, during daylight hours Tropocyclops is most abundant nearest the bottom and Chaoborus. The uniform distribution of Tropocyclops across depths at night (Fig. 3) may be because of the fact that temperature, food availability and predation risk at that time were similar across depths. Water temperatures at night varied only from 21 to 22 °C (Fig. 1). Oxygen concentrations at night did decrease with depth but probably were not sufficiently low at 1.0 m (6 ppm, Fig. 1) to be restrictive. Also, potential algal food for Tropocyclops, as estimated from the biovolume of cryptomonads and chrysophyte flagellates, was quite uniform across depths, especially at night (Fig. 2). Thus, the strategy of many crustacean zooplankton exhibiting typical diel vertical migrations to move up in the water column at night where food is more abundant and temperatures are higher should not apply to Tropocyclops in Johnson Pond. Regarding nocturnal predation, the risk near the surface from Buenoa and Notonecta should be very low. Buenoa is unable to feed effectively on this copepod in the dark or even in full moonlight (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished), and the larger-sized Notonecta should be less able to feed on small zooplankton like Tropocyclops than Buenoa. Chaoborus americanus and C. flavicans certainly prey on Tropocyclops when they are in the water column at night (M.C. Diéguez, unpublished), but their abundance may be similar across depths. Even if these predators were more abundant near the bottom, Tropocyclops may be unable to orient away from them at night. The reverse diel migration of P. remata in Johnson Pond may be an avoidance response to Tropocyclops. During the day when Tropocyclops is most abundant near the bottom, Polyarthra avoids the bottom and is most abundant near the surface (Figs 3 & 4). While T. extensus has been reported to be primarily herbivorous and to have very low feeding rates on small rotifers such as Polyarthra (DeMott & Watson, 1991; Adrian & Frost, 1992), it strongly suppresses P. remata in Johnson Pond. Enclosure experiments showed that population sizes of Polyarthra greatly increased when instar IV Buenoa was present and reduced abundances of Tropocyclops (Hampton et al., 2000). Furthermore, P. remata populations cultured in the laboratory on cryptomonad food grow rapidly in the absence of Tropocyclops but are dramatically suppressed in the presence of Tropocyclops (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished). The mechanism by which Tropocyclops inhibits P. remata appears to be direct and to be primarily predation (M.C. Diéguez & J.J. Gilbert, unpublished). While Polyarthra has an impressive escape response, in which it tumbles many body lengths at about one hundred times its normal swimming speed (Gilbert, 1985), it can be very susceptible to copepod predation (see below). In addition, Tropocyclops could mechanically interfere with Polyarthra. When encountering Polyarthra it could induce escape responses and thereby lead to a considerable expenditure of energy and reduction in feeding time. The diurnal ascent of P. remata is unlikely to be an avoidance response to Chaoborus. While all larval instars of Chaoborus probably readily eat rotifers (Moore & Gilbert, 1987; Moore, 1988; Swift, 1992; Lüning-Krizean, 1997; Wissel & Benndorf, 1998), the later ones select larger, crustacean prey (Moore, 1988; Swift, 1992; Lüning-Krizean, 1997). Polyarthra was consumed by C. punctipennis (Moore & Gilbert, 1987; Moore, 1988), but apparently not at all by C. flavicans (Lüning-Krizean 1997). At any rate, as the Chaoborus in Johnson Pond occur only at or near the bottom sediments during daytime, P. remata would not have to move very far up the water column to avoid this predator. The occurrence of P. remata at the surface of Johnson Pond during the day could make it susceptible to predation by Buenoa. However, even the smallest instars of Buenoa (I and II) cannot eat this rotifer (M.C. Diéguez, unpublished), probably because it is too small (<120 μm) to be visually detected or captured. Early instars of Anisops wakefieldi only ate rotifers larger than 150 μm (Gilbert & Burns, 1999). Therefore, concentration of P. remata at the surface during the day does not put this rotifer at risk from predation by Buenoa. Polyarthra remata in Johnson Pond, just like Tropocyclops, was uniformly distributed across depths at night (Fig. 3). Again, as with Tropocyclops, this probably reflects the fact that there was little variation across depths in temperature, food availability and predation risk. Polyarthra feeds primarily on flagellated cells (Pourriot, 1965; Bogdan & Gilbert, 1984, 1987); therefore, the estimate of similar food availability across depths at night, based on cryptomonads and chrysophyte flagellates (Fig. 2), probably applies to P. remata as well as to Tropocyclops. As Tropocyclops may be the primary predator of P. remata and is uniformly distributed across depths at night, predation risk to P. remata at night should be similar across depths. Thus, at night P. remata has no spatial refuge from Tropocyclops. It is noteworthy that P. remata was the only rotifer in Johnson Pond to exhibit a diel vertical migration. All other species either were similarly abundant across depths both mid-day and midnight (H. mira, K. cochlearis, A. fissa, As. ovalis) or else were found primarily near the bottom at both times of day (Pl. patulus). Perhaps P. remata is the only rotifer to migrate because it is the most susceptible to predation by Tropocyclops. Despite its escape response, Polyarthra generally is readily eaten, and often selected, by calanoid and cyclopoid copepods (Brandl & Fernando, 1978; Gilbert & Williamson, 1978; Karabin, 1978; Williamson & Gilbert, 1980; Williamson, 1984; Stemberger, 1985; Nero & Sprules, 1986; Williamson & Butler, 1986; Roche, 1990a,b; Adrian, 1991; Paul & Schindler, 1994; Couch, Gilbert & Burns, 1999). This probably is because of its soft body wall and the often limited effectiveness of its escape response against copepod predators. Reasons why the other rotifer species in Johnson Pond might be less susceptible than P. remata to Tropocyclops are not entirely clear. Hexarthra mira also has a soft body wall, but it is almost certainly too large (c. 200 μm) for Tropocyclops to eat. In addition, Hexarthra, like Polyarthra, has an escape response. This response is effective against the predatory rotifer Asplanchna (Sarma, 1993; Iyer & Rao, 1996; Hampton & Starkweather, 1998), and may also be against copepods. Keratella cochlearis is about the same size as P. remata (c. 130 μm, with spines, and 110 μm, respectively), but it has a tough, rigid lorica with anterior and posterior spines which may make it difficult for Tropocyclops to ingest. Several investigators have shown that other copepods have lower feeding rates on K. cochlearis than similarly sized rotifers with softer body walls (Gilbert & Williamson, 1978; Karabin, 1978; Williamson & Butler, 1986; Williamson, 1987; Roche, 1990a,b). Anuraeopsis fissa definitely is small enough (c. 80 μm) to be eaten by Tropocyclops, but it also may have a lorica rigid enough to deter ingestion. However, this species was one of several small rotifers eaten by Boeckella triarticulata and B. hamata (Couch et al., 1999). There appears to be no information on the ability of copepods to prey on Ascomorpha ovalis. This rotifer was very uncommon – mean abundances varied between 2 and 8 individuals L⁻¹ (Fig. 3) – and may have been avoided for this reason. Alternatively, it may be unpalatable. Its congener A. ecaudis is avoided by Diacyclops thomasi, possibly because the mucus house it produces is repellent (Stemberger, 1985, 1987). Mucus production appears to require light (Stemberger, 1987), and hence may depend on the symbiotic algal cells or plastids present in the wall of its stomach (de Beauchamp, 1932, 1965). Ascomorpha ovalis does not produce a mucus house, but it does similarly harbor symbiotic algal cells and possibly plastids (de Beauchamp, 1932, 1965); thus, it may also produce a distasteful mucus. Plationus patulus is a benthic species associated with sediment and aquatic vegetation (Koste, 1978; Koste & Shiel, 1987), and in the laboratory it usually attaches to substrata via a mucus thread (Hampton & Gilbert, 2001). Therefore, its greater abundance near the bottom in Johnson Pond at both mid-day and midnight, and its failure to exhibit a diel migration, was expected. While P. patulus consequently coexists with Tropocyclops near the bottom of the water column during the day, it probably is well defended against it by its size (c. 200 μm) and rigid lorica. There have been many reports of diel vertical migrations in rotifers (Ruttner, 1905; Pennak, 1944; Dumont, 1972; Fairchild et al., 1977; Miracle, 1977; Pivoda, 1977; Cruz-Pizarro, 1978; Magnien & Gilbert, 1983; Carillo, Cruz-Pizarro & Morales-Baquero, 1989; Williamson, 1993; González, 1998; Gilbert & Burns, 2001). However, clear reverse migrations, such as the one displayed by P. remata in Johnson Pond, have been documented only by Dumont (1972), Williamson (1993) and González (1998). In these three cases, the ecological significance of the migration also appears to be avoidance of predation by, or interference from, crustaceans exhibiting typical migrations. In the Dumont study, Asplanchna priodonta migrated out-of-phase with Bosmina spp. and Cyclops vicinus. In the Williamson study, As. ovalis, K. cochlearis and P. vulgaris reduced spatial overlap with Mesocyclops edax. In González’s study, a diurnal ascent of Polyarthra sp. occurred in enclosures without but not with Chaoborus, perhaps to rise above the more dense population of Daphnia pulicaria in the former. In conclusion, the present study in Johnson Pond demonstrates that a zooplankton community may exhibit pronounced vertical differentiation even in a very shallow (1.5 m) water column with little vertical stratification in temperature, dissolved oxygen concentration or phytoplankton. The pronounced diurnal segregation of T. extensus and P. remata may reflect a cascade of strong interspecific behavioural interactions dependent upon the presence of the notonectid Buenoa. In this hypothesized scheme, Tropocyclops migrates towards the bottom to avoid predation by Buenoa near the surface, while Polyarthra, in turn, migrates to the surface to avoid Tropocyclops. The stimuli for these migrations may be kairomones from Buenoa and Tropocyclops, respectively, and are currently under investigation. The migrations should greatly reduce the intensity of interactions between Buenoa and Tropocyclops, and between Tropocyclops and Polyarthra, and therefore promote the coexistence of Tropocyclops and Polyarthra with Buenoa in the ecosystem. Differences in the substrate spectrum of extracellular enzymes in shallow lakes of differing trophic status Kai Ziervogel · Dina Leech · Carol Arnosti Received: 29 October 2012 / Accepted: 23 May 2013 / Published online: 6 June 2013 © Springer Science+Business Media Dordrecht 2013 Abstract Organic matter fluxes and food web interactions in lakes depend on the abilities of heterotrophic microbial communities to access and degrade organic matter, a process that begins with extracellular hydrolysis of high molecular weight substrates. In order to determine whether patterns of enzymatic hydrolysis vary among shallow lakes of different trophic status, we investigated the hydrolysis of six specific organic macromolecules (polysaccharides) in the spring and late summer in four adjacent shallow lakes of eutrophic, oligotrophic, and dystrophic status in coastal North Carolina, USA. The spectrum of enzyme activities detected differed strongly between lakes, with all six polysaccharides hydrolyzed in West Mattamuskeet in May, while only two substrates were hydrolyzed in Lake Phelps in August/September. Differences in the spectrum of enzyme activities, and therefore the capabilities of heterotrophic microbial communities, were likely driven by variations among lakes in primary productivity patterns, sediment–water interactions, and/or water chemistry. Our data represent a first step towards a better understanding of carbon substrate availability and differences in carbon cycling pathways in shallow lakes of different trophic status. Keywords Enzymatic activities · Polysaccharide hydrolysis · Carbon cycling · Shallow lakes Introduction Shallow lakes and ponds with an average water depth of less than 3 m are important as habitats and water sources for a wide range of organisms (Scheffer 1998). The state of a lake’s ecosystem and thus the quality of the services provided is determined by the quality of the lake water. Water quality is usually a product of autochthonous and allochthonous carbon inputs, as well as the subsequent cycling of nutrients and carbon through the lake’s food webs (Hamilton and Schladow 1997), a process that is driven primarily by heterotrophic microbial communities (Wetzel 1995; Wetzel and Søndergaard 1997). Rates of organic matter degradation by microbial communities are often determined by the activities of extracellular enzymes, the primary means for microbes to access and degrade organic macromolecules (Chróst 1992; Arnosti 2011). Numerous studies have investigated enzymatic capabilities of microbial communities in a variety of (mainly) deep water lakes (Burns and Dick 2002; Chróst 1991, and references therein), demonstrating a close coupling between enzyme activities and primary productivity (e.g. Chróst and Siuda 2006; Kisand and Tammert 2000). However, microbial dynamics and organic matter fluxes in shallow lakes are likely to be fundamentally different from those of their deep water counterparts because of intense sediment–water interactions and the potentially significant impact of aquatic vegetation. Previous studies of hydrolytic capabilities in lakes—whether deep or shallow—have been conducted using small substrate proxies, consisting of a monomer linked to a fluorophore (Hoppe 1983). The complex constituents of natural organic matter, however, are hydrolyzed by enzymes that are selective for specific aspects of macromolecular structure (e.g. Boraston et al. 2004); small substrate proxies do not adequately represent this structural complexity (Warren 1996). Investigations to date using small substrate proxies therefore provide little information about the abilities of heterotrophic microbial communities to access the range of high molecular weight substrates potentially available for microbial processing in lakes. As a first step in investigating the extent to which pelagic microbial communities in shallow lakes are capable of enzymatically accessing macromolecular substrates, we compared the spectrum of extracellular enzymes hydrolyzing a suite of six specific polysaccharides (pullulan, laminarin, xylan, fucoidan, arabinogalactan, and chondroitin sulfate) in adjacent shallow lakes of different trophic status in North Carolina, USA. Previous work using these polysaccharide substrates in marine, riverine, and estuarine systems has demonstrated that pelagic microbial communities can differ strikingly in their abilities to hydrolyze structurally-related substrates, including those built of the same monomeric constituents (Keith and Arnosti 2001; Steen et al. 2008; Ziervogel and Arnosti 2009; Arnosti et al. 2011). The present study was intended to determine whether different patterns of substrate specificities are also found in shallow lakes of different trophic status. The focus on polysaccharides stems from the fact that they are major constituents of terrestrial as well as aquatic biomass; high molecular weight carbohydrates also make up a significant component of dissolved organic carbon in lakes (Münster 1993). The suite of substrates used in this study includes polysaccharides that are constituents of macroalgae and higher plants (Painter 1983). For example, laminarin, xylan, and fucoidan are found in phytoplankton and algae, while xylan and arabinogalactan are constituents of hemi-celluloses (Painter 1983), which are among the most abundant biopolymers on earth. Pullulan is produced by sea grass epiphytes, and pullulanase functions as a debranching enzyme of starch (White and Kennedy 1988), a common storage polysaccharide of algae (Lee 1980). Chondroitin sulfate is a sulfated glycosaminoglycan produced by mollusks, invertebrates and fish. Laminarin and pullulan are also both soluble glucose-containing polysaccharides, and glucose is one of the most abundant components of total carbohydrates in the environment (Cowie and Hedges 1984; Kennedy and White 1988). Measurements of glucose uptake also demonstrate that this monomer is a major carbon source for bacterioplankton in lakes (Münster 1993, and references therein). This suite of substrates can therefore be used to investigate the ability of heterotrophic microbial communities to initiate the cycling of organic matter that is characteristic of the types that might be found in shallow lakes. Materials and methods Study sites This study was conducted in Lake Mattamuskeet, Pungo Lake, and Lake Phelps, a group of coastal plain shallow lakes in North Carolina, USA, near the Albemarle-Pamlico Sound (Fig. 1; Table 1). Lake Mattamuskeet is a eutrophic–hypereutrophic lake that has been divided into two basins since the construction of a roadway in 1940. Since the lake’s division, macrophytes (mainly water celery or tapegrass) have been the dominant primary producers in the eastern basin (Sponberg and Lodge 2005), resulting in clear water conditions during peak growth in the summer months. The western basin of the lake remains phytoplankton-dominated and thus more turbid throughout the year (note that hereafter the two basins will be treated as two different lakes, i.e. East and West Mattamuskeet; Fig. 1; Table 1). Estimated annual primary productivity of phytoplankton in West Mattamuskeet is 300 g C m\(^{-2}\) year\(^{-1}\) compared to <100 g C m\(^{-2}\) year\(^{-1}\) of macrophytes; for East Mattamuskeet, annual primary productivity by phytoplankton and macrophytes are 29 and 600 g C m\(^{-2}\) y\(^{-1}\), respectively (phytoplankton data are from M. Piehler Fig. 1 Map of the investigated lakes (1 West Mattamuskeet, 2 East Mattamuskeet, 3 Pungo Lake, 4 Lake Phelps), with pictures of lakes’ water indicating their profound differences in trophic state. Inset for Pungo Lake shows a secchi disk partially submerged in the water (unpublished) and macrophyte data are from Sponberg and Lodge 2005). Pungo Lake is a dystrophic lake loaded with allochthonous carbon throughout the water column, which rapidly attenuates light and thus limits primary productivity (see Fig. 1). Lake Phelps is an oligotrophic clear water lake with sandy sediments throughout the lakebed. Given their close proximity (Fig. 1), the lakes have the same geologic underpinning, experiencing similar wind and precipitation patterns, but their trophic states differ remarkably (Table 1). They have remained internally stable over the last decades, despite similar extent of human impacts through canal construction, decreased forested catchment area, water level maintenance, and agriculture (Waters 2007; Waters et al. 2010). Our current knowledge of the lakes’ ecology and ecosystem responses to nutrient loading and anthropogenic stressors derives from a few recent studies on the paleolimnological sediment records (Waters 2007; Waters et al. 2010). We lack current information of the water quality and ecology of the four lakes, and there are no published data on the lakes’ microbial biomass and community structure. Water sampling The four lakes studied here are part of a national wildlife refuge. For the present study we were able to obtain water samples in May and August/September 2008 (Table 1). Surface water samples were collected by boat from the middle of the lakes, except for East Mattamuskeet in August/September when the water level was too low and the sample was taken near the shore. Prior to water sampling, physico-chemical water parameters were measured using a YSI sensor (Table 1). Water samples were taken from the surface using 250-mL PE bottles (for enzyme activities) and 100-mL dark bottles (for chlorophyll measurements). Samples were stored on ice in a cooler and transported to the laboratory at the UNC Institute of Marine Sciences (Moorhead City, NC) for chlorophyll measurements, and the UNC Department of Marine Sciences (Chapel Hill, NC) for enzyme activity measurements. Chlorophyll was measured in duplicates by filtering 50 mL of lake water GF/F filters that were then placed in 15 mL of 90 % acetone overnight at −20 °C (Holm-Hansen et al. 1965). Samples were run on a Shimadzu Trilogy fluorometer fitted with the non-acidification chlorophyll module. Enzyme activity measurements were initiated 7 days (May) and 9 days (August/September) after collection of water samples following the procedure described below. Unlabeled substrates were obtained from Fluka and Sigma, and fluorescently labeled with fluoresceinamine (FLA) using a modification of the method of Glabe et al. (1983), as described in Arnosti (1996, 2003). Single FLA-polysaccharide substrates were added to 50-ml portions of either unfiltered or autoclaved lake water (the latter served as a killed control) and separated into three clean glass vials, each at 10.5 μM monomer equivalents. Live and control water samples were incubated in the dark at 23 °C (room temperature) for 6 days. One mL per incubation vial was withdrawn immediately after the addition of the substrate, and after 2 as well as 6 days. Samples were filtered through a 0.2-μm pore size syringe filter and stored frozen until analysis. To determine enzymatic hydrolysis rates, samples from each time point were thawed and injected onto a HPLC/gel permeation chromatography (GPC) system consisting of a G-50 Sephadex gel column (20.5 × 1 cm) connected to a G-75 Sephadex gel column (18 × 1 cm). Column outflow passes through a fluorescence detector set to excitation and emission maxima of 490 and 530 nm, respectively. The column set was calibrated with a series of FITC-dextran standards (150, 10, 4 kD, FITC-galactose, and free fluorescent tag). Enzyme activity is measured as the changes in molecular weight of the total added polysaccharide pool over time, hence the requirement for extended incubation times. The information derived from these measurements therefore reflects the potential of heterotrophic microbial communities to access specific substrates, given sufficient time. Such responses potentially include microbial growth, as well as enzyme induction. Substrates incubated with autoclaved lake water showed no significant changes in molecular weights over time. The rates reported here should be regarded as potential hydrolysis rates, since added substrate is in competition with naturally-occurring substrates for enzyme active sites. Given that the level of carbon addition to each incubation (10.5 μM monomer, or 52.5–73.5 μM C) was very similar to previously reported concentrations of total dissolved carbohydrates in lakes (40 nM–60 μM C; Münster1993), hydrolysis rates are most likely zero-order with respect to substrate, and represent maximum potential rates. Statistical analysis Enzyme activities are given as their statistical mean (\( n = 3 \)) ± SD for analytical replicates. Differences of maximum hydrolysis rates measured for each of the six substrates were tested using a two-way ANOVA with lake and sampling time as factors (R Development Core Team 2010). A posthoc comparison using Tukey HSD was applied for significant (\( p \)-values < 0.05) lake-specific differences. Variations in substrate-specific maximum hydrolysis rates between the two sampling times were determined for each lake individually using a \( t \) test (Excel® data analysis toolpack). Results Physico-chemical parameters of the four lakes were very different between the two sampling times (Table 1). Surface water temperatures in the four lakes in August/September were 26–30 °C and thus 6 °C (Lake Phelps) to 10 °C (Pungo Lake) warmer compared to May; oxygen saturation levels were accordingly lower at higher water temperatures. Chlorophyll concentrations at both sampling times were generally highest in the eutrophic East and West Mattamuskeet and lowest in the oligotrophic Lake Phelps. Water conductivity in both basins of Lake Mattamuskeet was higher in August/September compared to May, and remained at the same level in the other two lakes. We also found considerably lower pH in August/September compared to May in three (East Mattamuskeet, Phelps, Pungo) of the four lakes. The difference in pH between the two sampling times was most pronounced in Pungo Lake, where pH dropped from 8.8 in May to 5.4 in August/September. Lake Phelps’ and East Mattamuskeets’ pH decreased from 6.2 and 8.6 in May to 4.9 and 7.6 in August/September, respectively. Along with changes in water chemistry and temperature, the four lakes showed distinct lake-specific as well as sampling time-specific differences in the spectrum of enzymatic activities (note that all polysaccharide incubations were conducted at constant room temperature, not in situ temperature, so temperature effects were not explicitly considered). The broadest enzymatic spectrum was measured in West Mattamuskeet, where all six substrates were hydrolyzed in May and all except fucoidan were hydrolyzed in August/September (Fig. 2a; Table 2). In East Mattamuskeet, in contrast, only 4 substrates (arabinogalactan, chondroitin, laminarin, xylan) were hydrolyzed at both sampling times (Fig. 2b; Table 2). An even narrower spectrum of polysaccharide hydrolases was measured in Lake Phelps and Pungo Lake: three (chondroitin, laminarin, xylan) and two substrates (laminarin, xylan) were hydrolyzed in Lake Phelps in May and August/September, respectively (Fig. 2c; Table 2), and only laminarin and xylan were hydrolyzed in Pungo Lake during both sampling times (Fig. 2d; Table 2). Maximum hydrolysis rate measured for each substrate varied significantly between lakes and sampling time (ANOVA; Table 3). Generally highest hydrolysis rates were found in the two basins of Lake Mattamuskeet, except for xylan, which was hydrolyzed at highest rates in Pungo Lake in May (Tables 2, 3). Considering each lake separately, we also found differences in hydrolysis rates for five of the six substrates between the two sampling times (t test; Table 3). Higher hydrolysis rates in May compared to August/September were found for xylan in West Mattamuskeet, Lake Phelps, and Pungo Lake, for chondroitin in West Mattamuskeet. Hydrolysis rates in August/September were higher for xylan and arabinogalactan in East Mattmuskeet, and for pullulan in West Mattmuskeet. Only lake-specific laminarin hydrolysis rates in May and August/September were statistically indistinguishable from one another. Differences in primary productivity (and potentially in hydrology) between these likes likely drive the remarkable differences in enzymatic capabilities of their respective microbial communities, as shown by the differences in the spectrum of substrates hydrolyzed (Tables 2, 3). All six substrates were only hydrolyzed in West Mattamuskeet in May when three (chondroitin, fucoidan, xylan) of the six substrates also showed higher maximum hydrolysis rates compared to August/September (Table 3). Neither fucoidan nor pullulan were hydrolyzed in East Mattamuskeet; in Lake Phelps and Pungo Lake, pullulan, fucoidan, and arabinogalactan were not hydrolyzed (Fig. 2; Table 2). The broad enzymatic spectrum observed in West Mattamuskeet reflects the ability of the bacterial community to degrade a diverse DOM pool that was likely dominated by phytoplankton primary productivity at the time of sampling. Phytoplankton are the dominant primary producers in the western basin of Lake Mattamuskeet, where overall highest oxygen saturation levels in the water column were measured in May (Table 1), suggesting elevated photosynthetic activities and thus phytoplankton metabolism at the first sampling time. Phytoplankton-derived DOM can include a wide range of carbohydrates, which may explain the broader range of substrates hydrolyzed in May relative to August/September. Phytoplankton exopolymeric substances, for example, have been found to be enriched in deoxysugar-containing sulfated polysaccharides, a description that fits fucoidan (Mopper et al. 1995). The narrower spectrum of polysaccharide hydrolases in East Mattamuskeet suggests a less diverse carbohydrate pool, or less diverse capabilities of the microbial communities to access substrates compared to West Mattamuskeet. We sampled at the beginning and at the end of the macrophyte growing season in East Mattamuskeet, assuming that macrophyte-DOM was a major carbohydrate source in the eastern basin at both sampling times. Bacterial decomposition of high levels of macrophyte DOM at the end of the growing season in East Mattamuskeet may explain significantly higher xylanase and arabinogalactan hydrolase activity in August/September compared to May (Tables 2, 3). Xylan hydrolysis in August/September was more than double the rate measured in May, and constituted more than half of the summed enzyme activities (Fig. 2; Table 2). Lake Phelps and Pungo Lake showed lower hydrolysis rates and lower functional diversity with respect to polysaccharide hydrolysis compared to East and West Mattamuskeet (Table 3). This difference may be a result of markedly lower primary productivity of the oligotrophic Lake Phelps, and the dystrophic waters of Pungo Lake (Table 1). In this context, the lack of hydrolysis of arabinogalactan in Lake Phelps and Pungo Lake is notable, since arabinogalactans are common constituents of hemicelluloses (Painter 1983), and are thus widespread in terrestrial ecosystems. Despite the obvious presence of humic substances in Pungo Lake (presumably due to allochthonous input into the lake, necessarily derived from terrestrial production), no arabinogalactan hydrolysis was observed in either this lake or in the clear water Lake Phelps. For shallow lakes such as these, the extent of sediment resuspension (which is far greater than in deep water lakes; Scheffer 1998) may also provide an explanation for the differences in the spectrum of substrates hydrolyzed in West and East Mattamuskeet. East Mattamuskeet is likely less prone to sediment resuspension events compared to West Mattamuskeet, which lacks the lake bed-stabilizing macrophytes. In general, mixing between the sediment and the overlying water can enhance the vertical transport of sediment-associated benthic microorganisms (e.g. Ritzrau and Graf 1992), increasing rates of enzyme activities in waters affected by sediment resuspension (Chróst and Riemann 1994; Cotner 2000; Ritzrau and Graf 1992; Ritzrau 1996; Wainright 1990). In addition to enhanced hydrolysis rates, sediment resuspension has been found to widen the spectrum of water column enzyme activities in coastal marine systems. Using the same suite of six polysaccharide substrates, Ziervogel and Arnosti (2009) found that sediment resuspension widened the spectrum from four to all six polysaccharide hydrolases in estuarine waters, likely reflecting a wider range of enzymatic capabilities of marine benthic microorganisms relative to bacterioplankton (Arnosti 2000, 2008; Teske et al. 2011; Ziervogel and Arnosti 2008). Comparisons of the spectrum of high molecular weight substrates hydrolyzed in benthic and pelagic lacustrine environments remain to be carried out. Published comparisons of enzyme activities in pelagic and benthic lacustrine environments are limited to a single study demonstrating more rapid hydrolysis of a wide range of small substrate proxies in sediments compared to overlying lake waters (Chróst and Siuda 2002). Differences in enzymatic capabilities of the microbial communities of these four lakes may also reflect the functional outcome of fundamental differences in the community structure of oligotrophic, dystrophic, and eutrophic lakes. Bacterial community structure in shallow lakes has been found to correlate with the lakes’ trophic status and suspended matter load (van der Gucht et al. 2005; Muylaert et al. 2002). Water chemistry can also lead to changes in the diversity of bacterial communities of a lake (Methe and Zehr 1999; Percent et al. 2008). Pungo Lake and Lake Phelps experienced a much larger drop in pH between May and August/September (Table 1) than did East Mattamuskeet; we hypothesize that this change in pH may have affected the lakes’ microbial communities. A reduction in community diversity in lower pH waters has been demonstrated by compositional analysis of the bacterial communities in 18 lakes affected by various degrees of acidic deposition (Percent et al. 2008). Reduced community diversity, caused by significant changes in water column pH between May and August/September, may also lead to a reduction in functional capabilities among the community members robust enough to withstand rapidly changing pH. Our initial investigation of geographically-proximate lakes of different trophic status demonstrates that the enzymatic capabilities of lacustrine pelagic communities differ profoundly from one another. Comparable differences in the spectrum of enzyme activities in marine pelagic systems have been found only across much broader spatial gradients (Arnosti et al. 2011). Determining the fundamental factors underlying these differences in enzymatic capabilities will require a coordinated study that integrates microbial community composition and metabolism with detailed analysis of organic matter sources and composition. Given that shallow lakes dominate the areal extent of inland waters (Downing 2010), which play an important role in global carbon cycling (Tranvik et al. 2009), better understanding of the breadth of substrates potentially available to microbial communities in shallow lakes will improve our abilities to understand disparate means of carbon cycling in these lakes, and ultimately to predict and model carbon transformations and CO₂ fluxes between inland waters and the atmosphere.
