The relative density of macrophyte communities in these hydrologically closed basins may strongly influence DOC concentrations in the lakes. In the water column, CH₄ concentrations are directly related to both conductivity and DOC, wherein high CH₄ concentrations correspond with both high conductivity and DOC (Fig. 8). However, we do not find a direct relationship between maximum CH₄ concentration and aquatic chemistry variables. Under open-water conditions of 2012, the maximum CH₄ concentration in the water column was from the hypolimnion of South Twin lake. While South Twin lake did exhibit relatively high conductivity, DOC concentrations were relatively low. Similarly, the highest CH₄ concentration was measured in Potentilla lake in 2013 under ice-covered conditions, corresponding to the lowest conductivity and DOC measured in the study. The lowest concentrations of CH₄ in all of the lakes were from epilimnetic waters, despite the wide range in aquatic chemistry lake to lake. In addition, EVV Upper lake had significantly higher concentrations of SO₄²⁻ than the other lakes in the study. Competition for substrates favors sulfate reduction (SR) and methanogenesis typically does not occur until SO₄²⁻ is exhausted and SR rates have decreased (Lovely and Klung, 1983, 1986; Scholten et al., 2002; Ward and Winfrey, 1985). However, EVV Upper lake did not have the lowest concentrations of CH₄ in the water column, suggesting there were sufficient reduced carbon substrates to fuel both SR and methanogenesis. Therefore, while aquatic chemistry in the water column could be a factor influencing CH₄ production, at the level of this investigation, it alone is likely insufficient to explain the variation in CH₄ concentrations observed lake to lake, as well as seasonally and annually. 5.2 Effect of temperature on lake stratification Ground-level air temperatures strongly influence the thermal stratification of lakes during the open-water season. Warm ground-level air temperatures during open-water conditions in 2012 (Fig. 3) resulted in epilimnetic temperatures being 1.5–5 °C higher in all of the study lakes relative to open-water conditions in 2013 (Fig. 4). Increased epilimnetic temperatures under open-water conditions in 2012 are consistent with both predictive models and measured temperatures indicating that warming climates result in higher epilimnetic temperatures (Honzo and Stefan, 1993; Fang and Stefan, 2009; Jankowski et al., 2006; Adrian et al., 2009; Coats et al., 2006). As a result of warmer epilimnetic waters, stronger thermal stratification occurred during open-water conditions in 2012 than in 2013, with \( \Delta T \) 4–9 \( ^\circ \)C higher in 2012 (Fig. 4). In addition, wind speeds were significantly lower and air pressures were higher during open-water conditions in 2012 compared with 2013 (Fig. 3), leading to reduced mixing of the water column and greater heat transfer to shallower epilimnia. Temperature and thermal structure strongly influence DO concentrations in lakes, wherein stronger thermal stratification leads to increased anoxia in the hypolimnion (Hanson et al., 2006; Adrian et al., 2009; Foley et al., 2012). For example, the extremely warm European summer of 2003 resulted in stronger thermal stratification and hypolimnetic DO depletion in Swiss lakes (Jankowski et al., 2006). Similarly, as a result of strong thermal stratification in 2012, the hypolimnia of EVV Upper lake, EVV Lower lake, Potentilla, and South Twin lake were anoxic. For comparison, 1–34 % of water column in the lakes was anoxic in 2012, whereas the percentages decreased to 0–7 % in 2013. 5.3 Effects of temperature on CH$_4$ Ground-level air temperature differences result in warmer surface waters and increased stratification between 2012 and 2013, but a weak linear relationship is observed between water temperatures and dissolved CH$_4$ concentrations (Fig. 8). Both the highest and lowest CH$_4$ concentrations are observed in waters <5 \( ^\circ \)C. In freshwater environments, the concentration of dissolved CH$_4$ reflects the balance between CH$_4$ production and CH$_4$ consumption by anaerobic or aerobic oxidation (Duc et al., 2010; Dzyuban, 2010; Encinas Fernandez et al., 2014; Kankaala et al., 2007; Martinez-Cruz et al., 2015; Segarra et al., 2015; Smemo and Yavitt, 2011). Methane production is affected by temperature, where higher temperatures result in increased production (Duc et al., 2010). However, methanogenesis only occurs under anaerobic conditions (Borrel et al., 2011; Valentine et al., 1994; Yvon-Durocher et al., 2011). Under open-water conditions in all of the lakes, the majority of the water column is oxygenated (Fig. 5); therefore, production was likely minimal in the water column in both 2012 and 2013. Concentration of CH$_4$ and DO are inversely related, wherein highest concentrations occur in anoxic waters and decrease with increasing DO (Fig. 8), suggesting MOx is driving the concentration of CH$_4$ in the water column. However, consumption of CH$_4$ by microbial methane oxidation is not strongly influenced by temperature (Duc et al., 2010) and has only been demonstrated to increase with increasing temperatures under CH$_4$ saturated conditions (Lofton et al., 2013). Despite the absence of a strong linear relationship between water temperature and CH$_4$ concentrations, warmer ground-level air temperatures correspond with increased CH$_4$ both in the water column and the sediments in the study lakes at the time of sampling. Under open-water conditions, CH$_4$ concentrations in the water column were significantly greater in 2012 than in 2013 (Fig. 8), corresponding with increased ground-level air temperatures. Similarly, under ice-covered conditions, ground-level air temperatures were \( \sim 6 \) \( ^\circ \)C higher in 2013 than in 2014 and CH$_4$ concentrations in the water column were greater for the two lakes in which there are data for both years (Fig. 9). The CH$_4$ concentration differences occur throughout the water column, but are more pronounced in the bottom waters close to the sediment–water interface. It is possible that increased ground-level air temperatures result in increased production of CH$_4$ in the profundal sediments, which lead to increased concentrations in the bottom waters of each lake. However, under open-water conditions in 2012, the bottom water temperatures were colder than in 2013, suggesting profundal sediments were not warmer due to increased ground-level air temperatures. More likely, the higher CH$_4$ concentrations in the bottom waters during open-water conditions in 2012 were the result of increased thermal stratification and subsequent anoxia, allowing a buildup of CH$_4$ in the bottom waters. The concentrations of CH$_4$ from profundal sediments during ice-covered conditions in 2013 were greater than from open-water conditions in 2013 (Table 4). While ground-level air temperatures were significantly colder during the 2013 ice-covered season compared to the 2013 open-water season (Fig. 3), the higher concentrations of CH$_4$ during ice-covered conditions may be a relic of the anomalously warm conditions from the previous open-water conditions in 2012. In the littoral sediments, where there are data for consecutive years, gas bubble CH$_4$ concentrations from 2012 were higher than in 2013 (Table 4), further suggesting that warmer ground-level air temperatures result in increased CH$_4$ production, consistent with experimental studies of methanogenesis response to higher temperature (Duc et al., 2010; Hoj et al., 2008; Lofton et al., 2013). However, it is important to note that littoral CH$_4$ concentrations are an estimate, as a volume of sediment/sample was unmeasured. Therefore, it is possible that the increase in littoral CH$_4$ concentrations is not the result of increased CH$_4$ production, but of a different amount of sediment disturbed. Without temperature data for profundal and littoral sediments, it is impossible to directly determine whether warmer temperatures result in an increase in CH$_4$ production or whether other factors may influence production of CH$_4$. However, because bottom water temperatures were colder during open-water conditions in 2012 than in 2013 (Fig. 4), it is unlikely that profundal sediments were warmer in response to warmer ground-level air temperatures. In addition to temperature, methanogenesis is also influenced by the amount and quality of organic carbon substrates (Borrel et al., 2011; West et al., 2012). Lakes in this study are all embedded within continuous permafrost, with an active layer <0.5 m thick. It is possible that the anomalously warm conditions in 2012 resulted in warming and thickening of the active permafrost layer, which could have caused organic carbon, nutrients, and ions to enter the lakes and be available for microbial utilization (Adrian et al., 2009; Kokelj et al., 2009; Lougheed et al., 2011; Weyhenmeyer and Karlsson, 2009). However, under open-water conditions, DOC was only higher in one lake in 2012 compared to 2013 and DOC concentrations during ice-covered conditions in 2013 and 2014 were similar (Table 2). Significantly higher specific conductivity during open-water conditions in 2012 compared to 2013 was observed for all of the lakes (Table 2), which could be attributed to an additional source from permafrost thaw. Increases in DOC and conductivity were observed in thaw ponds in western Siberia during the anomalous hot summer of 2012, but these were attributed to evaporation concentration effects (Pokrovsky et al., 2013). In the Greenlandic lakes, significant water level changes between the two consecutive years of this study were not observed, so it is unlikely that the higher conductivity in 2012 was the result of evaporation. 5.4 Effects of stratification on CH$_4$ Enhanced thermal stratification and anoxia during open-water conditions in 2012 corresponded with significantly higher CH$_4$ concentrations in the water column. The most notable difference in CH$_4$ concentrations between 2012 and 2013 occurred within the bottom waters, which were anoxic in 2012. Under open-water conditions in 2012, the amount of CH$_4$ stored in the hypolimnion was 2 to 300 times higher than in 2013. The higher CH$_4$ concentrations may be the result of increased CH$_4$ production due to more extensive anaerobic conditions. However, the higher CH$_4$ concentrations were more likely the result of larger pools of anoxic waters in 2012 allowing for a buildup of CH$_4$ that corresponded in increased CH$_4$ storage in the water column (Fig. 8). During fall overturn, the storage pool of CH$_4$ is susceptible to diffusion and/or oxidation (Encinas Fernandez et al., 2014; Kankaala et al., 2007; López Bellido et al., 2009). If half of the stored CH$_4$ is emitted during fall overturn, as suggested by results from Fernandez et al. (2014), the fall overturn CH$_4$ flux would be significantly larger in 2012 than that in 2013 as a result of the more extensive anoxia in 2012. Weaker thermal stratification during open-water conditions in 2013 meant that 93–100 % of the water column in the lakes had DO concentrations > 1 mg L$^{-1}$. When CH$_4$ diffusing from anoxic sediments reaches oxic sediment or water, the majority of it is oxidized (Bastviken et al., 2002; Dzyuban, 2010; Kankaala et al., 2007). MOx is highly efficient at consuming CH$_4$, thereby lowering CH$_4$ concentrations. The percentage of CH$_4$ oxidized can be estimated by assuming that CH$_4$ at the water–air interface originates from diffusion through the water column from the profundal sediments. Given that an increased proportion of the water column was oxic under open-water conditions 2013, we initially hypothesized that the percentage of CH$_4$ oxidized would be greater in 2013 than in 2012. However, under open-water conditions in 2013, the percentage of CH$_4$ oxidized was similar to, or less than, in 2012. Consistent with CH$_4$ oxidation rates from Alaskan lakes, MOx controls CH$_4$ concentrations when DO is present (Martinez-Cruz et al., 2015). Under warm conditions in 2012, not only were CH$_4$ concentrations in sediments and anoxic waters elevated but the percentage of CH$_4$ oxidized was also higher. Several studies suggest that MOx is important for mitigating CH$_4$ emissions to the atmosphere (Martinez-Cruz et al., 2015; Milucka et al., 2015; Segarra et al., 2015). However, despite the likelihood that MOx was more efficient in 2012 under warmer conditions, CH$_4$ concentrations in the stored pool were higher in 2012 than in 2013. While significant variations in CH$_4$ concentrations and inventories were observed under between the consecutive years under open-water conditions, the amount of CH$_4$ stored under ice cover was significantly greater than that stored in the anoxic hypolimnion under open-water conditions (Figs. 3–6). For South Twin lake, the CH$_4$ storage under ice cover in 2013 was more than an order of magnitude greater than that stored in the hypolimnion during open-water conditions in 2012, and in EVV Lower lake it was two orders of magnitude greater (Figs. 3–6). In these small Greenlandic lakes, emissions during spring overturn currently reflect the largest potential flux of CH$_4$ to the atmosphere. Similarly, in other Arctic lakes, CH$_4$ emissions during spring overturn after ice breakup are usually larger than CH$_4$ emissions during fall overturns (Juutinen et al., 2009; López Bellido et al., 2009; Karlsson et al., 2013; Miettinen et al., 2015). 5.5 Implications for a warmer Arctic In the Arctic, lakes are ice-covered for more than 8 months of the year (Belzile et al., 2001). The study lakes here are ice-covered ~ 10 months of the year. At sampling under ice-covered conditions, lakes have been covered ~ 8 months. In each of the study lakes, CH$_4$ concentrations are significantly higher under ice-covered conditions compared to open-water conditions (Fig. 7), which is also observed in other northern latitude lakes that are ice-covered the majority of the year (Juutinen et al., 2009; Martinez-Cruz et al., 2015). Ice cover impedes gas exchange between the water and the atmosphere, promoting buildup of CH$_4$ in the water column leading to increased CH$_4$ storage (Bastviken et al., 2004; Juutinen et al., 2009; Martinez-Cruz et al., 2015; Phelps et al., 1998). No holes or moats were observed in the ice cover during sampling; therefore, the total inventory of CH$_4$ in the water column under ice-covered conditions was stored. Similar to stored CH$_4$ during stratification in open-water conditions, CH$_4$ stored under ice is susceptible to emission to the atmosphere during spring overturns during and after ice breakup. Projected climate change is expected to change ice cover characteristics in lakes (Fang and Stefan, 2009; Mueller et al., 2009). Ice coverage duration has already decreased for many lakes as ground-level air temperatures have increased (Bertilsson et al., 2013; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2011). As perennially ice-covered lakes begin to develop open-water periods for at least some portions of the year, the number of seasonally frozen lakes will increase (Mueller et al., 2009). Currently, the largest efflux of CH4 from our study lakes will most likely occur during ice breakup and spring overturn, consistent with other Arctic lakes (Karlsson et al., 2013; Miettinen et al., 2015). Changes in the duration of seasonal ice cover will result in changes in inventories of under-ice CH4. We predict that, as the duration of ice cover decreases, the amount of CH4 stored under ice cover will likely decrease due to the shorter time for accumulation. If the amount of stored CH4 under ice cover decreases, this will potentially reduce the amount of CH4 emitted during ice breakup and spring overturn. In addition to a decrease in ice cover, our results also suggest that an increase in ground-level air temperatures will result in enhanced thermal stability and anoxia in Arctic lakes, as we observed during open-water conditions in 2012. The duration of open-water thermal stratification will also likely increase in concert with the decrease in ice cover. The combined effects of extended season and greater strength of stratification are likely to be development of higher CH4 inventories in the water column during open-water periods. Conceptually, as anoxic zones expand in space and duration, the influence of methanogenic sediments on water column inventories of methane should increase. Currently, small lakes emit substantially more CH4 per unit area than larger lakes during open-water conditions (Bastviken et al., 2004; Cole et al., 2007; Juutinen et al., 2009). Small, shallow likes are more susceptible to thermal change due to increased ground-level air temperatures and will likely continue to be major CH4 contributors to the atmosphere. In fact, our results suggest that increased warming in the Arctic will result in greater summer inventories of CH4 and consequently larger emissions of CH4 to the atmosphere during fall overturn in small lakes. 6 Conclusions Over the past half century, the Arctic has warmed at a rate greater than the global average, and climate models predict further polar amplification, with the Arctic continuing to warm at a faster rate than other regions. The anomalously warm summer of 2012 in Greenland corresponded with significantly higher CH4 concentrations under open-water conditions in a series of small lakes compared to the following year. Stronger thermal stratification under warmer conditions lead to increased CH4 storage in the lakes. With impending warming climate, increased stratification and CH4 storage in lakes will likely lead to greater potential fluxes during fall overturn. Currently, in these small, seasonally ice-covered Arctic lakes, the greatest concentrations of CH4 in the water column are occurring under ice-covered conditions. Changes in seasonal ice cover will result in changes in under ice CH4 inventories, and consequently lead to reductions in the amount of CH4 emitted during ice breakup and spring overturn. These results suggest that interannual variation in ground-level air temperatures may be the primary driver of changes in methane dynamics because it controls both the strength of thermal stratification and duration of ice cover. We predict that as the climate continues to warm, the greatest annual efflux of CH4 from small Arctic lakes will shift from spring overturn to fall overturn. 7 Data availability Data are available and can be requested by contacting the corresponding author (sbcadieux@gmail.com). Factors influencing macroinvertebrate assemblages in artificial subtropical ponds of Taiwan Sen-Her Shieh · Yao-Sheng Chi Received: 21 August 2009/Revised: 14 April 2010/Accepted: 17 April 2010/Published online: 2 May 2010 © Springer Science+Business Media B.V. 2010 Abstract Macroinvertebrate assemblages and its association with environmental factors at the 11 artificial subtropical ponds of Taiwan were examined using the multivariate analysis software STATICO. The aims of the study were to determine whether spatial and seasonal variation of macroinvertebrate assemblages changed seasonally, to examine which environmental factors determined the spatial and temporal structure of maroinvertebrate assemblages, and to compare between-pond variations in the taxon composition of macroinvertebrates. Macroinvertebrates were collected seasonally by a corer and a sweep net in 2007, and 13 physical and chemical factors were measured at the same time. A total of 31 macroinvertebrate taxa were collected during the sampling period, and the most dominant taxa were Chironomidae (31.7% of total animal abundance) and Tubificidae (22.4%). STATICO identified pond size, pond depth, sediment depth, and altitude as the major abiotic factors and Bufo melanostictus (Amphibia) as the major biotic factor to influence macroinvertebrate assemblages at these ponds. These factors changed with seasonality. For example, the abundance of B. melanostictus was the most important factor during the spring but became much less important in other seasons. According to the spatial distribution patterns of macroinvertebrate assemblages, macroinvertebrates could be split into two groups based on their dispersal. The active dispersers, such as insect taxa, were strongly associated with pond size and the passive dispersers, such as non-insect taxa, were strongly associated with the pond depth and/or sediment depth. The results of this study suggested that pond size might influence macroinvertebrate assemblages through their dispersal mechanisms and that the environmental factors which influenced the macroinvertebrate assemblages most changed with seasons in this study area. Keywords Pond size · Active dispersers · Passive dispersers · STATICO Introduction Ponds are rich and diverse habitats and play a key role in safeguarding aquatic biodiversity. They are defined as waterbodies between 1 m^2 and 2 ha in area which may be permanent or seasonal, including both artificial and natural waterbodies (Biggs et al., 2005). Despite their small surface area, they are exceptionally rich in biodiversity, as compared to streams and large lakes, and contribute significantly to regional freshwater biodiversity in many northern temperate regions (Oertli et al., 2002; Williams et al., 2003; Nicolet et al., 2004), but our understanding of the relative biodiversity importance of ponds elsewhere remains limited. However, the ponds are threatened due to anthropogenic activities, such as eutrophication, chemical pollution, acid rain, physical destruction, and invasion of exotic species (Heath & Whitehead, 1992; Brönmark & Hansson, 2002; Boothby, 2003). While monitoring programs for freshwaters have been widely carried out in many countries, particularly for streams and lakes, these programs have largely failed to include ponds (Oertli et al., 2005). The macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds are influenced by both abiotic and biotic factors. Abiotic factors, such as pond size (Rundle et al., 2002) and water chemistry (Friday, 1987), affect the number of taxa in the community. It has been suggested that large ponds support more macroinvertebrate taxa than small ones due to habitat heterogeneity (Della Bella et al., 2005). Biotic factors, such as the presence or absence of large predators (fish and amphibians) in a pond and the dispersal ability of macroinvertebrates, appear to be important in determining macroinvertebrate assemblages. Invertebrate biomass was found to be higher in fishless wetlands than in wetlands with fish (Zimmer et al., 2001). Rundle et al. (2002) indicated that the taxon richness of active dispersal macroinvertebrates was positively correlate with pond size, whereas the taxon richness of passive macroinvertebrates did not correlated with environmental variables. Assessing these influences on macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds are a key process to understand community structure and succession and to propose a man-made control before any pollution resulting from anthropogenic activities could occur. The relationships between environmental factors and macroinvertebrate distributions in freshwaters have often been studied using principal component analysis (Hinden et al., 2005), canonical correspondence analysis (Williams et al., 2003; Nicolet et al., 2004; Carchini et al., 2005), multidimensional scaling (Della Bella et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2006, 2009), or clustering (Collinson et al., 1995; Nicolet et al., 2004; Bilton et al., 2006). The main drawback of these methods is that they do not consider that both environmental factors and macroinvertebrate assemblages vary temporally and that the former affects the latter. In order to overcome this problem, the STATICO (STATIS and CO-inertia) has been developed (Thioulouse et al., 2004). It is a multivariate method allowing simultaneous analysis of a sequence of paired ecological tables recorded through a series of sampling occasions. Thioulouse et al. (2004) pointed that STATICO is particularly suited to study the relationship between the environmental and taxonomic tables when both vary time. Since ponds are not uniform as revealed by their shape, shoreline, and size, and a clear seasonal dynamics has been observed for the difference macroinvertebrate assemblages (Studinski & Grubbs, 2007), STATICO is a well-suited statistical tool to get a clear representation of the spatial and temporal variation of the macroinvertebrates assemblages in ponds. Most studies which examined macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds were conducted in Europe (Oertli et al., 2009). There are still relatively few such studies in Asia, especially artificial ponds, where the biodiversity has been poorly investigated. Because of the complexity of pond systems affected spatially and temporally by various abiotic and biotic factors, we analyzed using STATICO the relationships between these factors and maroinvertebrate assemblages in the 11 artificial subtropical ponds of Taiwan. The first aim of the study was to determine whether spatial and seasonal variation of macroinvertebrate assemblages changed among these subtropical ponds where seasonality was insignificant. The second aim was to examine which abiotic and biotic factors determined the spatial and temporal structure of these macroinvertebrate assemblages at these ponds. We assumed that the pond size and the presence and absence of large predators in ponds should be the most important factors to affect macroinvertebrate assemblages in these ponds. Therefore, it was predicted that ponds which were large and/or without large predators should support more taxon richness than ponds which were small and/or with large predators. The final aim was to compare between-pond variations in the taxon composition of active and passive dispersers of macroinvertebrates. We assumed that the active dispersal macroinvertebrate should be more associated with pond size. Materials and methods Study area Sampling sites were established in the coastal area of west central Taiwan. The area represents one of the biotopes most severely threatened by human impacts since the main land use of the area is municipal and agricultural. The area is flat, has low altitude (<300 m.a.s.l.), and has the annual precipitation of about 1,405 mm between 1998 and 2007, with the perhumid season from April to September and the relative drought season from October to December. Annual mean air temperature is about 23.2°C. The dominant vegetation of the area is Panicum maximum (Poaceae) and Acacia confuse (Fabaceae). Because our aims were to assess the relationships between environmental factors and macroinvertebrate assemblages among different ponds, 11 artificial ponds were selected in this area to insure that they were influenced by the same climate condition and land use. These ponds are situated in school grounds and located between the coordinates 24°6′N, 120°31′E and 24°24′N, 120°38′E. Sampling methods Macroinvertebrates samples were collected in January (winter), April (spring), July (summer), and October (autumn) 2007. Because different habitats and groups of macroinvertebrates require different sampling methods, the use of a single method for all habitats could yield misleading conclusion on macroinvertebrate richness. Therefore, two methods, e.g., the quantitative and qualitative methods (Studinski & Grubbs, 2007) were used in this study. A benthic corer sampler (diameter = 26 cm) was used as a quantitative method. During each sampling occasion, the longest transect of the pond was selected, and three benthic samples were taken at 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 of this transect. The benthic corer was pushed into the substrate until it reached an impermeable layer. The sediments within the corer were transferred by a hand with a cup to a bucket. Animals, organic matter, and remaining water in bucket were passed through a sieve with 0.8-mm apertures. These materials were preserved in 95% ethanol in the field. This procedure allowed us to sample benthic macroinvertebrates. For the qualitative method, ponds were sampled with a sweep net (with 20-cm D-frame and 200-μm mesh) at different microhabitats (such as emergent and submerged aquatic vegetation and pond margins) for 5 min (Batzer et al., 2004). This method allowed us to collect nekton macroinvertebrates and to get a representative sample from the system (Collinson et al., 1995). Sample sizes and sampling time were decided after a pilot study undertaken in these ponds. The main outcomes of this pilot study were that three corer samples and a total time of 5 min were good enough to have the representative taxa for these ponds. In the laboratory, all the samples were rinsed by tap water, and the animals were sorted and preserved in 75% ethanol for further analysis. The macroinvertebrate taxa were identified to the lowest taxonomic unit possible. Aquatic insects were identified according to Morse et al. (1994) and other macroinvertebrate taxa according to Dudgeon (1999) and Shy & Yu (1998). Members of Ostracoda were not identified further. Three vertebrate taxa were collected in this study, and they were common Asian toad (Bufo melanostictus), mosquitofish (Gambusia affinis), and paradise fish (Macropodus opercularis). Both B. melanostictus and G. affinis were almost found in each of the sampling ponds and were abundant, and so the two species were included in the following analyses. The physical and chemical factors were measured at each of the 11 ponds on each sampling occasion. Conductivity, pH value, dissolved oxygen, and water temperature were measured using WTW multi 340i. Water depth and sediment depth were measured using a graduated stick at 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 of the longest transect. The shoreline and area of ponds were assessed with a measuring tape by pacing in field. The shoreline development index (SDI) was calculated as follows: \[ \text{SDI} = \frac{L}{2 \sqrt{\pi A}} \] where \( L \) = the length of shoreline, and \( A \) = the area of pond (Wetzel, 2001). Finally, the percentage of plant cover at each sampling pond was measured by taking the pictures. The relative area of plant cover was estimated by ImageJ 1.42 software. Data analysis For each sampling occasion, three benthic corer samples were combined together as a sample unit and mean densities, taxon richness, Gastropoda richness, and Odonata richness were calculated as community parameters. Simple correlations between community parameters and environmental factors were made by the Spearman rank correlation test. Since the data sets of environmental variables were not normal and had no constant variance, the Kruskal–Wallis H test was used to test the differences of environmental factors among different ponds (Zar, 1999). Duncan’s multiple range test was conducted at a significance level of \( P < 0.05 \). STATICO was used to assess the spatial variability of macroinvertebrate assemblages and its dynamics in time and examine the dynamic trajectories of the physicochemical factors and macroinvertebrate assemblages. Before STATICO was carried out, data were organized into a succession of coupled environmental and taxonomic tables, each pair of tables corresponding to a sampling period. Four temporal pairs of tables (four sampling dates) were used in this study. Each table was first analyzed by principal component analysis (PCA), and each pair was then linked by a co-inertial analysis (Dray et al., 2003), producing a cross table. Partial triadic analysis (PTA) (Thioulouse & Chessel, 1987) was then used to analyze the series of cross tables. PTA involves three successive steps (Thioulouse et al., 2004). (1) The interstructure analysis gives the importance of each table and summarizes the global structure and the relationship between the tables. (2) The compromise analysis gives a picture of the structures common to all the tables. (3) The trajectory analysis summarizes the variability of the series of tables around the common structure defined by the compromise. In this analysis, three benthic corer and sweep samples for each pond on each sampling date were pooled together. Those taxa, which occurred only on one sampling date and their abundance were less than 1% of total abundance on the sampling date, were excluded from the analysis. A total of 21 taxa were included in the data set. Two vertebrate taxa, B. melanostictus and G. affinis, were used as environmental factors to detect their effect on macroinvertebrate assemblages. The relationships between pond size and shoreline length and between water temperature and dissolved oxygen were highly correlated, and so shoreline length and dissolved oxygen were excluded in this analysis. In total, therefore, 13 environmental factors were used in the analysis. All environmental factors, except pH values, and the macroinvertebrate abundances were \( \log(x + 1) \) transformed to approach a normal distribution (Legendre & Legendre, 1998). The analysis was performed with the ADE-4 software (Thioulouse et al., 1997). Results Environmental factors Environmental factors showed spatial differences among sampling ponds and temporal differences among seasons (Table 1). The mean conductivity of ponds varied from 148 to 783 \( \mu \)s/cm (mean = 288 \( \pm \) 54 (S.E.) \( \mu \)s/cm, median = 243 \( \mu \)s/cm). The high conductivity at site 2 was probably due to the location of pond 2 which was near the coast. Low dissolved oxygen was found at all ponds (mean = 3.13 \( \pm \) 0.37 mg/l, median = 3.23 mg/l). This reflected the fact that these ponds were more or less affected by human activities due to their location. With the exception of pond 10 (pH = 6.84), all ponds possessed pH values above 7.0. All ponds had mean water temperature between 21.6 and 24.7\( ^\circ \)C with the lowest in winter (9.9\( ^\circ \)C at site 1–15.0\( ^\circ \)C at pond 6) and the highest in summer (27.0\( ^\circ \)C at pond 10–31.0\( ^\circ \)C at pond 4). The mean depth of ponds ranged between 15.1 and 42.8 cm (mean = 29.1 \( \pm \) 3.0 cm, median = 30 cm). The sediment depth of ponds varied from 0.8 to 6.2 cm (mean = 2.18 \( \pm \) 0.47 cm, median = 1.6 cm). Macroinvertebrate communities In total, 31 macroinvertebrate taxa were recorded at the 11 sampling ponds during the sampling year (Table 2). In terms of taxon richness, pond fauna were dominated by Gastropoda, of which 10 taxa were recorded. Odonata were represented by nine taxa. Compared with Gastropoda and Odonata, Hemiptera (3 taxa), Hirudinea (2), Ephemeroptera (2), Decopoda (1), Coleoptera (1), Diptera (1), Oligochaeta (1), and Ostracoda (1) were relatively poor. For Diptera, Oligochaeta, and Ostracoda, it is likely to be an underestimate of the species-level diversity in these sampled ponds. The total macroinvertebrate species richness of ponds ranged between 2 and 13 (mean = 7.2 \( \pm \) 1.4 S.E.; median = 6) (Table 2). The abundance of B. melanostictus varied from 0 to 95.6% of total number of animals. At ponds 1, 2, 3, 7, and 11, the dominant taxa were Chironomidae, Tubificidae at ponds 5, 6, 8, and 10, Melanoides tuberculatus tubercul at pond 4, and Neocaridina denticulate at pond 9 (Table 2). There was a trend that the higher the mean water temperature, the higher the number of individuals and taxa (Table 3). The results were associated with the fact that the higher the temperature, the higher the number of gastropod and odonate taxa. In contrast, the number of individuals and taxa were negatively correlated with the altitudes of ponds. Interstructure The interstructure factor maps of the STATICO showed that the decrease of the eigenvalues was high between the first and second eigenvalues (59.3 and 16.3% of the total inertia, respectively) (Fig. 1A). This suggested that only the first axis might be chosen for the compromise analysis. The correlation circle showed all the sampling dates displaying same sign on the first interstructure factor (axis 1), indicating a positive correlation between the corresponding set of matrices (Fig. 1A). Such a uniform distribution on the first axis indicated a strong common structure of seasonality. The structure expressed through the first axis of the interstructure, therefore, corresponded to a community spatial pattern common to the different sampling dates. The second interstructure factor was characterized by the opposition between the sampling dates of winter and spring (positive correlation with axis 2) against the sampling dates of summer and autumn (negatively correlated with the axis). Compromise The contribution of the different sampling dates to the construction of the compromise table was similar (weights from 0.485 to 0.515) (Fig. 1D). Therefore, each of the four samplings played a similar role in the construction of the compromise table. Moreover, the fit of each of the tables to the compromise table (\( \cos^2 \)) was homogeneous (from 0.70 in autumn to 0.80 in winter). The share of the total variability accounted for by each of the first two axes of the compromise was 38.4 and 27.3%, respectively (Fig. 1B). Out of the 13 environmental factors taken into account, only a few were found to be correlated with the structure of macroinvertebrate assemblages (Fig. 1B). The first axis described a positive association with the sediment depth, water temperature, and distance from the major water bodies, and a negative association with the altitude. The second axis was mainly positively associated with pond depth but negatively with the pond size. The correspondence with the macroinvertebrate taxa allowed identifying these taxa which responded to the environmental gradients (Fig. 1C). On the first axis, the most abundant taxa (Tubificidae, Planorbidae, Ischnura senegalensis, and Physa acuta) caught in the ponds with deeper sediment and higher water temperature but with lower abundance of B. melanostictus were opposed to the taxa (Neocaridina denticulata) in the ponds with higher altitude. On the second axis, the most abundant taxa (Chironomidae, Orthetrum sabina, and Notonectidae) caught in the ponds with larger pond size which was opposed to the taxa (Tubificidae, Austropeplea ollula, and Melanoides tuberculatus tubercul) in the ponds with greater depth, higher plant cover, and higher abundance of Gambusia affinis. In addition, it was found that most insect taxa (e.g., Chironomidae, Orthetrum sabina, and Notonectidae) were located at the lower left part of the figure and associated with the pond size. The most non-insect taxa were located at the upper part of the figure and associated with the pond depth, except P. acuta, P. canaliculata, and Planorbidae which were associated with sediment depth. Trajectories The trajectories factor maps indicated that the relationships between the most abundant taxa in the assemblages and environmental factors differed between sampling periods (Figs. 2, 3). The stable part of the macroinvertebrate-environment dynamics was well expressed by the autumn survey due to the closer clustering around the center of the plot. The maps also enabled us to identify seasonal variations of the position of taxa around the common structure. In winter, Tubificidae and Ostracoda were positively associated with the pond depth, sediment depth, water temperature, and distance from the major water bodies but Chironomidae, Notonectidae, Orthetrum sabina, and P. acuta were positively associated with the pond size. In spring, the major macroinvertebrate taxa were I. senegalensis, P. acuta, Tubificidae, and A. ollula, and they were negatively associated with the abundance of B. melanostictus. In summer, I. senegalensis and Chironomidae were positively associated with the pond size, and Tubificidae was positively associated with the pond depth. In autumn, the pond size was the major factor to affect the abundance of Pomacea canaliculata, O. sabina, and I. senegalensis, and the pond depth were the major factors to affect the abundance of A. ollula and Tubificidae. Discussion The composition of macroinvertebrate assemblages The importance of ponds as a habitat of aquatic macroinvertebrates has been emphasized until recently (Biggs et al., 2005; Oertli et al., 2009). Bilton et al. (2009) studied ponds in two areas of southern England and found that the means of species richness of macroinvertebrates in each pond were 19.7 and 22.0, indicating the importance of such habitat in biodiversity. While the mean taxon richness in this study is lower than that found by Bilton et al. (2009), this is perhaps not surprising, as these ponds are relatively new, artificial ponds which are impacted by human activity. The result, therefore, might reflect the fact that the ponds sampled are not likely to be representative of less impacted sites in the region. Besides, the result might also reflect the fact that figures represented considerable underestimates of the true taxon richness of these ponds. For instance, the Chironomidae in this study were only simply enumerated. Many studies (Street & Titmus, 1979; Hinden et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2006) have pointed to the high diversity of chironomids in small ponds. The studied ponds, therefore, may be important for the freshwater biodiversity in this relatively impacted landscape, but more “natural” ponds elsewhere in the region are likely to hold more species. Moreover, this study found more taxon richness than Fig. 2 Trajectories factor map of macroinvertebrate taxa using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007. See Table 2 for the taxonomic abbreviations ![Trajectories factor map of macroinvertebrate taxa using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007.](page_320_180_1408_1092.png) the study of Lin et al. (2006) which found 4.6 taxa per pond in eight alpine ponds (>3,000 m.a.s.l.) in central Taiwan, indicating that taxon richness in Taiwan ponds was related to altitude, with increasing altitude being associated with a reduction in species richness. Hinden et al. (2005) also indicated that an altitude-related decline in taxon richness in the ponds of Switzerland. Carchini et al. (2005) pointed out that ponds at high altitude in central Italy had lower odonate richness than those at low altitude. Similarly, in this study, the average number of odonate richness in each pond was 1.8 (S.E. = 0.4), rising to 2.50 (S.E. = 0.38) when the pond without odonate were excluded. This was higher than the average of 0.88 (S.E. = 0.13) taxa per pond found in the high altitude ponds in central Taiwan (Lin et al., 2006). Similarly, while 10 gastropod taxa were found in this study, none was found by Lin et al. (2006). Many studies showed that Chironomidae and Coleoptrea typically made up the majority of the macroinvertebrate species richness in ponds worldwide (Della Bella et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2006, 2009). In our study, we also found that ponds were predominated by chironomids at ponds 1, 2, 3, and 7. However, only one taxon of aquatic beetles was found in any of our ponds under this study. It was probably due to the fact that these ponds were located at urban area and were relatively impacted sites. Therefore, they have much smaller regional species pools. Rundle et al. (2002) indicated that aquatic beetles are amongst vagile aquatic insect taxa. They would not access the ponds if these ponds are less suitable for their colonization. The result of this study might reflect the fact that these ponds, being in an urban area, were relatively impacted, should affect aquatic beetles more than other taxa. In this study, the most abundant taxa were chironomids and tubificids. The result was in accordant with the suggestion of Batzer et al. (2004) that most successful macroinvertebrates in ponds may be habitat generalists. They further suggested that the variation of these taxa among ponds might be largely stochastic. In this Fig. 3 Trajectories factor map of environmental variables using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007. See Table 1 for the environmental abbreviations ![Trajectories factor map of environmental variables using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007.](page_370_180_1407_1207.png) study, however, we found that the distributions of the chironomids and tubificids were mostly associated with the pond size and pond depth, respectively. Macroinvertebrate assemblages and environmental factors The results of STATICO suggested that the main common features of the organization patterns were first, the sediment depth and altitude, and second, the pond size and pond depth (Fig. 1B). Water chemistry, such as pH and conductivity values, seemed not to be important environmental factors to affect macroinvertebrate assemblages in this study. In contrast, Friday (1987) suggested that water chemistry was an important factor to shape macroinvertebrate assemblages. In addition, we found that the total macroinvertebrate taxa were not correlated with the pond age (Fig. 1B; Table 3). This finding concurred with the results of Jeffries (1991) and Gee et al. (1997) but contrasted with the result of Barnes (1983). Gee et al. (1997) indicated that invertebrate richness might be related to the age of the ponds whereas ponds were isolated from other wetlands. This was not the case in this study, because all the ponds in this study were not far away from the major water bodies (Table 1). Also, these ponds are relatively of recent origin. The strength of an age signal will depend on the relative importance of other drivers structuring the communities. Many studies (Oertli et al., 2002; Della Bella et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2009) found that the pond size and depth showed strong relationships with species’ occurrence across ponds. STATICO also identified pond size and depth as major environmental factors to influence macroinvertebrate assemblages in this study. The influence of pond size and depth on macroinvertebrate assemblages was generally a consequence of greater habitat heterogeneity (Della Bella et al., 2005), lower extinction risk due to larger population sizes (Gee et al., 1997), and buffering against fluctuations in physicochemical conditions in larger ponds (Connor & McCoy, 1979). In our study, however, we found that insect taxa, active dispersers, were highly associated with pond size and most non-insect taxa, passive dispersers, were associated with pond depth and/or sediment depth (Fig. 1B, C). Rundle et al. (2002) indicated that invertebrate taxa with different dispersal mechanisms show different distribution patterns across habitat gradients of size. Active dispersers show significant positive relationships with pond size and lead to non-random patterns in species distribution between ponds. The response of the passive taxa to depth might relate to relative permanence—deeper (and hence more permanent) ponds favoring desiccation-prone taxa such as molluscs. The effects of dispersal mechanisms on distribution patterns might reflect the lack of depth and area effects on taxon richness (Table 3). Similarly, Jeffries (1991) was unable to find a significant area effect on the richness of macroinvertebrates and suggested that other factors, such as biotic interactions, might be important. The biotic interactions, such as the presence or absence of fish or amphibian predators in a pond, appeared to be important in determining the abundance of macroinvertebrates (Zimmer et al., 2001). In this study, we found that ponds without amphibian predators contained more macroinvertebrate taxa than those with amphibian predators when pond 1 was excluded in the analysis. For instance, ponds 5, 10, and 11 which possessed relatively high abundance of B. melanostictus had only 2–4 macroinvertebrate taxa (Table 2). However, there was no evidence to show that fishless ponds (pond 5) contain more invertebrate taxa than those with fish. There might be other factors that explain the low taxon richness at pond 1. Similarly, the ponds described by Gee et al. (1997) as fish ponds were the most taxonomically rich amongst of those they sampled. On the other hand, abundance and species richness of odonate predators, such as I. senegalensis, O. sabina sabina, and P. flavescens, were little associated with the presence of B. melanostictus (Fig. 2B, C). This result was expected for amphibian because the predation of amphibian on odonate was low (Corbet, 1999). Seasonal variability of macroinvertebrate assemblages As we know, most studies on the seasonal changes in macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds focused on the effects of hydroperiod of temporary ponds on macroinvertebrate assemblages (e.g., Brooks, 2000, Batzer et al., 2004). There were very few studies on the seasonal changes in macroinvertebrate assemblages in permanent ponds. From the results of STATICO, the spatial patterns of macroinvertebrate assemblages at the 11 ponds were highly persistent during the course of the four seasons. Only a very limited number of taxa exhibited a strong variation of their abundance over seasons. The variations mainly reflected the shift in water temperatures which were negatively associated with altitude. Most taxa were positively correlated with water temperature (Fig. 1C). Both abundance and taxon richness of gastropod and odonate was positively related to water temperature (Table 3). Smith et al. (2003) also found similar results for gastropods. The seasonal variation was probably due to life-history patterns related to reproduction, dispersal, predation, temperature, and food (Tangen et al., 2003). The environmental factors which influenced the macroinvertebrate assemblages most in these ponds also changed with seasons. For example, pond size, though positively correlated with the sediment depth gradient in spring, became less correlated during the winter and summer. The abundance of B. melanostictus was inversely correlated with sediment depth and pond depth during the spring, and became the most important environmental factor during the spring, but was not correlated with them at the other seasons. In conclusion, macroinvertebrate assemblages varied spatially and temporally in response to the abiotic and biotic factors of these artificial subtropical ponds. Pond size, pond depth, sediment depth, altitude, and distance from the major water bodies were the major abiotic factors to determine the macroinvertebrate assemblages in these ponds, and the abundances of B. melanostictus were the major biotic factors. However, these factors changed with seasonality. According to the spatial distribution of macroinvertebrate assemblages in these ponds, macroinvertebrates could be classified into two groups based on their dispersal mechanisms. The active dispersers, such as insect taxa, were mostly associated with pond size, and the passive dispersers, such as non-insect taxa, with pond depth and sediment depth. The effect of pond size on macroinvertebrate assemblages might be through the dispersal mechanisms of macroinvertebrates. This effect needs to be further studied in the future. Factors influencing macroinvertebrate assemblages in artificial subtropical ponds of Taiwan Sen-Her Shieh · Yao-Sheng Chi Received: 21 August 2009/Revised: 14 April 2010/Accepted: 17 April 2010/Published online: 2 May 2010 © Springer Science+Business Media B.V. 2010 Abstract Macroinvertebrate assemblages and its association with environmental factors at the 11 artificial subtropical ponds of Taiwan were examined using the multivariate analysis software STATICO. The aims of the study were to determine whether spatial and seasonal variation of macroinvertebrate assemblages changed seasonally, to examine which environmental factors determined the spatial and temporal structure of maroinvertebrate assemblages, and to compare between-pond variations in the taxon composition of macroinvertebrates. Macroinvertebrates were collected seasonally by a corer and a sweep net in 2007, and 13 physical and chemical factors were measured at the same time. A total of 31 macroinvertebrate taxa were collected during the sampling period, and the most dominant taxa were Chironomidae (31.7% of total animal abundance) and Tubificidae (22.4%). STATICO identified pond size, pond depth, sediment depth, and altitude as the major abiotic factors and Bufo melanostictus (Amphibia) as the major biotic factor to influence macroinvertebrate assemblages at these ponds. These factors changed with seasonality. For example, the abundance of B. melanostictus was the most important factor during the spring but became much less important in other seasons. According to the spatial distribution patterns of macroinvertebrate assemblages, macroinvertebrates could be split into two groups based on their dispersal. The active dispersers, such as insect taxa, were strongly associated with pond size and the passive dispersers, such as non-insect taxa, were strongly associated with the pond depth and/or sediment depth. The results of this study suggested that pond size might influence macroinvertebrate assemblages through their dispersal mechanisms and that the environmental factors which influenced the macroinvertebrate assemblages most changed with seasons in this study area. Keywords Pond size · Active dispersers · Passive dispersers · STATICO Introduction Ponds are rich and diverse habitats and play a key role in safeguarding aquatic biodiversity. They are defined as waterbodies between 1 m^2 and 2 ha in area which may be permanent or seasonal, including both artificial and natural waterbodies (Biggs et al., 2005). Despite their small surface area, they are exceptionally rich in biodiversity, as compared to streams and large lakes, and contribute significantly to regional freshwater biodiversity in many northern temperate regions (Oertli et al., 2002; Williams et al., 2003; Nicolet et al., 2004), but our understanding of the relative biodiversity importance of ponds elsewhere remains limited. However, the ponds are threatened due to anthropogenic activities, such as eutrophication, chemical pollution, acid rain, physical destruction, and invasion of exotic species (Heath & Whitehead, 1992; Brönmark & Hansson, 2002; Boothby, 2003). While monitoring programs for freshwaters have been widely carried out in many countries, particularly for streams and lakes, these programs have largely failed to include ponds (Oertli et al., 2005). The macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds are influenced by both abiotic and biotic factors. Abiotic factors, such as pond size (Rundle et al., 2002) and water chemistry (Friday, 1987), affect the number of taxa in the community. It has been suggested that large ponds support more macroinvertebrate taxa than small ones due to habitat heterogeneity (Della Bella et al., 2005). Biotic factors, such as the presence or absence of large predators (fish and amphibians) in a pond and the dispersal ability of macroinvertebrates, appear to be important in determining macroinvertebrate assemblages. Invertebrate biomass was found to be higher in fishless wetlands than in wetlands with fish (Zimmer et al., 2001). Rundle et al. (2002) indicated that the taxon richness of active dispersal macroinvertebrates was positively correlate with pond size, whereas the taxon richness of passive macroinvertebrates did not correlated with environmental variables. Assessing these influences on macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds are a key process to understand community structure and succession and to propose a man-made control before any pollution resulting from anthropogenic activities could occur. The relationships between environmental factors and macroinvertebrate distributions in freshwaters have often been studied using principal component analysis (Hinden et al., 2005), canonical correspondence analysis (Williams et al., 2003; Nicolet et al., 2004; Carchini et al., 2005), multidimensional scaling (Della Bella et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2006, 2009), or clustering (Collinson et al., 1995; Nicolet et al., 2004; Bilton et al., 2006). The main drawback of these methods is that they do not consider that both environmental factors and macroinvertebrate assemblages vary temporally and that the former affects the latter. In order to overcome this problem, the STATICO (STATIS and CO-inertia) has been developed (Thioulouse et al., 2004). It is a multivariate method allowing simultaneous analysis of a sequence of paired ecological tables recorded through a series of sampling occasions. Thioulouse et al. (2004) pointed that STATICO is particularly suited to study the relationship between the environmental and taxonomic tables when both vary time. Since ponds are not uniform as revealed by their shape, shoreline, and size, and a clear seasonal dynamics has been observed for the difference macroinvertebrate assemblages (Studinski & Grubbs, 2007), STATICO is a well-suited statistical tool to get a clear representation of the spatial and temporal variation of the macroinvertebrates assemblages in ponds. Most studies which examined macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds were conducted in Europe (Oertli et al., 2009). There are still relatively few such studies in Asia, especially artificial ponds, where the biodiversity has been poorly investigated. Because of the complexity of pond systems affected spatially and temporally by various abiotic and biotic factors, we analyzed using STATICO the relationships between these factors and maroinvertebrate assemblages in the 11 artificial subtropical ponds of Taiwan. The first aim of the study was to determine whether spatial and seasonal variation of macroinvertebrate assemblages changed among these subtropical ponds where seasonality was insignificant. The second aim was to examine which abiotic and biotic factors determined the spatial and temporal structure of these macroinvertebrate assemblages at these ponds. We assumed that the pond size and the presence and absence of large predators in ponds should be the most important factors to affect macroinvertebrate assemblages in these ponds. Therefore, it was predicted that ponds which were large and/or without large predators should support more taxon richness than ponds which were small and/or with large predators. The final aim was to compare between-pond variations in the taxon composition of active and passive dispersers of macroinvertebrates. We assumed that the active dispersal macroinvertebrate should be more associated with pond size. Materials and methods Study area Sampling sites were established in the coastal area of west central Taiwan. The area represents one of the biotopes most severely threatened by human impacts since the main land use of the area is municipal and agricultural. The area is flat, has low altitude (<300 m.a.s.l.), and has the annual precipitation of about 1,405 mm between 1998 and 2007, with the perhumid season from April to September and the relative drought season from October to December. Annual mean air temperature is about 23.2°C. The dominant vegetation of the area is Panicum maximum (Poaceae) and Acacia confuse (Fabaceae). Because our aims were to assess the relationships between environmental factors and macroinvertebrate assemblages among different ponds, 11 artificial ponds were selected in this area to insure that they were influenced by the same climate condition and land use. These ponds are situated in school grounds and located between the coordinates 24°6′N, 120°31′E and 24°24′N, 120°38′E. Sampling methods Macroinvertebrates samples were collected in January (winter), April (spring), July (summer), and October (autumn) 2007. Because different habitats and groups of macroinvertebrates require different sampling methods, the use of a single method for all habitats could yield misleading conclusion on macroinvertebrate richness. Therefore, two methods, e.g., the quantitative and qualitative methods (Studinski & Grubbs, 2007) were used in this study. A benthic corer sampler (diameter = 26 cm) was used as a quantitative method. During each sampling occasion, the longest transect of the pond was selected, and three benthic samples were taken at 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 of this transect. The benthic corer was pushed into the substrate until it reached an impermeable layer. The sediments within the corer were transferred by a hand with a cup to a bucket. Animals, organic matter, and remaining water in bucket were passed through a sieve with 0.8-mm apertures. These materials were preserved in 95% ethanol in the field. This procedure allowed us to sample benthic macroinvertebrates. For the qualitative method, ponds were sampled with a sweep net (with 20-cm D-frame and 200-μm mesh) at different microhabitats (such as emergent and submerged aquatic vegetation and pond margins) for 5 min (Batzer et al., 2004). This method allowed us to collect nekton macroinvertebrates and to get a representative sample from the system (Collinson et al., 1995). Sample sizes and sampling time were decided after a pilot study undertaken in these ponds. The main outcomes of this pilot study were that three corer samples and a total time of 5 min were good enough to have the representative taxa for these ponds. In the laboratory, all the samples were rinsed by tap water, and the animals were sorted and preserved in 75% ethanol for further analysis. The macroinvertebrate taxa were identified to the lowest taxonomic unit possible. Aquatic insects were identified according to Morse et al. (1994) and other macroinvertebrate taxa according to Dudgeon (1999) and Shy & Yu (1998). Members of Ostracoda were not identified further. Three vertebrate taxa were collected in this study, and they were common Asian toad (Bufo melanostictus), mosquitofish (Gambusia affinis), and paradise fish (Macropodus opercularis). Both B. melanostictus and G. affinis were almost found in each of the sampling ponds and were abundant, and so the two species were included in the following analyses. The physical and chemical factors were measured at each of the 11 ponds on each sampling occasion. Conductivity, pH value, dissolved oxygen, and water temperature were measured using WTW multi 340i. Water depth and sediment depth were measured using a graduated stick at 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 of the longest transect. The shoreline and area of ponds were assessed with a measuring tape by pacing in field. The shoreline development index (SDI) was calculated as follows: \[ \text{SDI} = \frac{L}{2 \sqrt{\pi A}} \] where \( L \) = the length of shoreline, and \( A \) = the area of pond (Wetzel, 2001). Finally, the percentage of plant cover at each sampling pond was measured by taking the pictures. The relative area of plant cover was estimated by ImageJ 1.42 software. Data analysis For each sampling occasion, three benthic corer samples were combined together as a sample unit and mean densities, taxon richness, Gastropoda richness, and Odonata richness were calculated as community parameters. Simple correlations between community parameters and environmental factors were made by the Spearman rank correlation test. Since the data sets of environmental variables were not normal and had no constant variance, the Kruskal–Wallis H test was used to test the differences of environmental factors among different ponds (Zar, 1999). Duncan’s multiple range test was conducted at a significance level of \( P < 0.05 \). STATICO was used to assess the spatial variability of macroinvertebrate assemblages and its dynamics in time and examine the dynamic trajectories of the physicochemical factors and macroinvertebrate assemblages. Before STATICO was carried out, data were organized into a succession of coupled environmental and taxonomic tables, each pair of tables corresponding to a sampling period. Four temporal pairs of tables (four sampling dates) were used in this study. Each table was first analyzed by principal component analysis (PCA), and each pair was then linked by a co-inertial analysis (Dray et al., 2003), producing a cross table. Partial triadic analysis (PTA) (Thioulouse & Chessel, 1987) was then used to analyze the series of cross tables. PTA involves three successive steps (Thioulouse et al., 2004). (1) The interstructure analysis gives the importance of each table and summarizes the global structure and the relationship between the tables. (2) The compromise analysis gives a picture of the structures common to all the tables. (3) The trajectory analysis summarizes the variability of the series of tables around the common structure defined by the compromise. In this analysis, three benthic corer and sweep samples for each pond on each sampling date were pooled together. Those taxa, which occurred only on one sampling date and their abundance were less than 1% of total abundance on the sampling date, were excluded from the analysis. A total of 21 taxa were included in the data set. Two vertebrate taxa, B. melanostictus and G. affinis, were used as environmental factors to detect their effect on macroinvertebrate assemblages. The relationships between pond size and shoreline length and between water temperature and dissolved oxygen were highly correlated, and so shoreline length and dissolved oxygen were excluded in this analysis. In total, therefore, 13 environmental factors were used in the analysis. All environmental factors, except pH values, and the macroinvertebrate abundances were \( \log(x + 1) \) transformed to approach a normal distribution (Legendre & Legendre, 1998). The analysis was performed with the ADE-4 software (Thioulouse et al., 1997). Results Environmental factors Environmental factors showed spatial differences among sampling ponds and temporal differences among seasons (Table 1). The mean conductivity of ponds varied from 148 to 783 \( \mu \)s/cm (mean = 288 \( \pm \) 54 (S.E.) \( \mu \)s/cm, median = 243 \( \mu \)s/cm). The high conductivity at site 2 was probably due to the location of pond 2 which was near the coast. Low dissolved oxygen was found at all ponds (mean = 3.13 \( \pm \) 0.37 mg/l, median = 3.23 mg/l). This reflected the fact that these ponds were more or less affected by human activities due to their location. With the exception of pond 10 (pH = 6.84), all ponds possessed pH values above 7.0. All ponds had mean water temperature between 21.6 and 24.7\( ^\circ \)C with the lowest in winter (9.9\( ^\circ \)C at site 1–15.0\( ^\circ \)C at pond 6) and the highest in summer (27.0\( ^\circ \)C at pond 10–31.0\( ^\circ \)C at pond 4). The mean depth of ponds ranged between 15.1 and 42.8 cm (mean = 29.1 \( \pm \) 3.0 cm, median = 30 cm). The sediment depth of ponds varied from 0.8 to 6.2 cm (mean = 2.18 \( \pm \) 0.47 cm, median = 1.6 cm). Macroinvertebrate communities In total, 31 macroinvertebrate taxa were recorded at the 11 sampling ponds during the sampling year (Table 2). In terms of taxon richness, pond fauna were dominated by Gastropoda, of which 10 taxa were recorded. Odonata were represented by nine taxa. Compared with Gastropoda and Odonata, Hemiptera (3 taxa), Hirudinea (2), Ephemeroptera (2), Decopoda (1), Coleoptera (1), Diptera (1), Oligochaeta (1), and Ostracoda (1) were relatively poor. For Diptera, Oligochaeta, and Ostracoda, it is likely to be an underestimate of the species-level diversity in these sampled ponds. The total macroinvertebrate species richness of ponds ranged between 2 and 13 (mean = 7.2 \( \pm \) 1.4 S.E.; median = 6) (Table 2). The abundance of B. melanostictus varied from 0 to 95.6% of total number of animals. At ponds 1, 2, 3, 7, and 11, the dominant taxa were Chironomidae, Tubificidae at ponds 5, 6, 8, and 10, Melanoides tuberculatus tubercul at pond 4, and Neocaridina denticulate at pond 9 (Table 2). There was a trend that the higher the mean water temperature, the higher the number of individuals and taxa (Table 3). The results were associated with the fact that the higher the temperature, the higher the number of gastropod and odonate taxa. In contrast, the number of individuals and taxa were negatively correlated with the altitudes of ponds. Interstructure The interstructure factor maps of the STATICO showed that the decrease of the eigenvalues was high between the first and second eigenvalues (59.3 and 16.3% of the total inertia, respectively) (Fig. 1A). This suggested that only the first axis might be chosen for the compromise analysis. The correlation circle showed all the sampling dates displaying same sign on the first interstructure factor (axis 1), indicating a positive correlation between the corresponding set of matrices (Fig. 1A). Such a uniform distribution on the first axis indicated a strong common structure of seasonality. The structure expressed through the first axis of the interstructure, therefore, corresponded to a community spatial pattern common to the different sampling dates. The second interstructure factor was characterized by the opposition between the sampling dates of winter and spring (positive correlation with axis 2) against the sampling dates of summer and autumn (negatively correlated with the axis). Compromise The contribution of the different sampling dates to the construction of the compromise table was similar (weights from 0.485 to 0.515) (Fig. 1D). Therefore, each of the four samplings played a similar role in the construction of the compromise table. Moreover, the fit of each of the tables to the compromise table (\( \cos^2 \)) was homogeneous (from 0.70 in autumn to 0.80 in winter).
