Out of the 13 environmental factors taken into account, only a few were found to be correlated with the structure of macroinvertebrate assemblages (Fig. 1B). The first axis described a positive association with the sediment depth, water temperature, and distance from the major water bodies, and a negative association with the altitude. The second axis was mainly positively associated with pond depth but negatively with the pond size. The correspondence with the macroinvertebrate taxa allowed identifying these taxa which responded to the environmental gradients (Fig. 1C). On the first axis, the most abundant taxa (Tubificidae, Planorbidae, Ischnura senegalensis, and Physa acuta) caught in the ponds with deeper sediment and higher water temperature but with lower abundance of B. melanostictus were opposed to the taxa (Neocaridina denticulata) in the ponds with higher altitude. On the second axis, the most abundant taxa (Chironomidae, Orthetrum sabina, and Notonectidae) caught in the ponds with larger pond size which was opposed to the taxa (Tubificidae, Austropeplea ollula, and Melanoides tuberculatus tubercul) in the ponds with greater depth, higher plant cover, and higher abundance of Gambusia affinis. In addition, it was found that most insect taxa (e.g., Chironomidae, Orthetrum sabina, and Notonectidae) were located at the lower left part of the figure and associated with the pond size. The most non-insect taxa were located at the upper part of the figure and associated with the pond depth, except P. acuta, P. canaliculata, and Planorbidae which were associated with sediment depth. Trajectories The trajectories factor maps indicated that the relationships between the most abundant taxa in the assemblages and environmental factors differed between sampling periods (Figs. 2, 3). The stable part of the macroinvertebrate-environment dynamics was well expressed by the autumn survey due to the closer clustering around the center of the plot. The maps also enabled us to identify seasonal variations of the position of taxa around the common structure. In winter, Tubificidae and Ostracoda were positively associated with the pond depth, sediment depth, water temperature, and distance from the major water bodies but Chironomidae, Notonectidae, Orthetrum sabina, and P. acuta were positively associated with the pond size. In spring, the major macroinvertebrate taxa were I. senegalensis, P. acuta, Tubificidae, and A. ollula, and they were negatively associated with the abundance of B. melanostictus. In summer, I. senegalensis and Chironomidae were positively associated with the pond size, and Tubificidae was positively associated with the pond depth. In autumn, the pond size was the major factor to affect the abundance of Pomacea canaliculata, O. sabina, and I. senegalensis, and the pond depth were the major factors to affect the abundance of A. ollula and Tubificidae. Discussion The composition of macroinvertebrate assemblages The importance of ponds as a habitat of aquatic macroinvertebrates has been emphasized until recently (Biggs et al., 2005; Oertli et al., 2009). Bilton et al. (2009) studied ponds in two areas of southern England and found that the means of species richness of macroinvertebrates in each pond were 19.7 and 22.0, indicating the importance of such habitat in biodiversity. While the mean taxon richness in this study is lower than that found by Bilton et al. (2009), this is perhaps not surprising, as these ponds are relatively new, artificial ponds which are impacted by human activity. The result, therefore, might reflect the fact that the ponds sampled are not likely to be representative of less impacted sites in the region. Besides, the result might also reflect the fact that figures represented considerable underestimates of the true taxon richness of these ponds. For instance, the Chironomidae in this study were only simply enumerated. Many studies (Street & Titmus, 1979; Hinden et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2006) have pointed to the high diversity of chironomids in small ponds. The studied ponds, therefore, may be important for the freshwater biodiversity in this relatively impacted landscape, but more “natural” ponds elsewhere in the region are likely to hold more species. Moreover, this study found more taxon richness than Fig. 2 Trajectories factor map of macroinvertebrate taxa using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007. See Table 2 for the taxonomic abbreviations ![Trajectories factor map of macroinvertebrate taxa using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007.](page_320_180_1408_1092.png) the study of Lin et al. (2006) which found 4.6 taxa per pond in eight alpine ponds (>3,000 m.a.s.l.) in central Taiwan, indicating that taxon richness in Taiwan ponds was related to altitude, with increasing altitude being associated with a reduction in species richness. Hinden et al. (2005) also indicated that an altitude-related decline in taxon richness in the ponds of Switzerland. Carchini et al. (2005) pointed out that ponds at high altitude in central Italy had lower odonate richness than those at low altitude. Similarly, in this study, the average number of odonate richness in each pond was 1.8 (S.E. = 0.4), rising to 2.50 (S.E. = 0.38) when the pond without odonate were excluded. This was higher than the average of 0.88 (S.E. = 0.13) taxa per pond found in the high altitude ponds in central Taiwan (Lin et al., 2006). Similarly, while 10 gastropod taxa were found in this study, none was found by Lin et al. (2006). Many studies showed that Chironomidae and Coleoptrea typically made up the majority of the macroinvertebrate species richness in ponds worldwide (Della Bella et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2006, 2009). In our study, we also found that ponds were predominated by chironomids at ponds 1, 2, 3, and 7. However, only one taxon of aquatic beetles was found in any of our ponds under this study. It was probably due to the fact that these ponds were located at urban area and were relatively impacted sites. Therefore, they have much smaller regional species pools. Rundle et al. (2002) indicated that aquatic beetles are amongst vagile aquatic insect taxa. They would not access the ponds if these ponds are less suitable for their colonization. The result of this study might reflect the fact that these ponds, being in an urban area, were relatively impacted, should affect aquatic beetles more than other taxa. In this study, the most abundant taxa were chironomids and tubificids. The result was in accordant with the suggestion of Batzer et al. (2004) that most successful macroinvertebrates in ponds may be habitat generalists. They further suggested that the variation of these taxa among ponds might be largely stochastic. In this Fig. 3 Trajectories factor map of environmental variables using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007. See Table 1 for the environmental abbreviations ![Trajectories factor map of environmental variables using STATICO analysis on the 11 pond data in the coastal area of west central Taiwan from January to October 2007.](page_370_180_1407_1207.png) study, however, we found that the distributions of the chironomids and tubificids were mostly associated with the pond size and pond depth, respectively. Macroinvertebrate assemblages and environmental factors The results of STATICO suggested that the main common features of the organization patterns were first, the sediment depth and altitude, and second, the pond size and pond depth (Fig. 1B). Water chemistry, such as pH and conductivity values, seemed not to be important environmental factors to affect macroinvertebrate assemblages in this study. In contrast, Friday (1987) suggested that water chemistry was an important factor to shape macroinvertebrate assemblages. In addition, we found that the total macroinvertebrate taxa were not correlated with the pond age (Fig. 1B; Table 3). This finding concurred with the results of Jeffries (1991) and Gee et al. (1997) but contrasted with the result of Barnes (1983). Gee et al. (1997) indicated that invertebrate richness might be related to the age of the ponds whereas ponds were isolated from other wetlands. This was not the case in this study, because all the ponds in this study were not far away from the major water bodies (Table 1). Also, these ponds are relatively of recent origin. The strength of an age signal will depend on the relative importance of other drivers structuring the communities. Many studies (Oertli et al., 2002; Della Bella et al., 2005; Bilton et al., 2009) found that the pond size and depth showed strong relationships with species’ occurrence across ponds. STATICO also identified pond size and depth as major environmental factors to influence macroinvertebrate assemblages in this study. The influence of pond size and depth on macroinvertebrate assemblages was generally a consequence of greater habitat heterogeneity (Della Bella et al., 2005), lower extinction risk due to larger population sizes (Gee et al., 1997), and buffering against fluctuations in physicochemical conditions in larger ponds (Connor & McCoy, 1979). In our study, however, we found that insect taxa, active dispersers, were highly associated with pond size and most non-insect taxa, passive dispersers, were associated with pond depth and/or sediment depth (Fig. 1B, C). Rundle et al. (2002) indicated that invertebrate taxa with different dispersal mechanisms show different distribution patterns across habitat gradients of size. Active dispersers show significant positive relationships with pond size and lead to non-random patterns in species distribution between ponds. The response of the passive taxa to depth might relate to relative permanence—deeper (and hence more permanent) ponds favoring desiccation-prone taxa such as molluscs. The effects of dispersal mechanisms on distribution patterns might reflect the lack of depth and area effects on taxon richness (Table 3). Similarly, Jeffries (1991) was unable to find a significant area effect on the richness of macroinvertebrates and suggested that other factors, such as biotic interactions, might be important. The biotic interactions, such as the presence or absence of fish or amphibian predators in a pond, appeared to be important in determining the abundance of macroinvertebrates (Zimmer et al., 2001). In this study, we found that ponds without amphibian predators contained more macroinvertebrate taxa than those with amphibian predators when pond 1 was excluded in the analysis. For instance, ponds 5, 10, and 11 which possessed relatively high abundance of B. melanostictus had only 2–4 macroinvertebrate taxa (Table 2). However, there was no evidence to show that fishless ponds (pond 5) contain more invertebrate taxa than those with fish. There might be other factors that explain the low taxon richness at pond 1. Similarly, the ponds described by Gee et al. (1997) as fish ponds were the most taxonomically rich amongst of those they sampled. On the other hand, abundance and species richness of odonate predators, such as I. senegalensis, O. sabina sabina, and P. flavescens, were little associated with the presence of B. melanostictus (Fig. 2B, C). This result was expected for amphibian because the predation of amphibian on odonate was low (Corbet, 1999). Seasonal variability of macroinvertebrate assemblages As we know, most studies on the seasonal changes in macroinvertebrate assemblages in ponds focused on the effects of hydroperiod of temporary ponds on macroinvertebrate assemblages (e.g., Brooks, 2000, Batzer et al., 2004). There were very few studies on the seasonal changes in macroinvertebrate assemblages in permanent ponds. From the results of STATICO, the spatial patterns of macroinvertebrate assemblages at the 11 ponds were highly persistent during the course of the four seasons. Only a very limited number of taxa exhibited a strong variation of their abundance over seasons. The variations mainly reflected the shift in water temperatures which were negatively associated with altitude. Most taxa were positively correlated with water temperature (Fig. 1C). Both abundance and taxon richness of gastropod and odonate was positively related to water temperature (Table 3). Smith et al. (2003) also found similar results for gastropods. The seasonal variation was probably due to life-history patterns related to reproduction, dispersal, predation, temperature, and food (Tangen et al., 2003). The environmental factors which influenced the macroinvertebrate assemblages most in these ponds also changed with seasons. For example, pond size, though positively correlated with the sediment depth gradient in spring, became less correlated during the winter and summer. The abundance of B. melanostictus was inversely correlated with sediment depth and pond depth during the spring, and became the most important environmental factor during the spring, but was not correlated with them at the other seasons. In conclusion, macroinvertebrate assemblages varied spatially and temporally in response to the abiotic and biotic factors of these artificial subtropical ponds. Pond size, pond depth, sediment depth, altitude, and distance from the major water bodies were the major abiotic factors to determine the macroinvertebrate assemblages in these ponds, and the abundances of B. melanostictus were the major biotic factors. However, these factors changed with seasonality. According to the spatial distribution of macroinvertebrate assemblages in these ponds, macroinvertebrates could be classified into two groups based on their dispersal mechanisms. The active dispersers, such as insect taxa, were mostly associated with pond size, and the passive dispersers, such as non-insect taxa, with pond depth and sediment depth. The effect of pond size on macroinvertebrate assemblages might be through the dispersal mechanisms of macroinvertebrates. This effect needs to be further studied in the future. Széles University of Kaposvár 34 PUBLICATIONS 181 CITATIONS SEE PROFILE Fish preference of the Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra) on an abandoned fish pond and the role of fish sampling methods Éva A. Bauer-Haáz¹, Árpád Ferincz², Zoltán Szegvári³, Gabriella L. Széles¹ and József Lanszki¹, * With 1 figure and 2 tables Abstract: The role of small (< 10 ha) ponds in biodiversity conservation has been recently highlighted. As a top predator, the Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra) may have a powerful effect on the biodiversity and ecological functionality of small ponds, regardless of their purpose (e.g. aquaculture, angling or conservation). Our study sought to analyze the feeding habits of otter in a near-natural system (Csombárdi pond, SW Hungary). From December 2010 to November 2011, the annual composition of otter diet was assessed by the analysis of spraint samples (n = 483). Fish abundance was assessed from spring to autumn by electrofishing and fyke nets. Throughout the study period, the main food source of the otter was fish (73.5–84.9 % of occurrences), while amphibians represented a secondary resource. Otters behaved as opportunistic hunters, preying primarily on the most abundant fish species and size classes and conforming to seasonal variation in fish availability. Otter preferences in relation to fish habitat zones (shorezone or littoral, metaphyton, pelagic, benthic) and origin (native, non-native) differed according to the sampling method used to assess fish availability, suggesting that the sampling method chosen may distort the assessment of prey preference by otters. Two-thirds of fish eaten consisted of non-native species. Results may be useful for the conservation of otters, near-natural ponds, and associated native fish communities. Key words: Lutra lutra, diet, feeding habits, electrofishing, fyke net, fish selection, non-native fish, opportunism, conservation, Hungary. Introduction Since the beginning of the 21st century, both the number and total area (from 22,463 ha in 2001 to 24,364 ha in 2011; Pintér 2002, Jámborné & Bardócz 2012) of ponds under management for nature conservation have increased in Hungary. Ponds managed for conservation are buffer or shelter areas (i.e., year-round undisturbed habitats), where only the regulation of fish populations is applied. These near-natural habitats are suitable for investigating the ecological function and behaviour of piscivorous species (Erlinge 1967) in relation to fish farming. Surveys of fish assemblages in ponds and lakes are conducted using gillnets according to CEN standards (CEN 2003, CEN 2005). In small ponds (1–10 ha), the use of gillnets can be restricted due to dense macrophyte vegetation. In such cases, the most commonly used survey method is electrofishing (Diekmann et al. 2005, Erős et al. 2009). Alternatively, fyke netting can provide valuable additional data, particularly on benthic species (Lapointe et al. 2006, Ruetz et al. 2007). In Hungary, the Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra) is strictly protected as a Natura 2000 species (Heltai et al. 2012). After a dramatic decline occurred in the 1960s–1970s (Mason & Macdonald 1986), otter populations have begun to recover in the last two decades (Conroy & Chanin 2002, EEA 2009), sometimes leading to conflict with fish farmers and anglers (Kranz 2000, Britton et al. 2005, Marques et al. 2007). Although the feeding habits of the otter have been widely investigated both in natural freshwater habitats (e.g., Jedrzejewska et al 2001, Clavero et al. 2003) and in highly productive fish farms (e.g., Lanszki et al. 2001, Kloskowski 2005, Marques et al. 2007, Baltrunaite 2009), little is known about prey selection by otters in semi-natural ponds managed for nature conservation (but see Almeida et al. 2012). We studied otter diet in a near-natural pond to determine: 1) otter feeding preferences in relation to fish species, size class, habitat zone and origin (i.e., native or non-native) and 2) the influence of fish sampling methods on preference assessment. Material and methods Study area The study was carried out in SW Hungary on an abandoned artificial fish pond (Csombárdi pond, 7 ha; 46° 26′ N, 17° 39′ E, 147 m a.s.l.). The climate was continental with submediterranean influence. Annual rainfall was about 700 mm, of which more than 400 mm fell in the vegetation period (Dövényi 2010). The pond was included in a 54-ha nature conservation area, covered by meadows (Thymo serpylli-Festucetum pseudovinae; 50 %), water bodies and associated wetlands (Succiso-Molinietum hungaricae, Phragmition australis, Magnocaricion elatae; 20 %), marshes (Cirsio cani-Festucetum pratensis, Carici vulpinae-Alopecuretum pratensis), spontaneously reforested meadows, and degraded areas (ca. 10 % each). Two-thirds of the marsh-like pond surface was covered by vegetation (reed-mace Typha latifolia and, secondarily, reed Phragmites australis); the submerged vegetation (Potametea) was also dense. Water depth ranged between 1 m (in winter) and 1.5 m (in June). Since 2008, fish management has been limited to conservation measures. During the study period, the fish population of the pond originated from natural recruitment. The stable presence of otters (burrows, cub-rearing) was recorded on the site. Sampling and analysis Diet composition of the otter was determined by spraint (faecal) analysis (n = 483 samples), collected monthly from December 2010 to November 2011 along the banks and dike of the pond on a 600-m long standard route. Samples were soaked in water, then washed through a 0.5-mm sieve and dried at room temperature. All recognisable prey remains were separated and examined under a microscope. Fish species were identified on the basis of morphological differences of scales and bones, e.g., pharyngeal teeth, vertebrae, operculae, praecoperculae and maxillaries, using atlases and reference collections (e.g., Lanszki et al. 2001, Lanszki et al. 2007). Bones’ size combined with scale characters were used to assess the total number of items per sample to avoid over- or under-estimating the importance of a given fish taxon (Carss & Nelson 1998). The percent composition of otter diet was expressed as relative frequency of occurrence (O). Weight category of preyed fish was back-calculated using a reference collection of bones from fish of known size. Based on these weight estimates, food items (fish individuals) were divided into 4 categories (Lanszki et al. 2001, Lanszki & Sallai 2006): < 100 g, 100–500 g, 501–1000 g and > 1000 g. All other dry food remains were weighed and their weight multiplied by an appropriate coefficient of digestibility (rodents 9, birds 12, amphibians 18, fish 25, crayfish 7, insects 5, plant material 4; see Lanszki et al. 2006 for details) to obtain an estimate of the fresh biomass percentage (B) of the food consumed. Fish species were also grouped according to their preferred habitat zone (S – shorezone or littoral, M – metaphyton, P – pelagic, B – benthic) and origin (N – native and A – alien or non-native). Fish availability in the pond was investigated using electrofishing and fyke nets. Electrofishing was carried out in spring (5 May), summer (30 June), and autumn (4 October) 2011. Sampling was conducted for 60 minutes along the same vegetated shoreline transect in every season (mean length 1606 ± 210 m), by a boat-transported SAMUS 725MP, 12 V battery-powered device (used at Pulse DC 380–500 V; 50–70 Hz). Based on Specziár et al. (2012), this method provides reliable information regarding the fish assemblage structure. Each captured fish was identified at species level, weighed, and released, except for non-native gibel carp (Carassius gibelio) and pumpkinseed (Lepomis gibbosus), which were transported to the laboratory for further examinations. Seven fyke nets with a 10-mm mesh size were spaced evenly and consistently set on the water surface (5 large [60 × 110 cm], 1 medium [40 × 100 cm], 1 small [30 × 100 cm]), and seven on the bottom (5 large, 1 medium, 1 small) from the bank to the middle of the open water. Fyke nets were set for four consecutive days, twice in spring and autumn and three times in summer (5 × 4 × 14 = 280 trap-nights). Nets were checked every morning. To avoid multiple counts, specimens > 100 g were marked by cutting a ray of the dorsal fin. The Chi-squared test (\( \chi^2 \)) was used to compare raw frequency data of fish in otter diet (use) and in the environment (availability) in relation to survey method, season, fish size class and preferred habitat zone. Ivlev’s index (E_i) of preference was applied to each fish taxon and weight category as follows: \( E_i = (r_i - n_i)/(r_i + n_i) \), where \( r_i \) = percent occurrence of each (i^{th}) item in otter diet, and \( n_i \) = percent occurrence of the same item in the environment (Krebs 1989). As our data were fitted well to a normal distribution, we used an independent sample t-test to evaluate the effect of fish survey method on the normal E_i values of different fish species, in relation to fish weight, habitat zone and origin. Those fish species that were rarely (1–2 cases) identified by either fish surveys or spraint analyses were not included in the analyses. SPSS 10.0 for Windows (SPSS, Chicago, III) statistical package was used for data processing. A minimum probability level of \( p < 0.05 \) was accepted for all the statistics, and all \( p \)-values are two-tailed. Results The number of fish specimens (Table 1) captured by electrofishing increased from spring to autumn, whereas for fyke netting, it increased from spring to summer, then decreased in autumn. The composition of fish population (on the basis of 13 fish taxa) varied according to the type of sampling method applied (\( \chi^2_{10-11} = 24.25–333.59, p < 0.01 \)). Based on electrofishing, the composition of the fish resource varied seasonally (\( \chi^2_{18} = 67.16, p < 0.001 \)), with the pumpkinseed (particularly in spring and in autumn) and the gibel carp (particularly in summer and in autumn) being the most widespread species (Table 1). Besides these 2 main species, the topmouth gudgeon (Pseudorasbora parva) and the roach (Rutilus rutilus) were abundant in spring, while the rudd (Scardinius erythrophthalmus) and the common perch (Perca fluviatilis) were common in summer. According to sampling by fyke nets (Table 1), there were also significant seasonal differences (\( \chi^2_{22} = 398.07, p < 0.001 \)). The most common species was the rudd, although it was dominant (66.1 %) only in summer. Other abundant species were the topmouth gudgeon and the gibel carp in spring, and the common perch and the black bullhead (Ameiurus melas) in autumn. Other fish species were rarely detected. Fish weighing less than 100 g were predominant (Fig. 1). The main food of otter was fish in every season (O: 73.5–84.9 %, B: 85.2–97.8 %), with amphibians representing a secondary resource (O: 6.7–19.6 %, B: 2.4–13.0 %). Fish consumption increased from spring to autumn-winter, whereas consumption of amphibians (mainly Rana sp.) followed an opposite trend. Minor food types included birds in spring (O: 3.7 %; Anatidae) and summer (O: 2.0 %; small Passeriformes and Anatidae); reptiles (Colubridae) in spring and summer (O: 0.9–1.0 %); and mammals (small rodents) in winter (O: 0.6 %). Invertebrates (water beetles and larvae, and crayfish [Astacus sp.]) were frequently found (O: 0.9–7.4 %) but their percent contribution in terms of biomass was negligible (B: < 0.1 %). The relative frequency of main fish species in otter diet varied by season (\( \chi^2_{38} = 86.29, p < 0.001 \); Table 1). Three fish taxa formed the bulk (O: 75.5 %, B: 82.6 %) of otter diet throughout the year, namely Carassius sp. (mainly gibel carp) in spring and autumn, pumpkinseed in winter, and perch in summer. Beside these species, consumption of topmouth gudgeon (particularly in winter and autumn) and of black bullhead was considerable. Predation of economically important species, such as common carp (Cyprinus carpio), pike-perch (Sander lucioperca) and pike (Esox lucius), was only occasional. Two-thirds of fish eaten consisted of non-native species. Otter preferred the common carp, gibel carp (except for the largest size class), and perch, whilst rudd, roach, tench (Tinca tinca) and most size categories of pikeperch were avoided (Table 2). Bullhead were preferred by otter when its availability was assessed by electrofishing (\( t_4 = 3.41, p < 0.05 \)), whereas pumpkinseed were preferred based on availability as assessed by fyke nets (\( t_4 = 9.29, p < 0.01 \)). Otter consumed small-sized fish (< 100 g in weight) according to their occurrence in the environment as assessed by either electrofishing or fyke net sampling (\( E_i = 0.02 \) vs. 0.04, respectively; \( t_4 = 0.49, p = 0.648 \)), whereas 100–500 g fish were slightly avoided (\( E_i = –0.17 \) vs. –0.28, \( t_4 = 0.65, p = 0.550 \); Fig. 1). Larger fish categories rarely occurred (Fig. 1), but fish in the 501–1000 g category were slightly preferred (\( E_i = 0.31 \) vs. 0.32, \( t_3 = 0.16, p = 0.881 \)), and fish > 1000 g were avoided (\( E_i = –0.36 \) vs. –0.66, \( t_2 = 0.06, p = 0.956 \)). Preferences did not vary by sampling method for any size category. Otter preferences in relation to habitat zones and fish origin differed according to the sampling method used to assess fish availability. Otter preferred shore-zone fish (\( E_i = 0.44 \) vs. –0.06, \( t_4 = 3.67, p < 0.05 \)), but avoided fish living in the metaphyton (\( E_i = –0.35 \) vs. 0.17, \( t_4 = 2.76, p = 0.051 \)) and benthic zone (\( E_i = –0.35 \) vs. 0.81, \( t_4 = 5.69, p < 0.01 \)) when fish availability was assessed by fyke nets, but not by electrofishing. Pelagic fish were avoided according to both methods (\( E_i = –0.12 \) vs. –0.32, \( t_4 = 0.29, p = 0.786 \)). Native fishes were avoided and non-native fishes were preferred when availability was based on fyke netting (\( E_i = –0.33 \) and 0.29), while no preference was pointed out by electrofishing (\( E_i = 0.13 \) and –0.03). Discussion Fish preference Our data indicated that otters were opportunistic hunters on this near-natural pond, preying primarily on the most abundant fish species and size classes and conforming to seasonal variation in fish availability. These results are similar to studies in other natural habitats (ponds, lakes or rivers; e.g. Erlinge 1967, Kemenes & Nechay 1990, Copp & Roche 2003, Lanszki & Sallai 2006), while contrary or partially opposed to others (e.g., Lanszki et al. 2001, Marques et al. 2007, Sales-Luis et al. 2007, Miranda et al. 2008, Baltrunaite 2009), probably due to local differences in management policies (near-natural habitats vs. fish farms) and fish assemblage composition. As an example, otter preference for abundant, small-sized (< 100 g) gibel carp and avoidance of the rare, but larger (100–500 g) specimens found in this study is in contrast with the experience from fish ponds with low-density (< 2 % within fish community) gibel carp populations (Lanszki et al. 2001, Lanszki et al. 2007). Accordingly, in our study area otters preferred large (> 500 g) individuals of some rare commercial species such as the common carp and pike, while in a pond dominated by common carp in Poland (Kloskowski 2005), small-sized individuals were selected. Based on feeding experiments, otters prefer fish < 10 cm in length (Erlinge 1968); however, otters living on fish ponds mainly rely on small-sized fish when either fish biomass is low (Lanszki et al. 2001) or where small-bodied fish (e.g. gibel carp, topmouth gudgeon) are kept at relatively high density for commercial purposes (Lanszki et al. 2007). Contrary to earlier results from fish ponds in Hungary (Lanszki et al. 2001, Lanszki et al. 2007), the temporarily abundant, metaphyton-dwelling rudd was almost avoided by the otter. Our results may depend on the dense macrophyte vegetation covering almost 100 % of the lake surface and providing an appropriate refuge for this species (see also Miranda et al. 2008). Consumption of typical benthic fish species hidden in sediments (tench, Cobitidae, Gobio sp.) is also rarely occurring in other stagnant waters (e.g. Lanszki et al. 2001, Sales-Luis et al. 2007, Baltrunaite 2009). In fish ponds with fluctuating fish availability in cold periods (Kranz 2000, Kloskowski 2005, Lanszki et al. 2006) and in natural stagnant waters in summer or during drought periods (Erlinge 1967, Clavero et al. 2003, Lanszki & Sallai 2006, Lanszki & Széles 2006, Ruiz-Olmo & Jiménez 2009), fish availability may be inadequate to support otter populations. In these cases, otters use suboptimal (i.e., lower net energy) food items, e.g. amphibians, arthropods, birds in higher amounts; or they enlarge their home-range size (Erlinge 1967, Weber 1990, Mason & Macdonald 1986, Clavero et al. 2003, Kruuk 2006). Although fish biomass was not estimated in this study, fish formed the bulk of otter diet throughout the study period, suggesting that fish biomass was adequate to support the otter population. Accordingly, otter presence was stable and reproduction was observed. The effect of fish sampling method on prey preference Electrofishing is considered to be the least biased and least destructive method for fish sampling (Persat & Copp 1990). Our results suggested that the standard electrofishing method is more effective for catching shorezone- and metaphyton-dwelling fishes (Erős et al. 2009), whereas fyke nets, despite being used in both benthic and pelagic zones simultaneously, are primarily suitable for catching benthic and day-active fishes. As an example, adult black bullhead usually prefers benthic habitats (Kottelat & Freyhof 2007), where electrofishing is less effective (Cucherousset et al. 2006), while pumpkinseed, which is a shorezone species (McCairns & Fox 2004) was underrepresented in the catch of fyke nets, leading in both cases to apparent preference by otters. These results suggested that the sampling method could distort the assessment of prey preference by otters. We recommend the use of standardized methods (CEN 2003) in future studies conducted in near-natural ponds. Implications for conservation Our results indicate that the diet composition of the otter closely reflects the composition of the fish assemblage of natural or near-natural habitats (Erlinge 1967). The monitoring of fish faunas of such small ponds has not yet passed the standards of the EU Water Framework Directive, however, their crucial role in biodiversity conservation has been realized recently (Søndergaard et al. 2005, Cereghino et al. 2008). As fish sampling is usually expensive, the possible application of otter spraint analysis to fish assemblage monitoring, at least in special cases (e.g., detection of rare species) can be considered. The otter prefers easily available food (Erlinge 1967). According to this study, the diet may consist of non-native, undesirable (based on a conservation and economic point of view) fishes. Although otter predation on non-native fishes throughout their European range is still negligible (Balestrieri et al. 2013), occasionally, the consumption of non-native fishes by otters in a higher proportion than their availability has been reported for both Mediterranean and temperate stagnant waters (Lanszki et al. 2001, Sales-Luis et al. 2007, Lanszki & Sallai 2006). A high consumption ratio of non-native species suggests that otters may help to prevent habitat degradation of near-natural fishponds and man-altered water bodies by controlling non-native fish populations (Erős 2007, Mills et al. 2001). The gibel carp is one of the most problematic non-native fish species (Erős 2007, Sály et al. 2011) in the Pannonian biogeographical region. Expansion of this species was facilitated because several native predators, e.g., cormorants, herons and pike, avoid gibel carp due to a high dorsal profile and flattened body shape (Gere & Andrikovics 1991). Further research is needed to point out if, due to different feeding strategies, otter may be capable of controlling this invasive fish species. Acknowledgements Thanks to G. Bauer-Haáz¹, Árpád Ferincz², Zoltán Szegvári³, Gabriella L. Széles¹ and József Lanszki¹, * With 1 figure and 2 tables Abstract: The role of small (< 10 ha) ponds in biodiversity conservation has been recently highlighted. As a top predator, the Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra) may have a powerful effect on the biodiversity and ecological functionality of small ponds, regardless of their purpose (e.g. aquaculture, angling or conservation). Our study sought to analyze the feeding habits of otter in a near-natural system (Csombárdi pond, SW Hungary). From December 2010 to November 2011, the annual composition of otter diet was assessed by the analysis of spraint samples (n = 483). Fish abundance was assessed from spring to autumn by electrofishing and fyke nets. Throughout the study period, the main food source of the otter was fish (73.5–84.9 % of occurrences), while amphibians represented a secondary resource. Otters behaved as opportunistic hunters, preying primarily on the most abundant fish species and size classes and conforming to seasonal variation in fish availability. Otter preferences in relation to fish habitat zones (shorezone or littoral, metaphyton, pelagic, benthic) and origin (native, non-native) differed according to the sampling method used to assess fish availability, suggesting that the sampling method chosen may distort the assessment of prey preference by otters. Two-thirds of fish eaten consisted of non-native species. Results may be useful for the conservation of otters, near-natural ponds, and associated native fish communities. Key words: Lutra lutra, diet, feeding habits, electrofishing, fyke net, fish selection, non-native fish, opportunism, conservation, Hungary. Introduction Since the beginning of the 21st century, both the number and total area (from 22,463 ha in 2001 to 24,364 ha in 2011; Pintér 2002, Jámborné & Bardócz 2012) of ponds under management for nature conservation have increased in Hungary. Ponds managed for conservation are buffer or shelter areas (i.e., year-round undisturbed habitats), where only the regulation of fish populations is applied. These near-natural habitats are suitable for investigating the ecological function and behaviour of piscivorous species (Erlinge 1967) in relation to fish farming. Surveys of fish assemblages in ponds and lakes are conducted using gillnets according to CEN standards (CEN 2003, CEN 2005). In small ponds (1–10 ha), the use of gillnets can be restricted due to dense macrophyte vegetation. In such cases, the most commonly used survey method is electrofishing (Diekmann et al. 2005, Erős et al. 2009). Alternatively, fyke netting can provide valuable additional data, particularly on benthic species (Lapointe et al. 2006, Ruetz et al. 2007). In Hungary, the Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra) is strictly protected as a Natura 2000 species (Heltai et al. 2012). After a dramatic decline occurred in the 1960s–1970s (Mason & Macdonald 1986), otter populations have begun to recover in the last two decades (Conroy & Chanin 2002, EEA 2009), sometimes leading to conflict with fish farmers and anglers (Kranz 2000, Britton et al. 2005, Marques et al. 2007). Although the feeding habits of the otter have been widely investigated both in natural freshwater habitats (e.g., Jedrzejewska et al 2001, Clavero et al. 2003) and in highly productive fish farms (e.g., Lanszki et al. 2001, Kloskowski 2005, Marques et al. 2007, Baltrunaite 2009), little is known about prey selection by otters in semi-natural ponds managed for nature conservation (but see Almeida et al. 2012). We studied otter diet in a near-natural pond to determine: 1) otter feeding preferences in relation to fish species, size class, habitat zone and origin (i.e., native or non-native) and 2) the influence of fish sampling methods on preference assessment. Material and methods Study area The study was carried out in SW Hungary on an abandoned artificial fish pond (Csombárdi pond, 7 ha; 46° 26′ N, 17° 39′ E, 147 m a.s.l.). The climate was continental with submediterranean influence. Annual rainfall was about 700 mm, of which more than 400 mm fell in the vegetation period (Dövényi 2010). The pond was included in a 54-ha nature conservation area, covered by meadows (Thymo serpylli-Festucetum pseudovinae; 50 %), water bodies and associated wetlands (Succiso-Molinietum hungaricae, Phragmition australis, Magnocaricion elatae; 20 %), marshes (Cirsio cani-Festucetum pratensis, Carici vulpinae-Alopecuretum pratensis), spontaneously reforested meadows, and degraded areas (ca. 10 % each). Two-thirds of the marsh-like pond surface was covered by vegetation (reed-mace Typha latifolia and, secondarily, reed Phragmites australis); the submerged vegetation (Potametea) was also dense. Water depth ranged between 1 m (in winter) and 1.5 m (in June). Since 2008, fish management has been limited to conservation measures. During the study period, the fish population of the pond originated from natural recruitment. The stable presence of otters (burrows, cub-rearing) was recorded on the site. Sampling and analysis Diet composition of the otter was determined by spraint (faecal) analysis (n = 483 samples), collected monthly from December 2010 to November 2011 along the banks and dike of the pond on a 600-m long standard route. Samples were soaked in water, then washed through a 0.5-mm sieve and dried at room temperature. All recognisable prey remains were separated and examined under a microscope. Fish species were identified on the basis of morphological differences of scales and bones, e.g., pharyngeal teeth, vertebrae, operculae, praecoperculae and maxillaries, using atlases and reference collections (e.g., Lanszki et al. 2001, Lanszki et al. 2007). Bones’ size combined with scale characters were used to assess the total number of items per sample to avoid over- or under-estimating the importance of a given fish taxon (Carss & Nelson 1998). The percent composition of otter diet was expressed as relative frequency of occurrence (O). Weight category of preyed fish was back-calculated using a reference collection of bones from fish of known size. Based on these weight estimates, food items (fish individuals) were divided into 4 categories (Lanszki et al. 2001, Lanszki & Sallai 2006): < 100 g, 100–500 g, 501–1000 g and > 1000 g. All other dry food remains were weighed and their weight multiplied by an appropriate coefficient of digestibility (rodents 9, birds 12, amphibians 18, fish 25, crayfish 7, insects 5, plant material 4; see Lanszki et al. 2006 for details) to obtain an estimate of the fresh biomass percentage (B) of the food consumed. Fish species were also grouped according to their preferred habitat zone (S – shorezone or littoral, M – metaphyton, P – pelagic, B – benthic) and origin (N – native and A – alien or non-native). Fish availability in the pond was investigated using electrofishing and fyke nets. Electrofishing was carried out in spring (5 May), summer (30 June), and autumn (4 October) 2011. Sampling was conducted for 60 minutes along the same vegetated shoreline transect in every season (mean length 1606 ± 210 m), by a boat-transported SAMUS 725MP, 12 V battery-powered device (used at Pulse DC 380–500 V; 50–70 Hz). Based on Specziár et al. (2012), this method provides reliable information regarding the fish assemblage structure. Each captured fish was identified at species level, weighed, and released, except for non-native gibel carp (Carassius gibelio) and pumpkinseed (Lepomis gibbosus), which were transported to the laboratory for further examinations. Seven fyke nets with a 10-mm mesh size were spaced evenly and consistently set on the water surface (5 large [60 × 110 cm], 1 medium [40 × 100 cm], 1 small [30 × 100 cm]), and seven on the bottom (5 large, 1 medium, 1 small) from the bank to the middle of the open water. Fyke nets were set for four consecutive days, twice in spring and autumn and three times in summer (5 × 4 × 14 = 280 trap-nights). Nets were checked every morning. To avoid multiple counts, specimens > 100 g were marked by cutting a ray of the dorsal fin. The Chi-squared test (\( \chi^2 \)) was used to compare raw frequency data of fish in otter diet (use) and in the environment (availability) in relation to survey method, season, fish size class and preferred habitat zone. Ivlev’s index (E_i) of preference was applied to each fish taxon and weight category as follows: \( E_i = (r_i - n_i)/(r_i + n_i) \), where \( r_i \) = percent occurrence of each (i^{th}) item in otter diet, and \( n_i \) = percent occurrence of the same item in the environment (Krebs 1989). As our data were fitted well to a normal distribution, we used an independent sample t-test to evaluate the effect of fish survey method on the normal E_i values of different fish species, in relation to fish weight, habitat zone and origin. Those fish species that were rarely (1–2 cases) identified by either fish surveys or spraint analyses were not included in the analyses. SPSS 10.0 for Windows (SPSS, Chicago, III) statistical package was used for data processing. A minimum probability level of \( p < 0.05 \) was accepted for all the statistics, and all \( p \)-values are two-tailed. Results The number of fish specimens (Table 1) captured by electrofishing increased from spring to autumn, whereas for fyke netting, it increased from spring to summer, then decreased in autumn. The composition of fish population (on the basis of 13 fish taxa) varied according to the type of sampling method applied (\( \chi^2_{10-11} = 24.25–333.59, p < 0.01 \)). Based on electrofishing, the composition of the fish resource varied seasonally (\( \chi^2_{18} = 67.16, p < 0.001 \)), with the pumpkinseed (particularly in spring and in autumn) and the gibel carp (particularly in summer and in autumn) being the most widespread species (Table 1). Besides these 2 main species, the topmouth gudgeon (Pseudorasbora parva) and the roach (Rutilus rutilus) were abundant in spring, while the rudd (Scardinius erythrophthalmus) and the common perch (Perca fluviatilis) were common in summer. According to sampling by fyke nets (Table 1), there were also significant seasonal differences (\( \chi^2_{22} = 398.07, p < 0.001 \)). The most common species was the rudd, although it was dominant (66.1 %) only in summer. Other abundant species were the topmouth gudgeon and the gibel carp in spring, and the common perch and the black bullhead (Ameiurus melas) in autumn. Other fish species were rarely detected. Fish weighing less than 100 g were predominant (Fig. 1). The main food of otter was fish in every season (O: 73.5–84.9 %, B: 85.2–97.8 %), with amphibians representing a secondary resource (O: 6.7–19.6 %, B: 2.4–13.0 %). Fish consumption increased from spring to autumn-winter, whereas consumption of amphibians (mainly Rana sp.) followed an opposite trend. Minor food types included birds in spring (O: 3.7 %; Anatidae) and summer (O: 2.0 %; small Passeriformes and Anatidae); reptiles (Colubridae) in spring and summer (O: 0.9–1.0 %); and mammals (small rodents) in winter (O: 0.6 %). Invertebrates (water beetles and larvae, and crayfish [Astacus sp.]) were frequently found (O: 0.9–7.4 %) but their percent contribution in terms of biomass was negligible (B: < 0.1 %). The relative frequency of main fish species in otter diet varied by season (\( \chi^2_{38} = 86.29, p < 0.001 \); Table 1). Three fish taxa formed the bulk (O: 75.5 %, B: 82.6 %) of otter diet throughout the year, namely Carassius sp. (mainly gibel carp) in spring and autumn, pumpkinseed in winter, and perch in summer. Beside these species, consumption of topmouth gudgeon (particularly in winter and autumn) and of black bullhead was considerable. Predation of economically important species, such as common carp (Cyprinus carpio), pike-perch (Sander lucioperca) and pike (Esox lucius), was only occasional. Two-thirds of fish eaten consisted of non-native species. Otter preferred the common carp, gibel carp (except for the largest size class), and perch, whilst rudd, roach, tench (Tinca tinca) and most size categories of pikeperch were avoided (Table 2). Bullhead were preferred by otter when its availability was assessed by electrofishing (\( t_4 = 3.41, p < 0.05 \)), whereas pumpkinseed were preferred based on availability as assessed by fyke nets (\( t_4 = 9.29, p < 0.01 \)). Otter consumed small-sized fish (< 100 g in weight) according to their occurrence in the environment as assessed by either electrofishing or fyke net sampling (\( E_i = 0.02 \) vs. 0.04, respectively; \( t_4 = 0.49, p = 0.648 \)), whereas 100–500 g fish were slightly avoided (\( E_i = –0.17 \) vs. –0.28, \( t_4 = 0.65, p = 0.550 \); Fig. 1). Larger fish categories rarely occurred (Fig. 1), but fish in the 501–1000 g category were slightly preferred (\( E_i = 0.31 \) vs. 0.32, \( t_3 = 0.16, p = 0.881 \)), and fish > 1000 g were avoided (\( E_i = –0.36 \) vs. –0.66, \( t_2 = 0.06, p = 0.956 \)). Preferences did not vary by sampling method for any size category. Otter preferences in relation to habitat zones and fish origin differed according to the sampling method used to assess fish availability. Otter preferred shore-zone fish (\( E_i = 0.44 \) vs. –0.06, \( t_4 = 3.67, p < 0.05 \)), but avoided fish living in the metaphyton (\( E_i = –0.35 \) vs. 0.17, \( t_4 = 2.76, p = 0.051 \)) and benthic zone (\( E_i = –0.35 \) vs. 0.81, \( t_4 = 5.69, p < 0.01 \)) when fish availability was assessed by fyke nets, but not by electrofishing. Pelagic fish were avoided according to both methods (\( E_i = –0.12 \) vs. –0.32, \( t_4 = 0.29, p = 0.786 \)). Native fishes were avoided and non-native fishes were preferred when availability was based on fyke netting (\( E_i = –0.33 \) and 0.29), while no preference was pointed out by electrofishing (\( E_i = 0.13 \) and –0.03). Discussion Fish preference Our data indicated that otters were opportunistic hunters on this near-natural pond, preying primarily on the most abundant fish species and size classes and conforming to seasonal variation in fish availability. These results are similar to studies in other natural habitats (ponds, lakes or rivers; e.g. Erlinge 1967, Kemenes & Nechay 1990, Copp & Roche 2003, Lanszki & Sallai 2006), while contrary or partially opposed to others (e.g., Lanszki et al. 2001, Marques et al. 2007, Sales-Luis et al. 2007, Miranda et al. 2008, Baltrunaite 2009), probably due to local differences in management policies (near-natural habitats vs. fish farms) and fish assemblage composition. As an example, otter preference for abundant, small-sized (< 100 g) gibel carp and avoidance of the rare, but larger (100–500 g) specimens found in this study is in contrast with the experience from fish ponds with low-density (< 2 % within fish community) gibel carp populations (Lanszki et al. 2001, Lanszki et al. 2007). Accordingly, in our study area otters preferred large (> 500 g) individuals of some rare commercial species such as the common carp and pike, while in a pond dominated by common carp in Poland (Kloskowski 2005), small-sized individuals were selected. Based on feeding experiments, otters prefer fish < 10 cm in length (Erlinge 1968); however, otters living on fish ponds mainly rely on small-sized fish when either fish biomass is low (Lanszki et al. 2001) or where small-bodied fish (e.g. gibel carp, topmouth gudgeon) are kept at relatively high density for commercial purposes (Lanszki et al. 2007). Contrary to earlier results from fish ponds in Hungary (Lanszki et al. 2001, Lanszki et al. 2007), the temporarily abundant, metaphyton-dwelling rudd was almost avoided by the otter. Our results may depend on the dense macrophyte vegetation covering almost 100 % of the lake surface and providing an appropriate refuge for this species (see also Miranda et al. 2008). Consumption of typical benthic fish species hidden in sediments (tench, Cobitidae, Gobio sp.) is also rarely occurring in other stagnant waters (e.g. Lanszki et al. 2001, Sales-Luis et al. 2007, Baltrunaite 2009). In fish ponds with fluctuating fish availability in cold periods (Kranz 2000, Kloskowski 2005, Lanszki et al. 2006) and in natural stagnant waters in summer or during drought periods (Erlinge 1967, Clavero et al. 2003, Lanszki & Sallai 2006, Lanszki & Széles 2006, Ruiz-Olmo & Jiménez 2009), fish availability may be inadequate to support otter populations. In these cases, otters use suboptimal (i.e., lower net energy) food items, e.g. amphibians, arthropods, birds in higher amounts; or they enlarge their home-range size (Erlinge 1967, Weber 1990, Mason & Macdonald 1986, Clavero et al. 2003, Kruuk 2006). Although fish biomass was not estimated in this study, fish formed the bulk of otter diet throughout the study period, suggesting that fish biomass was adequate to support the otter population. Accordingly, otter presence was stable and reproduction was observed. The effect of fish sampling method on prey preference Electrofishing is considered to be the least biased and least destructive method for fish sampling (Persat & Copp 1990). Our results suggested that the standard electrofishing method is more effective for catching shorezone- and metaphyton-dwelling fishes (Erős et al. 2009), whereas fyke nets, despite being used in both benthic and pelagic zones simultaneously, are primarily suitable for catching benthic and day-active fishes. As an example, adult black bullhead usually prefers benthic habitats (Kottelat & Freyhof 2007), where electrofishing is less effective (Cucherousset et al. 2006), while pumpkinseed, which is a shorezone species (McCairns & Fox 2004) was underrepresented in the catch of fyke nets, leading in both cases to apparent preference by otters. These results suggested that the sampling method could distort the assessment of prey preference by otters. We recommend the use of standardized methods (CEN 2003) in future studies conducted in near-natural ponds. Implications for conservation Our results indicate that the diet composition of the otter closely reflects the composition of the fish assemblage of natural or near-natural habitats (Erlinge 1967). The monitoring of fish faunas of such small ponds has not yet passed the standards of the EU Water Framework Directive, however, their crucial role in biodiversity conservation has been realized recently (Søndergaard et al. 2005, Cereghino et al. 2008). As fish sampling is usually expensive, the possible application of otter spraint analysis to fish assemblage monitoring, at least in special cases (e.g., detection of rare species) can be considered. The otter prefers easily available food (Erlinge 1967). According to this study, the diet may consist of non-native, undesirable (based on a conservation and economic point of view) fishes. Although otter predation on non-native fishes throughout their European range is still negligible (Balestrieri et al. 2013), occasionally, the consumption of non-native fishes by otters in a higher proportion than their availability has been reported for both Mediterranean and temperate stagnant waters (Lanszki et al. 2001, Sales-Luis et al. 2007, Lanszki & Sallai 2006). A high consumption ratio of non-native species suggests that otters may help to prevent habitat degradation of near-natural fishponds and man-altered water bodies by controlling non-native fish populations (Erős 2007, Mills et al. 2001). The gibel carp is one of the most problematic non-native fish species (Erős 2007, Sály et al. 2011) in the Pannonian biogeographical region. Expansion of this species was facilitated because several native predators, e.g., cormorants, herons and pike, avoid gibel carp due to a high dorsal profile and flattened body shape (Gere & Andrikovics 1991). Further research is needed to point out if, due to different feeding strategies, otter may be capable of controlling this invasive fish species. Acknowledgements Thanks to G. Gas transfer velocities in small forested ponds Meredith A. Holgerson1,2, Emily R. Farr1, and Peter A. Raymond1 1School of Forestry and Environmental Studies, Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut, USA, 2Now at Department of Environmental Science and Management, Portland State University, Portland, Oregon, USA Abstract Inland waters actively exchange gases with the atmosphere, and the gas exchange rate informs system biogeochemistry, ecology, and global carbon budgets. Gas exchange in medium- to large-sized lakes is largely regulated by wind; yet less is known about processes regulating gas transfer in small ponds where wind speeds are low. In this study, we determined the gas transfer velocity, \( k_{600} \), in four small (<250 m\(^2\)) ponds by using a propane (C\(_3\)H\(_8\)) gas injection. When estimated across 12 h periods, the average \( k_{600} \) ranged from 0.19 to 0.72 m d\(^{-1}\) across the ponds. We also estimated \( k_{600} \) at 2 to 3 h intervals during the day and evaluated the relationship with environmental conditions. The average daytime \( k_{600} \) ranged from 0.33 to 1.83 m d\(^{-1}\) across the ponds and was best predicted by wind speed and air or air-water temperature; however, the explanatory power was weak (\( R^2 < 0.27 \)) with high variability within and among ponds. To compare our results to larger water bodies, we compiled direct measurements of \( k_{600} \) from 67 ponds and lakes worldwide. Our \( k_{600} \) estimates were within the range of estimates for other small ponds, and variability in \( k_{600} \) increased with lake size. However, the majority of studies were conducted on medium-sized lakes (0.01 to 1 km\(^2\)), leaving small ponds and large lakes understudied. Overall, this study adds four small ponds to the existing body of research on gas transfer velocities from inland waters and highlights uncertainty in \( k_{600} \), with implications for calculating metabolism and carbon emissions in inland waters. 1. Introduction Inland waters actively exchange gases with the atmosphere, with important consequences for ecosystem dynamics such as carbon emissions [Schilder et al., 2013; Seekell et al., 2014], oxygen availability [Melack and Fisher, 1983; Holgerson et al., 2016], and food web structure [Schindler et al., 1997; Devlin et al., 2015]. For instance, air-water gas exchange rates influence the extent to which greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide, are released by inland waters. The gas transfer velocity, \( k \), partly controls the exchange rate and is largely driven by turbulence at the air-water interface [MacIntyre et al., 1995]. In large water bodies, wind speed often drives turbulence because it creates surface waves and shear stress that increase \( k \) [MacIntyre et al., 1995]. As such, wind speed is often used to model \( k \) in lakes [Cole and Caraco, 1998] and the ocean [Wanninkhof, 1992]. However, the relationship between wind speed and \( k \) typically breaks down under low-wind conditions, characteristic of smaller and more sheltered waters [Clark et al., 1995; Cole and Caraco, 1998]. Considering that over 90% of lakes and ponds worldwide are less than 1 ha in size [Downing et al., 2006; Verpoorter et al., 2014] and that small ponds play a disproportionately large role in greenhouse gas emissions [Holgerson and Raymond, 2016], it is critical to determine their \( k \). Furthermore, because directly measuring \( k \) is time intensive, it is important to evaluate if any environmental parameters can be used to predict \( k \). Other than wind, environmental factors that influence turbulence and can be readily measured or estimated include surfactants, rainfall, and convection. Surfactants are formed by hydrophobic organic compounds, and they reduce wind stress at the surface, can obstruct molecular diffusion, and ultimately decrease gas transfer [MacIntyre et al., 1995]. Raindrops physically increase turbulence at the air-water interface and increase gas exchange [Ho et al., 1997]. Convection can influence \( k \) through seasonal and diurnal changes in air-water temperature, particularly in small water bodies [Matthews et al., 2003; Poindexter and Variano, 2013]. For instance, convection from cooling surface waters can increase gas transfer velocities by increasing turbulence in the surface mixing layer [MacIntyre et al., 2010; Holgerson et al., 2016]. The importance of convective cooling may be greater in small systems because they exhibit more extreme diurnal temperature changes than larger lakes, which increases sensible heat flux and convective turbulence [Woolway et al., 2016]. The relative importance of convection versus wind on \( k \) may be mediated by lake surface area, with wind dominating in larger systems and convection being more important in smaller, more sheltered lakes and ponds [Read et al., 2012]. There are multiple approaches for estimating \( k \), including whole-lake gas tracers, floating chambers, directly measuring turbulence, meteorological techniques (e.g., eddy flux), and modeling techniques, all of which have limitations [Matthews et al., 2003; Zappa et al., 2007; Cole et al., 2010]. Whole-lake tracers use gases such as sulfur hexafluoride, helium, or propane, which are added to a water body and the gas loss over time is used to estimate \( k \) [e.g., Wanninkhof et al., 1985; Clark et al., 1995; Frost and Upstill-Goddard, 2002; Cole et al., 2010; Jin et al., 2012]. However, this approach can be time-intensive and costly, particularly for large water bodies. Floating chambers are easy to deploy, but they create microenvironments within the chamber that exclude effects of wind and rainfall, generate artificial turbulence, change the atmospheric pressure, and alter the air-water concentration gradient [Matthews et al., 2003; Vachon et al., 2010]. Additionally, there are often high spatial and temporal variabilities that may not be captured by chambers that are only deployed for a short time [Schilder et al., 2013; Vachon and Prairie, 2013]. Flux chambers can also grossly overestimate \( k \) in low-turbulence environments [Vachon et al., 2010], characteristic of smaller water bodies. Directly measuring turbulence and eddy flux techniques works well but requires expensive equipment and is usually employed only in larger water bodies with adequate fetch [e.g., Jonsson et al., 2008]. Models offer the benefit that \( k \) can be estimated for water bodies that were never sampled, thus saving time, money, and allowing for gas exchange estimates to be extrapolated to the regional or global scale. Predictive models were originally based entirely on wind speed [Wanninkhof, 1992; Clark et al., 1995; Cole and Caraco, 1998] and more recently, models have included components for other variables such as lake area [Vachon and Prairie, 2013], wave breaking [Soloviev et al., 2007; Winslow et al., 2016], and buoyancy flux to capture convection [MacIntyre et al., 2010; Read et al., 2012]. For instance, the surface renewal model takes into account turbulence generated from both wind and heat loss, which creates instability at the air-water interface, particularly when the water becomes warmer than the air [MacIntyre et al., 1995]. Numerous models are now available for estimating \( k \), with varying data requirements [Winslow et al., 2016]. While these models are useful, they first require field sampling and validation across diverse water bodies. Field studies have shown that the wind speed-gas exchange relationship breaks down under low-wind speeds (\(<3\) m s\(^{-1}\)) [Clark et al., 1995; Cole and Caraco, 1998] and models that predict convection will dominate in these low-wind and oftentimes smaller water bodies [Read et al., 2012]. While some field studies have estimated \( k \) in small lakes, we are not aware of any study conducted in ponds smaller than 3000 m\(^2\) [Cole et al., 2010; Schilder et al., 2013]. Considering that there could be as many as 3 billion ponds between 100 and 1000 m\(^2\) globally [Downing, 2010] and that small ponds are hotspots for carbon emissions [Holgerson and Raymond, 2016], it is critical to determine their \( k \). Our study aims to fill this research gap by using whole-pond gas tracer studies to measure \( k \) in four small (<250 m\(^2\)), low-wind ponds. We then compared \( k \) to environmental parameters including wind speed, rain, light, and air and pond temperatures. We expected that pond cooling, indicative of convection, would be more important than wind in predicting \( k \). Lastly, we compiled data from 67 ponds and lakes worldwide where \( k \) was directly measured in order to compare values and variability across a spectrum of lake sizes. We expected that \( k \) would increase with lake size and were curious about variability across lake size classes. 2. Methods 2.1. Study Sites We evaluated the gas transfer velocity, \( k \), in four small, temporary ponds in Yale-Myers Forest in northeastern Connecticut during May and June 2013. The ponds ranged in surface area from 181 to 225 m\(^2\) and in mean depth from 31 to 56 cm (Table 1). The four ponds, Brookside, CH, RH, and Westford, were chosen for their closed basins with minimal emergent vegetation. The closed basin prevents the gas tracer from being diluted by inflow or escaping with outflow. The lack of emergent vegetation ensured that plant matter was not an important factor in regulating \( k \) [Poindexter and Variano, 2013]. During its sampling period, RH had ferns in about 20% of the basin along the edge and about 10 trees in the sides of the basin because it was sampled after a period of rain and therefore had higher water levels. All four ponds are heavily sheltered by the surrounding forest and thus have negligible fetch. Environmental Conditions To monitor environmental conditions at each pond, we used a data logger (Campbell Scientific CR300) to log measurements of wind speed (m s−1) and wind direction (degrees), air and water temperature (°C), photosynthetically active radiation (μmol s−1 m−2), and rainfall (mm) at 15 min intervals in each pond. We positioned the anemometer (height above water level: Westford 75 cm, Brookside 77 cm, CH 50 cm, and RH 35 cm), temperature probes, and photometer (LI-190 Quantum Sensor, LI-COR) on a stake at the deepest point of each pond. A tipping-bucket rain gauge located on a separate stake in the least canopy-covered region of each basin measured precipitation. We assessed pond bathymetry by measuring depth every meter along five transects per pond. We assumed that ponds had elliptical basins to estimate surface area and used depth measurements to estimate pond volume. 2.3. Gas Sampling We injected the ponds with propane because it is an inert gas with negligible background concentrations in the air and water. On the first day of sampling, we used an airstone to bubble propane into eight 18.9 L carboys filled with pond water for 10 min each at 13 psi. We added 3 mL of rhodamine to each carboy as a tracer to determine when the pond had completely mixed. The carboys were well mixed, and we sampled each carboy to determine initial propane concentrations. We then poured the carboy mixtures throughout the entire pond basin and walked through the pond to help with mixing. We used a handheld data logger (Turner Designs DataBank™) to measure rhodamine concentrations twice a day for the first 2 days to verify that the propane concentration mixed throughout the pond. We took our first measurements 6 h after the propane addition, which is when rhodamine concentrations indicated that the propane had mixed evenly throughout the pond basin. We measured propane concentrations from surface waters (~13 cm below the surface) at the deepest point of each pond by using a peristaltic pump (Cole-Parmer Masterflex E/S™ portable sampler 115 VAC). We took occasional samples manually without the pump as a result of instrument malfunction. We sampled every 2 h for the first 24 h, then every 3 h for the remaining 72 h, excluding the interval between 20 h and 08 h due to daylight constraints. We measured propane concentration by using a headspace equilibration technique [Raymond et al., 1997]. Briefly, we filled a beaker with water from the peristaltic pump and allowed it to flush for several volumes. We took three replicate 40 mL water samples from the beaker by using an airtight 60 mL syringe, then immediately drew in 20 mL of ambient air. We shook the syringe vigorously for 2 min in order to equilibrate the air and water phases. Samples of the headspace were then stored and transported to the laboratory in airtight, evacuated glass vials (Labco Limited, UK). We measured propane concentrations using a gas chromatograph (GC) (SRI 310C) with a 3.5 mm column. The GC temperature settings were as follows: detector temperature to 150°C and oven temperature to 100°C, resulting in a propane retention time of ~4.08 min. We injected all propane samples in 1 mL quantities with a 1 mL syringe. We also ran propane samples taken from the eight carboys for each pond on the GC with equivalent initial temperature settings but injected 0.5 mL volumes. PeakSimple 4.09 software measured the propane peak area in each sample, which we converted to concentration (ppmv) by using propane calibration curves. In order to obtain pond propane concentrations, we multiplied measured propane concentrations by 3/2 to correct for the dilution with ambient air during headspace equilibration. 2.4. Estimating Gas Transfer Velocity Gas transfer between aquatic surfaces and the atmosphere is described by the equation: \[ F = k (C_{\text{sur}} - C_{\text{eq}}) \] (1) where \( F \) is the gas flux (mmol m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\)), \( k \) is the gas transfer velocity (m d\(^{-1}\)), \( C_{\text{sur}} \) is the gas concentration in the surface water, and \( C_{\text{eq}} \) is the gas concentration when in equilibrium with the atmosphere. For the propane additions, we directly measured \( F \), \( C_{\text{sur}} \), and \( C_{\text{eq}} \), allowing for the derivation of \( k \). To derive \( k \), we first used a Grubbs outlier test to discount any erroneous propane concentrations that resulted from sampling error. We then converted the average propane concentrations (ppm\(_v\)) of the triplicates at each time point to units of mol L\(^{-1}\) by using Henry’s law constants [Mohebbi et al., 2012; Sander, 2015]. We calculated \( k \) across two different time scales: (1) for each 12 h sampling interval and (2) for each 2 or 3 h sampling period during the day. Longer time scales may more accurately reflect the overall ecosystem gas transfer velocity [Wanninkhof et al., 1987], while shorter time periods better allow for comparisons to be made to environmental conditions. To calculate \( k \) (m d\(^{-1}\)), we used the following equation [Wanninkhof et al., 1987]: \[ k = \frac{h}{\Delta t} \ln \frac{C_i - C_o}{C_f - C_o} \] (2) where \( h \) is the average depth of the pond, \( \Delta t \) is the time interval, \( C_i \) and \( C_f \) are the initial and final propane concentrations in the pond, respectively, and \( C_o \) is the background concentration of propane in the water. We computed average pond depth, \( h \), by taking the mean of the measured depths for each square meter measured in each pond. Since \( C_o \) of propane is negligible in this experiment, equation (2) becomes \[ k = \frac{h}{\Delta t} \ln \frac{C_i}{C_f} \] (3) Because we measured propane concentrations multiple times during the day, to estimate \( k \) for 12 h daytime periods, we performed a linear regression to determine the slope of concentration change over time for each 12 h daytime interval of sampling, and this slope replaced \( \frac{1}{\Delta t} \ln \frac{C_i}{C_f} \) in equation (3). We did not take any gas samples between 20 h and 08 h during the experiment, so we calculated the \( k \) values for each night of sampling by using \( C_f \) from the previous day as the initial propane concentration and \( C_i \) from the following day as the final propane concentration. We normalized \( k \) values to a \( k_{600} \) for propane by using the following equation [Jähne et al., 1987]: \[ \frac{k_{600}}{k_{\text{gas2}}} = \left( \frac{600}{\text{Sc}_{\text{gas2}}} \right)^n \] (4) where \( k_{600} \) is the \( k \) for propane at 20°C and corresponds to a Schmidt number of 600, which can be related to the \( k \) for any other gas [Raymond et al., 2012]. Sc denotes the Schmidt number for the particular gas of interest, and \( n \) is the Schmidt exponent, which varies from –0.5 to –0.67 depending on the boundary conditions. In low-wind environments (<3 m s\(^{-1}\)), \( n \) can be assumed to equal –0.67 [Jähne et al., 1987]. Occasionally, our measurements indicated that propane concentrations increased between sampling times, which likely resulted from spatial heterogeneity in the pond. We only report estimates of \( k \) for periods of time where propane concentrations decreased and indicate net propane evasion from the pond. 2.5. Comparison Across Lake Sizes We conducted a meta-analysis to compare our results to other water bodies where \( k_{600} \) was directly measured. We identified 18 studies, including ours, representing 67 ponds and lakes ranging in size from 181 m\(^2\) to 520 km\(^2\) (Data Set S2 in the supporting information). With this data set, we examined the mean and variability of \( k_{600} \) across lake sizes and also explored the relationship between surface area and gas exchange rate. 2.6. Models were created in R (R version 3.2.4, R Core Team) by using the “lme4” package [Bates et al., 2014]. Estimating Gas Transfer Velocity Surface water propane concentrations decreased exponentially over the sampling period in all four ponds (Figure 1), indicating continuous propane evasion from the ponds to the atmosphere. Initial concentrations of propane measured in the ponds ranged from 89 nmol L\(^{-1}\) in CH to 283 nmol L\(^{-1}\) in Westford and decreased between 51% and 93% during the sampling periods (Table 2). For 12 h periods, \( k_{600} \) averaged between 0.22 and 0.72 m d\(^{-1} \), with considerable variability within and among ponds (Table 2). For instance, estimates of \( k_{600} \) in CH differed by as much as 1.21 m d\(^{-1} \) among days. The maximum variability among ponds was 1.23 m d\(^{-1} \), with a minimum of 0.07 m d\(^{-1} \) in Westford and a maximum of 1.30 m d\(^{-1} \) in CH. There were no significant differences in average \( k_{600} \) during the day versus night (t test, \( t = 0.84 \), d.f. = 15.76, \( p = 0.42 \)); however, average daytime values (ranging from 0.37 to 1.30 m d\(^{-1} \)) were slightly higher than average nighttime values (ranging from 0.07 to 1.03 m d\(^{-1} \)) in CH, RH, and Westford, but not Brookside (Table 2). When measured across each 2 to 3 h period for daytime measurements only, the average \( k_{600} \) ranged between 0.33 and 1.83 m d\(^{-1} \) and was also variable within and among ponds (Table 2). For instance, during the 3 day study, daytime 2 to 3 h estimates of \( k_{600} \) differed by as much as 3.52 m d\(^{-1} \) in Brookside. Among ponds, there was a maximum variability of 3.94 m d\(^{-1} \), with a minimum of 0.01 m d\(^{-1} \) in RH and a maximum of 3.95 m d\(^{-1} \) in Brookside. 3.3.
