Implications for astrobiology On Mars, CH$_4$ is episodically observed in the atmosphere at low concentrations, but formation and oxidation processes are contentious unknowns and pathways for gas migration from the subsurface to surface have not been identified (Mumma et al., 2009; Webster et al., 2015). Low CH$_4$ concentrations in the martian atmosphere could reflect various combinations of low production rates, effective sequestration in the subsurface, and oxidation of CH$_4$ along pathways to the surface. Regardless of whether the formation of CH$_4$ on Mars is biological or geochemical, if enzyme-based microbial consumption is occurring then a kinetic isotope effect resulting in strong enrichment of $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ at low CH$_4$ concentrations could be a potent indicator of subsurface life. Microbial drawdown of CH$_4$ to sub-$\mu$M levels, accompanied by extreme enrichment of heavy isotopes in small lakes under Arctic conditions on Earth highlights the potential for measuring the isotopic compositions of CH$_4$ on Mars as a means to differentiate between biological and geochemical oxidation processes. 6. CONCLUSIONS In Greenland, small closed-basin lakes in close proximity to one another and located within continuous permafrost appear to operate independently, develop distinct chemical compositions, and express local microbial ecologies. For example, only EVV Upper lake has detectible sulfide and high concentrations of sulfate, whereas Teardrop lake is highly buffered throughout the water column, with pH of 9.2. As a result, CH$_4$ concentrations among Arctic lakes vary significantly both seasonally and annually. Carbon and hydrogen isotopic composition of CH$_4$ suggest that despite variations in concentration, CH$_4$ was produced via AM in the littoral sediments and HM in the profundal sediments in all of the lakes. In the water column of all of the studied lakes, when DO was present, a positive correlation in \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^2H_{CH_4} \) was observed, indicating that in these lakes, aerobic MOx was driving dissolved CH$_4$ dynamics. The low concentrations of CH$_4$ accompanied by extreme enrichment in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ reveals that MOx has the ability to fractionation C and H isotopes significantly more than previously recognized. We suggest that the enrichment in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ of CH$_4$ is the result of unusually efficient methanotrophic communities associated with photosynthetic algal mats. Additionally, the extreme enrichment of $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ of CH$_4$ from MOx has significant implications for interpretation of CH$_4$ cycles, which are necessary to define source estimates in emission modeling. Without understanding local geology and biology, stable isotopic values of CH$_4$ that are greater than $-30\%$ for \( \delta^{13}C \) and $-150\%$ for \( \delta^2H \) may be misinterpreted as thermogenic, geothermal, or abiogenic in origin. However, our understanding of the local bedrock combined with the statistically significant relationship between \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^2H_{CH_4} \) within the water-column and sediments confirms that the water-column CH$_4$ enriched in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ is the result of MOx. In order to fully appreciate the global extent to which MOx influences \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^2H \) of CH$_4$, detailed measurements of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^2H \) at depth intervals through water column of numerous lakes spanning low to high latitudes are needed. Large fractionations of C and H isotopes related to methane oxidation in Arctic lakes Sarah B. Cadieux a,*, Jeffrey R. White b, Peter E. Sauer a, Yongbo Peng a,1, Amy E. Goldman a,b,2, Lisa M. Pratt a a Department of Geological Sciences, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN 47405, USA b School of Public and Environmental Affairs, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN 47405, USA Received 14 November 2015; accepted in revised form 3 May 2016; available online 9 May 2016 Abstract Microbial oxidation of methane (CH4) plays a central role in carbon cycling in Arctic lakes, reducing potential CH4 emissions associated with warming. Isotopic signatures of CH4 (δ13C and δ2H) are indicators of microbial oxidation, wherein the process strongly enriches 13C and 2H in residual CH4. We present δ13C and δ2H measurements obtained from sampling the water column and sediment for dissolved CH4 from three, small Arctic lakes in western Greenland under both open-water and ice-covered conditions from 2013 to 2014. Despite substantial variations in aquatic chemistry among the lakes, δ13C and δ2H of CH4 suggested that CH4 was produced predominantly by acetoclastic methanogenesis in the littoral sediments and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis in the profundal sediments in all of the lakes. Surprisingly large variations for both δ13C and δ2H of CH4 were observed, with δ13C extending from −72‰ to +7.4‰ and δ2H from −390‰ to +250‰. The CH4 isotopic values reported here were significantly more enriched (p < 0.0001) in both 13C and 2H than values reported from other Arctic freshwater environments. As is characteristic of methanotrophy, the enrichment in 13C and 2H was associated with low CH4 concentrations. We suggest that the CH4 most enriched in 13C and 2H may reflect unusually efficient methanotrophic communities in Arctic ice-margin lakes. This study provides the first measurement of δ2H for CH4 in an Arctic freshwater environment at concentrations <10 μM. The extreme enrichment of 13C and 2H of CH4 from Arctic methanotrophy has significant implications for interpreting sources and sinks of CH4. Without knowledge of local geology, stable isotope values of CH4 higher than −30‰ for δ13C and −150‰ for δ2H could be misinterpreted as thermogenic, geothermal, or abiogenic origins. Given crystalline bedrock and the strong positive correlation between δ13C and δ2H throughout the water columns in three Arctic lakes confirms that CH4 heavily enriched in 13C and 2H is the result of methanotrophy. Keywords: Methane; Hydrogen isotopes; Carbon isotopes; Arctic; Lakes 1. INTRODUCTION Small lakes (<10 km^2) represent approximately half of the total area of surface water in Arctic environments (Abnizova et al., 2012) and emit more methane (CH4) per unit area than larger lakes (Bastviken et al., 2004; Cole et al., 2007; Juutinen et al., 2009; Downing, 2010). Microbial oxidation of CH4 is an important process in freshwater ecosystems, reincorporating CH4 back into the biogeochemical carbon cycle rather than being released as CH4 into the atmosphere. In northern lakes, up to 88% of the CH4 produced by microbes is oxidized by methanotrophs (Kankaala et al., 2006, 2007; Bastviken et al., 2008; López Bellido et al., 2009), leaving low concentrations of CH4 in surface water of lakes. Due to the challenge of reliably measuring stable isotope abundances at very low concentrations, the effect of methanotrophic oxidation on isotopes of CH4 in Arctic lakes has not previously been reported. The combination of concentration and isotopic signature is vital for understanding biogeochemical cycling of CH4 on Earth and for assessing pathways for production and oxidation of CH4 on Mars where episodic plumes of CH4 at low concentrations have been detected remotely and measured by instruments on martian rovers. In anticipation of returning samples from Mars to Earth and with increasing interest in astronauts as explorers on Mars, it is urgent to assess geochemical and/or biological processes influencing rates of CH4 formation and destruction (Mumma et al., 2009; Webster et al., 2015). Kinetic isotope effects associated with enzymatic processes during methanogenesis and methanotrophy are well established terrestrial biomarkers and are potential martian biomarkers for subsurface life. Measuring CH4 concentrations and CH4 fluxes are useful to assess the magnitude of emissions, but alone are unable to be used to decipher active production and pathways. Stable isotopic analysis of carbon (δ13C) and hydrogen (δ2H) is a well-established method to delineate the origin of CH4 gas, allowing for the differentiation of CH4 produced by microbial and thermal processes as well as microbial production and oxidation (Schoell, 1980; Whiticar and Faber, 1985; Whiticar et al., 1986; Whiticar, 1999). Despite a wide range of literature using 13C and 2H to interpret origin and thermal maturity of hydrocarbons in petroleum systems (Stahl and Carey, 1975; Schoell, 1980, 1988; Whiticar, 1989; Jackson et al., 2014), there has been limited work on δ13C and δ2H of CH4 in natural environments, most of which has been focused on wetlands (Martens et al., 1992; Hornibrook et al., 1997; Popp et al., 1999; Chanton et al., 2006; Sugimoto and Fujita, 2006; Alstad and Whiticar, 2011). Biogenic CH4 in freshwater environments is produced predominantly within anoxic sediments and is exported into the water column by ebullition (bubbling) or diffusion (Strayer and Tiedje, 1978; Bastviken et al., 2008). Microbial CH4 is produced by methanogens, strictly anaerobic Archaea, who are responsible for 10–50% of overall carbon mineralization in freshwater lakes (Bastviken et al., 2008). In freshwater environments, there are two primary metabolic pathways for CH4 production, acetoclastic methanogenesis (AM) and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis (HM), which have been demonstrated to vary spatially in permafrost-influenced ecosystems (Prater et al., 2007). Both AM and HM are associated with a kinetic isotope effect resulting in depletion of 13C in the product CH4 relative to the pre-cursor substrate (Whiticar et al., 1986; Balabane et al., 1987; Valentine et al., 2004a,b). However, the magnitude of the carbon isotope effect is different for the two primary methanogenic pathways, with AM resulting in δ13CCH4 ranging from −60‰ to −40‰, and HM ranging from −110‰ to −60‰ (Whiticar et al., 1986). Hydrogen isotopes of CH4 similarly become depleted in 2H during microbial CH4 production. The δ2H value of CH4 depends on the precursor for CH4 hydrogen, which is either from cleavage of H2O or acetate (Woltemate et al., 1984; Whiticar, 1999; Chanton et al., 2006). Although this remains contentious, it is generally assumed that during HM, all 4 H atoms are supplied by formation water, whereas during AM, the transfer of the methyl group to CH4 supplies 3 H atoms, and the additional H atom is derived from formation water (Whiticar et al., 1986). As a result, the magnitude of the kinetic isotope effect of hydrogen is different for the two pathways, dependent on value of precursor δ2H, with AM resulting in δ2HCH4 ranging from −530‰ to −250‰, and HM ranging from −250‰ to −170‰ (Sugimoto and Wada, 1995). The isotope systematics of hydrogen for homoacetogenesis in competition with methanogenesis under substrate-limiting conditions and low temperatures of natural systems is not well known (Kotsyurbenko et al., 2001), although culture studies suggest that there is rapid hydrogen isotope exchange between H2 and H2O during homoacetogenesis (Valentine et al., 2004a,b). Methane oxidation (MOx) depends on both the availability of CH4 and dissolved oxygen (DO); high CH4 oxidation rates are usually found at the oxic/anoxic interface where both CH4 and DO are abundant (Bastviken et al., 2002; Dzyuban, 2010; Martinez-Cruz et al., 2015). Anaerobic oxidation of CH4 (AOM) can also occur by utilizing alternative terminal electron acceptors in lieu of dissolved oxygen (Valentine, 2002; Nordi et al., 2013; Segarra et al., 2013, 2015; Milucka et al., 2015). High affinity methanotrophs are able to oxidize CH4 at or below atmospheric concentrations (Bárcena et al., 2010, 2011; Martineau et al., 2014; Christiansen et al., 2015). Isotope fractionation associated with microbial CH4 oxidation leads to systematic enrichment in both 13C and 2H of CH4 in the residual un-oxidized pool (Coleman et al., 1981; Happell et al., 1994; Templeton et al., 2006; Kinnaman et al., 2007). The enrichment in both 13C and 2H during oxidation results in values being increased by <1–30‰ for δ13CCH4 and 3–200‰ for δ2HCH4 (Coleman et al., 1981; Happell et al., 1994; Bastviken et al., 2002). In this study, we report values of δ13C and δ2H for CH4 collected from three, small Arctic lakes in western Greenland to assess seasonal sources and sinks of CH4. Lakes were sampled during open-water conditions in July 2013 and under ice-cover in April 2014 when the lakes had been ice-covered and isolated from the atmosphere for 7–8 months. The studied lakes show considerable variation in concentration and proportions of major ions despite being located along a 6 km segment of a narrow valley. Therefore, we hypothesize that due to chemical heterogeneity, sources and sinks of CH4 in each lake would vary lake-to-lake as well as seasonally. Hundreds of thousands of Holocene lakes dot the landscape in southwestern Greenland (Anderson et al., 2001; Anderson and Stedmon, 2007) and are underlain by continuous permafrost (Jorgensen and Andreasen, 2007). Deglaciation began in the region ~11,000 BP (Van Tatenhove and van der Meer, 1996; Leng et al., 2012), exposing Precambrian metamorphic crystalline bedrock, primarily felsic gneisses (Jensen et al., 2002). As a result, CH4 in these lakes has had little to no influence from buried ancient organic matter, allowing biogenic CH4 cycles to be studied in isolation. To our knowledge, this work provides the first coupled measurements of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) of CH4 under both open-water and ice-covered conditions in a relatively undisturbed, periglacial, lacustrine setting thereby filling critical knowledge gaps concerning biogeochemical cycles of CH4 within small Arctic lakes and isotope fractionation of CH4 in low concentration environments. 2. STUDY AREA Lakes in this study are located between the village of Kangerlussuaq, Greenland at the head of Søndre Strømfjord and the active terminus of the Russell Glacier (Fig. 1). During the last Glacial Maximum, the Greenland ice sheet (GIS) covered the area. Retreat of the GIS likely resulted in formation of the lakes in glacially scoured hollows (Leng et al., 2012). Currently, the margin of the GIS is ~2 km away from the study lakes. The region has continuous permafrost <50 cm below the surface, extending down to 130 m at Kangerlussuaq and 500 m at the edge of the ice sheet (Jorgensen and Andreasen, 2007). Bedrock is predominantly garnet-grade, Archean gneisses with Quaternary glacial, fluvial and alluvial deposits present in low-lying areas. Mean annual air temperature at the Kangerlussuaq weather station from 1974 to 2012 was −6 °C. During warm months of late May to early September, mean temperatures often exceed +11 °C and peak to +20 °C in July. The cold season extends from November to late March, with mean daily temperature averaging −21 °C in February. Precipitation in the Kangerlussuaq area is minimal, with annual precipitation <150 mm yr−1, mostly from June to August (Ohmura and Reeh, 1991). Dwarf shrubs (Salix, Vaccinium and Betula), Sphagnum spp., and graminoids (Carex and Calamagrostis) dominate the tundra vegetation in the region. 2.1. Study lakes In this paper three, small adjacent lakes (surface area <3 ha, maximum depth <8 m) with a range of different morphometries and aquatic chemistries (Fig. 1; Table 1) are studied. Lake names used herein are informal names. The study lakes are part of a series of lakes within a narrow valley overlying a structural shear zone extending from the Russell Glacier to the Søndre Strømfjord (Fig. 1). The smallest lake (0.2 ha), EVV Upper lake, has the highest concentration of sulfate and is the only lake with detectible sulfide in the water column (Table 1). Teardrop lake is the most brackish of the lakes, with conductivity >2500 \( \mu \)S cm\(^{-1}\). In addition, it is highly buffered throughout the water column, with pH of 9.2. Potentilla lake is the most dilute lake (conductivity <250 \( \mu \)S cm\(^{-1}\)) and the largest lake in the study (Table 1). Within the study area, there are isolated patches of bedrock containing thinly interbedded, pyrite-mineralized, metasiltstones and quartzites. Sulfate crusts are present on bedrock exposures of these metasediments. Elevated sulfate contents in some lakes are inferred to be sourced by leaching of pyrite-mineralized metasediments that underlie the lake or adjacent wetlands. Elevated carbonate contents are inferred to be sourced by rare pods of marble reported in the region (Anderson et al., 2001). All of the study lakes are dimictic, exhibiting ice cover from late October to early June. Currently the study lakes are all hydrologically closed-basins, with no direct inflow or outflow channels observed from 2011 to 2014. Due to continuous permafrost, groundwater seepage into the lakes is assumed to be limited. 3. METHODS 3.1. Field methods 3.1.1. Sample collection and physico-chemical analysis Lakes were sampled both in July 2013 and April 2014 in order to capture maximum summer and winter conditions. Henceforth, July samplings will be referred to as open-water and April will be referred to as ice-covered. All water samples and measurements were taken at maximum water depth (\( Z_{\text{max}} \)), determined using bathymetric maps (Appendix 1). Under open-water conditions, samples and measurements were collected using an inflatable Alpaca raft (Anchorage, Alaska, USA), and under ice-covered conditions, a hole (~30 cm in diameter) was augered into the ~2 m of ice cover in order to access the water column. Dissolved oxygen (DO, mg L\(^{-1}\)), pH, and specific conductivity (\( \mu \)S cm\(^{-1}\)) were measured using a YSI 6093 Data Sonde (Yellow Springs Inc., Yellow Springs, OH, USA) deployed at 0.5 m depth intervals. Hydrogen isotopes of water collected from the epilimnion, metalimnion and hypolimnion from each lake were analyzed on a Picarro L2120-i isotopic liquid water and water vapor analyzer equipped with a high precision vaporizer in the Stable Isotope Laboratory at the Department of Geosciences, University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA. 3.1.2. Water-column \( CH_4 \) collection A submersible electronic pump was used to collect water samples for dissolved \( CH_4 \) in the water column for all lakes under open-water conditions and for EVV Upper lake and Teardrop lake under ice-covered conditions. Samples were collected at 0.5–1.0 m intervals through the water column and \( CH_4 \) was immediately stripped in the field using a headspace-equilibrium technique (Westendorp, 1985). For each sample, 500 mL of lake water was collected into a capped 1 L Erlenmeyer flask and vigorously hand shaken for 1 min. Headspace gas in the flask was displaced into a Cali-5-Bond bag using syringes of water collected from the surface of the lake. Dissolved \( CH_4 \) in Potentilla lake under ice-covered conditions was collected using passive diffusion bags (PDBs) in order to obtain a high-resolution profile of dissolved \( CH_4 \) in the water column. The PDBs are composed of a polyethylene membrane with a protective plastic mesh and are commercially available from EON Products Inc. (Georgia, USA). For field deployment, PDBs were attached to a polypropylene rope using stainless steel S-Biners attached to the plastic mesh so that PDBs were oriented perpendicular to the rope and parallel to ice, and the rope was anchored to the ice. After 5 days, PDBs were retrieved from the lake and dissolved gas was sampled immediately in the field using the equilibrium gas stripping method with 500 mL Ball® jars (as opposed to an Erlenmeyer flask). Further details regarding PDB methodology, preparation and applicability can be found in Goldman et al. (2015). 3.1.3. Profundal sediment \( CH_4 \) Profundal sediment samples were taken from \( Z_{\text{max}} \) of each lake during open-water conditions using a Wildco push-coring device. Sediment was collected in polycarbonate plastic barrels with an internal diameter of 6.7 cm. Dissolved gas in the sediment was sampled using an equilibrium gas stripping method similar to the water-column CH₄ (Section 3.1.2.1). Sediment cores were subsectioned into 6–10 cm intervals and put into 8 L Nalgene bottles, with lids altered to include two syringe ports connected to Luer-Lock fittings. Once the sediment was put into the bottle and the lid was shut, the bottle was evacuated using a hand pump connected to a lid port. After evacuation, zero-CH₄ water was injected to create a 4 L sediment–water slurry. The bottle was vigorously shaken for 5 min to displace gas from the sediment-slurry into the headspace. 3.1.4. Littoral sediment CH₄ Littoral sediment gas samples were collected during open-water conditions by physically disturbing the sediment in order to release entrained gas bubbles. Each sample was collected from a vegetated region where water depth was <0.5 m. Gas bubbles were collected using an inverted plastic funnel (28 cm diameter) with a gas-tight sampling tube and 3-way Luer-Lock valve attached to the neck. Gas in the funnel was transferred to a Cali-5-Bond bag using a plastic syringe. Note that we were unable to quantify the volume of sediment sampled. Consequently, concentrations of CH₄ in gas collected from littoral sediments cannot be converted into pool size of CH₄ in the littoral sediments. Rather, the samples were used to constrain the isotopic composition of CH₄ present in the littoral sediments (Chanton, 2005). 3.2. Laboratory methods 3.2.1. Concentration of CH₄ Concentration of water-column CH₄ and sediment CH₄ was measured using a Los Gatos Research (LGR) Methane Carbon Isotope Analyzer (MCIA) (LGR, Mountain View CA, USA) at the Kangerlussuaq International Science Support facility (KISS). The LGR MCIA is a portable, off-axis, integrated cavity output spectrometer that measures CH₄ without sample preparation. All samples were processed within 24 h of collection. For each analysis, 400–600 mL of gas sample was required. Calibration was repeated every 10 samples, with Scotty® gas standards of 50 and 100 ppmv CH₄. Samples were diluted with a known volume of zero-air in order to bring them within the range of the calibration gases. The total concentration of CH₄ in each sample was corrected for dilution and calculated from the sum of the measured headspace partial pressure and the dissolved CH₄ remaining after gas stripping, calculated according to Henry’s law using values after Lide and Fredrikse (1995). Instrumental uncertainty of CH₄ from the MCIA was ±0.5 ppmv, which is one standard deviation of the gas standards analyzed during sample runs. Previously, concentrations of CH₄ from MCIA were analyzed on a Gas Chromatograph Flame Ionization Detector (GC-FID) to confirm validity (Appendix 2). Aliquots of each sample were transferred to pre-evacuated glass vials and returned to Indiana University, USA for carbon and hydrogen isotopic analysis of CH₄. 3.3. Carbon and hydrogen isotopic analysis of CH₄ Stable C and H isotopes of CH₄ were analyzed using two approaches. MCIA was used for C isotopic analysis on samples with CH₄ concentrations >50 ppmv, but the MCIA produces unreliable results at lower concentrations (Appendix 3). Therefore, stable isotope ratios of both carbon and hydrogen of CH₄ were measured using continuous-flow gas chromatography-oxidation/pyrolysis isotope ratio mass spectrometry (GC-ox/pyr-IRMS) with a laboratory-built gas pre-concentrator interfaced with a ThermoFinnigan GCC and Delta Plus XP IRMS at the Stable Isotope Research Facility (SIRF) at Indiana University in Bloomington, Indiana. The pre-concentrator design was modeled after principles described by Merritt et al. (1995) and inlet system developed by Miller et al. (2002) for carbon isotope analysis and Brass and Rockmann (2010) for carbon and hydrogen isotopes. The gas sample containing CH₄ is first dried by passing through a cold trap and then passed into a stainless steel sample loop packed with HayeSep D and kept at −130 °C. After the CH₄ is extracted, the trap is warmed to −20 °C and the CH₄ is cryofocused at the head of Varian Porabond Q GC column. Carbon of CH₄ is converted to CO₂ at 950 °C and H is converted to H₂ in an alumina reactor at 1450 °C. Carbon and hydrogen isotope ratios are expressed in standard δ notation (δ¹³C and δ²H): \[ \delta = [(R_{\text{sample}} - R_{\text{standard}})/R_{\text{standard}}] \times 1000 = \%o \] where \( R \) is the molar ratio of heavy to light isotopes (¹³C/¹²C, ²H/¹H) for both sample and standard. Carbon isotope values are referenced to VPDB and hydrogen isotope values are referenced to VSMOW by comparison with pure CH₄ where the isotopic composition has been measured by off-line combustion (http://mypage.iu.edu/~aschimme/compounds.html). Instrumental uncertainty of δ¹³C and δ²H from the GC-C-IRMS was calculated as ±0.4‰ and as ±10‰ respectively, which is one standard deviation for repeated measures of the gas standards analyzed during sample runs. 3.4. Statistical analyses Statistical analyses were made using IBM SPSS Statistics. Combined concentrations of CH₄ and isotopic compositions for all study lakes during each season were assessed for normal distribution via the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, and were found to be non-normally distributed. Student’s t tests of unequal variance were used for testing statistically significant differences in concentrations of CH₄ and isotopic values of CH₄ between seasons and between study results and reported isotopic values from other natural, freshwater environments above 55° latitude. Systematic changes in δ¹³C and δ²H were analyzed using linear regression, based upon the pathway of oxidation leading to systematic enrichment in both ¹³C and ²H of CH₄ in the residual unoxidized pool (Coleman et al., 1981; Happell et al., 1994; Templeton et al., 2006; Kinnaman et al., 2007). 4. RESULTS 4.1. Water-column CH₄ 4.1.1. Concentration of CH₄ Under open-water conditions, concentrations of CH₄ were strongly related to DO dynamics (Fig. 2). Dissolved CH₄ concentrations in the surface waters of the three lakes ranged from 0.9 to 2.4 µM (Fig. 3). Clinograde DO profiles were measured in EVV Upper and Potentilla lakes with DO saturated in surface water (9.5 and 11.0 mg L⁻¹ respectively), and decreasing with depth to anoxia (<0.5 mg L⁻¹; Fig. 3). In EVV Upper lake and Potentilla lake, CH₄ concentrations increased down the water column with decreasing DO, with the maximum CH₄ observed in the anoxic water at the sediment–water interface (150 and 67 µM respectively). Teardrop lake was oxic to suboxic (DO > 1 mg L⁻¹) throughout the water column with an oxygen anomaly at 4.0 m, wherein DO drastically shifted from >10 mg L⁻¹ at 3.5 m to 1.8 mg L⁻¹ at 4 m, and then returned to 7 mg L⁻¹ at 4.5 m. Throughout the water column of Teardrop lake, there were low CH₄ concentrations (<8.1 µM; Fig. 3). In all three lakes, concentrations of CH₄ were significantly greater under ice-covered conditions compared to open-water conditions (n = 31, p = 0.0002). A downward increase in CH₄ concentration from below ice-cover to the sediment–water interface was measured in all three lakes under ice-covered conditions (Fig. 3). Potentilla lake was the only lake with measurable DO under ice-cover (Fig. 3). Consequently, CH₄ concentrations dynamically followed DO with highest concentrations (220 µM) observed within the anoxic bottom waters and decreasing concentrations tracking increasing dissolved DO upward through the water column until concentrations of CH₄ reached levels <1 µM immediately below the ice (Fig. 3). EVV Upper and Teardrop lakes were entirely anoxic below ice-cover with concentrations of CH₄ >50 µM throughout the water column (Fig. 3). 4.1.2. \( \delta^{13}C \) of water-column CH₄ Under open-water conditions, \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) in the three lakes ranged from −68.7‰ to +7.4‰ (Fig. 3). In both EVV Upper lake and Potentilla lake, CH₄ was enriched in \( ^{13}C \) in the surface waters relative to the bottom waters (Fig. 3). At 4.0 m depth, an anomalously heavy \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) value of +7.4‰ was observed (Fig. 3). In Potentilla lake, with the exception of 2.0 m, \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) was stable from the surface down the water column to 6.0 m. Isotopic evidence of production pathways for CH4 in Greenlandic lakes Bedrock in the Kangerlussuaq region consists of tightly folded, felsic gneisses exposed to garnet-grade metamorphism and contains no measurable organic C, therefore we assume that all CH4 within the study lakes is biologically produced. To look at differences in microbial production of CH4, we focus our discussion on the sediment CH4 in the study lakes from open-water conditions. In order to distinguish AM and HM CH4 production pathways from each other isotopically, isotopic compositions of H2O, dissolved inorganic matter (DIC), and organic matter (OM) must be constant. If not, the variation in δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 reflect not only different production pathways, but also variation in environmental factors that affect isotopic composition of reactants. In the study lakes, δ2H2O in the water column slightly decreases with distance away from the margin of the GIS, from a median of −91.5‰ in EVV Upper lake to −97.4‰ in Potentilla lake. Despite the spatial variation in δ2H2O among the lakes, there is no significant relationship between δ2H2O from the water column and δ2HCH4 from sediments (Fig. 5), suggesting that δ2HCH4 is not a direct reflection of variation in 2H2O. In addition to differences in δ2H2O among the lakes, there are also variations in δ13CDIC from the water column among the lakes (Stern et al., 2014). However, there is not enough data to confirm or deny if δ13CCH4 is reflecting variation in δ13CDIC. Approximately a 5‰ difference in δ13COM of particulate OM from profundal sediments was observed lake-to-lake, ranging from −29.2‰ in EVV Upper lake to −24.5‰ (Table 1). Data suggest that the ~45‰ difference in δ13CCH4 of profundal sediment may reflect the δ13COM of precursor OM (Fig. 5b). However, the range in δ13COM is narrow compared to the overall range observed in aquatic chemistry and δ13CCH4 among the lakes. In both the profundal and littoral sediments of the study lakes, values of δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 are consistent with microbial CH4 production (Fig. 4) (Whiticar et al., 1986; Whiticar, 1999). Profundal sediment CH4 is more depleted in 13C and enriched in 2H relative to littoral sediment CH4 (Table 2), suggesting different microbial production pathways, partial oxidation of the littoral sediments, or higher precursor δ13COM in the littoral sediments. However, δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 values from both profundal and littoral sediments plot primarily within the AM field (Fig. 4). The HM pathway field in the δ13CCH4 and δ2HCH4 classification diagram was determined from marine samples where δ2H2O is ~0‰ (Whiticar, 1999; Waldron et al., 1999b). As a result, the HM pathway field may not accurately represent Arctic waters where δ2H2O ≪ 0‰. Using the assumptions from Chanton et al. (2006), we can adjust the measured sediment δ2HCH4 for the δ2H2O of the water in the lake where the CH4 was formed using the following equation: \[ \delta^{2}\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{CH}_4\text{-measured}} - \delta^{2}\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\text{ water}} = \delta^{2}\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{CH}_4\text{-adjusted}} \] In order to use this equation, δ2HCH4 in the sediments must reflect CH4 production without isotopic overprinting from oxidation. If CH4 in the sediments was subjected to oxidation then a positive correlation between δ13CCH4 and δ²HCH₄ would be observed (Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Alperin and Reeburgh, 1988; Whiticar, 1999). An inverse relationship is observed between δ¹³CCH₄ and δ²HCH₄ from sediments, confirming CH₄ in the sediments had not been oxidized (Fig. 4). The adjustment for δ²H₂O shifted δ²HCH₄ of profundal sediments into the HM pathways field, whereas the littoral sediment δ²HCH₄ remains primarily in the AM pathway field (Fig. 6). Without δ¹³COM in the littoral sediments of each lake, we are unable to assess if the variations between the sediments are the result of different microbial pathways, or if there is also variations in precursor OM. However, δ¹³COM and C/N ratios of littoral sediments from EVV Upper lake suggested OM is sourced from in-lake primary production (Thompson, 2015). The difference in CH₄ production pathway between the littoral and profundal sediments likely reflects the supply of labile organic compounds and δ¹³COM, which would influence CH₄ formation (Duc et al., 2010). In the littoral sediments, aquatic macrophytes and phytoplankton supply a source of labile OM, resulting in AM. Correspondingly, the lake with the highest CH₄ concentrations in the littoral sediments (EVV Upper lake) has the highest concentration of aquatic macrophytes, with the shoreline dominated by Hippuris vulgaris. In freshwater environments, CH₄ typically is produced by AM (Whiticar et al., 1986; Conrad, 1999) because plant root exudates and fresh OM provide a ready supply of labile OM to the bacteria. Previous theoretical values predict that HM accounts for ~30% of overall CH₄ production in freshwater lakes (Conrad, 1999). In high-latitude Sphagnum bogs, CH₄ production via HM is dominant because of an inhibition of the AM pathway, whereas AM is dominant in Carex-rich environments (Popp et al., 1999; Chanton et al., 2006). Sphagnum spp. was a significant component of littoral communities of lakes in this study. In closed lake basins, OM from these areas may represent important carbon inputs, which could be influencing the HM pathway for CH₄ production in the profundal sediments. We were surprised to discover that despite significant variations in DOC, SO₄²⁻ and conductivity among the lakes, formation pathways of CH₄ in littoral and profundal sediments seem to be identical in all of the lakes. Competition for substrates (particularly acetate and H₂) favors sulfate reduction (SR), inhibiting CH₄ production (Lovely and Klung, 1983, 1986; Ward and Winfrey, 1985; Scholten et al., 2002). Methanogenesis typically does not occur until SO₄²⁻ is exhausted and SR rates have decreased because SR can very effectively uptake both H₂ and acetate, maintaining H₂ and acetate concentrations too low for methanogens (Lovely and Klung, 1986). In the study lakes, EVV Upper lake has the highest SO₄²⁻ concentrations and is the only lake with detectable H₂S in the water column during open-water conditions (Table 1). The presence and accumulation of CH₄ in the sediments indicates that there is sufficient carbon to both fuel reduction of the SO₄²⁻ pool and support methanogenesis in EVV Upper lake. Given the current data, there is no way to assess if communities are spatially coexisting or separated by vertical stratification. However, EVV Upper lake does have the lowest concentration of CH₄ in the profundal sediments, which could be due to SR reducing methanogenesis. Isotopic evidence of consumption of CH₄ by methanotrophic oxidation Under both open-water and ice-covered conditions, concentrations of CH₄ are strongly related to dissolved oxygen dynamics, suggesting MOx is reducing water column CH₄. Methane can also be consumed under anoxic conditions, by AOM (Valentine, 2002; Nordi et al., 2013; Segarra et al., 2013, 2015; Milucka et al., 2015). However, the strong relationship between CH₄ and DO suggests that in the lakes here, aerobic MOx is the dominant pathway consuming CH₄. Oxidation of CH₄ leads to a systematic enrichment in both ¹³C and ²H of the residual un-oxidized CH₄ (Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Whiticar and Faber, 1985; Alperin and Reeburgh, 1988; Whiticar, 1999). In the profundal and littoral sediments of all of the lakes, an inverse relationship is observed between δ¹³CCH₄ and δ²HCH₄, suggesting the CH₄ has not been fully oxidized. In the water column under both open-water and ice-covered conditions, a strong, positive correlation between δ¹³CCH₄ and δ²HCH₄ is observed in all the lakes (\( n = 51, R = 0.93, p < 0.001 \); Fig. 2c), indicating CH₄ has been oxidized. In oxic waters, CH₄ is systematically enriched in both ¹³C and ²H, which is consistent with MOx (Whiticar and Faber, 1985; Happell et al., 1994; Whiticar, 1999; Bastviken et al., 2002; Alstad and Whiticar, 2011). The slope of enrichment of ¹³C and 2H for our lake sample, calculated as \( \delta^{2}H/\delta^{13}C \) (7.9), is within the slope of projected oxidation predicted by previous experimental studies, which range from 5.9 to 13 (Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Whiticar, 1999; Kinnaman et al., 2007). In general, the lower concentrations of CH4 are from oxic waters and are strongly related to higher values of both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \). However, the CH4 most enriched in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) is from samples with concentrations of CH4 above 1 \( \mu \)M. It should be noted that these extreme values are from a single depth interval with duplicate measurements in Teardrop lake under open-water conditions and correspond with an oxygen anomaly. Assuming the sediments are the only source of CH4 to the water column in the study lakes, 75–99% of all CH4 from the sediment–water interface is reduced by the time it reaches the lake surface. If MOx is driving the depletion of CH4 concentrations through the water column then fractionation factors (\( \alpha \)) for methanotrophy can be estimated for each CH4 profile using an open system model at steady state (Happell et al., 1994): \[ f_{MOx} = (\delta_i - \delta_f)/((\alpha - 1) \times 1000) \] where \( f_{MOx} \) is the fraction of CH4 removed by oxidization, \( \delta_i \) and \( \delta_f \) are the \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) or \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) of the initial pool from the sediment–water interface and final un-oxidized residue at the lake surface, respectively, and \( \alpha \) is the fractionation factor. Resulting \( \alpha \) values range from 1.02 to 1.06 for C and 1.2 to 1.8 for H. With the exception of \( \alpha \) values for \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) from EVV Upper lake during open-water conditions (1.2), \( \alpha \) values for \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) in this study are higher than \( \alpha \) values previously reported in both laboratory and natural environments (1.002–1.013 for C and 1.095–1.325 for H) (Zyakun et al., 1979; Coleman and Risatti, 1981; Whiticar et al., 1986; Alperin and Reeburgh, 1988; Whiticar, 1999). Estimation of \( \alpha \) for \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) from CH4 concentrations and \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) from a series of small European lakes under open-water conditions suggests comparable \( \alpha \) from MOx (Rinta et al., 2015). The higher \( \alpha \) values calculated here suggest a unique microbial community is present in these lakes that hasn’t been observed in the laboratory may be carrying out MOx. The largest \( \alpha \) for methanotrophy calculated in this study for both C and H (1.06 and 1.8) is from under open-water conditions in Teardrop lake. Congruently, the CH4 most enriched in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) is from 4.0 m depth in Teardrop lake under open-water conditions. Concentrations of DO are >1 mg L\(^{-1}\) through the water column of Teardrop lake, but do not follow a clinograde DO profile like the other lakes. At 4.0 m, an anomalous DO shift is observed, corresponding with a strong enrichment in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) of CH4. In addition, whereas in the other lakes the concentration of CH4 increases down the water column under open-water conditions, the concentration of CH4 in Teardrop lake is higher in the epilimnion (2.02–8.05 \( \mu \)M) than in the bottom waters (1.4–1.6 \( \mu \)M), likely caused by methanotrophy in the lower waters or lateral addition of dissolved CH4 from productive, littoral waters (Schilder et al., 2013). Recently, evidence of methanotrophy fueled by DO production by photosynthetic algae was reported from a meromictic lake (Milucka et al., 2015), but corresponding \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and/or \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) were not analyzed. In Teardrop lake during under open-water conditions, the entire water column is euphotic and suspended calcareous algal mats are observed within the water column, potentially responsible for the anomalous DO profile. We suspect that the anomalously-enriched \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) of CH4 from these intervals may be the result of a dynamic microbial community associated with the calcareous mats, with processes not previously identified in laboratory studies of MOx isotope systematics. The elevated CH4 concentrations in the epilimnion of Teardrop lake may reflect inputs from littoral sediments (Bastviken et al., 2004), as the \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) in the upper water column falls within the range observed in the littoral sediments. Additionally, elevated CH4 concentrations in the epilimnion of Teardrop lake may also be the result of CH4 that escaped the suspended mat communities, or aerobic methanogenesis (Grossart et al., 2011; Bogard et al., 2014). 5.3. Regional comparison of isotopic data In Arctic lakes, measurements of both \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^{2}H_{CH_4} \) have only been reported from ebullition (Martens et al., 1992; Nakagawa et al., 2002; Negandhi et al., 2013), profundal sediments (Woltemate et al., 1984; Oremland et al., 1987), anoxic waters (Oremland et al., 1987) and an Antarctic perennially ice-covered lake (Wand et al., 2006). A compilation of data for all natural, freshwater environments above 55° latitude from studies reporting both \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) for CH4 show isotopic values clustered within the field associated with microbial production (Fig. 7). Values more positive than −30‰ for \( \delta^{13}C \) and −150‰ for \( \delta^{2}H \) have not been previously reported in CH4 from Arctic freshwater environments. The values of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) for CH4 reported here from the water column in small Greenlandic lakes are significantly more enriched in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) (\( n_1 = 61, n_2 = 301, p < 0.0001 \)) than values reported from other Arctic freshwater environments (Fig. 7) (Woltemate et al., 1984; Hermichen et al., 1985; Martens et al., 1992; Popp et al., 1999; Waldron et al., 1999a; Nakagawa et al., 2002; Chanton et al., 2006; Alstad and Whiticar, 2011; Negandhi et al., 2013). The extremely large H isotope shifts (up to 550‰) in this study appear to be unprecedented for natural environments, having only previously been documented in laboratory oxidation experiments of C2+ n-alkanes and substituted aromatics (Kinnaman et al., 2007; Wijker et al., 2013). As a result, low \( \mu \)M concentrations of CH4 accompanied by an extreme enrichment in both \( ^{13}C \) and \( ^{2}H \) here reveals that MOx has the ability to fractionate C and H isotopes significantly more than previously recognized. High affinity methanotrophs in Arctic soils have been demonstrated to be able to oxidize CH4 at concentrations at or below atmospheric levels, however there are no corresponding isotopic measurements to suggest that high affinity methanotrophy is driving the extreme isotope enrichment (Bárcena et al., 2010, 2011; Martineau et al., 2014; Christiansen et al., 2015). Therefore, it is possible that the results here are not unique to small, Arctic lakes but reflect our ability to measure \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^{2}H \) of CH4 at lower concentrations than have previously been reported. The shaded area denotes the field of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^2H \) associated with microbial CH$_4$ production (Whiticar et al., 1986; Whiticar, 1999). (For interpretation of the references to colour in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.) 5.4. Implications for astrobiology On Mars, CH$_4$ is episodically observed in the atmosphere at low concentrations, but formation and oxidation processes are contentious unknowns and pathways for gas migration from the subsurface to surface have not been identified (Mumma et al., 2009; Webster et al., 2015). Low CH$_4$ concentrations in the martian atmosphere could reflect various combinations of low production rates, effective sequestration in the subsurface, and oxidation of CH$_4$ along pathways to the surface. Regardless of whether the formation of CH$_4$ on Mars is biological or geochemical, if enzyme-based microbial consumption is occurring then a kinetic isotope effect resulting in strong enrichment of $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ at low CH$_4$ concentrations could be a potent indicator of subsurface life. Microbial drawdown of CH$_4$ to sub-$\mu$M levels, accompanied by extreme enrichment of heavy isotopes in small lakes under Arctic conditions on Earth highlights the potential for measuring the isotopic compositions of CH$_4$ on Mars as a means to differentiate between biological and geochemical oxidation processes. 6. CONCLUSIONS In Greenland, small closed-basin lakes in close proximity to one another and located within continuous permafrost appear to operate independently, develop distinct chemical compositions, and express local microbial ecologies. For example, only EVV Upper lake has detectible sulfide and high concentrations of sulfate, whereas Teardrop lake is highly buffered throughout the water column, with pH of 9.2. As a result, CH$_4$ concentrations among Arctic lakes vary significantly both seasonally and annually. Carbon and hydrogen isotopic composition of CH$_4$ suggest that despite variations in concentration, CH$_4$ was produced via AM in the littoral sediments and HM in the profundal sediments in all of the lakes. In the water column of all of the studied lakes, when DO was present, a positive correlation in \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^2H_{CH_4} \) was observed, indicating that in these lakes, aerobic MOx was driving dissolved CH$_4$ dynamics. The low concentrations of CH$_4$ accompanied by extreme enrichment in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ reveals that MOx has the ability to fractionation C and H isotopes significantly more than previously recognized. We suggest that the enrichment in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ of CH$_4$ is the result of unusually efficient methanotrophic communities associated with photosynthetic algal mats. Additionally, the extreme enrichment of $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ of CH$_4$ from MOx has significant implications for interpretation of CH$_4$ cycles, which are necessary to define source estimates in emission modeling. Without understanding local geology and biology, stable isotopic values of CH$_4$ that are greater than $-30\%$ for \( \delta^{13}C \) and $-150\%$ for \( \delta^2H \) may be misinterpreted as thermogenic, geothermal, or abiogenic in origin. However, our understanding of the local bedrock combined with the statistically significant relationship between \( \delta^{13}C_{CH_4} \) and \( \delta^2H_{CH_4} \) within the water-column and sediments confirms that the water-column CH$_4$ enriched in $^{13}C$ and $^2H$ is the result of MOx. In order to fully appreciate the global extent to which MOx influences \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^2H \) of CH$_4$, detailed measurements of \( \delta^{13}C \) and \( \delta^2H \) at depth intervals through water column of numerous lakes spanning low to high latitudes are needed. Lentic small water bodies: Variability of pesticide transport and transformation patterns Uta Ulrich a,*, Georg Hörmann a, Malte Unger b, Matthias Pfannerstill c, Frank Steinmann c, Nicola Fohrer a a Institute of Natural Resource Conservation, Christian-Albrechts University Kiel, Olshausenstr. 75, 24118 Kiel, Germany b Gesellschaft für Freilandökologie und Naturschutzplanung, Stuthagen 25, 24113 Molfsee, Germany c State Agency for Agriculture, the Environment and Rural Areas Schleswig-Holstein, Hamburger Chaussee 25, 24220 Flinthbek, Germany HIGHLIGHTS • Transformation products of applied in the previous year were clearly detected in the following year. • Parent compounds were measured in the year of application only. • Consistent concentration patterns were observed for metazachlor and for the transformation products but not for flufenacet. • Positives of a pesticide probably present a snapshot, they may originate from former applications at larger distance. • Subsurface inputs are a crucial entry path for pesticides into lentic small water bodies and are not well understood, yet. ARTICLE INFO Article history: Received 6 July 2017 Received in revised form 2 November 2017 Accepted 3 November 2017 Available online 9 November 2017 Editor: Kevin V. Thomas Keywords: Lentic small water bodies Flufenacet Metazachlor Pesticides Transformation products Input pathways Pond GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT A B S T R A C T Lentic small water bodies have a high ecological potential as they fulfill several ecosystem services such as the retention of water and pollutants. They serve as a hot spot of biodiversity. Due to their location in or adjacent to agricultural fields, they can be influenced by inputs of pesticides and their transformation products. Since small water bodies have rarely been part of monitorings/campaigns up to now, their current exposure and processes guiding the pesticide input are not understood, yet. This study presents results of a sampling campaign of 10 lentic small water bodies from 2015 to 2016. They were sampled once after the spring application for a pesticide target screening, before autumn application and three times after rainfall events following the application. The autumn sampling focused on the herbicides metazachlor, flufenacet and their transformation products - oxalic acid and - sulfonic acid as representatives for common pesticides in the study region. The concentrations were associated with rainfall before and after application, characteristics of the site and the water bodies, physicochemical parameters and the applied amount of pesticides. The key results of the pesticide screening in spring indicate positive detections of pesticides which have not been applied for years to the single fields. The autumn sampling showed frequent occurrences of the transformation products, which are formed in soil, from 39% to 94% of all samples (n = 71). Discharge patterns were observed for metazachlor with highest concentrations in the first sample after application and then decreasing, but not for flufenacet. The concentrations of the 1. Introduction The environmental fate of pesticides and their effects on non-target areas and organisms has been investigated for many decades (among others Kreuger, 1998; Leu et al., 2004). Due to the European Water Framework Directive (WFD) (2009/128/EC, 2009), a monitoring of pesticide concentrations in rivers with a catchment > 10 km², in lakes with a surface area >50 ha and groundwater has been obligatory in the European member states since 2000. Surface water bodies below these surface/catchment sizes are not considered within the EU-WFD. These so called small water bodies (SWB) are often located in rural areas with intensive agricultural use and have a considerable potential to be harmed by agrochemicals since they are adjacent and in direct contact with agricultural fields (Schäfer et al., 2007; Liess et al., 2008; Bunzel et al., 2014). Potential input pathways are by air and water. Water related transport pathways are by surface runoff, lateral flow in the unsaturated zone or shallow groundwater in the saturated zone (Du et al., 2016; Fares, 2016). However, SWB should receive more attention since they perform important hydro-ecological functions: they collect storm water directly by tile drainages and surface runoff or indirectly by subsurface flow and can interact with groundwater (EPCN, 2010; Céréghino et al., 2014; Golus and Bajkiewicz-Grabowska, 2016). Furthermore, SWB retain pollutants by sorption/sedimentation processes, support microbiological degradation and plant uptake (Steidl et al., 2008; Das Gupta et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2016). Due to the changing physicochemical environment in SWB (Lischeid and Kalettka, 2012), they provide a variety of different habitats which leads to a high biodiversity in these ecosystems (Downing, 2010; Biggs et al., 2016; Hill et al., 2016). Especially for amphibians, lentic SWB are of importance since they enable the change between aquatic and terrestrial habitat according to the current life cycle. If SWB are located in an appropriate setting, they act as step stones for migrating species and support genetic exchange as well as meta-populations in habitats (Roe and Georges, 2007; Jeliazkov et al., 2014). Such a patchy spatial arrangement of SWB allows species to migrate to favored habitats when climate change alters environmental conditions (Rosset and Oertli, 2011). According to their high number at global scale, SWB are assessed to be a relevant part of the carbon cycle and contribute significantly to carbon sequestration (Gilbert et al., 2016; Holgerson and Raymond, 2016). So far, SWB have just been protected by the Council Directive 92/43/EEC on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora (92/43/EEC, 1992). Since authorities/researchers are aware of the importance of SWB, they attract more attention by selected monitoring programs (Brinke et al., 2015; Tamis et al., 2017) or legal instruments such as National Action Plans for the sustainable use of Pesticides (NAP). The mentions of SWB s in NAPs of other European states are listed in (Table 1). Considerable pesticide contaminations have been found in lotic SWB with maximum concentrations up to 130 µg L⁻¹ for prosulfocarb, 129 µg L⁻¹ for ethofumesat and 92 µg L⁻¹ for metamitron and several exceedances of environmental quality standards were reported (Neumann et al., 2003; Brinke et al., 2015; Szöcs et al., 2017). However, these studies demonstrate that the data base for SWB is too small to give a representative status of contamination, especially for lentic SWB (LSWB). The collected data are inconsistent in sampling procedure, strategy, amount and selection of the active compound and solely demonstrate the current status at the date of sampling (Schreiner et al., 2016; Ulrich et al., 2015; Brinke et al., 2015). Besides, driving factors of pesticide transport into LSWB and of their transformation processes have not been investigated and are not understood, yet. To better understand pesticide fate at sites with lentic SWB and to protect valuable functions of these water bodies, the objectives of our study are (i) to improve and enhance the data base for pesticide contamination in lentic SWB, (ii) to observe the spatial and temporal heterogeneity of pesticide input into these water bodies within one catchment, (iii) to record transformation patterns of the mother compounds into their transformation products and (iv) to relate physico-chemical characteristics of the target compounds, hydrological parameters and site characteristics to the findings. Despite of several definitions of SWB in terms of size or water levels, the authors refer to perennial rivers/lotic water bodies with catchments <10 km² and lakes/lentic water bodies with a surface area <50 ha based on the EU Water Framework Directive. 2. Material and methods In our study, 10 LSWB were monitored in autumns 2015 and 2016 after pesticide application. Event-based grab samples were analyzed for the applied herbicides flufenacet and metazachlor as well as their transformation products - oxalic acid (OA) and - sulfonic acid (ESA). 2.1. Description of the study site and sampling points The catchment of the lowland river Kielstau is located in the North of Germany, Federal State Schleswig-Holstein (Fig. 1). Briefly summarized, it is a catchment with an area of 50 km² and the river Kielstau has a length of 17 km. The region with plain topography is intensively used for agriculture (63% of catchment area). Due to the lowland character, hydraulic gradients are low and there is a high potential for water retention in the landscape (Kiesel et al., 2010). The groundwater levels are high and the shallow groundwater is in close interaction with surface water (Pfannerstill et al., 2014). Approximately 38% of the agricultural fields are drained to improve management practices and plant growth (Fohrer et al., 2007). The prevalent soil types are Planosols and Luvisols and Gleysols and Histosols in the depressions. The average annual temperature is 8.9 °C, the annual precipitation is 885 mm and the annual sunshine duration is 1631 h (data from 1990 to 2016; DWD, 2017a). The Kielstau catchment was appointed as Unesco demosite in 2010 (Fohrer and Schmalz, 2012). As selection criteria, the target pesticides had to be applied to the surrounding fields, the owners had to agree to the sampling and provisioning of application data. Since metazachlor and flufenacet are the most common herbicides applied in rape and winter grain in autumn, the LSWB are located in either rape or winter grain fields with sizes of 4–15 ha. The LSWB are closed depression not connected to discharging or supplying drainage pipes. Evaporation and seepage are assumed to be the loss components. The LSWB are mainly surrounded by a furrow/dam. Exemplarily, Fig. 2 shows the variety of the LSWB concerning size and vegetation. The land use changed from 2015 to 2016 due to the crop rotation system (Table 2). The farmers reported about the date of application, product used, amount applied, field size and drainage system. 2.2. Sampling procedure and chemical analyses In both years, samples were collected in each LSWB once before application of the herbicides on 27/08/2015 and 23/08/2016 and at three dates after application. The individual sampling was event based depending on the date of application and the occurrence of rainfall (see chapter 2.4). The samples were collected at 1 to 3 locations of the water body in a depth of approximately 10–20 cm below the surface with a grab sampler and merged to a mixed sample. These locations were marked and used for subsequent sampling. The samples were stored in glass bottles at −18 °C until analysis. The water samples were analyzed for pH, Oxygen content, electrical conductivity, temperature and redox potential (WTW 3540) in the field according to the common guidelines (DIN 384044, 1976; DIN 384046, 1984; ISO 5814, 2012; ISO 7888, 1993; ISO 10523, 2008). The autumn samples were analyzed after 24 h sedimentation using an AB Sciex 5500 Qtrap with a Synergi 4 μm HydroRP 80A (Phenomenex) column in negative modus for flufenacet-ESA, -OA and metazachlor-ESA. The mobile phase consists of 1 mmol L−1 ammonium acetate buffer and acetonitrile/methanol 50:50, both acidificated with 20 μL acidic acid L−1. Flufenacet, metazachlor and -OA were analyzed with an AB Sciex 6500 Qtrap and a Zorbax Eclipse XDB 3.5 μm (Agilent) column in negative modus with mobile phase of 100% ultrapure water and 100% acetonitrile, both acidificated with 1 mL formic acid L−1. The injection volume of both methods accounted for 100 μL. The Limit of Quantification (LOQ) was 0.01 μg L−1 for flufenacet and metazachlor and 0.025 μg L−1 for the other compounds. Results below the LOQ were set to 0.5 LOQ for illustration in figures and further calculations. The recovery rate for all compounds is in the range of 80–120% determined with addition of a 0.25 ng mL−1 standard of each compound in every fifth sample. To estimate the pesticide contamination of the spring applications, all LSWB were sampled as described above on 7th July 2015 and 5th July 2016, and were analyzed for a target screening of 108 pesticides including 7 TPs. The TPs of metazachlor and flufenacet were not part of the target screening. Here, just concentrations above the LOQ are used for further statistical analysis. The samples were first centrifuged for 30 min at 4 °C with 20,000 rotations min−1. The analyses were then carried out with an Agilent 6460 Triple Quadrupole LC/MS and a Hypersil ODS 250 mm, 3 μm (MZ Analysentechnik) column in both, positive and negative modus. The mobile phase consists of 100% acetonitrile and a 11 mmol L−1 ammonium formate buffer. The recovery rate for the compounds is in the range of 80–110% determined with addition of a 0.12 ng mL−1 standard of each compound in every seventh sample. Fig. 2. Hydrological data The effect of pesticide input via drift during the application procedure was estimated with data of wind speed and wind direction from the station “Flensburg Schäferhaus” of the German Weather Service, situated approximately 12 km from the catchment (DWD, 2017b). Water flow into the LSWB during the sampling period may either increase input of pesticides or dilute pesticide concentrations. The changes of the water level in the LSWB were used as indicator for water inflow/outflow since inputs via precipitation were assessed to be negligible due to the small surface area of the LSWB. Simple rods were installed in the water body close to the bank in August 2016. At every sampling date, the distance between water surface and end of rod was measured and relative water level changes were determined. Precipitation data were measured with an automatic rain gauge (Ott Pluvio, Germany) (LLUR, 2017a) as daily sums at Satrup village, in 8 km distance from most LSWB. Additionally, daily sums were measured with a Hellmann rain gauge at a distance of 2–4 km away from the ISWB in Maasbüll to analyze small-scale variation of precipitation (Hansen, 2016). 2.4. Sampling patterns Previous studies within the Kielstau revealed that on average, a rainfall event of approximately 10 mm causes an increase of the main river's discharge (Ulrich, 2011; Ulrich et al., 2012; Fohrer et al., 2014). Hence, the LSWB were sampled after precipitation sums of at least 10 mm. The decision for a sampling was made based on the weather forecast and the rainfall of the last 24 h. The sampling dates varied according to the date of application and the rainfall patterns (Table 3). In 2015, the third sampling took place approximately four weeks after the second sampling to leave time for transformation processes of the studied pesticides. The results from 2015 showed that these processes occur soon after application. Therefore, the third sampling in 2016 was conducted after the third relevant rainfall event. Digital maps and data analysis Landscape parameters in the surrounding of each LSWB were derived from a digital soil type map based on “Reichsbodenschätzung und Bodenübersichtskarte” BUEK25 (LLUR, 2017b), with data of soil type and the humic content classes. A digital elevation grid with a 1 × 1 m (LVermGeo, 2005b) resolution was used to calculate the slopes with spatial analyst of ArcMap 10 (2010). The surface area, the circumference of the LSWB and the shoreline with higher vegetation such as shrubs, bushes and trees, which prevent input via drift, and the width of the buffer strips were quantified with Digital Ortho Photos (GeoBasis-DE, 2012) and field mappings. The analysis of the collected data was carried out with the statistical program R, version 3.3.3 (R Developing Core Team, 2008). The GGally package creates a matrix of plots with a given data set. Here, the following correlations were calculated: • Concentration of target compounds applied with physicochemical data • Concentration of target compounds applied with site characteristics • Mean concentration of target compounds applied at current year with physicochemical data • Mean concentration of target compounds applied at current year with site characteristics • Median concentration of target compounds applied at current year with physicochemical data • Median concentration of target compounds applied at current year with site characteristics 3. Results and discussion of pesticide analyses 4.1. Pesticide target screening after spring application The analyses showed that from the measured 108 compounds, ten compounds in 2015 and twelve compounds in 2016 were quantified above the LOQ (Fig. 5). Most of the compounds with positive findings were detected in one or few LSWB, but metolachlor, terbuthylazine and its TP desethylterbuthylazine were found in each LSWB. Comparing both years, azoxystrobin, cyproconazole, diflufenican were measured solely in 2016, while pirimicarb was found only in 2015. The pesticide concentrations in 2015 were close to the LOQ with four exemptions clearly above 0.1 μg L⁻¹. In 2016, seven findings were higher than 0.1 μg L⁻¹. The highest detected concentration after the spring application was 0.63 μg metolachlor L⁻¹ in A10. Multiple-pesticide contaminations from 3 to 7 compounds were observed in the single LSWB whereas the number of contaminants increased from 2015 to 2016. The highest number of compounds was observed in A7 with 6 compounds in 2015 and 7 compounds in 2016. Due to their high uncertainty, the values of methyldesphenylchloridazone were not considered. Within the twelve compounds detected in concentrations higher than the LOQ, there are four herbicides, three fungicides, three insecticides and two TP of herbicides. Their properties vary concerning mobility and persistence in a broad range (PPDB, 2017, Lewis et al., 2016;) so that inputs cannot be addressed to certain physicochemical characteristics. Considering the land use, none of these compounds had been applied in that year directly to the fields in which the LSWB were located as the crops grown there did not require them. However, in all cases these pesticides had been applied to the crops on either one of the neighbouring fields that year or in autumn/spring of the previous year to the LSWB field. Hence, the pesticide inputs may originate from these adjacent fields or former applications. Exemplarily, diflufenican is a herbicide which is applied in autumn and is part of a widely distributed product. In autumn 2015, this product was applied to field A7 (winter grain) so that the measured concentration in A7 in spring 2016 may result from that application. The same product was applied to A1, A3, A6 and A10 as well in 2015, but residues in July 2016 were not found. These results may lead to the assumption that A7 is more susceptible to pesticide inputs than the other LSWB of the study. The key results of the target screenings are that (i) metolachlor, terbuthylazine and its TP desethyltriazine were found in all LSWB and that (ii) the concentrations of the twelve compounds were lower in 2015 than in 2016. (i) Metolachlor and terbuthylazine are herbicides which are applied to corn. However, they were neither applied in 2015 nor in 2016 and often not for years to the fields of the ten LSWB. In most of the LSWB, the three compounds were detected in both years in background concentrations.01–0.03 μg L⁻¹. In 2016 in A10, 0.315 μg L⁻¹ terbuthylazine and 0.63 μg L⁻¹ metolachlor were found. Since a field with corn cultivation in 2016 is next to A10, it can be assumed that these concentrations are caused by the release from this field to A10. There were no further fields with corn cultivation close to the other LSWB which could explain the findings of terbuthylazine and metolachlor. Sandin et al. In addition to water-related transport into water bodies, atmospheric deposition has to be considered as a potential input pathway as well. Several studies show that pesticides can be transported via air or rainfall to non-target areas (Epple et al., 2002; Sauret et al., 2009; Jiménez et al., 2015). Metolachlor, terbuthylazine and desethylterbuthylazine were mainly detected in wet deposition in amounts of 0.01–1.39 g ha⁻¹ a⁻¹, 0.04–1.11 g ha⁻¹ a⁻¹ and 0.08 g ha⁻¹ a⁻¹, respectively (Sauret et al., 2009; Kreuger et al., 2017). Especially for triazines like terbuthylazine and its TP, long-range transport is observed due to their high persistence in air (Epple et al., 2002; Kreuger et al., 2017). As a consequence of the use of metolachlor since 1976 and terbuthylazine since 1971 it becomes probable that they have spread ubiquitously over time and cause the low but permanent background concentrations. These background concentrations have been recognized in studies with a large number of sampling points and sampling dates (LFU, 2014; LLUR, 2014; Schreiner et al., 2016). As a consequence of the long period of terbuthylazine application, its TP desethylterbuthylazine, was measured in background concentrations of 0.01–0.03 µg L⁻¹ and up to 0.114 µg L⁻¹ in A6 in 2016.
