Invertebrates were preserved in the field in 5% formalin, identified in the laboratory and then preserved in 70% ethanol. Life-history and growth Twenty-one species were found in sufficient numbers throughout their developmental period to allow their life histories and growth patterns to be studied. All larvae were divided into size categories (0.1 mm) based either on head capsule width or tibia length of the third leg. Size–frequency plots for life-cycle determination were based on direct identification of larval instars (four species of Heteroptera, seven Coleoptera, five Diptera), or on head or tibia measurements when larval instars could not be easily identified (one species of Ephemeroptera, four Odonata). Sets of larvae (at least 10 individuals) from different size categories were dried at 60°C for 24 h and then weighed. Larval mean individual dry weights (\( W \), mg) were derived from linear regressions (\( \ln W = a + bL \) with 95% C.L.) between the natural log of weight (\( \ln W \)) and tibia length or head capsule width. Mean individual dry weights of cohorts from each site were natural log transformed to generate a series of subsegment linear regressions that represent a generation’s seasonal growth patterns over the year (see, for example, Figure 8). RESULTS Life-history patterns The life-history patterns of the 21 study species (Figures 1–7) can be divided into five main types. (1) The semivoltine life-cycle of Anax imperator began in summer (June–September). It lasted 2 years and ended in late spring (June). There was a large range of larval sizes throughout the year, with two overlapping generations. (2) Five species showed slow cycles with one generation per year. The eggs began to hatch in the spring (Coenagrion scitulum, Libellula depressa, Agabus nitidus, Haliplus lineatocollis) or late summer (Odontomyia ornata), and growth occurred over a long period (9–12 months) before spring or early summer emergences. (3) Ten species exhibited fast univoltine cycles (one generation per year), with hatching periods in late winter (Hygrotus inaequalis, Acilius sulcatus), spring (Chalcolestes viridis, Corixa punctata, Plea leachi, Hygrobia hermanni, Phaenobezzia sp.), or early summer (Haliplus mucronatus, Noterus clavicornis, Stratiomys potamida) with a short growth period (2–4 months), and were adult by spring, summer, or autumn. (4) Three species were multivoltine (two or three generations per year) with a long winter generation (September to May) and one (Culicoides sp., Dicrotendipes tritomus) or two (Cloeon dipterum) short summer generations (from July to August). It should be noted that two additional mayflies, Cloeon simile and Caenis luctuosa, occurred in pond 1 (but not in ponds 2 and 3). Their life-cycle patterns were previously described in Cayrou and Céréghino (2003): both species had a long winter and a short summer generation. (5) Two species were clearly bivoltine, with two short generations per year, i.e., in spring and summer (Naucoris maculatus), or both in spring (Notonecta maculata). Growth A simple regression (\( \ln W = a + bL \)) provided the best means for measuring the relationship between dry weight (\( W \)) and head width or tibia length (\( L \)). Table 2 presents values for constants a and b (\( \pm 95\% \) CL) obtained for the 21 species studied. The ‘\( r \)’ values ranged from 0.82 to 0.99, and were significant for each species (\( p < 0.05 \) or \( p < 0.01 \)). Growth was exponential either over the whole developmental period for a given cohort, or over two or three successive periods during which the growth rate was fairly constant. During these periods, there was a Figure 1. Life-history of Cloeon dipterum in ponds 2 and 3. Frequency distribution of head capsule width (L, mm) at each sampling date (November 2000–November 2001). Three cohort growth pattern types could be perceived (Figure 8): (I) growth occurred mainly in autumn and spring; it was low in winter; (II) growth was higher in summer and autumn than in winter and spring; and (III) all of the growth occurred continuously over 2–4 months in spring or summer. DISCUSSION Compared with previous reports, some species seemed to exhibit flexible life histories. Cloeon dipterum occurs throughout much of Europe, and most authors have described univoltine and bivoltine (with a short summer generation) life-cycles (Clifford, 1982), whereas three generations per year were recorded in ponds 2 and 3 (see also Elliott et al., 1988). Libellula depressa was clearly univoltine in ponds 2 and 3. However, Di Giovanni et al. (2000) noted that Libellula depressa had a 2-yr life-cycle, although some more rapidly growing individuals were able to emerge after 1 yr. The data in the present study suggested that Anax imperator had a 2-yr life-cycle. However, in colder regions (e.g. Germany, United Kingdom), A. imperator shows larval cycles extending either over 1 or 2 yr (Corbet, 1955; Sternberg and Buchwald, 2000), even at a given locality (which remains likely in our study area). Corixa punctata is mostly univoltine, but a second generation was observed by Papáček and Bohoněk (1989). According to Svensson et al. (2000), Notonecta maculata has one generation per year in Sweden, with adult emergence in August (compared with two generations per year and emergence from May to July in this study). Acilius sulcatus grew from February to June in pond 2 (this study), but from May to June in Wisconsin, USA (Hilsenhoff, 1993). Finally, previously undescribed life-cycle and growth patterns were detailed for the following species: Naucoris maculatus, Haliplus lineatocollis, Haliplus mucronatus, Hygrotus inaequalis, Noterus clavicornis, Odontomyia ornata, Stratiomys potamida, Dicrotendipes tritomus – thus contributing further to an understanding of the population dynamics of wetland insects. Figure 7. Life-history of Diptera species in pond 1 (Dicrotendipes tritomus) and 2 (other species). Frequency distribution of the various larval instars (I–IV) at each sampling date (November 2000–November 2001). See caption to Figure 1. As wetland habitats, ponds have only recently started receiving some attention, and most of the current research still focuses on assessing the biodiversity they support (Briers and Biggs, 2003; Angélbert et al., 2004) or are likely to host (Davies et al., 2004; Gaston et al., 2005). Among wetland inhabitants, aquatic insects have the potential to be relevant ecological indicators. Indeed, they are already widely used to reveal short- and long-term environmental changes in both running and still waters (Céréghino et al., 2003; Verneaux et al., 2004), most notably through the strong influence of human disturbance on the species richness of aquatic insects (Rosenberg and Resh, 1993). Such disturbances usually lead to losses of taxa (Compin and Céréghino, 2003). However, in a given area, biodiversity estimates (e.g. species richness, evenness, etc.) strongly depend on the spatial scale (type of habitat) and temporal scale (week, month, or season) over which observations are made. Water temperature is usually considered to be the major abiotic factor affecting the life-cycle phenology of aquatic invertebrates (Vannote and Sweeney, 1980; Sweeney et al., 1986), influencing the seasonality and development patterns of aquatic insects through growth, adult size, and fecundity (Lavandier, 1988; Giberson and Rosenberg, 1992; Pritchard and Zloty, 1994). This study suggested that the increased growth of those species with long generations (e.g., Cloeon dipterum) seemed to correspond to the rise in water temperature in spring (March), and that the warmest period (spring–summer) favoured the hatching and rapid development of short summer generations in most species. Whatever the biotic and/or abiotic factors controlling the life-cycle phenologies, and, subsequently, the temporal patterns of aquatic insect communities within ponds, this study clearly emphasizes the temporal dimension of biodiversity in small bodies of water. The seasonality of wetland-dependent insects in particular may influence the biodiversity ponds may support. pay attention to the time-frame needed to survey ponds, as many species (chiefly those with short cycles and/or egg-diapause periods) could be overlooked. Similar recommendations are already part of protocols for sampling and assessment of both riverine and wetland habitats, e.g. RIVPACS sampling for rivers (Wright et al., 2000), and UK National Pond Survey methods (Pond Action, 1989). Life-cycle attributes (e.g., reproduction, hatching and emergence periods) need to be carefully considered when restoring, managing and/or creating new ponds for conservation purposes (Ripley et al., 2004). Owing to the difficulty of pond creation in the study area (a limestone plateau), dredging the abandoned ponds is the only option for wetland restoration. Therefore, environmental managers should minimize the likelihood that dredging will eliminate populations (e.g., during the main growth or hatching periods). Theoretically, the acceptable period for dredging would be between adult emergence and egg-laying, i.e. during the flight and reproduction period. Given that most populations show a temporal sequence of species replacements (e.g. certain Coleoptera, Heteroptera), or have delayed life-cycle events (certain Odonata), defining an optimal period for dredging seems to be an impossible task. As an alternative, a plan of pond management should be envisaged over a large spatial scale to maintain the heterogeneity of pond networks in the area. Such a plan would imply promoting the conservation of all ponds, regardless of their successional stages. This is especially important when the density of ponds in the network is very sparse. Indeed, a recent study in the same area (Angélibert and Giani, 2003) on the dispersal capability of Odonata showed that dispersal phenomena were low because of the distance separating ponds. Thus, after dredging, species adapted to late succession ponds have little hope of finding suitable conditions in other ponds to ensure their development. The insects studied are widely distributed throughout Europe (see the Limnofauna Europaea (Illies, 1978)) and are regarded as having a low conservation priority. Broader conservation strategies should therefore ensure that such currently common organisms do not become the endangered species of the future (Rustigian et al., 2003). Ponds also provide useful models for studying how life-history patterns enable many populations to utilize small ecosystems, temporal segregation and/or differences in the size of coexisting nymphs certainly reducing interspecific competition for food and habitat resources (Svensson et al., 2000; Cayrou and Céréghino, 2003). Subsequently, interesting ideas and/or alternative strategies can be derived for conservation planning. Because the growth of most species is markedly seasonal and many species are temporally segregated, the spatial scale needed to manage threatened habitats must be enlarged. Thus, when possible, pond networks should primarily be preserved rather than attempting to target some bodies of water for particular management actions. ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS We wish to thank N. Life-cycle phenology of some aquatic insects: implications for pond conservation JÉRÔME CAYROU and RÉGIS CÉRÉGHINO* Laboratoire d’Ecologie des Hydrosystèmes, Université Paul Sabatier, Toulouse, France ABSTRACT 1. Life-cycles and growth patterns were determined for 21 dominant aquatic insect species in small permanent ponds in an arid, karstic region (SW France, site fr7300909 of the Natura 2000 conservation network). The species studied are widely distributed throughout Europe, but some life-cycle patterns are reported here for the first time. 2. The life-history patterns of the 21 species can be divided into five main types: (i) a semivoltine cycle spreading over 2 years; (ii) slow univoltine cycles; (iii) fast univoltine cycles; (iv) multivoltine life-cycles with a long winter generation and two or three summer generations per year; and (v) bivoltine life-cycles with two fast generations per year. Growth was either exponential over the whole developmental period for a given cohort, or divided into two or three successive periods during each of which the growth rate was fairly constant. 3. Biodiversity estimates strongly depend on the temporal and spatial scale over which observations are made. Ponds thus provide useful models to show how life-history patterns enable many temporally segregated populations to utilize small ecosystems. Conservation frameworks should therefore carefully consider the time-frame needed to survey ponds, as many species with fast cycles could be overlooked. The spatial scale needed to manage threatened habitats and thus preserve pond networks must be broadened, rather than attempting to target individual water bodies for particular management actions. KEY WORDS: aquatic insects; wetlands; ponds; life-history; growth; temporal niche segregation; temperature; conservation INTRODUCTION The diversity of habitat types within wetlands allows them to be colonized by a wide range of specialist and generalist species (Masing et al., 2000). Wetlands are thus often considered as ‘hot spots’ of biodiversity within a region or a landscape (Gopal et al., 2001; Williams et al., 2004). However, wetlands and the biodiversity they support are threatened by human activity (e.g. agriculture, industry, urban development), though these ecosystems have significant ecological functions (Dugan, 1990) and recognized social and economic uses (Chapman et al., 2001). During the 20th century, wetland losses reached 40–90% in a number of north-western European countries (Hull, 1997), and in the United States more than 50% of these ecosystems have been destroyed by man (Tiner, 1984; Williams, 1990). Due to such large-scale habitat loss, many species are also endangered. This threat has prompted specific studies aimed at understanding the dynamics of wetland populations. Such an understanding is expected to help in planning conservation efforts such as the creation or restoration of ecosystems (Biggs et al., 1994). Although ponds have only recently started receiving some attention (Oertli, 1995; Hull, 1997; Angélbert et al., 2004), it is now well established that their management and conservation is closely linked to an understanding of the biodiversity and ecology of the biota they host (Gee et al., 1997; Gaston et al., 2005). Many of the models used to predict the consequences of future conservation strategies require life-history data (Rustigian et al., 2003). Therefore, information on the life-cycles of aquatic species is of fundamental importance for virtually all aspects of wetland conservation, including the conservation of ponds. Aquatic insects constitute an important part of animal production within wetlands (Oertli, 1993), and are tightly integrated into the structure and functioning of their habitats (e.g. organic matter processing, nutrient retention, food resources for vertebrates such as amphibians, fish, or birds). In a given area, the spatial and temporal variability of habitat types are key factors influencing the biodiversity of insect communities (Minshall, 1984; Hanquet et al., 2004), and are reflected in the ecological strategies and adaptation exhibited by species (Townsend, 1989; Townsend et al., 1997). In contrast to the large volume of studies in river ecology, very little research has addressed the population dynamics of pond insects. Most attention has instead been paid to patterns of biodiversity such as spatial variations in species richness (Oertli, 1995), or species diversity vs. area relationships (Oertli et al., 2002). Information on the life-history of pond insects is generally sparse, and usually available for a few, separately studied, species (e.g., Di Giovanni et al., 2000). However, there have been no previous attempts to gather – in a single investigation – detailed life-cycle and growth data on a large number of pond insects that are likely to coexist. Such an investigation would provide an overview of life-history traits and would consequently have significant implications for planning management and/or conservation actions in a particular area. In this investigation, the life-cycle phenologies, including growth patterns, of 21 aquatic insect species were determined in three small, permanent ponds in the arid, karstic region of the ‘Causses du Quercy’ (SW France). This area belongs to the Natura 2000 conservation network, and the results are discussed with reference to the implications for broader conservation strategies. STUDY AREA Located in south-western France, the ‘Causses du Quercy’ is a 2156 km\(^2\) limestone plateau. This arid area is affected by Mediterranean, Atlantic, and Continental climates, and this is reflected in its distinctive weather conditions and vegetation cover. The dominant plant species found in the area are *Quercus pubescens* Willd. and *Acer monspessulanum* L., while the moorland vegetation is principally composed of *Juniperus communis* L. The area belongs to the Natura 2000 conservation network, and is identified as site fr7300909. The plateau has no natural surface fresh water; however, it has more than 300 artificial ponds (typically permanent, rectangular in shape, and shallow, with a density of less than one pond per square kilometre). These ponds, bored into the calcareous rock, were created to hold rain water and support agricultural activities, and it is a technique that has been practised since the 12th century. Abandoned during the 1960s, the ponds are progressively filling with sediment and aquatic vegetation. Although they are now at various stages of natural succession, they support an aquatic vegetation community classified for conservation by the European Fauna-Flora-Habitat guideline 92/43/CEE: ‘22.12X22.44, oligo-mesotrophic calcareous waters with benthic vegetation of Characea’. This study was conducted from November 2000 to November 2001 in three such permanent ponds with a rocky substrate (hereafter called 1, 2 and 3). These three ponds are at different stages of natural succession; their main characteristics are shown in Table 1. A thorough study of their physical and chemical features (together with a fauna and flora species list) can be found in Angélibert et al. (2004). METHODS Sampling In each pond, samples were collected monthly from November 2000 to February 2001, then every 2 weeks from March to November 2001. Different techniques were used to obtain qualitative samples of aquatic insects within each pond. First, samples were randomly taken in each pond and at each sampling date by intensive sweeping of a hand net (mesh size = 250 μm) through the various habitats for 15–20 min. In order to maximize the number of available individuals on each sampling occasion, additional samples were specifically taken from the various substrate types (Table 1), each requiring a specific sampling technique (Oertli, 1993). Thin layers of mud (< 5 cm) deposited on the calcareous substrate and bryophytes were sampled using an air-lift sampler (Boulton, 1985) (sampling area 186 cm², mesh size of the net: 250 μm). Thick layers of mud (> 5 cm) were sampled using a plastic core sampler (sampling area: 28.2 cm²). Specific cores (40 cm high and 4.4 cm in diameter) were used to sample the submerged section of Typha stems. The aerial part of the plant was cut at water level, and the remaining submerged part was quickly enclosed in the core and cut at approximately 35 cm under the surface of the water. Chara beds at mid-depth were sampled by rapidly enclosing plants in a plastic box (7.5 × 16 × 11.5 cm). The Chara plants were then cut with shears. Table 1. Invertebrates were preserved in the field in 5% formalin, identified in the laboratory and then preserved in 70% ethanol. Life-history and growth Twenty-one species were found in sufficient numbers throughout their developmental period to allow their life histories and growth patterns to be studied. All larvae were divided into size categories (0.1 mm) based either on head capsule width or tibia length of the third leg. Size–frequency plots for life-cycle determination were based on direct identification of larval instars (four species of Heteroptera, seven Coleoptera, five Diptera), or on head or tibia measurements when larval instars could not be easily identified (one species of Ephemeroptera, four Odonata). Sets of larvae (at least 10 individuals) from different size categories were dried at 60°C for 24 h and then weighed. Larval mean individual dry weights (\( W \), mg) were derived from linear regressions (\( \ln W = a + bL \) with 95% C.L.) between the natural log of weight (\( \ln W \)) and tibia length or head capsule width. Mean individual dry weights of cohorts from each site were natural log transformed to generate a series of subsegment linear regressions that represent a generation’s seasonal growth patterns over the year (see, for example, Figure 8). RESULTS Life-history patterns The life-history patterns of the 21 study species (Figures 1–7) can be divided into five main types. (1) The semivoltine life-cycle of Anax imperator began in summer (June–September). It lasted 2 years and ended in late spring (June). There was a large range of larval sizes throughout the year, with two overlapping generations. (2) Five species showed slow cycles with one generation per year. The eggs began to hatch in the spring (Coenagrion scitulum, Libellula depressa, Agabus nitidus, Haliplus lineatocollis) or late summer (Odontomyia ornata), and growth occurred over a long period (9–12 months) before spring or early summer emergences. (3) Ten species exhibited fast univoltine cycles (one generation per year), with hatching periods in late winter (Hygrotus inaequalis, Acilius sulcatus), spring (Chalcolestes viridis, Corixa punctata, Plea leachi, Hygrobia hermanni, Phaenobezzia sp.), or early summer (Haliplus mucronatus, Noterus clavicornis, Stratiomys potamida) with a short growth period (2–4 months), and were adult by spring, summer, or autumn. (4) Three species were multivoltine (two or three generations per year) with a long winter generation (September to May) and one (Culicoides sp., Dicrotendipes tritomus) or two (Cloeon dipterum) short summer generations (from July to August). It should be noted that two additional mayflies, Cloeon simile and Caenis luctuosa, occurred in pond 1 (but not in ponds 2 and 3). Their life-cycle patterns were previously described in Cayrou and Céréghino (2003): both species had a long winter and a short summer generation. (5) Two species were clearly bivoltine, with two short generations per year, i.e., in spring and summer (Naucoris maculatus), or both in spring (Notonecta maculata). Growth A simple regression (\( \ln W = a + bL \)) provided the best means for measuring the relationship between dry weight (\( W \)) and head width or tibia length (\( L \)). Table 2 presents values for constants a and b (\( \pm 95\% \) CL) obtained for the 21 species studied. The ‘\( r \)’ values ranged from 0.82 to 0.99, and were significant for each species (\( p < 0.05 \) or \( p < 0.01 \)). Growth was exponential either over the whole developmental period for a given cohort, or over two or three successive periods during which the growth rate was fairly constant. Three cohort growth pattern types could be perceived (Figure 8): (I) growth occurred mainly in autumn and spring; it was low in winter; (II) growth was higher in summer and autumn than in winter and spring; and (III) all of the growth occurred continuously over 2–4 months in spring or summer. DISCUSSION Compared with previous reports, some species seemed to exhibit flexible life histories. Cloeon dipterum occurs throughout much of Europe, and most authors have described univoltine and bivoltine (with a short summer generation) life-cycles (Clifford, 1982), whereas three generations per year were recorded in ponds 2 and 3 (see also Elliott et al., 1988). Libellula depressa was clearly univoltine in ponds 2 and 3. However, Di Giovanni et al. (2000) noted that Libellula depressa had a 2-yr life-cycle, although some more rapidly growing individuals were able to emerge after 1 yr. The data in the present study suggested that Anax imperator had a 2-yr life-cycle. However, in colder regions (e.g. Germany, United Kingdom), A. imperator shows larval cycles extending either over 1 or 2 yr (Corbet, 1955; Sternberg and Buchwald, 2000), even at a given locality (which remains likely in our study area). Corixa punctata is mostly univoltine, but a second generation was observed by Papáček and Bohoněk (1989). According to Svensson et al. (2000), Notonecta maculata has one generation per year in Sweden, with adult emergence in August (compared with two generations per year and emergence from May to July in this study). Acilius sulcatus grew from February to June in pond 2 (this study), but from May to June in Wisconsin, USA (Hilsenhoff, 1993). Finally, previously undescribed life-cycle and growth patterns were detailed for the following species: Naucoris maculatus, Haliplus lineatocollis, Haliplus mucronatus, Hygrotus inaequalis, Noterus clavicornis, Odontomyia ornata, Stratiomys potamida, Dicrotendipes tritomus – thus contributing further to an understanding of the population dynamics of wetland insects. Figure 7. Life-history of Diptera species in pond 1 (Dicrotendipes tritomus) and 2 (other species). Frequency distribution of the various larval instars (I–IV) at each sampling date (November 2000–November 2001). See caption to Figure 1. As wetland habitats, ponds have only recently started receiving some attention, and most of the current research still focuses on assessing the biodiversity they support (Briers and Biggs, 2003; Angélbert et al., 2004) or are likely to host (Davies et al., 2004; Gaston et al., 2005). Among wetland inhabitants, aquatic insects have the potential to be relevant ecological indicators. Indeed, they are already widely used to reveal short- and long-term environmental changes in both running and still waters (Céréghino et al., 2003; Verneaux et al., 2004), most notably through the strong influence of human disturbance on the species richness of aquatic insects (Rosenberg and Resh, 1993). Such disturbances usually lead to losses of taxa (Compin and Céréghino, 2003). However, in a given area, biodiversity estimates (e.g. species richness, evenness, etc.) strongly depend on the spatial scale (type of habitat) and temporal scale (week, month, or season) over which observations are made. Water temperature is usually considered to be the major abiotic factor affecting the life-cycle phenology of aquatic invertebrates (Vannote and Sweeney, 1980; Sweeney et al., 1986), influencing the seasonality and development patterns of aquatic insects through growth, adult size, and fecundity (Lavandier, 1988; Giberson and Rosenberg, 1992; Pritchard and Zloty, 1994). This study suggested that the increased growth of those species with long generations (e.g., Cloeon dipterum) seemed to correspond to the rise in water temperature in spring (March), and that the warmest period (spring–summer) favoured the hatching and rapid development of short summer generations in most species. Whatever the biotic and/or abiotic factors controlling the life-cycle phenologies, and, subsequently, the temporal patterns of aquatic insect communities within ponds, this study clearly emphasizes the temporal dimension of biodiversity in small bodies of water. The seasonality of wetland-dependent insects in particular may influence the biodiversity ponds may support. Similar recommendations are already part of protocols for sampling and assessment of both riverine and wetland habitats, e.g. RIVPACS sampling for rivers (Wright et al., 2000), and UK National Pond Survey methods (Pond Action, 1989). Life-cycle attributes (e.g., reproduction, hatching and emergence periods) need to be carefully considered when restoring, managing and/or creating new ponds for conservation purposes (Ripley et al., 2004). Owing to the difficulty of pond creation in the study area (a limestone plateau), dredging the abandoned ponds is the only option for wetland restoration. Therefore, environmental managers should minimize the likelihood that dredging will eliminate populations (e.g., during the main growth or hatching periods). Theoretically, the acceptable period for dredging would be between adult emergence and egg-laying, i.e. during the flight and reproduction period. Given that most populations show a temporal sequence of species replacements (e.g. certain Coleoptera, Heteroptera), or have delayed life-cycle events (certain Odonata), defining an optimal period for dredging seems to be an impossible task. As an alternative, a plan of pond management should be envisaged over a large spatial scale to maintain the heterogeneity of pond networks in the area. Such a plan would imply promoting the conservation of all ponds, regardless of their successional stages. This is especially important when the density of ponds in the network is very sparse. Indeed, a recent study in the same area (Angélibert and Giani, 2003) on the dispersal capability of Odonata showed that dispersal phenomena were low because of the distance separating ponds. Thus, after dredging, species adapted to late succession ponds have little hope of finding suitable conditions in other ponds to ensure their development. The insects studied are widely distributed throughout Europe (see the Limnofauna Europaea (Illies, 1978)) and are regarded as having a low conservation priority. Broader conservation strategies should therefore ensure that such currently common organisms do not become the endangered species of the future (Rustigian et al., 2003). Ponds also provide useful models for studying how life-history patterns enable many populations to utilize small ecosystems, temporal segregation and/or differences in the size of coexisting nymphs certainly reducing interspecific competition for food and habitat resources (Svensson et al., 2000; Cayrou and Céréghino, 2003). Subsequently, interesting ideas and/or alternative strategies can be derived for conservation planning. Because the growth of most species is markedly seasonal and many species are temporally segregated, the spatial scale needed to manage threatened habitats must be enlarged. Thus, when possible, pond networks should primarily be preserved rather than attempting to target some bodies of water for particular management actions. ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS We wish to thank N. Measurements of chlorophyll-a from phytoplankton using ethanol as extraction solvent By ANNE-METTE JESPERSEN and KIRSTEN CHRISTOFFERSEN With 2 figures and 4 tables in the text Abstract The use of ethanol as extraction solvent for the determination of chlorophyll-a was evaluated on a variety of cultures and natural populations of phytoplankton. Ethanol was equally efficient as methanol in the extraction of chlorophyll-a from cultures or natural populations of phytoplankton. An extraction period of 6 hours in cold ethanol was in most cases sufficient to complete the extraction, but longer extraction time or heating the solvent may be necessary when green algae dominate the plankton. The extraction efficiency decreases 10—25 %, when water reduced the ethanol concentration from 96 % to 83.5 %. Interference from chlorophyll-b in the spectrophotometric determination of chlorophyll-a in ethanol comprised 3—9 % and should be ignored in routine determinations of chlorophyll-a from phytoplankton. Introduction Measurement of the chlorophyll-a content in phytoplankton is often used as an index for biomass, which is an important parameter in many ecological studies in aquatic environments. Since Strickland & Parsons published a procedure in 1968 involving extraction in 90 % acetone a large number of methodological changes have been published. Despite the fact that acetone is still commonly used in many marine studies, it is now recognised, that the extraction efficiency is low in the presence of many green and bluegreen algae (Marker 1972, Holm-Hansen & Riemann 1978, Riemann & Ernst 1982), which are commonly found in eutrophic lakes and coastal marine environments. As an alternative, alcoholic extraction solvents have been proposed. Holm-Hansen & Riemann (1978) concluded that methanol was a fast and efficient extraction solvent, but it has been criticized because of its unhealthy characteristics (Nusch & Palme 1980). Ethanol was introduced several years ago (Nusch & Palme 1975), but the extent to which calibrations and evaluations have been carried out is still limited. However, some studies (Moed & Hallegraef 1978, Nusch 1980, Arvola 1981) have demonstrated that the extraction efficiency of ethanol is comparable to that obtained by methanol. The Danish Standardization Council recently has chosen ethanol as the Danish Standard (DS 1985) and this solvent may emerge as the general extraction solvent for both freshwater and marine environments. The aim of this work was to evaluate (1) the extraction efficiency of hot and cold ethanol using a variety of phytoplankton cultures and natural populations, (2) the effect of water content in the solvent, and (3) the interference of chlorophyll-b on the spectrophotometric determination of chlorophyll-a. Materials and methods Water samples were collected from 12 different lakes situated in the central part of Jutland and North Zealand (Denmark) from september to december 1983. Phytoplankton primary productivity and the algal composition of the lakes are listed in Table 1. Surface water samples were collected in 5-litre plastic bottles, and subsamples were filtered through Whatman GF/C (47 mm) filters using a vacuum pressure of approximately 20 cm Hg. The filters were sucked dry and stored at −20 °C prior to use. The algae composition was determined from water samples fixed with Lugols iodine. Phytoplankton cultures included Scenedesmus quadricauda (Brebisson), Chlorella vulgaris (Beijerinck), Selenastrum capricornutum (Printz) and Pediastrum duplex (Meyen), grown in a modified Österlind B medium (Steemann Nielsen & Wiium-Andersen 1970), in a 12/12 hours light and dark cycle at 25 °C. Light source was a Phillips LTD 18w/84 and light intensity was 260 \( \mu \)E m\(^{-2}\) s\(^{-1}\). The growth conditions of the culture were checked from cell counts using a haemocytometer. Aliquots of cultures in log or stationary phases were filtered through Whatman GF/C filters (25 mm) at 20 cm Hg and used immediately. Filters containing phytoplankton cultures and natural phytoplankton were extracted in 5 ml of either 96 % ethanol or absolute methanol. In one experiment, ethanol concentrations from 96 % to 83.5 % were used. Table 1. Dominating species and annual phytoplankton primary productivity from the 12 Danish lakes studied.

In another experiment, 96 % ethanol were heated to 70 °C (in water bath) for 2—6 minutes, otherwise "cold" (20 °C) ethanol were used. Extraction time varied from 6 to 24 hours. All samples were measured spectrophotometrically after refiltering the pigment extract through Whatman GF/C filters (25 mm) as described in Riemann & Ernst (1982). A Beckmann 26 spectrophotometer was used (1 cm cuvettes). Maximum absorbance in the red region of the spectrum was at 665 nm for chlorophyll-a in absolute methanol and 96 % ethanol. Corrections for turbidity were made by subtracting the absorbance at 750 nm which never exceeded 5 % of the 665 nm measurements. Maximum absorbance for chlorophyll-b was at 650 nm and 652 nm in ethanol and methanol, respectively. The following specific absorption coefficients were applied: chlorophyll-a in ethanol 83.4 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) (Winthermans & Demots 1965), in methanol 77.9 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) cm (Riemann 1978), and chlorophyll-b in ethanol 45.9 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) (Winthermans & Demots 1965). Reproducibility of the chlorophyll measurements was tested using two phytoplankton cultures and one natural phytoplankton population. The coefficient of variation ranged from 1.7 % to 7.8 % (n = 10). Analysis of data were performed using Student t-test and two-factor analysis of variance (P < 0.05). Results and discussion The extraction efficiency of ethanol Two experiments were set up to compare the extraction efficiencies of ethanol and methanol. In the first experiment, four species of green algae and one natural population of phytoplankton were extracted for 6 hours in 96 % ethanol and absolute methanol. In addition, the pigments were extracted in hot and cold ethanol for various times. Except for Scenedesmus and Chlorella in stationary phases, no significant differences were found in the amount of chlorophyll-a extracted from any of the cultures, regardless solvent, heating procedure or length of extraction period (Fig. 1A—D). Furthermore, no significant differences were observed between the methanol, cold and hot ethanol extractions in the natural population of phytoplankton (Fig. 1 E). The chlorophyll-a extracted from Scenedesmus after 6 hours using hot ethanol was 54 % higher than after 6 hours methanol extraction (Fig. 1F). No significant differences were observed after 6 hours using methanol and cold ethanol, but the chlorophyll-a concentration in cold ethanol increased during the extraction period, and after 24 hours the chlorophyll concentration was 46 % higher, compared with the results obtained from methanol extraction. There were no significant differences between the extracted chlorophyll-a concentrations after 18 hours in cold and hot ethanol. Assuming that 6 hours is a sufficient extraction period using methanol (Riemann & Ernst 1982), the results obtained from Chlorella (in log phase), Selenastrum, Pediastrum and the natural population of phytoplankton from Frederiksborg Slotssø suggested a complete extraction after 6 hours in cold Fig. 1 A—F. Chlorophyll-a (mg l^{-1}) extracted from various algae cultures using absolute methanol for 6 hours or 96% cold and hot ethanol for 6, 12, 18 and 24 hours. Chlorella vulgaris was extracted during both stationary and exponential growth phase, Selenastrum capricornutum, Pediastrum duplex, and Scenedesmus quadricauda during exponential growth phase. The sample after 12 hours extraction using Pediastrum was lost. Black columns represent methanol, white columns cold ethanol, and hatched columns hot ethanol extrations (n = 3). Bars represent standard deviations. ethanol. In contrast, methanol extraction of Scenedesmus was not efficient enough to remove chlorophyll-a from the cells, since hot ethanol gave more chlorophyll-a than the cold solvents. In a similar experiment Nusch (1980) reported that methanol and ethanol were equally efficient and always more efficient than acetone. This is in contradiction to the results reported by Arvola (1981), who found that methanol was superior to ethanol. Riemann & Ernst (1982) demonstrated that methanol extracted more chlorophyll-a from Scenedesmus acutus compared with ethanol extractions. Thus, extraction efficiencies for the various solvents may be species specific. According to our results a 6 hour extraction in cold ethanol, without further treatment, is sufficient to complete the extraction in most cases. When certain green algae are dominating, longer extraction time or heating the solvents may be necessary. In a second experiment, the extraction efficiency of cold ethanol was compared with methanol extraction on natural populations of phytoplankton, to investigate the influence of phytoplankton composition on the extraction efficiency. Based on the first experiment, an 18 hour extraction time was chosen. No significant differences were found between the results obtained from ethanol or methanol extractions (Table 2), except in the samples from Ellesø and Thorsø. In Ellesø, 7% more chlorophyll was extracted with ethanol than with methanol, and in Thorsø the methanol extraction gave 3% more chlorophyll than the ethanol extraction. Table 2. To investigate the influence of temperature on the extraction efficiency, samples from 6 different lakes were heated for 2 to 6 minutes and the results were compared with results obtained from cold ethanol extraction (Table 3). The hot ethanol extractions were generally more efficient than the cold ethanol, but no significant differences were found except from Skanderborg Lillesø, where 10—15 % more chlorophyll was obtained by heating for 2 to 6 minutes, and from Ellesø after 4 minutes. The results from the natural populations of phytoplankton support the conclusion that cold ethanol is an equally efficient extraction solvent as methanol. In the samples from Skanderborg Lillesø, which was totally dominated by *Scenedesmus*, more chlorophyll was obtained by heating the solvent. It is known from the literature that different treatments such as homogenization, ultrasonic treatments and heating (Holm-Hansen & Riemann 1978, Nusch 1980, Riemann & Ernst 1982) optimize the extraction conditions, especially when algae belonging to Chlorophyceae and Cyanophyceae dominate. However, the pigment concentration in the samples from Skanderborg Lillesø was extremely high and this may have reduced the extraction efficiency and furthermore caused an increased amount of water in the solvent, which also result in reduced extraction efficiency (see below). The effect of water content in the extraction solvent The effect of water in the ethanol was tested on *Chlorella, Scenedesmus* and on a natural population of phytoplankton. When distilled water was passed through GF/C filters during the standard procedure, the retained water was 0.139 ml (SD = 0.006; n = 3) on 25 mm GF/C filters, and 0.396 ml (SD = 0.003; n = 3) on 47 mm GF/C filters. This increased water content resulted in a 3—7 % reduction in the ethanol concentration. Based on these data, ethanol concentrations between 83.5 % and 96 % were tested. Fig. 2 A—C. Chlorophyll-a (mg l\(^{-1}\)) extracted from *Chlorella vulgaris*, *Scenedesmus quadricauda* and a natural population of phytoplankton from Frederiksborg Slotssø, using varying percentages of ethanol (diluted with distilled water). Bars represent standard deviations (n = 3). When the ethanol concentration was reduced from 96% to 83.5%, 10% less chlorophyll was extracted from *Chlorella*, 14% less from the natural population of phytoplankton, and 25% less from *Scenedesmus* (Fig. 2). The relative large reduction in chlorophyll extracted from *Scenedesmus* is probably related to its morphology, which increases the possibility of water adhesion to the cells. Furthermore, the results in Fig. 2 are underestimated, since the true water content on filters containing algae, bacteria, and detritus is higher than those predicted from experiments using distilled water. Previous findings have demonstrated that the extraction efficiencies in methanol (Rie- MANN 1980) and ethanol (NUSCH 1980), were reduced when the water content was increased. Thus, the water content in ethanol extraction should be kept as low as possible. Spectrophotometric interference of chlorophyll-b on the determination of chlorophyll-a in ethanol Pigment extracts from natural populations of phytoplankton often contain chlorophyll-b and -c, which have absorption maxima close to that of chlorophyll-a in the red region of the spectrum. The interference from chlorophyll-b leads to an overestimation of chlorophyll-a, while the interference of chlorophyll-c in most cases may be ignored, since the absorption maximum of chlorophyll-c is 30—35 nm from the absorption peak of chlorophyll-a (MARKER et al. 1980). To investigate the interference of chlorophyll-b on the determination of chlorophyll-a in ethanol, the absorption at 665 nm was read at different mixed solutions of the two pigments (Table 4). When chlorophyll-b constituted from 5 % to 100 % of the chlorophyll-a (by weight), the absorbance at 665 nm increased from 1.5 % to 35.1 %. In similar experiments using methanol RIEMANN (1978) found an 1.4 % to 44.6 % overestimation, when chlorophyll-b constituted 5 % to 90 % of the chlorophyll-a content. This interference is higher than for ethanol, because the maximum absorbance of chlorophyll-b is closer to the peak of chlorophyll-a in methanol. LOFTUS & CARPENTER (1971) reported, that chlorophyll-b rarely constituted more than 10—20 % of the chlorophyll-a content in natural populations of phytoplankton, dominated by green algae or other algae containing chlorophyll-b. Only in one sample they found 40 % chlorophyll-b. RIEMANN & ERNST (1982) investigated six green algae and found, after optimal extraction, that chlorophyll-b constituted 13—33 % of the chlorophyll-a in methanol extracts. Table 4. Assuming that chlorophyll-b will constitute at most 30% of chlorophyll-a in natural populations of phytoplankton, the maximum interference of chlorophyll-b leads to an 9.3% overestimation of chlorophyll-a in ethanol. To correct for this interference involves either 1) a detailed spectrophotometric determination at different wavelengths (Strickland & Parsons 1972), or 2) a chromatographic separation of the chlorophylls. The first method is not recommended (Marker et al. 1980) because chlorophyll-a thereby is overestimated and a chromatographic separation is still not applicable in routine measurements. Measurements of chlorophyll-a from phytoplankton using ethanol as extraction solvent By ANNE-METTE JESPERSEN and KIRSTEN CHRISTOFFERSEN With 2 figures and 4 tables in the text Abstract The use of ethanol as extraction solvent for the determination of chlorophyll-a was evaluated on a variety of cultures and natural populations of phytoplankton. Ethanol was equally efficient as methanol in the extraction of chlorophyll-a from cultures or natural populations of phytoplankton. An extraction period of 6 hours in cold ethanol was in most cases sufficient to complete the extraction, but longer extraction time or heating the solvent may be necessary when green algae dominate the plankton. The extraction efficiency decreases 10—25 %, when water reduced the ethanol concentration from 96 % to 83.5 %. Interference from chlorophyll-b in the spectrophotometric determination of chlorophyll-a in ethanol comprised 3—9 % and should be ignored in routine determinations of chlorophyll-a from phytoplankton. Introduction Measurement of the chlorophyll-a content in phytoplankton is often used as an index for biomass, which is an important parameter in many ecological studies in aquatic environments. Since Strickland & Parsons published a procedure in 1968 involving extraction in 90 % acetone a large number of methodological changes have been published. Despite the fact that acetone is still commonly used in many marine studies, it is now recognised, that the extraction efficiency is low in the presence of many green and bluegreen algae (Marker 1972, Holm-Hansen & Riemann 1978, Riemann & Ernst 1982), which are commonly found in eutrophic lakes and coastal marine environments. As an alternative, alcoholic extraction solvents have been proposed. Holm-Hansen & Riemann (1978) concluded that methanol was a fast and efficient extraction solvent, but it has been criticized because of its unhealthy characteristics (Nusch & Palme 1980). Ethanol was introduced several years ago (Nusch & Palme 1975), but the extent to which calibrations and evaluations have been carried out is still limited. However, some studies (Moed & Hallegraef 1978, Nusch 1980, Arvola 1981) have demonstrated that the extraction efficiency of ethanol is comparable to that obtained by methanol. The Danish Standardization Council recently has chosen ethanol as the Danish Standard (DS 1985) and this solvent may emerge as the general extraction solvent for both freshwater and marine environments. The aim of this work was to evaluate (1) the extraction efficiency of hot and cold ethanol using a variety of phytoplankton cultures and natural populations, (2) the effect of water content in the solvent, and (3) the interference of chlorophyll-b on the spectrophotometric determination of chlorophyll-a. Materials and methods Water samples were collected from 12 different lakes situated in the central part of Jutland and North Zealand (Denmark) from september to december 1983. Phytoplankton primary productivity and the algal composition of the lakes are listed in Table 1. Surface water samples were collected in 5-litre plastic bottles, and subsamples were filtered through Whatman GF/C (47 mm) filters using a vacuum pressure of approximately 20 cm Hg. The filters were sucked dry and stored at −20 °C prior to use. The algae composition was determined from water samples fixed with Lugols iodine. Phytoplankton cultures included Scenedesmus quadricauda (Brebisson), Chlorella vulgaris (Beijerinck), Selenastrum capricornutum (Printz) and Pediastrum duplex (Meyen), grown in a modified Österlind B medium (Steemann Nielsen & Wiium-Andersen 1970), in a 12/12 hours light and dark cycle at 25 °C. Light source was a Phillips LTD 18w/84 and light intensity was 260 \( \mu \)E m\(^{-2}\) s\(^{-1}\). The growth conditions of the culture were checked from cell counts using a haemocytometer. Aliquots of cultures in log or stationary phases were filtered through Whatman GF/C filters (25 mm) at 20 cm Hg and used immediately. Filters containing phytoplankton cultures and natural phytoplankton were extracted in 5 ml of either 96 % ethanol or absolute methanol. In one experiment, ethanol concentrations from 96 % to 83.5 % were used. Table 1. Dominating species and annual phytoplankton primary productivity from the 12 Danish lakes studied.

In another experiment, 96 % ethanol were heated to 70 °C (in water bath) for 2—6 minutes, otherwise "cold" (20 °C) ethanol were used. Extraction time varied from 6 to 24 hours. All samples were measured spectrophotometrically after refiltering the pigment extract through Whatman GF/C filters (25 mm) as described in Riemann & Ernst (1982). A Beckmann 26 spectrophotometer was used (1 cm cuvettes). Maximum absorbance in the red region of the spectrum was at 665 nm for chlorophyll-a in absolute methanol and 96 % ethanol. Corrections for turbidity were made by subtracting the absorbance at 750 nm which never exceeded 5 % of the 665 nm measurements. Maximum absorbance for chlorophyll-b was at 650 nm and 652 nm in ethanol and methanol, respectively. The following specific absorption coefficients were applied: chlorophyll-a in ethanol 83.4 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) (Winthermans & Demots 1965), in methanol 77.9 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) cm (Riemann 1978), and chlorophyll-b in ethanol 45.9 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) (Winthermans & Demots 1965). Reproducibility of the chlorophyll measurements was tested using two phytoplankton cultures and one natural phytoplankton population. The coefficient of variation ranged from 1.7 % to 7.8 % (n = 10). Analysis of data were performed using Student t-test and two-factor analysis of variance (P < 0.05). Results and discussion The extraction efficiency of ethanol Two experiments were set up to compare the extraction efficiencies of ethanol and methanol. In the first experiment, four species of green algae and one natural population of phytoplankton were extracted for 6 hours in 96 % ethanol and absolute methanol. In addition, the pigments were extracted in hot and cold ethanol for various times. Except for Scenedesmus and Chlorella in stationary phases, no significant differences were found in the amount of chlorophyll-a extracted from any of the cultures, regardless solvent, heating procedure or length of extraction period (Fig. 1A—D). Furthermore, no significant differences were observed between the methanol, cold and hot ethanol extractions in the natural population of phytoplankton (Fig. 1 E). The chlorophyll-a extracted from Scenedesmus after 6 hours using hot ethanol was 54 % higher than after 6 hours methanol extraction (Fig. 1F). No significant differences were observed after 6 hours using methanol and cold ethanol, but the chlorophyll-a concentration in cold ethanol increased during the extraction period, and after 24 hours the chlorophyll concentration was 46 % higher, compared with the results obtained from methanol extraction. There were no significant differences between the extracted chlorophyll-a concentrations after 18 hours in cold and hot ethanol. Assuming that 6 hours is a sufficient extraction period using methanol (Riemann & Ernst 1982), the results obtained from Chlorella (in log phase), Selenastrum, Pediastrum and the natural population of phytoplankton from Frederiksborg Slotssø suggested a complete extraction after 6 hours in cold Fig. 1 A—F. Chlorella vulgaris was extracted during both stationary and exponential growth phase, Selenastrum capricornutum, Pediastrum duplex, and Scenedesmus quadricauda during exponential growth phase. The sample after 12 hours extraction using Pediastrum was lost. Black columns represent methanol, white columns cold ethanol, and hatched columns hot ethanol extrations (n = 3). Bars represent standard deviations. ethanol. In contrast, methanol extraction of Scenedesmus was not efficient enough to remove chlorophyll-a from the cells, since hot ethanol gave more chlorophyll-a than the cold solvents. In a similar experiment Nusch (1980) reported that methanol and ethanol were equally efficient and always more efficient than acetone. This is in contradiction to the results reported by Arvola (1981), who found that methanol was superior to ethanol. Riemann & Ernst (1982) demonstrated that methanol extracted more chlorophyll-a from Scenedesmus acutus compared with ethanol extractions. Thus, extraction efficiencies for the various solvents may be species specific. According to our results a 6 hour extraction in cold ethanol, without further treatment, is sufficient to complete the extraction in most cases. When certain green algae are dominating, longer extraction time or heating the solvents may be necessary. Based on the first experiment, an 18 hour extraction time was chosen. Measuring the trophic status of ponds: Relationships between summer rate of periphytic net primary productivity and water physico-chemistry Lionel Sager* Laboratory of Ecology and Aquatic Biology (LEBA), University of Geneva, Chemin des Clochettes 18, CH-1206 Geneva, Switzerland ARTICLE INFO Article history: Received 2 July 2008 Received in revised form 22 December 2008 Accepted 23 December 2008 Published online 3 January 2009 Keywords: AFDW Alternative stable states Assessment Eutrophication Nitrogen Phosphorus Submerged macrophytes ABSTRACT The monitoring of the water quality is a major environmental concern and specific method of assessment needs to be addressed for ponds. Among threats on freshwater, eutrophication remains an important and widespread problem. To assess if the trophic state of ponds can be significantly predicted by physico-chemical surrogates, parallel measurements of water physico-chemistry and of summer rates of periphytic net primary productivity (NPP) were performed on a set of nine lowland Swiss ponds representing the whole spectrum of trophic states. The developed methods to measure periphytic NPP on artificial substrates give similar values between the pseudo-replicates and are functional for ponds. The winter concentration of total nitrogen (TN) in the water is a significant predictor of the average summer rates of NPP while in submerged macrophyte beds total phosphorus (TP) is a better predictor. Rates of NPP measured in open water were most often higher and water transparency lower than in macrophyte beds, highlighting the positive influence of macrophytes on water quality and a possible co-occurrence in a pond of contrasting conditions when submerged species are present. This emphasizes the importance of maintaining or restoring submerged macrophyte stands in ponds to improve the water quality. 1. Introduction Monitoring and quality improvement of surface freshwater are major environmental concerns worldwide (Johnson et al., 2001). In European countries, the Water Framework Directive (WFD, Council of the European Communities, 2000) provides clear objectives to obtain at least a good qualitative and quantitative status of all waters in Europe by 2015. To attain these goals, all the aquatic compartments have to be considered and assessed with specific methods to classify them into high, good, moderate, bad and poor ecological quality. As ponds are recognized as distinct aquatic compartments from rivers and lakes (Søndergaard et al., 2005a) and react in a different manner to impacts, specific methods are required for their assessment; some are currently being developed (Menetrey et al., 2005) or are already operational (Biggs et al., 2000; Boix et al., 2005; Oertli et al., 2005), review in Indermuehle et al. (2005). Moreover, recent works have established ponds as being very significant components of the freshwater resource, in terms of their contribution to both local and regional biodiversity (Murphy, 2002; Oertli et al., 2002; Williams et al., 2003), confirming their importance to the concept of integrated catchments management. Practically, however, ponds are neglected in the implementation of the WFD as many countries have set a lower size limit of 50 ha to apply the directive on water bodies (Nicolet et al., 2007). Among the current threat on freshwater, eutrophication through diffuse pollution from agriculture (Havens et al., 2001) remain as an important, widespread and even growing problem for freshwater and coastal oceans (Carpenter et al., 1999; Bronmark and Hansson, 2002; Vadeboncoeur et al., 2003; Craft et al., 2007). Accelerated rates of eutrophication linked to human activities have generated much interest during the last decades and many studies have been carried out, particularly in large lakes and rivers. Notably, an international research program of OECD (Vollenweider and Kerekes, 1982) associated ranges of quantifiable environmental parameters to each of 5 classes of trophic state (ultra-oligotrophic, oligotrophic, mesotrophic, eutrophic, hypertrophic) that were previously attributed with an expert system to 100 northern temperate lakes. To implement the WFD in Danish lakes, Sondergaard et al. (2005b) proposed a pre-classification of lakes based on their trophic status given by the concentration of total phosphorus (TP), in order to identify biological indicators of eutrophication. Focusing on the assessment of eutrophication, one must take into account that high nutrient concentration in small lakes or ponds do not necessarily bring a high phytoplankton biomass and a turbid water as observed in larger lakes (Sondergaard et al., 2005a), because other controlling factors are implicated including a possible scale effect (Schindler, 1998). In this way, the ranges of concentrations of nutrients in the water assigned by OECD (Vollenweider and Kerekes, 1982) to each trophic class for lakes are not necessarily valid for ponds. Eutrophication is historically described as a regular increase of the phytoplankton primary productivity following larger inputs of inorganic nutrients (Naumann, 1927). This emphasis that any classification of water bodies in trophic state is an artificial reading of a continuous biological process. This continuity in eutrophication process complicates the establishment of well-defined limits between classes and furthermore the assignment of biological indicators values to a trophic state (Sondergaard et al., 2005b). As already pointed out by Rodhe (1969), the trophic state is expressed by a rate and must be determined by measuring primary production. Thus measuring rates of primary production in ponds varying in water concentration of major nutrients would permit to determine which parameters are best correlated and best predictors of the measured production and so eutrophication, even if these parameters are not the only factors determining the primary productivity as early underlined by Naumann (1932). Additionally, eutrophication is coupled at least in lakes by a shift from the dominance of benthic to pelagic production (Sand-Jensen and Borum, 1991; Vadeboncoeur et al., 2003). As the rate of primary productivity can be spatially and temporally heterogeneous for a given water body (Liboriussen and Jeppesen, 2006), a simple physico-chemical surrogate valid for ponds would be very valuable for ecological assessment. To record primary productivity in ponds varying in trophic status, the chosen method must be standardized and usable on the full range of trophic conditions. Ponds have generally a high littoral surface area relative to their pelagic volume and therefore an important potential for macrophyte and periphyton growth (Wetzel, 1990). For that reason, the benthic contribution to primary production can be more important in shallow systems like ponds than in deep lakes. Taking this benthic fraction into account is of prime importance, particularly for oligotrophic systems where it can represent the majority of the primary production (Vadeboncoeur et al., 2002). In addition, measuring periphytic productivity rather than macrophyte biomass could be more pertinent as the development of submerged vegetation is known to be discontinuous along trophic gradients (Scheffer, 1990). Moreover, Smoot et al. (1998) have shown that on artificial substrate the response of periphyton growth to nutrients is similar to the response of phytoplankton, making periphyton a valuable descriptor of phytoplankton response. This property allows the use of this indicator on the full spectrum of trophic conditions as it can grow in ponds with oligotrophic to hypertrophic conditions, where planktonic algae become the main producers and replace the benthic fraction. To focus on water quality, submerged macrophytes have the capacity to link the sediment with the overlying water and so to mobilize nutrients from the sediments (Graneli and Solander, 1988), in contrast to periphyton that cannot directly uptake nutrients stocked in the sediment (except for the epipelon (Hansson, 1992)). To standardize the measure of periphytic productivity, independent of the grazing pressure by zooplankton and macroinvertebrates, it has to be performed in controlled conditions with no access to grazers. Furthermore, the measurement must take into account the presence of macrophyte beds. Actually these can influence the abundance of periphyton by several mechanisms, notably competition for nutrient resources, release of allelopathic substances (Wium-Andersen, 1987; Ervin and Wetzel, 2003; Gross et al., 2003) or sheltering of the zooplanktonic and macroinvertebrate communities from predation (Timms and Brian, 1984; Jeppesen et al., 1997). Moreover, parallel measurements of periphytic productivity performed outside and inside beds of submerged plants permit to calculate a mean value of productivity between results obtained in open water and in macrophyte beds and also to detect potential co-occurrence within a pond of contrasting conditions linked by a continuous gradient between clear water zone colonized by submerged macrophytes and turbid zone without submerged vegetation. Co-occurring contrasting conditions have already been described by Scheffer et al. (1994) in shallow lakes of greater surfaces than the ponds considered here. Since there is an important nutrient recycling and rapid turnover in ponds and other shallow systems, water concentrations of nutrients show considerable fluctuation during the growing season, and a large part are mobilized in the biota and are not measurable in the water. During winter however, for ponds located at medium and high latitude, biological activity and primary productivity are very low and nutrients are in the water column for the most part, in dissolved or particle forms (Linton and Goulder, 2000). Hansson (1992) notably observed the peak of total phosphorus (TP) in open water occurring during winter for high latitudes lakes. Thus, winter values are expected to give a better picture of the potential of primary productivity by quantifying the amounts available in spring for the growth of producers. Furthermore, winter values avoid the confounding effects of uptake of phosphorus and denitrification that occur with summer readings (James et al., 2005). By performing parallel measurements of winter water physico-chemistry and of summer rates of periphytic productivity on a small dataset of ponds, this study aims to: 1) identify correlations between periphytic productivity and physico-chemical indicators of the trophic state, 2) detect a possible co-occurrence of contrasting conditions of turbidity and periphytic productivity in a given pond, 3) assess if a single chemical surrogate of primary productivity can potentially be used to classify ponds in the same biogeographic area according to their trophic state. Such a surrogate could serve as a basis to calibrate ecological value by species and select biological metrics of eutrophication. Additionally, this study will provide an opportunity to test the reliability of the method adapted for measuring the periphytic net primary productivity in ponds. 2. Material and methods 2.1. Study sites This study took place in the western part of the Swiss Plateau, a distinct biogeographic area (sensus Gonseth et al., 2001). The landscape of this area, where human population and agriculture are concentrated, has been intensely modified during the 20th century by increase in urbanisation and the intensification of agricultural practices (Lundstrom-Gillieron and Schlaepfer, 2003), resulting in the fragmentation of natural areas. The nine permanent ponds surveyed for this analysis represent a gradient of primary productivity from oligomesotrophic to hypertrophic. These ponds, located between 420 and 773 m a.s.l, are small and shallow, ranging from 327 to 10,616 m^2 in surface area, (mean: 3087 m^2, median: 2733 m^2) and from 0.38 to 1.03 m in mean depths (mean and median: 0.7 m). All these sites are colonized by fish. Four of the nine water bodies are colonized by submerged species of macrophytes (S), three by floating-leaves species (F) but without submerged hydrophytes and two supports only emerged vegetation (E). The location and the main morphometric characteristics of the ponds are given in Fig. 1 and Table 1. The sampling of the vegetation was made with the standardized method of Oertli et al. (2005) and consists of prospection by square quadrats (0.25 m^2) disposed equidistantly along transects perpendicular to the longest axis of the pond and located at regular intervals according to the pond size. The minimum number of quadrat prospected per pond (n) is related to the water surface area (m^2) by the equation \( n = 1.96 - 2.8 \times \log_{10}(\text{area}) + 2.6 \times (\log_{10}(\text{area}))^2 \). Such a strategy was shown to sample at least 70% of the real richness. A specie list was noted for each quadrat along with abundance in semi-quantitative classes. The number of quadrats prospected and the main species of macrophytes by site are given in Table 2 along with an estimation of their abundance at the pond scale. ![Map showing the study area in the western part of Switzerland and location of the ponds.](page_1092_186_1017_670.png) Fig. 1 – Study area in the western part of Switzerland and location of the ponds. 2.2. Periphytic primary productivity Rates of periphytic net primary productivity (NPP) on artificial substrates and in absence of herbivores (method adapted from Clesceri et al., 1998; Chase, 2003) were directly recorded in situ in each pond as a measure of periphytic primary productivity at two points chosen with criterion detailed thereafter. All measures were performed at location with similar water depths (0.8 m) and in areas with minimal shading from terrestrial vegetation or from surrounding plants for measures in macrophyte beds. In all cases the shading at the location of the measurement point never attain five percent of the surface. Measurements were performed continuously from June 6, 2005 to August 2, 2005, across the period of longest daytime in northern hemisphere and until the aquatic vegetation biomass summer peak (Jackson et al., 1994). This period correspond to the time of optimal growth conditions for periphyton on artificial substrate as identified by Jobgen et al. (2004). Submerged macrophyte presence in four ponds and floating-leaves species presence in three ponds were taken into account by measuring productivity inside vegetation stands and in open water. Growth rates were determined by measuring the accumulation of periphyton on the inner side of transparent plastic boxes (polystyrene PS) offering each a colonisable surface of 0.023 m^2 (Fig. 2). Boxes were covered by a net on their open face (mesh size 0.25 mm) to prevent, or at least limit the income of grazers, and were positioned two to three centimeters below the water surface in groups of three pseudo-replicates fixed around a pole planted in the pond base. According to Chase and Ryberg (2004), such a mesh retains about 10% of the available light “but did not significantly reduce algal growth in a controlled experiment performed in the absence of grazers”. Preventing the access of grazers is of prime importance for this study and as Jones et al. (2002) pointed out, the grazing pressure is a stronger limiting factor of the net production of periphyton than the water nutrient concentration. To reduce to the minimum meteorologically related variation among ponds, sampling and replacement of the boxes of all nine ponds were carried out over the shortest possible time period (two days). 2.3. Physico-chemistry Water physico-chemistry was measured once in winter and physical parameters were measured five times in summer (at each box replacement). The winter fieldwork was undertaken during three consecutive days (from 9 to 11 February, 2005) after a long frost period. Water sampling and field measurements were made at the deeper central point of each pond by drilling a hole in the ice cover. Water samples were taken at 20 cm below the icy surface with a sampling bottle, and then stocked in acid pre-rinse PE plastic bottles immediately before being stored in the dark in a refrigerated box. Water samples for the analysis of dissolved components (PO₄-P (soluble reactive phosphorus = SRP), NO₃-N, NH₃-N) were filtered in situ trough 0.45 μm filters (Schleicher & Schuell ME 25). Unfiltered samples were kept for total phosphorus (TP) and total nitrogen (TN) analyses. All samples were stored in the dark at 4 °C and analysed within 48 h after field collection. The SESA water quality laboratory (VD) analyzed all the water samples with standard methods. TP was determined after potassium persulphate digestion at 121 °C and under pressure for half an hour; SRP was further measured by the ascorbate acid/molybdenum blue method (Clesceri et al., 1998). TN was determined by chemiluminescence after oxidization in NO at high temperature and reaction with ozone. NH₃-N was determined by colorimetry with the salicylate method. NO₃-N was determined by ion chromatography. A deep profile was made in the field for physical parameters (temperature, pH, conductivity) using a multi-parameters probe (YSI 556®, YSI Incorporated, Yellowspring, USA). Water turbidity (NTU) and transparency (cm) were also measured in the field with a turbidity meter (WTW Turb 355 IR®, WTW GmbH, Weilheim, D) and a Snellen tube of 60 cm length. 2.4. Data analyses To assess the reliability of the primary productivity measurement method, mean rate of productivity and variance were calculated for each measurement point and sampling occasion. In parallel, productivity rates by pseudo-replicates were box-plotted by point and sampling occasion to visually detect eventual outliers. To test if any measured physical and chemical variables could explain the differences of periphytic productivity among ponds, multiple stepwise linear regressions were performed (threshold of entry \( p \leq 0.05 \), removal \( \geq 0.1 \)). As we wanted to explore the relationships between summer periphytic growth rate and winter concentrations of TP or TN, linear stepwise regressions were performed with these two parameters in a first set of predictors and physical parameters in a second set to see if their inclusion could improve the \( R^2 \) and significance of the models. Regressions were performed between seasonal productivity rates of each pond and the corresponding mean of physical parameters of the water as well as winter concentrations of nutrients. Mean productivity rate by pond is the sum of the means of the two sampling points of each sampling occasion. To refine the regressions according to the sampling points, the same above procedure was applied separately for three subsets of the data (open water (O), submerged species (S) and floating-leaves species (F)). As one of the ponds shows very high rates of productivity, we reapplied the whole procedure after removing this extreme value from the dataset to verify if the identified regressions remained significant. The critical \( \alpha \) values were corrected by applying the Bonferroni corrections for non-independent comparisons (Maxwell and Delaney, 1990). As a second objective we wanted to compare the rates of periphytic productivity between sampling points located in the same pond, respectively inside versus outside macrophyte stands. With all sampling occasions, there were enough data to test the significance of the differences among locations with an unparametric test (Mann–Whitney) between productivity by boxes at the sampling points. As there were not enough pseudo-replicates to validate the statistical test by sampling occasion, simple box plot by sampling points and by sampling occasion were plotted for each pond. This revealed if differences were detectable, and helped rank productivity rates at each vegetated sampling point in space and time as lower, equal or higher to unvegetated points. 3. Results The set of ponds display a wide range of periphytic growth rate, nutrient concentrations and water physical parameters. Measures of periphytic growth rate by single point and sampling occasion ranged from 0.022 to 48.406 gC/m²/14 days (0.0016–3.458 gC/m²/day) and the mean seasonal value for ponds ranged from 1.284 to 52.950 gC/m²/56 days (0.023– 0.946 gC/m²/day). The daily mean seasonal value by point and by pond and the mean value by point and by sampling occasions are given in Table 3 along with variance between pseudo-replicates, except for the first sampling occasions where the three boxes by point were weighted together. Rates for the last sampling occasion in open water of pond P3 could not be retained for the analyses because the boxes emerged during sampling. Six exposed boxes were also damaged and the measurements were removed from the dataset. Winter nutrient concentrations of TP ranged from 0.002 to 0.346 mg L⁻¹ and TN varied from 0.7 to 5.83 mg L⁻¹. Ranges and mean values for summer and winter measurements of physico-chemical parameters are given in Table 4 3.1. Regressions of productivity rates with physico-chemical parameters The mean seasonal rates of periphytic primary productivity by pond defined as the sum of the mean value by pond for each sampling occasion are positively correlated to the water concentration of total nitrogen (TN) measured during the previous winter (linear regression for the whole season, Table 5, model 1, \( r^2 = 0.974, p = 8.55e-07 \)). With the stepwise procedure, the regression remained the same with winter TN as unique predictor. Without the extreme value of the hypertrophic site (P6), the regression between the seasonal productivity by pond and the winter concentration of TN remained valid, even if less significant and less strong (model 2, Table 5, \( r^2 = 0.754, p = 5.16e-03 \)). In that case, the stepwise regression retained the mean water transparency as second predictor negatively correlated with productivity, improving the performance of the model (model 3, Table 5). The scatter plot of the seasonal values of productivity versus TN or TP presented in Fig. 3 shows additionally the OECD (Vollenweider and Kerekes, 1982; Wetzel, 1983; Forsberg and Ryding, 1980) limits of nutrient concentration between trophic classes as well as the limits between the classes of ecological quality included for shallow lakes by Sondergaard et al. (2005b). For the measures located in open water, regressions with TN were also significant for seasonal productivity (model 1, Table 6, \( r^2 = 0.937, p = 1.68e-05 \)). The stepwise procedure even improves the model by including the mean turbidity as second predictor (model 2 Table 6). Without the upper value of productivity (pond P6), the regressions are less strong but the predictors remain the same.

Productivity rates were very similar between location at the two sites colonized by Polygonum amphibium (P1 and P2), and on the remaining site (P8), rates in macrophyte stands were higher at first, but then lower than in open water even if the stands remained stable over the eight weeks of measurement. 4. Discussion 4.1. Reliability and limitations of the method for ponds The rates of productivity measured for each pseudo-replicate for a given point and sampling occasion were similar even if the variance between the boxes increased for high means (see Table 3 and Fig. 4). Despite this uncontrolled effect, the method is sensitive and allows classifying ponds of this dataset by trophic states characterized by TN as a higher variance between pseudo-replicates occurs in systems already hypertrophic. However as the data material is small and restricted to a limited geographic area, these results need to be confirmed on a broader scale to generalize this outcome for ponds in the area. Observed rates (Table 3) were low compared with other studies (for instance see Chase (2003) with measured productivity ranging between 6.12 and 56.2 g/m²/day). This could be due to the smaller net mesh size used to cover the open face of boxes, which could have limited the colonization by algae. On the other hand this net allowed inter-sites comparisons by strongly reducing and homogenising the residual grazing factor. The nature of the artificial substrate can also be involved. Actually, the review of Cattaneo and Amireault (1992) suggested that the type of artificial substrate is not crucial but Danilov and Ekelund (2001) observed no growth of periphyton on PVC substrate and the formation of a slim layer of bacteria covering the artificial substrate. No such layer was observed in the current study and the poly-styrene plastic often employed in biology, notably for the Petri dishes, is more likely to have played an inhibitory effect as it seems to be the case with PVC. 4.2. Periphytic productivity and nutrients The significant positive regression observed between TN and mean periphytic growth rate is consistent with other studies, for instance Luttenton and Lowe (2006) found significant correlation between nitrogen concentration on nutrient-diffusive substrata (NDS) and total biovolume of periphyton growing on this substrate. Similarly Chase and Ryberg (2004) found positive correlations between primary productivity measured with a method similar to this study and TP and TN in order of importance. Kahlert and Pettersson (2002) also measured an increase in the biomass of benthic algae with trophic levels even if it was not correlated with the nutrient status of the algae itself.
