Effectively, TN is often highly correlated with TP in freshwater (Downing and Mccauley, 1992; this study) and with other trophic state variables like chlorophyll a (Forsberg and Ryding, 1980). Moreover, rooted plants can obtain phosphorus from the sediment and in this way act as a source for the water column (Carignan and Kalff, 1982) while nitrogen on the other hand tends to be lost through denitrification within plant stands (Weisner et al., 1994). Peretyatko et al. (2007) observed notably that dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) tends to decrease in pond water during the warmer month, especially in sites without submerged species and abundant phytoplankton. Therefore, in shallow lakes with macrophyte stands, algal populations can be nitrogen limited during summer (Moss et al., 2005) even if, as in this study, the winter TN/TP ratio does not indicate a nitrogen limitation in most of the ponds. Additionally, on NDS spanning a large range of molar N/P ratios and nutrient concentrations, Luttenton and Lowe (2006) showed that nitrogen concentration is a significant predictor of the algal biovolume growing on the substrate and that neither the N/P ratio nor the phosphorus concentration of the NDS were significantly correlated with this biovolume. These results suggest that the TP concentration measured in winter is an underestimation of the available phosphorus during the growing season. As all the ponds were icy at the time of the winter sampling, the absence of turbulence under the ice cover should have limited the suspension of fine particles in the water column. During warm months with a high water temperature and a low concentration of dissolved oxygen, ponds with organic P-saturated sediment can be net source of P by release of the iron-bound P (Søndergaard et al., 1999; Fairchild and Velinsky, 2006). Conversely the winter concentrations of TN could be an over estimation of the available nutrient in summer as a significant part can be lost through denitrification. This could explain the relatively high concentrations of TN and the corresponding trophic levels attributed to the ponds when compared to the TP concentrations and corresponding trophic classes (Fig. 3). It is therefore likely that the trophic status of the ponds is overestimated when the limits of Wetzel (1983) or Forsberg and Ryding (1980) set for large lakes are directly applied to the winter concentration of TN as in Fig. 3. On the other hand the limits of nutrient concentration proposed by Søndergaard et al. (2005b) to set ecological quality classes for shallow lakes (Fig. 3, dashed lines) seems to be more appropriate for ponds. In particular, it reassigned the sites classified as eutrophic following the TP or TN scales of Vollenweider and Kerekes (1982), Forsberg and Ryding (1980) and Wetzel (1983) into moderate to good quality, and the mesotrophic sites into high quality while keeping the hypertrophic ponds in poor to bad quality classes. These scales, even if not giving a trophic status, rely directly on water quality and distribute the gradient of nutrient concentrations observed in ponds in all the quality classes based either on TP or TN. 4.3. Roles and effects of submerged macrophytes The observed lower rates of periphytic productivity within boxes placed in the submerged macrophyte stands of two truly stagnant sites harboring continuously submerged species show the influences of submerged plants on nutrient cycling. Notably, macrophytes and their associated epiphytes mobilize and store nutrients prior to releasing it during their senescence. This competitive storage involves a reduced nutrient availability for phytoplankton (Kufel and Ozimek, 1994) and for the periphyton colonizing the artificial substrate. These results are concordant with the observation of Takamura et al. (2003) who found at a similar nutrient level a significantly lower concentration of planktonic chlorophyll within submerged macrophytes than in lakes without submerged species. Similarly, Liboriussen and Jeppesen (2003) and Vadeboncoeur et al. (2001) observed lower gross primary productivity in clear water compared to turbid one. When measuring biomass of phytoplankton, Peretyatko et al. (2007) reported lower amount in ponds supporting submerged plants when compared to unvegetated ponds or those with floating-leaved species only. With a measure of the total lake net primary production, Blindow et al. (2006) observed higher level in a clear lake compared to a turbid one but the two lakes considered in that study were deeper than the ponds considered here, and their water column, if turbid, experienced more self-shading and higher rates of community respiration than shallower sites. In fact, Blindow et al. (2006) pointed out that this difference of total net primary productivity between clear and turbid water tends to decrease with the mean depth by reducing the water volume below the compensation depth. As the artificial substrates used in our study were set 2–3 cm below the water surface, the measured growths of periphyton are less influenced by phytoplankton shading. The contrasting conditions of turbidity and transparency observed between macrophyte stands and open water were previously described by Scheffer et al. (1994) in shallow lakes. Other factors could also explain the lower periphytic productivity rates often measured within plant stands, for example shading by the macrophytes canopy (Ozimek et al., 1990), strong evidence of release of allelopathic substances by macrophytes (Gross et al., 2007) or increased rates of sedimentation (Carpenter, 1981; Petticrew et al., 1991) accompanied by a reduced resuspension within macrophyte stands (Scheffer et al., 1993). A lower or a negative net production of the epiphyte communities colonizing the artificial substrate placed within submerged species, as seasonally observed on natural substrate by Vis et al. (2006), can also explain the difference between open water and macrophyte stands. If the respiration process is more important than in open water, the amount of carbon measured after two weeks underestimates primary production. Conversely, the refuge effect of submerged macrophyte for grazers (Timms and Brian, 1984; Jeppesen et al., 1997) must be here less important as the experimental design that we used strongly limit the influence of large macroinvertebrates grazers. On one of the four sites harboring submerged species (P5), the early senescence of Myriophyllum spicatum (represented by the upward arrow in Fig. 4) during the second part of June was accompanied by a strong increase in the rate of productivity at the corresponding location that even surpasses the rate measured in open water. This is probably due to the direct recycling of nutrients released by macrophytes as periphyton can directly exploit this resource (Cattaneo and Kalff, 1979; Carignan and Kalff, 1982; Rooney and Kalff, 2003). Moreover, Carpenter (1980) but also Smith and Adams (1986) showed that the importance of macrophyte-derived nutrients for epiphyton increases with the degree of senescence of the plant. Additionally, Carignan and Kalff (1982) have specifically measured that M. spicatum is a significant source of highly available P for the surrounding epiphyton and phytoplankton. Interestingly, the water transparency remains inversely correlated to the rate of primary productivity and became simultaneously lower within macrophytes than in open water (data not shown). This peak of productivity was follow by a rapid growth of dense beds of Ceratophyllum demersum in early July along with a reduction of the rate measured in the box even if transparency remained low (downward arrow in Fig. 4). During this period, the rate of productivity continued to increase in open water to reach the seasonal peak during the first fortnight of July (Fig. 4). This delayed growth in open water compared to the growth measured in senescing beds during the previous two weeks can be linked to the horizontal diffusion from beds to open water of the available nutrients, similarly to what was observed by Rooney and Kalff (2003) studying active cycling from the sediment mediated by macrophytes. During the last fortnight of July, open water was progressively colonized by stands of C. demersum generating a net reduction in the productivity rate and resulting in similar values between the two sampling points becoming gradually both vegetated. The site P9 is a bit different as it has a flow-through regime, which is not the case in the other sites. In this case the mean rates of productivity were higher in macrophyte stands than in open water (118.7%–226.5% of the rates measured in open water). As already mentioned, measured rates as well as absolute differences were very low and the values were even overlapping between pseudo-replicates of the two sampling points (Fig. 4). Nevertheless, this trend differs notably from the other sites characterized by well-marked differences in periphytic productivity measured in the boxes between plant stands and open water. This difference can be due to different factors, notably a lower current speed through the dense macrophyte stands (Gessner, 1950; Stephan and Gutknecht, 2002) increasing the water retention time and potentially enhancing both sedimentation and the use of dissolved nutrients. Other factors could be involved, notably a release of nutrients by macrophytes, as mentioned earlier. Actually, this pond exhibits low concentration of dissolved nutrients (Table 4) and the nutritive contribution of healthy plants to periphyton, even if little, is known to be more important in oligotrophic water (Eminson and Moss, 1980; Burkholder and Wetzel, 1990). Additionally, nutrient diffusion may be facilitated and mixing of the water mediated by the current tends to also homogenize the conditions across the site. In this pond, transparency was always at the maximum value at the two sampling points and the turbidity remained low in value and range (inferior to four NTU among all measurements). 5. Conclusions and perspectives Firstly, the method of periphytic productivity measurement adapted in this study operates well with this dataset of ponds and gives repeatable measures except for the hypertrophic sites that showed an increase of the variance between pseudo-replicates. Secondly the results indicated that for the study area considered, the winter concentration of total nitrogen was a significant predictor of the summer rates of periphytic productivity measured in open water or averaged by ponds. When beds of submerged macrophytes were present, the periphytic productivity within the plant stands was generally lower and the transparency higher. In that case, the winter concentration of TP was a stronger and better predictor of the productivity. This limited growth of periphyton within the boxes placed in submerged macrophyte beds puts in evidence for the positive effects of submerged plants on water quality and emphasizes the importance of maintaining or restoring submerged macrophyte stands in ponds. Extending these results for assessing pond water quality in other region of Switzerland would require a similar study on a broader scale notably with sites located at higher altitudes, as the range of environmental parameters of particular concern for primary productivity differs broadly between Alps and lowlands (Hinden et al., 2005). Measuring the trophic status of ponds: Relationships between summer rate of periphytic net primary productivity and water physico-chemistry Lionel Sager* Laboratory of Ecology and Aquatic Biology (LEBA), University of Geneva, Chemin des Clochettes 18, CH-1206 Geneva, Switzerland ARTICLE INFO Article history: Received 2 July 2008 Received in revised form 22 December 2008 Accepted 23 December 2008 Published online 3 January 2009 Keywords: AFDW Alternative stable states Assessment Eutrophication Nitrogen Phosphorus Submerged macrophytes ABSTRACT The monitoring of the water quality is a major environmental concern and specific method of assessment needs to be addressed for ponds. Among threats on freshwater, eutrophication remains an important and widespread problem. To assess if the trophic state of ponds can be significantly predicted by physico-chemical surrogates, parallel measurements of water physico-chemistry and of summer rates of periphytic net primary productivity (NPP) were performed on a set of nine lowland Swiss ponds representing the whole spectrum of trophic states. The developed methods to measure periphytic NPP on artificial substrates give similar values between the pseudo-replicates and are functional for ponds. The winter concentration of total nitrogen (TN) in the water is a significant predictor of the average summer rates of NPP while in submerged macrophyte beds total phosphorus (TP) is a better predictor. Rates of NPP measured in open water were most often higher and water transparency lower than in macrophyte beds, highlighting the positive influence of macrophytes on water quality and a possible co-occurrence in a pond of contrasting conditions when submerged species are present. This emphasizes the importance of maintaining or restoring submerged macrophyte stands in ponds to improve the water quality. 1. Introduction Monitoring and quality improvement of surface freshwater are major environmental concerns worldwide (Johnson et al., 2001). In European countries, the Water Framework Directive (WFD, Council of the European Communities, 2000) provides clear objectives to obtain at least a good qualitative and quantitative status of all waters in Europe by 2015. To attain these goals, all the aquatic compartments have to be considered and assessed with specific methods to classify them into high, good, moderate, bad and poor ecological quality. As ponds are recognized as distinct aquatic compartments from rivers and lakes (Søndergaard et al., 2005a) and react in a different manner to impacts, specific methods are required for their assessment; some are currently being developed (Menetrey et al., 2005) or are already operational (Biggs et al., 2000; Boix et al., 2005; Oertli et al., 2005), review in Indermuehle et al. (2005). Moreover, recent works have established ponds as being very significant components of the freshwater resource, in terms of their contribution to both local and regional biodiversity (Murphy, 2002; Oertli et al., 2002; Williams et al., 2003), confirming their importance to the concept of integrated catchments management. Practically, however, ponds are neglected in the implementation of the WFD as many countries have set a lower size limit of 50 ha to apply the directive on water bodies (Nicolet et al., 2007). Among the current threat on freshwater, eutrophication through diffuse pollution from agriculture (Havens et al., 2001) remain as an important, widespread and even growing problem for freshwater and coastal oceans (Carpenter et al., 1999; Bronmark and Hansson, 2002; Vadeboncoeur et al., 2003; Craft et al., 2007). Accelerated rates of eutrophication linked to human activities have generated much interest during the last decades and many studies have been carried out, particularly in large lakes and rivers. Notably, an international research program of OECD (Vollenweider and Kerekes, 1982) associated ranges of quantifiable environmental parameters to each of 5 classes of trophic state (ultra-oligotrophic, oligotrophic, mesotrophic, eutrophic, hypertrophic) that were previously attributed with an expert system to 100 northern temperate lakes. To implement the WFD in Danish lakes, Sondergaard et al. (2005b) proposed a pre-classification of lakes based on their trophic status given by the concentration of total phosphorus (TP), in order to identify biological indicators of eutrophication. Focusing on the assessment of eutrophication, one must take into account that high nutrient concentration in small lakes or ponds do not necessarily bring a high phytoplankton biomass and a turbid water as observed in larger lakes (Sondergaard et al., 2005a), because other controlling factors are implicated including a possible scale effect (Schindler, 1998). In this way, the ranges of concentrations of nutrients in the water assigned by OECD (Vollenweider and Kerekes, 1982) to each trophic class for lakes are not necessarily valid for ponds. Eutrophication is historically described as a regular increase of the phytoplankton primary productivity following larger inputs of inorganic nutrients (Naumann, 1927). This emphasis that any classification of water bodies in trophic state is an artificial reading of a continuous biological process. This continuity in eutrophication process complicates the establishment of well-defined limits between classes and furthermore the assignment of biological indicators values to a trophic state (Sondergaard et al., 2005b). As already pointed out by Rodhe (1969), the trophic state is expressed by a rate and must be determined by measuring primary production. Thus measuring rates of primary production in ponds varying in water concentration of major nutrients would permit to determine which parameters are best correlated and best predictors of the measured production and so eutrophication, even if these parameters are not the only factors determining the primary productivity as early underlined by Naumann (1932). Additionally, eutrophication is coupled at least in lakes by a shift from the dominance of benthic to pelagic production (Sand-Jensen and Borum, 1991; Vadeboncoeur et al., 2003). As the rate of primary productivity can be spatially and temporally heterogeneous for a given water body (Liboriussen and Jeppesen, 2006), a simple physico-chemical surrogate valid for ponds would be very valuable for ecological assessment. To record primary productivity in ponds varying in trophic status, the chosen method must be standardized and usable on the full range of trophic conditions. Ponds have generally a high littoral surface area relative to their pelagic volume and therefore an important potential for macrophyte and periphyton growth (Wetzel, 1990). For that reason, the benthic contribution to primary production can be more important in shallow systems like ponds than in deep lakes. Taking this benthic fraction into account is of prime importance, particularly for oligotrophic systems where it can represent the majority of the primary production (Vadeboncoeur et al., 2002). In addition, measuring periphytic productivity rather than macrophyte biomass could be more pertinent as the development of submerged vegetation is known to be discontinuous along trophic gradients (Scheffer, 1990). Moreover, Smoot et al. (1998) have shown that on artificial substrate the response of periphyton growth to nutrients is similar to the response of phytoplankton, making periphyton a valuable descriptor of phytoplankton response. This property allows the use of this indicator on the full spectrum of trophic conditions as it can grow in ponds with oligotrophic to hypertrophic conditions, where planktonic algae become the main producers and replace the benthic fraction. To focus on water quality, submerged macrophytes have the capacity to link the sediment with the overlying water and so to mobilize nutrients from the sediments (Graneli and Solander, 1988), in contrast to periphyton that cannot directly uptake nutrients stocked in the sediment (except for the epipelon (Hansson, 1992)). To standardize the measure of periphytic productivity, independent of the grazing pressure by zooplankton and macroinvertebrates, it has to be performed in controlled conditions with no access to grazers. Furthermore, the measurement must take into account the presence of macrophyte beds. Actually these can influence the abundance of periphyton by several mechanisms, notably competition for nutrient resources, release of allelopathic substances (Wium-Andersen, 1987; Ervin and Wetzel, 2003; Gross et al., 2003) or sheltering of the zooplanktonic and macroinvertebrate communities from predation (Timms and Brian, 1984; Jeppesen et al., 1997). Moreover, parallel measurements of periphytic productivity performed outside and inside beds of submerged plants permit to calculate a mean value of productivity between results obtained in open water and in macrophyte beds and also to detect potential co-occurrence within a pond of contrasting conditions linked by a continuous gradient between clear water zone colonized by submerged macrophytes and turbid zone without submerged vegetation. Co-occurring contrasting conditions have already been described by Scheffer et al. (1994) in shallow lakes of greater surfaces than the ponds considered here. Since there is an important nutrient recycling and rapid turnover in ponds and other shallow systems, water concentrations of nutrients show considerable fluctuation during the growing season, and a large part are mobilized in the biota and are not measurable in the water. During winter however, for ponds located at medium and high latitude, biological activity and primary productivity are very low and nutrients are in the water column for the most part, in dissolved or particle forms (Linton and Goulder, 2000). Hansson (1992) notably observed the peak of total phosphorus (TP) in open water occurring during winter for high latitudes lakes. Thus, winter values are expected to give a better picture of the potential of primary productivity by quantifying the amounts available in spring for the growth of producers. Furthermore, winter values avoid the confounding effects of uptake of phosphorus and denitrification that occur with summer readings (James et al., 2005). By performing parallel measurements of winter water physico-chemistry and of summer rates of periphytic productivity on a small dataset of ponds, this study aims to: 1) identify correlations between periphytic productivity and physico-chemical indicators of the trophic state, 2) detect a possible co-occurrence of contrasting conditions of turbidity and periphytic productivity in a given pond, 3) assess if a single chemical surrogate of primary productivity can potentially be used to classify ponds in the same biogeographic area according to their trophic state. Such a surrogate could serve as a basis to calibrate ecological value by species and select biological metrics of eutrophication. Additionally, this study will provide an opportunity to test the reliability of the method adapted for measuring the periphytic net primary productivity in ponds. 2. Material and methods 2.1. Study sites This study took place in the western part of the Swiss Plateau, a distinct biogeographic area (sensus Gonseth et al., 2001). The landscape of this area, where human population and agriculture are concentrated, has been intensely modified during the 20th century by increase in urbanisation and the intensification of agricultural practices (Lundstrom-Gillieron and Schlaepfer, 2003), resulting in the fragmentation of natural areas. The nine permanent ponds surveyed for this analysis represent a gradient of primary productivity from oligomesotrophic to hypertrophic. These ponds, located between 420 and 773 m a.s.l, are small and shallow, ranging from 327 to 10,616 m^2 in surface area, (mean: 3087 m^2, median: 2733 m^2) and from 0.38 to 1.03 m in mean depths (mean and median: 0.7 m). All these sites are colonized by fish. Four of the nine water bodies are colonized by submerged species of macrophytes (S), three by floating-leaves species (F) but without submerged hydrophytes and two supports only emerged vegetation (E). The location and the main morphometric characteristics of the ponds are given in Fig. 1 and Table 1. The sampling of the vegetation was made with the standardized method of Oertli et al. (2005) and consists of prospection by square quadrats (0.25 m^2) disposed equidistantly along transects perpendicular to the longest axis of the pond and located at regular intervals according to the pond size. The minimum number of quadrat prospected per pond (n) is related to the water surface area (m^2) by the equation \( n = 1.96 - 2.8 \times \log_{10}(\text{area}) + 2.6 \times (\log_{10}(\text{area}))^2 \). Such a strategy was shown to sample at least 70% of the real richness. A specie list was noted for each quadrat along with abundance in semi-quantitative classes. The number of quadrats prospected and the main species of macrophytes by site are given in Table 2 along with an estimation of their abundance at the pond scale. ![Map showing the study area in the western part of Switzerland and location of the ponds.](page_1092_186_1017_670.png) Fig. 1 – Study area in the western part of Switzerland and location of the ponds. 2.2. Periphytic primary productivity Rates of periphytic net primary productivity (NPP) on artificial substrates and in absence of herbivores (method adapted from Clesceri et al., 1998; Chase, 2003) were directly recorded in situ in each pond as a measure of periphytic primary productivity at two points chosen with criterion detailed thereafter. All measures were performed at location with similar water depths (0.8 m) and in areas with minimal shading from terrestrial vegetation or from surrounding plants for measures in macrophyte beds. In all cases the shading at the location of the measurement point never attain five percent of the surface. Measurements were performed continuously from June 6, 2005 to August 2, 2005, across the period of longest daytime in northern hemisphere and until the aquatic vegetation biomass summer peak (Jackson et al., 1994). This period correspond to the time of optimal growth conditions for periphyton on artificial substrate as identified by Jobgen et al. (2004). Submerged macrophyte presence in four ponds and floating-leaves species presence in three ponds were taken into account by measuring productivity inside vegetation stands and in open water. Growth rates were determined by measuring the accumulation of periphyton on the inner side of transparent plastic boxes (polystyrene PS) offering each a colonisable surface of 0.023 m^2 (Fig. 2). Boxes were covered by a net on their open face (mesh size 0.25 mm) to prevent, or at least limit the income of grazers, and were positioned two to three centimeters below the water surface in groups of three pseudo-replicates fixed around a pole planted in the pond base. According to Chase and Ryberg (2004), such a mesh retains about 10% of the available light “but did not significantly reduce algal growth in a controlled experiment performed in the absence of grazers”. Preventing the access of grazers is of prime importance for this study and as Jones et al. (2002) pointed out, the grazing pressure is a stronger limiting factor of the net production of periphyton than the water nutrient concentration. To reduce to the minimum meteorologically related variation among ponds, sampling and replacement of the boxes of all nine ponds were carried out over the shortest possible time period (two days). 2.3. Physico-chemistry Water physico-chemistry was measured once in winter and physical parameters were measured five times in summer (at each box replacement). The winter fieldwork was undertaken during three consecutive days (from 9 to 11 February, 2005) after a long frost period. Water sampling and field measurements were made at the deeper central point of each pond by drilling a hole in the ice cover. Water samples were taken at 20 cm below the icy surface with a sampling bottle, and then stocked in acid pre-rinse PE plastic bottles immediately before being stored in the dark in a refrigerated box. Water samples for the analysis of dissolved components (PO₄-P (soluble reactive phosphorus = SRP), NO₃-N, NH₃-N) were filtered in situ trough 0.45 μm filters (Schleicher & Schuell ME 25). Unfiltered samples were kept for total phosphorus (TP) and total nitrogen (TN) analyses. All samples were stored in the dark at 4 °C and analysed within 48 h after field collection. The SESA water quality laboratory (VD) analyzed all the water samples with standard methods. TP was determined after potassium persulphate digestion at 121 °C and under pressure for half an hour; SRP was further measured by the ascorbate acid/molybdenum blue method (Clesceri et al., 1998). TN was determined by chemiluminescence after oxidization in NO at high temperature and reaction with ozone. NH₃-N was determined by colorimetry with the salicylate method. NO₃-N was determined by ion chromatography. A deep profile was made in the field for physical parameters (temperature, pH, conductivity) using a multi-parameters probe (YSI 556®, YSI Incorporated, Yellowspring, USA). Water turbidity (NTU) and transparency (cm) were also measured in the field with a turbidity meter (WTW Turb 355 IR®, WTW GmbH, Weilheim, D) and a Snellen tube of 60 cm length. 2.4. Data analyses To assess the reliability of the primary productivity measurement method, mean rate of productivity and variance were calculated for each measurement point and sampling occasion. In parallel, productivity rates by pseudo-replicates were box-plotted by point and sampling occasion to visually detect eventual outliers. To test if any measured physical and chemical variables could explain the differences of periphytic productivity among ponds, multiple stepwise linear regressions were performed (threshold of entry \( p \leq 0.05 \), removal \( \geq 0.1 \)). As we wanted to explore the relationships between summer periphytic growth rate and winter concentrations of TP or TN, linear stepwise regressions were performed with these two parameters in a first set of predictors and physical parameters in a second set to see if their inclusion could improve the \( R^2 \) and significance of the models. Regressions were performed between seasonal productivity rates of each pond and the corresponding mean of physical parameters of the water as well as winter concentrations of nutrients. Mean productivity rate by pond is the sum of the means of the two sampling points of each sampling occasion. To refine the regressions according to the sampling points, the same above procedure was applied separately for three subsets of the data (open water (O), submerged species (S) and floating-leaves species (F)). As one of the ponds shows very high rates of productivity, we reapplied the whole procedure after removing this extreme value from the dataset to verify if the identified regressions remained significant. The critical \( \alpha \) values were corrected by applying the Bonferroni corrections for non-independent comparisons (Maxwell and Delaney, 1990). As a second objective we wanted to compare the rates of periphytic productivity between sampling points located in the same pond, respectively inside versus outside macrophyte stands. With all sampling occasions, there were enough data to test the significance of the differences among locations with an unparametric test (Mann–Whitney) between productivity by boxes at the sampling points. As there were not enough pseudo-replicates to validate the statistical test by sampling occasion, simple box plot by sampling points and by sampling occasion were plotted for each pond. This revealed if differences were detectable, and helped rank productivity rates at each vegetated sampling point in space and time as lower, equal or higher to unvegetated points. 3. Results The set of ponds display a wide range of periphytic growth rate, nutrient concentrations and water physical parameters. Measures of periphytic growth rate by single point and sampling occasion ranged from 0.022 to 48.406 gC/m²/14 days (0.0016–3.458 gC/m²/day) and the mean seasonal value for ponds ranged from 1.284 to 52.950 gC/m²/56 days (0.023– 0.946 gC/m²/day). The daily mean seasonal value by point and by pond and the mean value by point and by sampling occasions are given in Table 3 along with variance between pseudo-replicates, except for the first sampling occasions where the three boxes by point were weighted together. Rates for the last sampling occasion in open water of pond P3 could not be retained for the analyses because the boxes emerged during sampling. Six exposed boxes were also damaged and the measurements were removed from the dataset. Winter nutrient concentrations of TP ranged from 0.002 to 0.346 mg L⁻¹ and TN varied from 0.7 to 5.83 mg L⁻¹. Ranges and mean values for summer and winter measurements of physico-chemical parameters are given in Table 4 3.1. Regressions of productivity rates with physico-chemical parameters The mean seasonal rates of periphytic primary productivity by pond defined as the sum of the mean value by pond for each sampling occasion are positively correlated to the water concentration of total nitrogen (TN) measured during the previous winter (linear regression for the whole season, Table 5, model 1, \( r^2 = 0.974, p = 8.55e-07 \)). With the stepwise procedure, the regression remained the same with winter TN as unique predictor. Without the extreme value of the hypertrophic site (P6), the regression between the seasonal productivity by pond and the winter concentration of TN remained valid, even if less significant and less strong (model 2, Table 5, \( r^2 = 0.754, p = 5.16e-03 \)). In that case, the stepwise regression retained the mean water transparency as second predictor negatively correlated with productivity, improving the performance of the model (model 3, Table 5). The scatter plot of the seasonal values of productivity versus TN or TP presented in Fig. 3 shows additionally the OECD (Vollenweider and Kerekes, 1982; Wetzel, 1983; Forsberg and Ryding, 1980) limits of nutrient concentration between trophic classes as well as the limits between the classes of ecological quality included for shallow lakes by Sondergaard et al. (2005b). For the measures located in open water, regressions with TN were also significant for seasonal productivity (model 1, Table 6, \( r^2 = 0.937, p = 1.68e-05 \)). The stepwise procedure even improves the model by including the mean turbidity as second predictor (model 2 Table 6). Without the upper value of productivity (pond P6), the regressions are less strong but the predictors remain the same.

Discussion 4.1. Reliability and limitations of the method for ponds The rates of productivity measured for each pseudo-replicate for a given point and sampling occasion were similar even if the variance between the boxes increased for high means (see Table 3 and Fig. 4). Despite this uncontrolled effect, the method is sensitive and allows classifying ponds of this dataset by trophic states characterized by TN as a higher variance between pseudo-replicates occurs in systems already hypertrophic. However as the data material is small and restricted to a limited geographic area, these results need to be confirmed on a broader scale to generalize this outcome for ponds in the area. Observed rates (Table 3) were low compared with other studies (for instance see Chase (2003) with measured productivity ranging between 6.12 and 56.2 g/m²/day). This could be due to the smaller net mesh size used to cover the open face of boxes, which could have limited the colonization by algae. On the other hand this net allowed inter-sites comparisons by strongly reducing and homogenising the residual grazing factor. The nature of the artificial substrate can also be involved. Actually, the review of Cattaneo and Amireault (1992) suggested that the type of artificial substrate is not crucial but Danilov and Ekelund (2001) observed no growth of periphyton on PVC substrate and the formation of a slim layer of bacteria covering the artificial substrate. No such layer was observed in the current study and the poly-styrene plastic often employed in biology, notably for the Petri dishes, is more likely to have played an inhibitory effect as it seems to be the case with PVC. 4.2. Periphytic productivity and nutrients The significant positive regression observed between TN and mean periphytic growth rate is consistent with other studies, for instance Luttenton and Lowe (2006) found significant correlation between nitrogen concentration on nutrient-diffusive substrata (NDS) and total biovolume of periphyton growing on this substrate. Similarly Chase and Ryberg (2004) found positive correlations between primary productivity measured with a method similar to this study and TP and TN in order of importance. Kahlert and Pettersson (2002) also measured an increase in the biomass of benthic algae with trophic levels even if it was not correlated with the nutrient status of the algae itself. Moreover, rooted plants can obtain phosphorus from the sediment and in this way act as a source for the water column (Carignan and Kalff, 1982) while nitrogen on the other hand tends to be lost through denitrification within plant stands (Weisner et al., 1994). Peretyatko et al. (2007) observed notably that dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) tends to decrease in pond water during the warmer month, especially in sites without submerged species and abundant phytoplankton. Therefore, in shallow lakes with macrophyte stands, algal populations can be nitrogen limited during summer (Moss et al., 2005) even if, as in this study, the winter TN/TP ratio does not indicate a nitrogen limitation in most of the ponds. Additionally, on NDS spanning a large range of molar N/P ratios and nutrient concentrations, Luttenton and Lowe (2006) showed that nitrogen concentration is a significant predictor of the algal biovolume growing on the substrate and that neither the N/P ratio nor the phosphorus concentration of the NDS were significantly correlated with this biovolume. These results suggest that the TP concentration measured in winter is an underestimation of the available phosphorus during the growing season. As all the ponds were icy at the time of the winter sampling, the absence of turbulence under the ice cover should have limited the suspension of fine particles in the water column. During warm months with a high water temperature and a low concentration of dissolved oxygen, ponds with organic P-saturated sediment can be net source of P by release of the iron-bound P (Søndergaard et al., 1999; Fairchild and Velinsky, 2006). Conversely the winter concentrations of TN could be an over estimation of the available nutrient in summer as a significant part can be lost through denitrification. This could explain the relatively high concentrations of TN and the corresponding trophic levels attributed to the ponds when compared to the TP concentrations and corresponding trophic classes (Fig. 3). It is therefore likely that the trophic status of the ponds is overestimated when the limits of Wetzel (1983) or Forsberg and Ryding (1980) set for large lakes are directly applied to the winter concentration of TN as in Fig. 3. On the other hand the limits of nutrient concentration proposed by Søndergaard et al. (2005b) to set ecological quality classes for shallow lakes (Fig. 3, dashed lines) seems to be more appropriate for ponds. In particular, it reassigned the sites classified as eutrophic following the TP or TN scales of Vollenweider and Kerekes (1982), Forsberg and Ryding (1980) and Wetzel (1983) into moderate to good quality, and the mesotrophic sites into high quality while keeping the hypertrophic ponds in poor to bad quality classes. These scales, even if not giving a trophic status, rely directly on water quality and distribute the gradient of nutrient concentrations observed in ponds in all the quality classes based either on TP or TN. 4.3. Roles and effects of submerged macrophytes The observed lower rates of periphytic productivity within boxes placed in the submerged macrophyte stands of two truly stagnant sites harboring continuously submerged species show the influences of submerged plants on nutrient cycling. Notably, macrophytes and their associated epiphytes mobilize and store nutrients prior to releasing it during their senescence. This competitive storage involves a reduced nutrient availability for phytoplankton (Kufel and Ozimek, 1994) and for the periphyton colonizing the artificial substrate. These results are concordant with the observation of Takamura et al. (2003) who found at a similar nutrient level a significantly lower concentration of planktonic chlorophyll within submerged macrophytes than in lakes without submerged species. Similarly, Liboriussen and Jeppesen (2003) and Vadeboncoeur et al. (2001) observed lower gross primary productivity in clear water compared to turbid one. When measuring biomass of phytoplankton, Peretyatko et al. (2007) reported lower amount in ponds supporting submerged plants when compared to unvegetated ponds or those with floating-leaved species only. With a measure of the total lake net primary production, Blindow et al. (2006) observed higher level in a clear lake compared to a turbid one but the two lakes considered in that study were deeper than the ponds considered here, and their water column, if turbid, experienced more self-shading and higher rates of community respiration than shallower sites. In fact, Blindow et al. (2006) pointed out that this difference of total net primary productivity between clear and turbid water tends to decrease with the mean depth by reducing the water volume below the compensation depth. As the artificial substrates used in our study were set 2–3 cm below the water surface, the measured growths of periphyton are less influenced by phytoplankton shading. The contrasting conditions of turbidity and transparency observed between macrophyte stands and open water were previously described by Scheffer et al. (1994) in shallow lakes. Other factors could also explain the lower periphytic productivity rates often measured within plant stands, for example shading by the macrophytes canopy (Ozimek et al., 1990), strong evidence of release of allelopathic substances by macrophytes (Gross et al., 2007) or increased rates of sedimentation (Carpenter, 1981; Petticrew et al., 1991) accompanied by a reduced resuspension within macrophyte stands (Scheffer et al., 1993). A lower or a negative net production of the epiphyte communities colonizing the artificial substrate placed within submerged species, as seasonally observed on natural substrate by Vis et al. (2006), can also explain the difference between open water and macrophyte stands. If the respiration process is more important than in open water, the amount of carbon measured after two weeks underestimates primary production. Conversely, the refuge effect of submerged macrophyte for grazers (Timms and Brian, 1984; Jeppesen et al., 1997) must be here less important as the experimental design that we used strongly limit the influence of large macroinvertebrates grazers. On one of the four sites harboring submerged species (P5), the early senescence of Myriophyllum spicatum (represented by the upward arrow in Fig. 4) during the second part of June was accompanied by a strong increase in the rate of productivity at the corresponding location that even surpasses the rate measured in open water. This is probably due to the direct recycling of nutrients released by macrophytes as periphyton can directly exploit this resource (Cattaneo and Kalff, 1979; Carignan and Kalff, 1982; Rooney and Kalff, 2003). Moreover, Carpenter (1980) but also Smith and Adams (1986) showed that the importance of macrophyte-derived nutrients for epiphyton increases with the degree of senescence of the plant. Additionally, Carignan and Kalff (1982) have specifically measured that M. spicatum is a significant source of highly available P for the surrounding epiphyton and phytoplankton. Interestingly, the water transparency remains inversely correlated to the rate of primary productivity and became simultaneously lower within macrophytes than in open water (data not shown). This peak of productivity was follow by a rapid growth of dense beds of Ceratophyllum demersum in early July along with a reduction of the rate measured in the box even if transparency remained low (downward arrow in Fig. 4). During this period, the rate of productivity continued to increase in open water to reach the seasonal peak during the first fortnight of July (Fig. 4). This delayed growth in open water compared to the growth measured in senescing beds during the previous two weeks can be linked to the horizontal diffusion from beds to open water of the available nutrients, similarly to what was observed by Rooney and Kalff (2003) studying active cycling from the sediment mediated by macrophytes. During the last fortnight of July, open water was progressively colonized by stands of C. demersum generating a net reduction in the productivity rate and resulting in similar values between the two sampling points becoming gradually both vegetated. The site P9 is a bit different as it has a flow-through regime, which is not the case in the other sites. In this case the mean rates of productivity were higher in macrophyte stands than in open water (118.7%–226.5% of the rates measured in open water). As already mentioned, measured rates as well as absolute differences were very low and the values were even overlapping between pseudo-replicates of the two sampling points (Fig. 4). Nevertheless, this trend differs notably from the other sites characterized by well-marked differences in periphytic productivity measured in the boxes between plant stands and open water. This difference can be due to different factors, notably a lower current speed through the dense macrophyte stands (Gessner, 1950; Stephan and Gutknecht, 2002) increasing the water retention time and potentially enhancing both sedimentation and the use of dissolved nutrients. Other factors could be involved, notably a release of nutrients by macrophytes, as mentioned earlier. Actually, this pond exhibits low concentration of dissolved nutrients (Table 4) and the nutritive contribution of healthy plants to periphyton, even if little, is known to be more important in oligotrophic water (Eminson and Moss, 1980; Burkholder and Wetzel, 1990). Additionally, nutrient diffusion may be facilitated and mixing of the water mediated by the current tends to also homogenize the conditions across the site. In this pond, transparency was always at the maximum value at the two sampling points and the turbidity remained low in value and range (inferior to four NTU among all measurements). 5. Conclusions and perspectives Firstly, the method of periphytic productivity measurement adapted in this study operates well with this dataset of ponds and gives repeatable measures except for the hypertrophic sites that showed an increase of the variance between pseudo-replicates. Secondly the results indicated that for the study area considered, the winter concentration of total nitrogen was a significant predictor of the summer rates of periphytic productivity measured in open water or averaged by ponds. When beds of submerged macrophytes were present, the periphytic productivity within the plant stands was generally lower and the transparency higher. In that case, the winter concentration of TP was a stronger and better predictor of the productivity. This limited growth of periphyton within the boxes placed in submerged macrophyte beds puts in evidence for the positive effects of submerged plants on water quality and emphasizes the importance of maintaining or restoring submerged macrophyte stands in ponds. Extending these results for assessing pond water quality in other region of Switzerland would require a similar study on a broader scale notably with sites located at higher altitudes, as the range of environmental parameters of particular concern for primary productivity differs broadly between Alps and lowlands (Hinden et al., 2005). Multiyear measurements of ebullitive methane flux from three subarctic lakes Martin Wik,1 Patrick M. Crill,1 Ruth K. Varner,2 and David Bastviken1,3 Received 24 April 2013; revised 29 July 2013; accepted 3 August 2013; published 20 September 2013. [1] Ebullition (bubbling) from small lakes and ponds at high latitudes is an important yet unconstrained source of atmospheric methane (CH4). Small water bodies are most abundant in permanently frozen peatlands, and it is speculated that their emissions will increase as the permafrost thaws. We made 6806 measurements of CH4 ebullition during four consecutive summers using a total of 40 bubble traps that were systematically distributed across the depth zones of three lakes in a sporadic permafrost landscape in northernmost Sweden. We identified significant spatial and temporal variations in ebullition and observed a large spread in the bubbles’ CH4 concentration, ranging from 0.04% to 98.6%. Ebullition followed lake temperatures, and releases were significantly larger during periods with decreasing atmospheric pressure. Although shallow zone ebullition dominated the seasonal bubble CH4 flux, we found a shift in the depth dependency towards higher fluxes from intermediate and deep zones in early fall. The average daily flux of 13.4 mg CH4 m−2 was lower than those measured in most other high-latitude lakes. Locally, however, our study lakes are a substantial CH4 source; we estimate that 350 kg of CH4 is released via ebullition during summer (June–September), which is approximately 40% of total whole year emissions from the nearby peatland. In order to capture the large variability and to accurately scale lake CH4 ebullition temporally and spatially, frequent measurements over long time periods are critical. Citation: Wik, M., P. M. Crill, R. K. Varner, and D. Bastviken (2013), Multiyear measurements of ebullitive methane flux from three subarctic lakes, J. Geophys. Res. Biogeosci., 118, 1307–1321, doi:10.1002/jgrg.20103. 1. Introduction [2] Lakes are common features of the terrestrial landscape and known sources of methane (CH4) [Bastviken et al., 2004], an important radiatively active trace gas in Earth’s atmosphere [Cicerone and Oremland, 1988; Reeburgh, 2003]. There is much uncertainty in the contributions of water bodies to atmospheric CH4 due to few measurements on even fewer lakes and because of large unknowns in the spatiotemporal variability in emission [Bastviken et al., 2004]. Particularly numerous small lakes and ponds are critical for improved understanding of the role of water bodies, both in the global carbon (C) cycle and in quantifying the global CH4 budget [Cole et al., 2007; Tranvik et al., 2009; Downing, 2010]. [3] Bastviken et al. [2011] have recently estimated global lake CH4 emissions of 72 ± 69 Tg yr−1, which is approximately 40% of the global contribution by wetlands, considered the single largest natural source of atmospheric CH4 [Denman et al., 2007]. Although reported global lake CH4 emissions are dominated by releases from temperate, subtropical, and tropical surface waters [Bastviken et al., 2011], lakes and ponds most frequently occur at higher latitudes, particularly in climate-sensitive permafrost landscapes [Lehner and Döll, 2004; Smith et al., 2007]. The available data sets for these high-latitude environments are limited, and therefore, they cannot be seen as fully representative. In a warming Arctic, permafrost degradation is likely to cause increased wetness and widespread formation of ponds and small lakes [Sannel and Kuhry, 2011]. Large amounts of labile organic C, currently stored in frozen peatlands, can potentially be mobilized following thaw and transported to anoxic lake sediments that favor CH4 production and release to the atmosphere [van Huissteden et al., 2011]. Hence, there is speculation that the source contribution of CH4 from high-latitude lakes will increase and be a positive feedback to projected future warming [Walter et al., 2006; Cole et al., 2007]. [4] Ebullition is a spatially and temporally complex, yet major, transport mode of CH4 from anoxic lake bottoms. It has been estimated to dominate over diffusional losses from the water column [Crill et al., 1988; Keller and Stallard, 1994; Bastviken et al., 2011]. The bubbles are gas mixtures that can be almost entirely CH4, but more often, they also Figure 1. Location of our study lakes within the Stordalen Mire, 11 km east of Abisko in northern Sweden (68°21'N, 19°02'E). Colored contours and solid white circles indicate water depth and bubble trap placement, respectively. Note that Lake Villasjön is evenly shallow around 1 m. The aerial infrared photograph was taken in July 2000 (available at the Abisko Scientific Research Station (ANS)). contain percent concentrations of nitrogen (N_2) and trace amounts of carbon dioxide (CO_2) and hydrogen (H_2) [Fendinger et al., 1992; Walter et al., 2008]. Methane formation in anoxic sediments is through both acetate fermentation and CO_2 reduction by H_2 and is controlled by heat energy and the availability of organic substrate [Zeikus and Winfrey, 1976; Kelly and Chynoweth, 1981; Duc et al., 2010]. Bubbling events are believed to occur when the pressure of the gas in the sediment exceeds the overlying hydrostatic loading [Fendinger et al., 1992]; negative changes in atmospheric pressure as well as decreasing water level have been found to coincide with gas eruptions from surface waters [Mattson and Likens, 1990; Varadharajan and Hemond, 2012]. [5] Observations suggest that bubbles are more frequently released in shallow zones close to lake margins [Keller and Stallard, 1994; Zimov et al., 1997; Bastviken et al., 2004]. Apart from a lower hydrostatic pressure, shallow areas often support plant growth, providing an autochthonous source of fresh organic C. Labile allochthonous organic loading is also likely to have a shorter residence time in the water column and a higher likelihood to be deposited to sediments in shallow zones. At depth, it eventually accumulates in a more decomposed state after a longer transit time and a prolonged period in the water column [Torres et al., 2010]. Shallow zones also favor bubble formation because they are generally warmer, which both stimulates methanogenesis [Duc et al., 2010] and makes CH_4 less soluble [Yamamoto et al., 1976]. After release, ebullitive CH_4 is largely unaffected by oxidation and dissolution in the water column because of the bubbles' buoyancy and rapid ascent to the surface [Chanton, 2005], although in deeper water bodies, exchange between the rising bubbles and the surrounding water occurs [McGinnis et al., 2006]. [6] A large amount of bubbles are emitted from point sources (seeps) in the sediment that are capable of more or less reoccurring releases [Walter et al., 2007; Wik et al., 2011]. Studies of Arctic lakes in permafrost regions in Alaska and Siberia report that seep ebullition can be persistent enough to maintain open holes (hot spots) in the ice during winter [e.g., Anthony et al., 2012]. Furthermore, Walter et al. [2007] argue that seeps in lake sediments are spatially fixed and that randomly dispersed measurements, or those that are not located directly over seeps, are likely to fail to capture large bubbling events and only monitor what they label as background ebullition, an overall smaller part of the total ebullitive flux. However, fluxes quantified irrespective of predetermined seep locations should not be neglected. Lake systems differ morphologically, and long-term spatially fixed seeps are likely absent in sediments that are not linked to deeper gas-rich structures or geological C-rich deposits such as coal seams [Etiope et al., 2009] and Table 1. Ice surveys of trapped bubbles on frozen high-latitude lakes indicate that seeps are often short-lived, emitting bubbles episodically during a limited time only [Wik et al., 2011]. [7] Bottom-up estimates and predictions of northern lake CH$_4$ emissions are limited not only by large uncertainties in the vulnerability and fate of permafrost [Hugelius et al., 2012] but also by the lack of long-term flux measurements that address highly heterogeneous emission pathways and large unknowns in release mechanisms [Bastviken et al., 2004; Tranvik et al., 2009]. This paper reports four years of seasonal (June–September) measurements of CH$_4$ ebullition from three lakes in subarctic Sweden that lie within a peatland underlain by sporadic permafrost. We identify the distribution of ebullition rates, bubble CH$_4$ concentrations, and fluxes with this unique data set. The core of this study focuses on determining the temporal and spatial variability of ebullition. We use analysis of variance (ANOVA) to compare bubble CH$_4$ concentrations and fluxes among our study lakes and among sampling locations and different depth zones. Using the same approach, we also investigate annual, monthly, and daily variability among the four years, from June to September. Furthermore, the bubble CH$_4$ concentrations and fluxes are compared with those measured in previous studies on other northern lakes. We also compare the flux magnitudes with CH$_4$ emissions from the major subhabitats of the surrounding landscape, and we highlight the importance of long-term measurements and use cumulative fluxes when extrapolating seasonal fluxes across entire lake areas. 2. Methods 2.1. Study Site [8] We focused on three lakes (Inre Harrsjön, Mellan Harrsjön, and Villasjön) located within the Stordalen Mire ![Bubble trap design consisting of an inverted funnel of which the tip is elongated to fit a 10 mL polypropylene syringe. (b) We used foam to keep the trap floating at the surface and a separate float to prevent it from being pulled by the mooring line. This way, the trap was almost never positioned directly over the mooring. Figure 3. Dark and light grey bars indicate linear and logarithmic occurrence probabilities, respectively. Note the different scales on the y axes. complex, a dynamic subarctic peatland 11 km east of Abisko in northern Sweden (68°21′N, 19°02′E; Figure 1). The mire is 350 m above sea level and underlain by sporadic permafrost visible as ombrotrophic palsas that rise above semiwet and wet minerotrophic fens, streams, and shallow lakes. The Abisko region has warmed 1.5°C in recent decades, from a mean annual temperature of −0.9°C in 1974 to 0.6°C in 2006 [Callaghan et al., 2010]. At the Stordalen Mire, warming above the 0°C threshold has caused substantial permafrost degradation, shallow water pool formation, and shorter ice-covered seasons [Christensen, 2004; Johansson et al., 2006]. Although the elevated parts of the mire experience permafrost degradation, there are limited erosional margins around the lakes. Instead, the lakes are mostly surrounded by wet fens (dominated by Eriophorum angustifolium, Carex rostrata, and Sphagnum spp.) and semiwet subalpine birch forest [Malmer et al., 2005]. [9] Mellan Harrsjön and Inre Harrsjön are smaller but deeper lakes than Villasjön, which is overall shallow (Table 1) and bottom freezes during winter. Mellan Harrsjön and Inre Harrsjön share water via Yttre Harrsjön, and during high flow, Villasjön drains into Inre Harrsjön through a fen and southwest into the continuously north flowing stream. Mellan Harrsjön receives the majority of its water from the same stream, and there is a small inflow feeding water into Villasjön from the east. Inre Harrsjön, on the other hand, lacks a comparable surface water source [Olefeldt et al., 2012]. Both Inre Harrsjön and Villasjön are considered partly spring fed; springs have been located north and south of Inre Harrsjön [Nilsson, 2006], and water upwelling has been observed in Villasjön. The lakes are usually ice free from mid-May to mid-October. [10] Little is known about the lake sediments. Radiocarbon dating of sediment sequences in Inre Harrsjön and Villasjön suggests that initial sedimentation began 2650 and 3400 calibrated years B.P., respectively [Kokfelt et al., 2010]. The organic layer in the central intermediately deep (3.5 m) part of Inre Harrsjön consists of 275 cm gyttja with a 40% C content [loss on ignition (LOI)] in the top meter. In the northeastern part of Villasjön, the organic layer measures 323 cm of peat-rich detritus gyttja with a C content of up to 80% (LOI) [Kokfelt et al., 2010]. The lakes have similar drainage basins and are shallow enough to have similar wind mixing and resuspension of surface sediments during storm events. Inre Harrsjön and Mellan Harrsjön are underlain by schist bedrock, whereas Villasjön is underlain by granite [Lindström et al., 1985]. 2.2. Ebullition Sampling [11] We measured lake CH4 ebullition during consecutive summers (June–September) of 2009–2012 at 40 locations using bubble traps. The trap design consisted of an inverted 50 cm wide circular funnel fitted with a closed scaled cylinder (10 ml polypropylene syringe and three-way stopcock; Figure 2). The narrow neck of the sampler was designed to limit the potential surface area that could promote diffusion of CH4 from the trap back into the water. Each funnel was stabilized by floating foam and three equally sized weights and attached to a separate float connected to a mooring, allowing it to roam in an area of 12 m². This ensured that the traps were not affected by their moorings. [12] In Mellan Harrsjön and Inre Harrsjön, 13 and 17 bubble traps were distributed along transects that stretched over the entire lakes, covering different water depth zones (Figure 1). The transect locations were also chosen with respect to the distribution of trapped bubbles in the ice in winter reported by Wik et al. [2011]. We measured not only zones with high spatial density of clustered bubble morphologies but also areas where clusters were minimal. In shallow Villasjön, 10 traps were deployed across the southwestern part of the lake, a zone that stretches from the central peat plateau toward a rockier bottom with little aquatic vegetation. No measurements were made in Villasjön during the summer of 2009. Similar transect locations were used in each year. Table 2. [13] Apart from a few weekly sampling periods (mainly in 2009), we surveyed all bubble traps frequently, most often within a 24–72 h period. Accumulated gas volumes were collected manually using syringes, and notes were made of headspace volumes and time of sampling. Undetectably small volumes were referred to as zero. All gas samples were analyzed for CH4 the same day. 2.3. Gas Analysis and Bubble CH4 Flux Calculation [14] The gas samples were analyzed for CH4 at ANS using a Shimadzu 2014 gas chromatograph with a flame ionization detector, a 2 m 80/100 mesh HayeSep-Q packed column, and a 200 μL injection loop. Helium carrier gas was used at a flow rate of 50 mL min−1. Because of high CH4 concentrations in the bubbles, 1 mL of each sample was diluted before injection with 59 mL of ambient air using a 60 mL polypropylene syringe. The dilution factor was 65.7 ± 3.0 [mean ± standard deviation (SD)] as determined by analysis of multiple (n = 94) dilutions of 2000 ppm CH4 standard. Instrument precision ranged from 0.02% to 0.5%; injections with standard were made both before and after each daily set of samples. Lake Water Temperature and Atmospheric Pressure [15] We measured lake water temperatures throughout the year using arrays of intercalibrated temperature sensors (HOBO Water Temp Pro v2, model U22, Onset Computer) that logged every 5 and 15 min in summer and winter, respectively. The top of the water column was monitored equally in all three lakes, at 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, and 1 m below the surface. In Villasjön, the 1 m sensor penetrated the surface sediment. The arrays in Inre Harrsjön and Mellan Harrsjön had additional sensors every second meter down into the surface sediments of the deep holes. We inferred surface sediment temperatures in other zones using the depth profiles of the water temperatures. The temperature gradient between the water and the uppermost 5–10 cm of lake sediments has been measured to near zero [Gudasz et al., 2010]. Atmospheric pressure data were measured hourly at ANS. 2.5. Statistical Analysis and Spatial Scaling [16] The overall distributions of ebullition rate, bubble CH4 concentration, and flux were characterized using the Figure 5. Bubble CH4 flux during periods with decreasing and increasing atmospheric pressure. Open circles and horizontal lines indicate mean and median bubble fluxes, respectively. Boxes show the range between the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers denote the 90th percentile. Negative and positive pressure changes used for grouping were defined as the overall slope in hourly pressure during each individual sampling period. Anderson-Darling goodness of fit in EasyFit 5.5. Because of highly skewed data with large numbers of zeros, means in bubble CH4 flux magnitudes are reported with 10–90 percentile ranges instead of SDs. We examined the temporal variability in bubble CH4 concentration and flux by year, month, and day (sampling period). The spatial variability was examined by lake and trap location and by depth zone of shallow (0–2 m), intermediate (2–4 m), and deep (4–7 m). Differences among groups of data were examined using analysis of variance (ANOVA), both one way and that of a multiple regression approach specified as a general linear model, in Minitab 16. All statistical tests used a significance level of 5% (α = 0.05). Test results are compiled in Table S1 in the supporting information. The use of parametric tests with nonnormal data was justified, according to the central limit theorem, by the large set of samples. Parametric tests were also suitable because they compare means instead of medians (nonparametric tests), i.e., they account for large bubbling events that were outliers in the distribution but yet contributed disproportionally and in a numerative sense to the total flux. [17] We calculated seasonal cumulative bubble CH4 fluxes for all three lakes combined by successive additions of the average fluxes of each sampling period, both overall (all 40 traps) and for each specific depth zone. Overall whole lake extrapolated fluxes were calculated by multiplying the overall cumulative bubble CH4 fluxes per square meter with the total area of the lakes (20.3 ha) and depth-weighted whole lake fluxes by summing the products of the depth zone-specific cumulative fluxes and their corresponding surface area. We estimated that the shallow, intermediate, and deep zones covered 19.2, 0.8, and 0.3 ha, respectively, using the depth contour map developed by Wik et al. [2011]. 3. Results 3.1. Overall Bubble Volume, CH4 Concentration, and Flux [18] Altogether, we measured 6806 headspace volumes from the bubble traps, of which 45% were greater than zero and 88% were sampled in periods of 24–72 h. Ebullition rates were on average 39.9 mL m−2 d−1 (10–90 percentile range: 0–103.6, n = 6806) and ranged from 0 to 2771.8 mL m−2 d−1. Bubble CH4 concentrations averaged 34.8% (SD = 25.2, n = 3763) and ranged from 0.04% to 98.6%. No relationship was found between CH4 concentration and corresponding headspace volume (R2 = 0.012, n = 3763). The calculated bubble fluxes were on average 13.4 mg CH4 m−2 d−1 (10–90 percentile range: 0–33.9, n = 6806) and ranged from 0 to 1682.5 mg CH4 m−2 d−1. Both the frequency distributions of ebullition rates and bubble CH4 fluxes followed a gamma distribution with a median close to zero (α = 0.14576 and 0.07663, β = 273.13 and 174.05; Figures 3a and 3c). The bubble CH4 concentrations were less positively skewed, following a Dagum distribution with a median close to the mean (k = 0.06023, α = 11.98, β = 80.883; Figure 3b). 3.2. Temporal Variability and Trends [19] Bubble CH4 concentrations and fluxes were highly variable among the four summer periods (p < 0.001, n = 3763 and 6806; Table 2). The average concentration was highest in 2010 and lowest in 2009, whereas the average flux was highest in 2009 and lowest in 2012. Monthly variations from June to September were larger than interannual variabilities (Table 3). We found a near twofold overall increase in bubble CH4 concentration during summer (p < 0.001, n = 3763; Table 2). Bubble CH4 flux magnitudes followed the heating and cooling of the lakes with a threefold overall increase from June to late August, after which they decreased in September (p < 0.001, n = 6806; Figure 4 and Table 2). [20] Ebullition was most variable on a daily basis (Table 3); average bubble fluxes (all 40 traps) ranged from 0 to 143.5 mg CH4 m−2 among the individual sampling periods. Days of peak ebullition often coincided with steep drops in atmospheric pressure and were observed as increased bubbling across the different depth zones (Figure 4). On average, the bubble CH4 flux was twofold higher and more variable during periods with an overall decreasing atmospheric pressure (p < 0.001, n = 6604; Figure 5). 3.3. Spatial and Depth-Dependent Variability [21] Bubble CH4 concentrations and fluxes were highly variable among and within the three lakes (p < 0.001, n = 3763 and 6806; Figure 6 and Table 2). Lake-specific averages were highest in Villasjön and lowest in Inre Harrsjön. Trap-specific averages ranged from 6.5% to 55.4% and from 0.4 to 52.8 mg CH4 m−2 d−1 and were lowest in the eastern shallow end of Inre Harrsjön (traps 1 and 2). Methane concentrations were highest in bubbles captured over the deep hole in Mellan Harrsjön (trap 20), and bubble CH4 fluxes were highest near the western shore of Villasjön (traps 31–34). [22] Altogether, bubble CH4 concentrations were similar among depth zones (p = 0.404, n = 3762). In contrast, bubble CH4 fluxes in the lakes’ shallow zones (0–2 m) averaged almost two- and fourfold higher than those in the intermediate Figure 6. [23] The depth dependency of ebullition varied temporally. In June, shallow zone bubble CH₄ concentrations were on average higher than those from deep zones, whereas it was vice versa in September after a linear increase of CH₄ in deep zone bubbles over summer (Figure 7a). The dominance of shallow zone bubble CH₄ fluxes decreased over summer relative to an increase in intermediate and deep zone fluxes (Figures 4 and 7c). In September, flux magnitudes were similar between shallow and deep zones and highest from intermediate depths (Figure 7b). At the same time, average water and surface sediment temperatures at different depths merged around 8.5°C (Figure 7d). 3.4. Overall Bubble Volume, CH$_4$ Concentration, and Flux [25] The distribution of ebullition rates reflects the nature of gas venting in the Stordalen lakes. The low rate ebullition (<30 mL m$^{-2}$ d$^{-1}$) that dominated approximately 80% of the distribution occurred frequently on a daily basis. Although larger bubbling events (>100 mL m$^{-2}$ d$^{-1}$) occurred less frequently, they were not rare, accounting for nearly 8% of the observations. Large episodic events reflected the recharge and depletion of gas in the sediment, and they were important in shifting the mean within the distribution. We did not measure CH$_4$ production in the sediments; however, we expect it to be a function of labile C availability and sediment temperature [e.g., Zeikus and Winfrey, 1976]. The positively skewed gamma distribution of the ebullition rates (Figure 3a) mirrored the distribution of our calculated bubble CH$_4$ fluxes (Figure 3c), implying that the mass transport of CH$_4$ via ebullition was largely determined by total bubble volume over time. Similar highly skewed distributions of ebullition have been described in the Upper Mystic Lake, MA [Varadharajan and Hemond, 2012], and at Sallie’s Fen, NH [Goodrich et al., 2011]. [26] Although bubble CH$_4$ fluxes were primarily determined by ebullition rate, bubble CH$_4$ concentration was important; fluxes could potentially vary by 3 orders of magnitude based on the observed range of the concentrations (0.04%–98.6%). The positively skewed Dagum distribution (Figure 3b) shows that most bubbles had CH$_4$ concentrations in the low to mid percent range (10%–50%). The large number of bubbles at the very low end of the distribution implies that there are substantial temporal and spatial shifts in CH$_4$ production rates as well as physical parameters affecting the bubbles in the sediment and gas accumulation and loss of CH$_4$ in our bubble traps (sections 4.2 and 4.3). [27] The overall bubble flux from our study lakes (13.4 mg CH$_4$ m$^{-2}$ d$^{-1}$) was lower than what has been reported in most other high-latitude lake systems. The bubble flux across two north Siberian thermokarst lakes, measured from June to September using randomly placed bubble traps, was 46.7 mg CH$_4$ m$^{-2}$ d$^{-1}$ (calculated as a daily flux from 5.7 g CH$_4$ m$^{-2}$ yr$^{-1}$) [Walter et al., 2006]. Bubble fluxes from a northern boreal beaver pond averaged 83.8 ± 141 mg CH$_4$ m$^{-2}$ d$^{-1}$ [Dove et al., 1999], and Huttunen et al. [2001] measured 36 mg CH$_4$ m$^{-2}$ d$^{-1}$ from a midboreal lake in Finland. Our average bubble CH$_4$ concentration of 34.8 ± 25.2% ($n$ = 3763) was similar to background (39 ± 25%, $n$ = 39) and twofold lower than that of reported seep ebullition (82 ± 7%, $n$ = 55) measured in Alaskan and Siberian thermokarst lakes by Walter et al. [2008]. Furthermore, it ranged within the bubble CH$_4$ concentrations reported by Dove et al. [1999] from open water and vegetated sites in the beaver pond (47.2 ± 20.8% and 26.6 ± 12.4%, $n$ = 771). [28] One major difference between our study lakes at Stordalen and those, for example, in northern Siberia [Walter et al., 2006] is that they lack erosional margins and underlying permafrost. This implies that the Stordalen lakes are likely to receive less labile organic material and therefore cannot sustain the high rates of ebullition or persistent seeps observed in other high-latitude lakes. Because lakes similar to those in Stordalen are numerous across high latitudes, they are important when constraining northern lake emissions. In fact, the sporadic permafrost terrain representative for Stordalen is a common landscape with the highest lake area fraction (lakes are estimated to cover 3.12% of the area) across northern glaciated environments) [Smith et al., 2007]. In 2009 and 2011, when bubble CH₄ fluxes averaged higher than in 2010 and 2012 (Table 2), the lakes warmed earlier, and they did not cool as rapidly in the fall
