The diversity of macroinvertebrate and macrophyte communities in ponds LAURIE E. FRIDAY Department of Biological Sciences, University of Exeter SUMMARY. 1. The range of factors which may influence the wide variation in the structure of pond communities is reviewed. 2. Factors explaining the variation in numbers of macroinvertebrate and macrophyte taxa are investigated, using multiple regression analysis, for a group of ponds in which biogeographical effects are likely to be minimal. 3. Numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa in these ponds are highly correlated with pH and probably, therefore, with other associated aspects of water chemistry. 4. Many invertebrate taxa, from species to entire phyla, were not found below pH 5.5, but few characteristically 'acidophilic' taxa were apparent. 5. Details of species composition of the macroinvertebrate fauna differ widely even between ponds of similar pH. 6. The diversity and composition of macrophyte communities are not adequately predicted by any of the factors investigated. Introduction Ponds and other small water bodies are highly individual habitats: the fauna and flora usually vary widely, and often unpredictably, between ponds even within a small geographical area. While it is sometimes possible to find correlations between observed faunal or floral diversity and various factors, it is rarely possible, except by rigorous experimental treatment, to establish the causes of inter-pond variation. A wide variety of explanatory factors has been put forward, as a result of field studies of small water bodies or on theoretical grounds, as possible influences on the diversity and composition of pond communities. These factors may be grouped together under two broad headings: 'biogeographical' factors, operating via the dispersal of organisms to essentially insular habitats, and 'habitat' characteristics, both physico-chemical and biotic, influencing the establishment and persistence of colonizing species. These categories are not mutually exclusive, but form a useful basis for reviewing the wide range of factors which might explain inter-pond variation in the number and identities of species. Correspondence: Dr L. E. Friday, Department of Applied Biology, Pembroke Street, Cambridge CB2 3DX. (i) Biogeographical factors (a) Pond age. Studies of the initial colonization of newly created ponds show a general increase in the numbers of species of invertebrates and macrophytes (Gates, 1927; Street & Titmus, 1979; Barnes, 1983). Where dispersal distances are short, the rate of acquisition of new species has been observed to decline within a few years (Barnes, 1983), suggesting an approach to an 'equilibrium number of species', as predicted by MacArthur & Wilson's (1967) theory of island biogeography. However, Godwin's (1923) observations on the flora of much older ponds suggest that numbers of less vagile species (i.e. those with weak or passive dispersal) may continue to rise over many decades. As a pond ages, so the habitat it presents to colonists changes, partly due to increases in the extent and diversity of aquatic vegetation and in the production of autochthonous detritus. These changes are accompanied by changes in the identity of the dominant invertebrate taxa (Street & Titmus, 1979; Barnes, 1983). While it is possible to fit a model to the observed rise in numbers of taxa with age, the order in which individual colonists establish is not easy to predict. Invasion by an individual species depends on the availability of suitable propagules in 'source' habitats, the species' dispersal mechanisms, and the distance over which it has to disperse, but is also subject to chance (Talling, 1951). (b) Isolation. MacArthur & Wilson's model predicts a decrease in the equilibrium number of species on an island, and changes in the species represented, with increasing isolation from the source of colonists. Aho (1978a) found a significant correlation between isolation of small, productive Finnish lakes and the diversity of their molluscan faunas. Several authors have suggested that changes in isolation over historical or geological time (due to flooding, changes in river courses, creation or destruction of source habitats) have influenced the diversity of less vagile organisms in lakes (e.g. Boycott, 1919; Godwin, 1923; Aho, 1978b; Barbour & Brown, 1974). The immediate surroundings of ponds may also influence their chances of discovery by actively dispersing organisms, but surrounding vegetation and land use are likely to be of greater importance in their effect on aspects of the pond habitat, namely hydrology, water chemistry and allochthonous organic inputs. (c) Pond area. Connor & McCoy (1979), in their review of the species–area relationship, point out that the possible effects of area on community diversity have both biogeographical and biotic elements: as area increases, so the number of habitat types, with their associated species, is likely to increase; population sizes should also increase with area, thus reducing the extinction rate of resident species (MacArthur & Wilson, 1967); and large 'target' areas may simply receive a larger number of colonizing propagules, and therefore a chance of a greater variety of species, than smaller ones. Lassen (1975), Aho (1978a), Driver (1977) and Fryer (1985) found correlations between area (or log area) and the numbers of species of molluscs, chironomids and crustaceans respectively. Which of these aspects may account for the observed relationships is not possible to determine from diversity data alone, but Fryer (1985) suggests that the types of habitats found in different sized water bodies ('pond' as opposed to 'lake' habitats) may partly explain the composition of the crustacean faunas in his study area. Area, as an expression of the size of a water body, is also related to its persistence. Small ponds tend to be less permanent than larger ones, may show greater fluctuations in physical and chemical conditions, and so present quite a different type of habitat. Macan (1954, 1962) discusses the probable influence of habitat stability on the identity, and possibly on the diversity, of corixid species in a water body. (ii) Characteristics of the habitat (a) Habitat diversity. Factors contributing to the diversity of habitat for pond macrophytes include details of the bank topography and changes in substratum associated with irregularities in the shoreline. For the macroinvertebrate fauna, the diversity of macrophytic vegetation and local changes in substratum may be major factors. Observations by several authors on invertebrate communities associated with different species of macrophytes (e.g. Soszka, 1975; Dvorak & Best, 1982; Lodge, 1985), suggest that a correlation might be expected between macrophyte and macroinvertebrate numbers of species. Palmer (1981) found a close relationship between macrophyte species diversity and the number of species of Coleoptera and Hemiptera in a survey of base-rich ponds in Norfolk. (b) Competition and predation. Little direct evidence has been put forward to show that biotic interactions are major determinants of pond biotic diversity. However, changes in fish populations are often accompanied by changes in the plant and invertebrate communities (Macan, 1965, 1977b; Korinkova, 1967; Henrickson & Oscarson, 1985) and the effect of fish predation on zooplankton community structure is well documented (see Zaret, 1980). Biotic interactions might possibly be a major influence from the very earliest stages of pond colonization. In new ponds, extensive pure stands of emergent or floating-leaved macrophytes may establish within a few years (Barnes, 1983) and preclude other species by competition for light or space. They may constitute very distinctive habitats for invertebrates and if, by chance, different aggressive species colonize neighbouring ponds, then quite different communities may result. (c) Water chemistry. Many workers have found a correlation between pond biotic diversity and water chemistry. Scandinavian studies of molluscan communities (e.g. Aho, 1987a; Økland, 1980) link species diversity to a combination of pH and calcium levels. Strong positive correlations between pH and numbers of species of Crustacea have been reported from acidic, low-calcium ponds and lakes in Northern Britain (Fryer, 1980) and Norway (Økland & Økland, 1980). The composition of macrophytic communities may also be changed during lake acidification (Grahn, 1975). Green (1986) found a non-linear relationship between conductivity and zooplankton diversity in crater lakes. Several authors stress the importance of the general level of productivity of a water body (usually gauged by concentrations of nutrient ions) in determining the assortment of species found there, e.g. Saether (1975). In the present study, the distribution of littoral macroinvertebrates and macrophytes in a group of ponds within a small geographical area were investigated to discover which factors best predict the numbers of taxa and the types of communities found in each pond. In view of the difficulties inherent in distinguishing the confounding effects of different types of variables, the ponds were chosen to minimize the possible influence of pond age and isolation. Sites Sixteen ponds were chosen from among the large number of water bodies created by open-cast extraction of ball-clay in the Isle of Purbeck, Dorset, U.K. The study ponds all lie within an area of heath, woodland and pasture, 5×2 km, centred on National Grid Reference SY935835, just north of the chalk escarpment (Fig. 1). The ponds were chosen to represent as wide a range of physico-chemical and habitat conditions (as judged from terrestrial and aquatic vegetation) as possible. The exact ages of individual ponds are not known, but all date from the nineteenth century, with the exception of pond Q, which was formed in the eighteenth century (English China Clays (Ball Clays) Ltd, pers. comm.). From a study of the rate of colonization of newly created ball-clay ponds in the area (Barnes, 1983), it appears that the equilibrium number of macroinvertebrate taxa for small ponds is approached within 20 years of the first appearance of the water body. It is expected, therefore, that the ponds chosen for this study have attained the colonization asymptote, at least as far as macroinvertebrates are concerned, and any differences in age between them are not likely to be of importance. Dispersal distances between the ponds are small, the greatest nearest-neighbour distance being <1 km. No discrete source of colonizing propagules is recognizable, there being numerous small water bodies (ball-clay ponds, bomb craters and streams) in the area as well as the Corfe River to the east and the River Stour to the north-west. It is therefore assumed that the source pool of colonists is diffuse, so that no pond is substantially more isolated than any other. All the ponds contain at least 1 m depth of water throughout the year and none is connected, at any time, to any other water body. Methods (i) Morphometry Pond areas and shore lengths were estimated from large-scale maps produced by English China Clays (Ball Clays) Ltd surveyors. For the larger ponds, maximum depths and basin profiles were obtained from depth measure- FIG. 1. Location of the study site and map of the sixteen ball-clay ponds, labelled A–R. ments taken at 5 m intervals along transects; depths of smaller ponds were measured using a lead line from the bank. (ii) Chemistry Water samples were taken from 20 cm below the surface, 2 m from the shore, away from dense vegetation. All ponds were sampled within 2 h around noon on 12 April 1979 and again on 8 August 1979. Temperature and dissolved oxygen were recorded in situ and samples were analysed the same day by the Wessex Water Authority chemical laboratory, Poole, using standard methods (see Barnes, 1981; for details). For each sample, pH, electrical conductivity, turbidity, total hardness, alkalinity, nitrate, ammonium, orthophosphate, and 5-day B.O.D. were determined. Seven samples were later analysed for calcium and two for total aluminium, using an atomic absorption spectrophotometer at the University of Exeter. (iii) Macrophytes All ponds were surveyed during a 2-week period in August 1979 to determine the total area vegetated, the number of species, and their relative abundance, expressed as cover abundance scores as follows: 1 = 0.1–5% of vegetated area 2 = 6–25% of vegetated area 3 = 26–50% of vegetated area 4 = 51–75% of vegetated area 5 = 76–100% of vegetated area (iv) Macroinvertebrates The macroinvertebrate communities of the shallow littoral were sampled using standard sampling units, each consisting of five separate 2 m sweeps with an F.B.A. pond net (mesh aperture 1 mm). Trials showed that five sweeps obtained at least 85% of the species to be discovered by repeated sweeping within a given weed bed. Pond nets tend to under-sample certain elements of the fauna (see Macan, 1977a, for a critique), and the species lists obtained from one period of sampling will not be complete. However, such samples, taken in a standard manner and within a short space of time, may be used to compare communities between ponds. All sixteen ponds were sampled in a 3-day period in early April 1979. All were sampled with equal intensity, that is the number of sampling units employed in each pond was proportional to the extent of the shallow littoral habitat. An increase in the number of samples as pond size increased was deemed necessary to incorporate the apparent greater diversity of littoral habitats in larger ponds. The shoreline of each pond was divided arbitrarily into 100 m stretches and one sampling unit was taken in each 100 m stretch. The positions of the five individual sweeps in each sampling unit were determined by possibility of access to the water. Identification was taken to species wherever possible, but chironomid larvae were identified only to genus, and some members of other groups could be identified only to family. The relative numerical abundance of taxa were expressed as abundance scores as follows: 1 = present, but a mean of <1 individual per sampling unit 2 = 1–10 individuals per sampling unit 3 = 11–100 individuals per sampling unit 4 = >100 individuals per sampling unit The use of approximately logarithmic abundance categories to some extent overcomes the problem of comparing relative abundance of taxa of very different body size and reduces the dominating effect of seasonal swarms of small individuals. Results Numbers of taxa The numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa and macrophyte species found in each pond are shown in Table 1, together with values for selected physical and chemical parameters. The wide range of all these parameters over the sixteen ponds is apparent: for example, the number of macroinvertebrate taxa ranges from twenty-four to eighty-eight; pH from 3.8 to 7.5; and pond area from 0.023 to 2.0 ha. The total number of macroinvertebrate taxa found was 174 and the total number of macrophyte species thirty-one. The relationships between numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa (INVERTS) and macrophyte species (PLANTS) and physical and chemical characteristics of the ponds were investigated by correlation and regression analyses carried out using the statistical package MINITAB 81.1 (Ryan, 1981). Regression analyses were used to discover which, if any, of the biotic, physical and chemical factors might adequately explain the variation in numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa or macrophyte species found in these ponds. Preliminary analyses suggested that regression analysis would not be inappropriate, since the measurement errors in the y-variables (INVERTS or PLANTS) are great relative to those in the x-variables (predictors), and the individual variables are approximately normally distributed. Bivariate plots suggested the need to log-transform INVERTS, PLANTS, area and vegetated area for regression analysis (i.e. LINVERTS, LPLANTS, LAREA, LVAREA); this gave an acceptable degree of homoscedasticity in the residuals (Draper & Smith, 1981). Regression analyses proceeded by using predicator variables in turn, and, for multiple regression, adding them one at a time, using a correlation matrix as a guide and inspecting residuals and coefficients at each stage. The effectiveness of the various regression equations for predicting numbers of taxa in individual ponds was assessed by plotting the number of taxa predicted v. the number observed for each pond ('predicted-y v. observed-y' plots). Points falling above the line of equality indicate an over-estimation by the equation, those below an under-estimation (see Fig. 3). As a first step, Pearson correlation coefficients were computed between all pairs of the fourteen variables given in Table 1, log-transformed as appropriate. Sixteen pairs of observations were used in each case, except those involving calcium, for which only seven pairs could be used. Table 2, the correlation half-matrix, shows a number of distinct patterns: (i) LINVERTS is positively correlated with calcium and pH (\( P < 0.01 \)) and with LPLANTS, alkalinity, and LVAREA (\( P < 0.05 \)). (ii) All pairwise correlations between pH, conductivity, B.O.D., total hardness, alkalinity and calcium are significant at the 1% level. (iii) LAREA and LVAREA are correlated (\( P < 0.05 \)), depth is correlated with LAREA (\( P < 0.01 \)), and LVAREA with LINVERTS (\( P < 0.05 \)) but none of these morphometric variables is correlated with any chemical factor. Discussion For the majority of the Purbeck ball-clay ponds considered here, the numbers of littoral macroinvertebrate taxa present are closely predicted by a single environmental variable, namely pH. Below pH 5.5, Mollusca, Malacostraca and Ephemeroptera are completely absent, while other taxa, notably the Trichoptera and Chironomini (Diptera), show a reduction in the numbers of taxa present. These patterns concur well with those reported from Scandinavian acidified lakes and North American dystrophic waters, where Gastropoda, Malacostraca and Ephemeroptera are characteristically absent at low pH (Wetzel, 1975; Økland, 1980; Stenson, 1985). In terms of the identities of taxa present, faunal similarities are greatest between ponds of similar pH (Fig. 5a), which suggests that successful colonization of at least some ponds is restricted to a subset of the total Purbeck species pool by chemical, or associated, factors. Marked faunal differences between acid and circum-neutral ball-clay ponds are apparent from the earliest stages of colonization of new ponds in the Isle of Purbeck (Barnes, 1983) so that differences between acid and circum-neutral 'mature' pond faunas are not the result of successional changes or differential dispersal rates between acid-sensitive and acid-tolerant species. Absence of taxa from ponds of low pH is probably due to a suite of factors, both chemical and biotic, which are directly or indirectly consequential on pH. The adverse effects of high hydrogen ion concentrations per se are exacerbated where calcium concentrations are low and levels of toxic metal ions, notably Al^{3+}, are high (Howells, 1984). The toxic effects of low pH have been demonstrated experimentally for a number of freshwater invertebrate groups, notably Crustacea (e.g. Steigen & Raddum, 1981), Ephemeroptera (Bell, 1971), and some Plecoptera and Trichoptera (Raddum & Steigen, 1981). In the Purbeck ponds, calcium levels are very highly correlated with pH, and although total aluminium levels were not measured systematically, two measurements of 70 \( \mu \)g l^{-1} in pond J and 570 \( \mu \)g l^{-1} in pond Q indicate that some of the acid ponds are probably well within the range of Al^{3+} concentrations known to be toxic to fish (Howells, 1984). The water chemistry in acid ponds E, J, P, Q and R is likely to cause severe physiological stress and prevent completion of the life-cycle in sensitive groups and thus ensure that any incoming propagules of these species cannot colonize. Furthermore, changes in certain biotic elements brought about by physiological stress may so change the habitat as to preclude colonization by species which are not themselves acid-sensitive. Stenson (1985) suggests that a loss of grazers (gastropods) and shredders (malacostracans) may have a major influence on littoral feeding relationships in the acidified Lake Gårdsjön. In the present study the macroinvertebrate faunas of acid ponds are characterized by what is absent, rather than what is present. Few taxa are recognizably 'acidophilic' in their distribution, with the possible exceptions of the chironomid Acamptocladius ?submontanus and the mayfly Leptophlebia marginata. The Odonata also appear to be better represented in ponds of pH<6.8. There is no evidence in these data of the biologically mediated pH effect reported by Hendrikson & Oscarson (1985), namely that loss of fish, the major visual predators, during lake acidification results in increased abundance of large, active invertebrates such as corixids and Notonecta (Hemiptera) and dytiscids (Coleoptera). Fish are absent from most of the ponds below pH 6.5 (A, B, C, D, E, J, P, Q and R), but there is no indication of a greater relative abundance of Hemiptera or Coleoptera in these ponds. This lack of agreement may be because the open water ('limnetic') species included by Hendrikson & Oscarson were not specifically sampled here. Over the wide range of pH represented in the study ponds, then, differences in faunal composition and diversity between the opposite ends of the pH spectrum may be due to a number of factors, probably acting in combina- tion. Many of these are themselves a direct or indirect consequence of hydrogen ion concentration, and pH alone would seem to provide a convenient index of the macroinvertebrate diversity to be expected in a pond. However, spot pH measurements from different water bodies can meaningfully be compared only if all are taken at approximately the same time and in a comparable way, since the pH of a given water body may vary both spatially and temporally, and with different methods of measurement. Although the general character of the macroinvertebrate communities of the Purbeck ponds is set by water chemistry, there is considerable variation in the details of the assemblages, even in ponds of similar pH. In general, ponds which fall within a narrow range of water chemistry, and not affected by any other overwhelmingly influential factor, may be expected to display a considerable diversity of assemblages, each created by a multiplicity of abiotic and biotic factors acting in unique combinations. Two ponds, F and L, clearly do not fit the linear model relating numbers of taxa to pH. Their faunal impoverishment may be linked to the lack of extensive weed beds in both ponds. The paucity of macrophytes may, in turn, be due to a number of factors, such as dense phytoplankton in the summer, supported by high nitrate and phosphate levels (Table 1), unbroken tree-shade round the margins and disturbance of the littoral sediment by bottom-feeding carp and tench. (The latter two points apply equally well to the richly-vegetated pond H, however.) Ponds F and L both have highly organic littoral substrata which support some distinctive faunal elements: pond F, in common with the other woodland ponds H and K, is dominated by shredders (mainly Trichoptera), while pond L, which also receives run-off from a nearby pig-farm, is dominated by organisms typical of organically enriched habitats, such as Tubificidae (Oligochaeta) and Chironomus spp. (Diptera). The number of species of macrophyte found in the Purbeck ponds bears no clear relationship with any of the factors considered. Some of the species distributions are clearly linked with pH: Sphagnum cuspidatum and Juncus bulbosus, in particular, are typical of the acid ponds. Grahn (1975) shows that Sphagnum species rapidly dominate acidified Swedish lakes, and this creates a characteristic biotope for invertebrates quite different from the habitat provided by aquatic angiosperms. The tenuous link observed here between macrophyte assemblages and water chemistry is in sharp contrast to the close relationship known to occur between lake diatom assemblages and pH (e.g. Battarbee, 1984). It remains to ask why such a wide range of pH occurs in the Purbeck ball-clay ponds. Two main sources of possible variation can be identified: local variations in geology, and differences in the land-use and vegetation immediately surrounding the ponds. Ball-clays are themselves chemically inert, but some clay sequences contain pyritic plant remains, which may be oxidized during changes in the water-table and cause acidification. The incidence of acid and neutral ponds is, however, independent of the oxidation state of the clays in this study area. A far greater influence on water chemistry would appear to be the use and vegetation of the surrounding land. The ponds all lie within the Bagshot Beds sandy deposits, which support Calluna heathland over much of the area (Fig. 1). Water passing through these heathland soils is likely to be acidic and low in nutrient ions. Pinus and Rhododendron occur on the sandier soils producing acidic drainage water, while the various species of deciduous

A few of the ponds also receive water from pasture, and other areas used for raising animals, which is likely to be of higher pH and richer in nutrients than drainage water from other land-use types. The diversity of macroinvertebrate and macrophyte communities in ponds LAURIE E. FRIDAY Department of Biological Sciences, University of Exeter SUMMARY. 1. The range of factors which may influence the wide variation in the structure of pond communities is reviewed. 2. Factors explaining the variation in numbers of macroinvertebrate and macrophyte taxa are investigated, using multiple regression analysis, for a group of ponds in which biogeographical effects are likely to be minimal. 3. Numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa in these ponds are highly correlated with pH and probably, therefore, with other associated aspects of water chemistry. 4. Many invertebrate taxa, from species to entire phyla, were not found below pH 5.5, but few characteristically 'acidophilic' taxa were apparent. 5. Details of species composition of the macroinvertebrate fauna differ widely even between ponds of similar pH. 6. The diversity and composition of macrophyte communities are not adequately predicted by any of the factors investigated. Introduction Ponds and other small water bodies are highly individual habitats: the fauna and flora usually vary widely, and often unpredictably, between ponds even within a small geographical area. While it is sometimes possible to find correlations between observed faunal or floral diversity and various factors, it is rarely possible, except by rigorous experimental treatment, to establish the causes of inter-pond variation. A wide variety of explanatory factors has been put forward, as a result of field studies of small water bodies or on theoretical grounds, as possible influences on the diversity and composition of pond communities. These factors may be grouped together under two broad headings: 'biogeographical' factors, operating via the dispersal of organisms to essentially insular habitats, and 'habitat' characteristics, both physico-chemical and biotic, influencing the establishment and persistence of colonizing species. These categories are not mutually exclusive, but form a useful basis for reviewing the wide range of factors which might explain inter-pond variation in the number and identities of species. Correspondence: Dr L. E. Friday, Department of Applied Biology, Pembroke Street, Cambridge CB2 3DX. (i) Biogeographical factors (a) Pond age. Studies of the initial colonization of newly created ponds show a general increase in the numbers of species of invertebrates and macrophytes (Gates, 1927; Street & Titmus, 1979; Barnes, 1983). Where dispersal distances are short, the rate of acquisition of new species has been observed to decline within a few years (Barnes, 1983), suggesting an approach to an 'equilibrium number of species', as predicted by MacArthur & Wilson's (1967) theory of island biogeography. However, Godwin's (1923) observations on the flora of much older ponds suggest that numbers of less vagile species (i.e. those with weak or passive dispersal) may continue to rise over many decades. As a pond ages, so the habitat it presents to colonists changes, partly due to increases in the extent and diversity of aquatic vegetation and in the production of autochthonous detritus. These changes are accompanied by changes in the identity of the dominant invertebrate taxa (Street & Titmus, 1979; Barnes, 1983). While it is possible to fit a model to the observed rise in numbers of taxa with age, the order in which individual colonists establish is not easy to predict. Invasion by an individual species depends on the availability of suitable propagules in 'source' habitats, the species' dispersal mechanisms, and the distance over which it has to disperse, but is also subject to chance (Talling, 1951). (b) Isolation. MacArthur & Wilson's model predicts a decrease in the equilibrium number of species on an island, and changes in the species represented, with increasing isolation from the source of colonists. Aho (1978a) found a significant correlation between isolation of small, productive Finnish lakes and the diversity of their molluscan faunas. Several authors have suggested that changes in isolation over historical or geological time (due to flooding, changes in river courses, creation or destruction of source habitats) have influenced the diversity of less vagile organisms in lakes (e.g. Boycott, 1919; Godwin, 1923; Aho, 1978b; Barbour & Brown, 1974). The immediate surroundings of ponds may also influence their chances of discovery by actively dispersing organisms, but surrounding vegetation and land use are likely to be of greater importance in their effect on aspects of the pond habitat, namely hydrology, water chemistry and allochthonous organic inputs. (c) Pond area. Connor & McCoy (1979), in their review of the species–area relationship, point out that the possible effects of area on community diversity have both biogeographical and biotic elements: as area increases, so the number of habitat types, with their associated species, is likely to increase; population sizes should also increase with area, thus reducing the extinction rate of resident species (MacArthur & Wilson, 1967); and large 'target' areas may simply receive a larger number of colonizing propagules, and therefore a chance of a greater variety of species, than smaller ones. Lassen (1975), Aho (1978a), Driver (1977) and Fryer (1985) found correlations between area (or log area) and the numbers of species of molluscs, chironomids and crustaceans respectively. Which of these aspects may account for the observed relationships is not possible to determine from diversity data alone, but Fryer (1985) suggests that the types of habitats found in different sized water bodies ('pond' as opposed to 'lake' habitats) may partly explain the composition of the crustacean faunas in his study area. Area, as an expression of the size of a water body, is also related to its persistence. Small ponds tend to be less permanent than larger ones, may show greater fluctuations in physical and chemical conditions, and so present quite a different type of habitat. Macan (1954, 1962) discusses the probable influence of habitat stability on the identity, and possibly on the diversity, of corixid species in a water body. (ii) Characteristics of the habitat (a) Habitat diversity. Factors contributing to the diversity of habitat for pond macrophytes include details of the bank topography and changes in substratum associated with irregularities in the shoreline. For the macroinvertebrate fauna, the diversity of macrophytic vegetation and local changes in substratum may be major factors. Observations by several authors on invertebrate communities associated with different species of macrophytes (e.g. Soszka, 1975; Dvorak & Best, 1982; Lodge, 1985), suggest that a correlation might be expected between macrophyte and macroinvertebrate numbers of species. Palmer (1981) found a close relationship between macrophyte species diversity and the number of species of Coleoptera and Hemiptera in a survey of base-rich ponds in Norfolk. (b) Competition and predation. Little direct evidence has been put forward to show that biotic interactions are major determinants of pond biotic diversity. However, changes in fish populations are often accompanied by changes in the plant and invertebrate communities (Macan, 1965, 1977b; Korinkova, 1967; Henrickson & Oscarson, 1985) and the effect of fish predation on zooplankton community structure is well documented (see Zaret, 1980). Biotic interactions might possibly be a major influence from the very earliest stages of pond colonization. In new ponds, extensive pure stands of emergent or floating-leaved macrophytes may establish within a few years (Barnes, 1983) and preclude other species by competition for light or space. They may constitute very distinctive habitats for invertebrates and if, by chance, different aggressive species colonize neighbouring ponds, then quite different communities may result. (c) Water chemistry. Many workers have found a correlation between pond biotic diversity and water chemistry. Scandinavian studies of molluscan communities (e.g. Aho, 1987a; Økland, 1980) link species diversity to a combination of pH and calcium levels. Strong positive correlations between pH and numbers of species of Crustacea have been reported from acidic, low-calcium ponds and lakes in Northern Britain (Fryer, 1980) and Norway (Økland & Økland, 1980). The composition of macrophytic communities may also be changed during lake acidification (Grahn, 1975). Green (1986) found a non-linear relationship between conductivity and zooplankton diversity in crater lakes. Several authors stress the importance of the general level of productivity of a water body (usually gauged by concentrations of nutrient ions) in determining the assortment of species found there, e.g. Saether (1975). In the present study, the distribution of littoral macroinvertebrates and macrophytes in a group of ponds within a small geographical area were investigated to discover which factors best predict the numbers of taxa and the types of communities found in each pond. In view of the difficulties inherent in distinguishing the confounding effects of different types of variables, the ponds were chosen to minimize the possible influence of pond age and isolation. Sites Sixteen ponds were chosen from among the large number of water bodies created by open-cast extraction of ball-clay in the Isle of Purbeck, Dorset, U.K. The study ponds all lie within an area of heath, woodland and pasture, 5×2 km, centred on National Grid Reference SY935835, just north of the chalk escarpment (Fig. 1). The ponds were chosen to represent as wide a range of physico-chemical and habitat conditions (as judged from terrestrial and aquatic vegetation) as possible. The exact ages of individual ponds are not known, but all date from the nineteenth century, with the exception of pond Q, which was formed in the eighteenth century (English China Clays (Ball Clays) Ltd, pers. comm.). From a study of the rate of colonization of newly created ball-clay ponds in the area (Barnes, 1983), it appears that the equilibrium number of macroinvertebrate taxa for small ponds is approached within 20 years of the first appearance of the water body. It is expected, therefore, that the ponds chosen for this study have attained the colonization asymptote, at least as far as macroinvertebrates are concerned, and any differences in age between them are not likely to be of importance. Dispersal distances between the ponds are small, the greatest nearest-neighbour distance being <1 km. No discrete source of colonizing propagules is recognizable, there being numerous small water bodies (ball-clay ponds, bomb craters and streams) in the area as well as the Corfe River to the east and the River Stour to the north-west. It is therefore assumed that the source pool of colonists is diffuse, so that no pond is substantially more isolated than any other. All the ponds contain at least 1 m depth of water throughout the year and none is connected, at any time, to any other water body. Methods (i) Morphometry Pond areas and shore lengths were estimated from large-scale maps produced by English China Clays (Ball Clays) Ltd surveyors. For the larger ponds, maximum depths and basin profiles were obtained from depth measure- FIG. 1. Location of the study site and map of the sixteen ball-clay ponds, labelled A–R. ments taken at 5 m intervals along transects; depths of smaller ponds were measured using a lead line from the bank. (ii) Chemistry Water samples were taken from 20 cm below the surface, 2 m from the shore, away from dense vegetation. All ponds were sampled within 2 h around noon on 12 April 1979 and again on 8 August 1979. Temperature and dissolved oxygen were recorded in situ and samples were analysed the same day by the Wessex Water Authority chemical laboratory, Poole, using standard methods (see Barnes, 1981; for details). For each sample, pH, electrical conductivity, turbidity, total hardness, alkalinity, nitrate, ammonium, orthophosphate, and 5-day B.O.D. were determined. Seven samples were later analysed for calcium and two for total aluminium, using an atomic absorption spectrophotometer at the University of Exeter. (iii) Macrophytes All ponds were surveyed during a 2-week period in August 1979 to determine the total area vegetated, the number of species, and their relative abundance, expressed as cover abundance scores as follows: 1 = 0.1–5% of vegetated area 2 = 6–25% of vegetated area 3 = 26–50% of vegetated area 4 = 51–75% of vegetated area 5 = 76–100% of vegetated area (iv) Macroinvertebrates The macroinvertebrate communities of the shallow littoral were sampled using standard sampling units, each consisting of five separate 2 m sweeps with an F.B.A. pond net (mesh aperture 1 mm). Trials showed that five sweeps obtained at least 85% of the species to be discovered by repeated sweeping within a given weed bed. Pond nets tend to under-sample certain elements of the fauna (see Macan, 1977a, for a critique), and the species lists obtained from one period of sampling will not be complete. However, such samples, taken in a standard manner and within a short space of time, may be used to compare communities between ponds. All sixteen ponds were sampled in a 3-day period in early April 1979. All were sampled with equal intensity, that is the number of sampling units employed in each pond was proportional to the extent of the shallow littoral habitat. An increase in the number of samples as pond size increased was deemed necessary to incorporate the apparent greater diversity of littoral habitats in larger ponds. The shoreline of each pond was divided arbitrarily into 100 m stretches and one sampling unit was taken in each 100 m stretch. The positions of the five individual sweeps in each sampling unit were determined by possibility of access to the water. Identification was taken to species wherever possible, but chironomid larvae were identified only to genus, and some members of other groups could be identified only to family. The relative numerical abundance of taxa were expressed as abundance scores as follows: 1 = present, but a mean of <1 individual per sampling unit 2 = 1–10 individuals per sampling unit 3 = 11–100 individuals per sampling unit 4 = >100 individuals per sampling unit The use of approximately logarithmic abundance categories to some extent overcomes the problem of comparing relative abundance of taxa of very different body size and reduces the dominating effect of seasonal swarms of small individuals. Results Numbers of taxa The numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa and macrophyte species found in each pond are shown in Table 1, together with values for selected physical and chemical parameters. The wide range of all these parameters over the sixteen ponds is apparent: for example, the number of macroinvertebrate taxa ranges from twenty-four to eighty-eight; pH from 3.8 to 7.5; and pond area from 0.023 to 2.0 ha. The total number of macroinvertebrate taxa found was 174 and the total number of macrophyte species thirty-one. The relationships between numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa (INVERTS) and macrophyte species (PLANTS) and physical and chemical characteristics of the ponds were investigated by correlation and regression analyses carried out using the statistical package MINITAB 81.1 (Ryan, 1981). Regression analyses were used to discover which, if any, of the biotic, physical and chemical factors might adequately explain the variation in numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa or macrophyte species found in these ponds. Preliminary analyses suggested that regression analysis would not be inappropriate, since the measurement errors in the y-variables (INVERTS or PLANTS) are great relative to those in the x-variables (predictors), and the individual variables are approximately normally distributed. Bivariate plots suggested the need to log-transform INVERTS, PLANTS, area and vegetated area for regression analysis (i.e. LINVERTS, LPLANTS, LAREA, LVAREA); this gave an acceptable degree of homoscedasticity in the residuals (Draper & Smith, 1981). Regression analyses proceeded by using predicator variables in turn, and, for multiple regression, adding them one at a time, using a correlation matrix as a guide and inspecting residuals and coefficients at each stage. The effectiveness of the various regression equations for predicting numbers of taxa in individual ponds was assessed by plotting the number of taxa predicted v. the number observed for each pond ('predicted-y v. observed-y' plots). Points falling above the line of equality indicate an over-estimation by the equation, those below an under-estimation (see Fig. 3). As a first step, Pearson correlation coefficients were computed between all pairs of the fourteen variables given in Table 1, log-transformed as appropriate. Sixteen pairs of observations were used in each case, except those involving calcium, for which only seven pairs could be used. Table 2, the correlation half-matrix, shows a number of distinct patterns: (i) LINVERTS is positively correlated with calcium and pH (\( P < 0.01 \)) and with LPLANTS, alkalinity, and LVAREA (\( P < 0.05 \)). (ii) All pairwise correlations between pH, conductivity, B.O.D., total hardness, alkalinity and calcium are significant at the 1% level. (iii) LAREA and LVAREA are correlated (\( P < 0.05 \)), depth is correlated with LAREA (\( P < 0.01 \)), and LVAREA with LINVERTS (\( P < 0.05 \)) but none of these morphometric variables is correlated with any chemical factor. The same patterns emerge, and correlations between the April and August values for each determinand were all significant (\( P<0.01 \)). The predictor variable accounting for the largest proportion (59.4%) of the variance in LINVERTS is pH. Discussion For the majority of the Purbeck ball-clay ponds considered here, the numbers of littoral macroinvertebrate taxa present are closely predicted by a single environmental variable, namely pH. Below pH 5.5, Mollusca, Malacostraca and Ephemeroptera are completely absent, while other taxa, notably the Trichoptera and Chironomini (Diptera), show a reduction in the numbers of taxa present. These patterns concur well with those reported from Scandinavian acidified lakes and North American dystrophic waters, where Gastropoda, Malacostraca and Ephemeroptera are characteristically absent at low pH (Wetzel, 1975; Økland, 1980; Stenson, 1985). In terms of the identities of taxa present, faunal similarities are greatest between ponds of similar pH (Fig. 5a), which suggests that successful colonization of at least some ponds is restricted to a subset of the total Purbeck species pool by chemical, or associated, factors. Marked faunal differences between acid and circum-neutral ball-clay ponds are apparent from the earliest stages of colonization of new ponds in the Isle of Purbeck (Barnes, 1983) so that differences between acid and circum-neutral 'mature' pond faunas are not the result of successional changes or differential dispersal rates between acid-sensitive and acid-tolerant species. Absence of taxa from ponds of low pH is probably due to a suite of factors, both chemical and biotic, which are directly or indirectly consequential on pH. The adverse effects of high hydrogen ion concentrations per se are exacerbated where calcium concentrations are low and levels of toxic metal ions, notably Al^{3+}, are high (Howells, 1984). The toxic effects of low pH have been demonstrated experimentally for a number of freshwater invertebrate groups, notably Crustacea (e.g. Steigen & Raddum, 1981), Ephemeroptera (Bell, 1971), and some Plecoptera and Trichoptera (Raddum & Steigen, 1981). In the Purbeck ponds, calcium levels are very highly correlated with pH, and although total aluminium levels were not measured systematically, two measurements of 70 \( \mu \)g l^{-1} in pond J and 570 \( \mu \)g l^{-1} in pond Q indicate that some of the acid ponds are probably well within the range of Al^{3+} concentrations known to be toxic to fish (Howells, 1984). The water chemistry in acid ponds E, J, P, Q and R is likely to cause severe physiological stress and prevent completion of the life-cycle in sensitive groups and thus ensure that any incoming propagules of these species cannot colonize. Furthermore, changes in certain biotic elements brought about by physiological stress may so change the habitat as to preclude colonization by species which are not themselves acid-sensitive. Stenson (1985) suggests that a loss of grazers (gastropods) and shredders (malacostracans) may have a major influence on littoral feeding relationships in the acidified Lake Gårdsjön. In the present study the macroinvertebrate faunas of acid ponds are characterized by what is absent, rather than what is present. Few taxa are recognizably 'acidophilic' in their distribution, with the possible exceptions of the chironomid Acamptocladius ?submontanus and the mayfly Leptophlebia marginata. The Odonata also appear to be better represented in ponds of pH<6.8. There is no evidence in these data of the biologically mediated pH effect reported by Hendrikson & Oscarson (1985), namely that loss of fish, the major visual predators, during lake acidification results in increased abundance of large, active invertebrates such as corixids and Notonecta (Hemiptera) and dytiscids (Coleoptera). Fish are absent from most of the ponds below pH 6.5 (A, B, C, D, E, J, P, Q and R), but there is no indication of a greater relative abundance of Hemiptera or Coleoptera in these ponds. This lack of agreement may be because the open water ('limnetic') species included by Hendrikson & Oscarson were not specifically sampled here. Over the wide range of pH represented in the study ponds, then, differences in faunal composition and diversity between the opposite ends of the pH spectrum may be due to a number of factors, probably acting in combina- tion. Many of these are themselves a direct or indirect consequence of hydrogen ion concentration, and pH alone would seem to provide a convenient index of the macroinvertebrate diversity to be expected in a pond. However, spot pH measurements from different water bodies can meaningfully be compared only if all are taken at approximately the same time and in a comparable way, since the pH of a given water body may vary both spatially and temporally, and with different methods of measurement. Although the general character of the macroinvertebrate communities of the Purbeck ponds is set by water chemistry, there is considerable variation in the details of the assemblages, even in ponds of similar pH. In general, ponds which fall within a narrow range of water chemistry, and not affected by any other overwhelmingly influential factor, may be expected to display a considerable diversity of assemblages, each created by a multiplicity of abiotic and biotic factors acting in unique combinations. Two ponds, F and L, clearly do not fit the linear model relating numbers of taxa to pH. Their faunal impoverishment may be linked to the lack of extensive weed beds in both ponds. The paucity of macrophytes may, in turn, be due to a number of factors, such as dense phytoplankton in the summer, supported by high nitrate and phosphate levels (Table 1), unbroken tree-shade round the margins and disturbance of the littoral sediment by bottom-feeding carp and tench. (The latter two points apply equally well to the richly-vegetated pond H, however.) Ponds F and L both have highly organic littoral substrata which support some distinctive faunal elements: pond F, in common with the other woodland ponds H and K, is dominated by shredders (mainly Trichoptera), while pond L, which also receives run-off from a nearby pig-farm, is dominated by organisms typical of organically enriched habitats, such as Tubificidae (Oligochaeta) and Chironomus spp. (Diptera). The number of species of macrophyte found in the Purbeck ponds bears no clear relationship with any of the factors considered. Some of the species distributions are clearly linked with pH: Sphagnum cuspidatum and Juncus bulbosus, in particular, are typical of the acid ponds. Grahn (1975) shows that Sphagnum species rapidly dominate acidified Swedish lakes, and this creates a characteristic biotope for invertebrates quite different from the habitat provided by aquatic angiosperms. The tenuous link observed here between macrophyte assemblages and water chemistry is in sharp contrast to the close relationship known to occur between lake diatom assemblages and pH (e.g. Battarbee, 1984). It remains to ask why such a wide range of pH occurs in the Purbeck ball-clay ponds. Two main sources of possible variation can be identified: local variations in geology, and differences in the land-use and vegetation immediately surrounding the ponds. Ball-clays are themselves chemically inert, but some clay sequences contain pyritic plant remains, which may be oxidized during changes in the water-table and cause acidification. The incidence of acid and neutral ponds is, however, independent of the oxidation state of the clays in this study area. A far greater influence on water chemistry would appear to be the use and vegetation of the surrounding land. The ponds all lie within the Bagshot Beds sandy deposits, which support Calluna heathland over much of the area (Fig. 1). Water passing through these heathland soils is likely to be acidic and low in nutrient ions. Pinus and Rhododendron occur on the sandier soils producing acidic drainage water, while the various species of deciduous

The potential of the zooplankton resting-stage bank to restore communities in permanent and temporary waterbodies ENEIDA MARIA ESKINAZI-SANT’ANNA1* AND MICHAEL L. PACE2 1LABORATORY OF AQUATIC ECOLOGY, DEPARTMENT OF BIODIVERSITY, EVOLUTION AND ENVIRONMENT, FEDERAL UNIVERSITY OF OURO PRETO, OURO PRETO, MINAS GERAIS, BRAZIL AND 2DEPARTMENT OF ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCES, UNIVERSITY OF VIRGINIA, CHARLOTTESVILLE, VA, USA *CORRESPONDING AUTHOR: eskinazi@iceb.ufop.br Received September 2, 2017; editorial decision May 31, 2018; accepted June 1, 2018 Corresponding editor: Karl Havens We assessed how the viability and diversity of the zooplankton resting-stage bank can be affected by predictable and unpredictable hydroperiods using permanent and temporary lakes. We hypothesized that the zooplankton resting-stage bank in temporary waterbodies would be affected by the length of the dry period (seasonal, intermittent and episodic). We also tested the role of dried macrophyte mats in preserving resting-stage banks in temporary lakes. Laboratory experiments were conducted with sediment samples from two permanent waterbodies and three temporary shallow lakes that undergo dry periods of different lengths (seasonal, intermittent and >10 years dry). The results of the experiments suggested that the dry period length significantly affected the viability and diversity of the resting-stage bank, affecting its potential role in zooplankton community recovery. Longer dry periods also affected the temporal hatching response of resting stages from temporary lakes: species from unpredictably drying waterbodies experienced delayed hatching. Resting-stage viability and richness were largely and positively influenced by dried macrophyte mats, which surpassed the efficiency of the sediment as a substrate for conserving resting stages. Our results provide new insight on the functional role of macrophytes indicating that these beds are pivotal in conserving resting stages and increasing zooplankton community resilience. KEYWORDS: zooplankton; resting-stages bank; hatching; hydroperiod; macrophytes mats INTRODUCTION Temporary and permanent waterbodies are important landscape elements (Downing, 2010; Ewald et al., 2012) and are classified as permanent or temporary depending on the length and the predictability of wetting and drying (William, 1998; Brock, 2011; Ewald et al., 2012). For temporary ecosystems, loss of water (dry period) is a natural phase of their hydrological variability (Brocks et al., 2003), and aquatic organisms living in these special habitats have developed extraordinary adaptations to survive drying. Of particular importance is the production of resting stages that can survive during unfavorable (dry) conditions (De Stasio, 1990; Hairston et al., 1995; Brendonck and De Meester, 2003). The production of resting structures and dormant phases of the life cycle is a well-known characteristic of zooplankton (Radzikowski, 2013). Although the robust structure of the resting-stage covering possessed by many (but not all) species can enable them to survive for long periods under adverse conditions, the temporal viability of these dormant forms can be affected by long-term drought (Fryer, 1996; Cáceres, 1998; Havel et al., 2000; Boven and Brendock, 2009). Under these circumstances, recovery of the zooplankton community would require dispersal from adjacent habitats. Thus, recovery of a completely dried waterbody in the absence of a bank of viable resting-stages would depend on the integrity of the local aquatic habitats and their biota, and the dispersal of viable resistant forms (Shurin, 2000; Clarke, 2003; Franco et al., 2006; Incagnone et al., 2015; Schwartz and Jenkins, 2000). Understanding the resilience of the zooplankton assembly in temporary habitats can help to predict how the community structure could be affected by changes in water regimes, and which habitats can preserve viable resting-egg banks after unpredictable and/or long dry periods. If it is possible to determine the temporal viability and the time response of the resting-stage bank, as well as the most resilient species ensemble, it could be possible to forecast the recovery time and composition of the aquatic ecosystems affected by changes in water regimes, as predicted under climate-change scenarios (Brock, 1998; Mertens et al., 2008; Williams et al., 2008). Biological responses of aquatic populations from temporary aquatic ecosystems, including species strategies to adapt in changing environments, must be understood and taken into account in conservation actions (Angeler, 2007). The present contribution explores the composition (species richness) and viability (temporal response and hatching abundance) of zooplankton resting-stage banks in waterbodies that experience different wetting and drying regimes. Although zooplankton communities from tropical shallow lakes are considered under influence of constant seasonal patterns of light and temperature, which trigger and maintain high rates of resting-stage hatching, the prevalence of harsh drying conditions and its effect on the viability and resilience of resting stages bank is still largely unexplored. To evaluate the influence of local constraints on the viability of zooplankton resting stages, two permanent lakes and three temporary waterbodies were selected. The permanent lakes are representative of the potential optimal hydrological conditions for longevity of the resting-stage bank (no desiccation period). To test if different climate conditions could affect the hatching response in permanent habitats, experiments were carried out for a tropical lake (water and sediment under warm temperatures) and a temperate lake, where seasonality, including cold conditions, affects the water and sediment. We tested the hypothesis that the composition and viability of the zooplankton resting-stage bank are influenced by the water regime. Specifically, we predicted that resting-stage banks from temporary habitats exposed to prolonged dry periods would hatch fewer animals and have lower species richness, due to environmental harshness (especially in Coutos and Meio lakes). We assessed this hypothesis by investigating the following questions: (i) how long does the resting-stage bank survive in habitats that experience extreme dry periods; (ii) how is the abundance and species composition of hatchlings from the resting bank influenced by the length of the dry period; and (iii) how does the species richness and hatching of the resting-stage bank respond to different water regimes? In addition to the above hypotheses, we considered the importance of macrophytes as source of hatching zooplankton. In shallow temporary waterbodies, extensive macrophyte beds usually cover the bottom, where they augment the environmental heterogeneity, habitat and refuge for aquatic invertebrates. During the dry period, the macrophyte banks collapse and become part of the organic fraction of the lake sediment, as dried aquatic vegetation. To assess the role of dried macrophyte mats as a substrate for zooplankton resting stages in temporary lakes, hatching experiments were also carried out with this material. This approach, to our knowledge, is the first to address the potential importance of the dried mats of aquatic plants for the preservation of the zooplankton resting-stage bank. METHOD Study sites Sediment samples were collected in five shallow waterbodies in Brazil and the USA. Limnological features of these waterbodies are summarized in Table I. In Brazil, samples were obtained in one permanent lake (Carioca Lake) and three temporary lakes (Coutos, Seca and Meio) with different hydrological pulses, according to Table I: Limnological features of the studied waterbodies (mean values). * = Exclusively hatched from macrophyte mats.

Source of data: Beaver Creek: Emery et al. (2015). Carioca Lake: Pinto-Coelho et al. (2008). Coutos Lake: FW Moreira et al. (2015); Seca Lake: R Moreira et al. (2015). For Meio Lake, biological and chemical variables are unknown, since the lake remains dried since 2004. Hydrological classification according to Brocks et al. (2003). Brock et al. (2003). Carioca Lake is a natural lake surrounded by Atlantic Rain Forest located in the State Park of Rio Doce (Minas Gerais state, Southeast Brazil). In the USA, sampling was conducted in Beaver Creek Reservoir, a permanent waterbody located at Albemarle County, Virginia. (Fig. 1). The temporary lakes were selected according to a dryness gradient. Seca is a seasonal pond that fills each year during the rainy period. Coutos and Meio lakes are representative of the harshest conditions of dryness. These two shallow lakes are located on an outcrop with iron-rich duricrust, under severe edapho-climatic conditions, including high ultraviolet (UV) intensities and daily temperature variations of the substrate that can easily exceed 50°C (Jacobi et al., 2007). Coutos is an intermittent shallow lake that remains dry even during the rainy period, if rains are sparse. Meio Lake has been completely dry since 2004. We considered that Coutos and Meio lakes constitute natural models of the extreme environmental stresses that can affect the viability of resting stages: dryness and high soil temperatures. Field sampling In Brazil, sediment sampling was conducted during the dry period (August and September of 2014), when all the temporary lakes were completely dry. In the USA, sampling was conducted in early spring (April 2015), after the resting stages had been under influence of cold temperatures, but before the temperature had warmed enough to trigger hatching in the growing season. For temporary lakes, sediments were collected with a garden trowel from the top 6 cm at 10 random sampling points, 5 from the littoral (covered by emergent macrophytes) and another 5 randomly points selected from the open-water area (mainly covered by submerged macrophytes). From these 10 locations, a pooled sample was created for each lake by combining all sediment samples. Sediments from permanent lakes (Carioca Lake and Beaver Creek Reservoir) were obtained with a core (60-cm long acrylic tube, diameter 8 cm), in three randomly sampled locations. The sediment samples were immediately transported to the laboratory in a cool box, and kept in the dark in a refrigerator at 4°C. The upper 5 cm of each sediment core from the permanent lakes was sliced and integrated into a single sample. Sample processing The wet sediment samples from the permanent lake were first processed before the hatching experiments, to kill any remaining active stages of aquatic invertebrates. Each sample was spread into a thin layer onto a plastic surface and dried for 1 week at room temperature. Although some studies have reported that isolation of resting stages from the sediments can increase the hatching rates (Cáceres and Schwalbach, 2001; Vandekerkhove et al., 2004), this method can also decrease the efficiency of sorting of smaller resting stages such as rotifers and the more delicate dormant stages of some copepods (Brendonck and De Meester, 2003). Considering that the main goal of this study was to observe the recovery of the zooplankton assembly, resting stages were not isolated from the sediment. For hatching experiments, subsamples of 50 g of sediment from every lake were manually agitated in a plastic tray for 30 min and then placed into individual 25 × 10 cm covered plastic boxes. We used three replicate boxes for each lake. Each of the boxes for every lake was flooded with 1 L of distilled water and then incubated at 25°C under fluorescent lights (4000 lux) and a 16:8 h light/dark cycle. Samples were incubated for 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 days. Every 2 days, the entire volume of the water was removed with a volumetric transfer pipette, and new water was added to the sediment. The water removed was filtered through a 35-μm plankton mesh and preserved with Lugol’s solution. These samples were used to assess zooplankton composition, richness and to estimate the time hatching response of the resting bank. Fig. 1. Map of the studied waterbodies. Brazil: Carioca Lake, Seca Lake, Coutos and Meio lakes. USA: Beaver Creek Reservoir (Albemarle County, Virginia). Hatching experiments of zooplankton resting stages from dried macrophyte mats were carried out by carefully separating the macrophyte mats from the sediment samples from the temporary waterbodies (Coutos Lake, Meio Lake and Seca Lake), under a stereomicroscope. Macrophyte banks in Seca Lake are almost entirely dominated by Eleocharis minima Kunth, Juncus densiflorus Kunth and Egeria minima Planchon. In Coutos Lake, besides E. minima, several other species of macrophytes can be found, such as Nymphaoides indica (L.) Kuntze, Polygonum sp., Helanthium tenellum (Mart. Ex R. & S.) Britton, Utricularia sp. and Egeria najas Planch. Three subsamples of 50 g of macrophytes mats were placed in three individual covered 50 × 20-cm plastic boxes. Each box was flooded with 2 L of distilled water, and then incubated in the same temperature and light regimes used for the sediment samples. Since it was difficult to separate hatched individuals from the macrophyte fragments, samples were incubated for 30 days. At the end of this period, the entire sample was filtered and washed with distilled water under a 35-μm plankton mesh. Samples were preserved in 4% formalin solution with Rose Bengal stain to aid in separating organisms from macrophyte detritus. In these experiments, zooplankton richness was considered as the number of species detected on the 30th day of the experiment. The entire content of each zooplankton sample was sorted under a stereomicroscope (Zeiss Discovery V20) at 50–150× magnification. When necessary, samples were also analyzed under an inverted microscope (Zeiss AXIO Observer A1) at 400–1000× magnification. Rotifers were identified to the lowest taxonomic level possible, following the keys of Ruttner-Kolisko (1974), Koste (1978) and Stemberg (1979). Additional information available at the website http://cfb.unh.edu/cfbkey/html/begin.html was also consulted. For cladocerans, taxonomic references included those by Brooks (1959), Hebert and Finston (1997), Elmoor-Loureiro (2007) and Van Damme and Dumont (2010) and the descriptions found in the following website: https://cladocera.wordpress.com/. For cyclopoid copepods, we consulted the key by Reid (1985). For Anostraca the descriptions by Chaves et al. (2011) were followed, and for Conchostraca we followed Pereira and García (2001). Zooplankton richness was obtained by counting the number of species that hatched during the experiments from the 5th to the 30th days of experiment. Hatching abundance was estimated by counting the individuals in the zooplankton samples. Statistical analyses were performed in Statistica (9.0) and EstimateS. To find differences in zooplankton richness among waterbodies and to test the hypotheses regarding the importance of sediment samples versus macrophyte mats to conserve resting-stages banks, ANOVA was used on log-transformed data to reduce heteroscedasticity, followed by Tukey test. The statistical analyses comprised two fixed factors: temporal aspects of the dryness period (permanent or temporary lakes) and length of dryness (permanent, seasonal and intermittent). Meio Lake was removed from these analyses, as it clearly differed from the other two shallow lakes. Hatching data were also log-transformed to homogenize the variance. For regressions, we examined residual plots to check that models were not biased and the models were used to test the a priori hypotheses regarding the effects of dryness length on (i) zooplankton richness and (ii) hatching of the resting-stage bank. RESULTS Zooplankton richness from sediment and dried macrophyte mats A total of 95 species hatched during the experiments, confirming the presence of a residual stage bank in the permanent and temporary lakes. Overall, 10 species hatched from Beaver Creek, 21 from Carioca, 51 from Coutos, 54 from Seca and 10 from Meio Lake (Table II). In permanent waterbodies, rotifers were the most frequent forms hatched from resting stages, especially Brachionus calyciflorus, Brachionus mirus, Filinia longiseta, Hexarthra intermedia and Plygura sp., and bdelloideans, which could not be identified to genus level. Crustaceans hatched in low numbers (usually <10 daily hatchings), and were represented mainly by Daphnia species (D. ambigua, D. parvula and D. rosea in Beaver Creek and D. gessneri and D. laevis in Carioca). Cyclopoid copepods were also found in low numbers. In the temporary shallow lakes, the proportion of epibenthic cladoceran species was over-represented, while widespread limnetic forms such as Moina minuta were under-represented. The cladocerans Chydorus pubescens, Ilyocryptus spinifer, Chydorus cf. sphaericus and Alona ossiani can be considered the most resilient species in the temporary habitats, since they were the most frequent and abundant species hatched from the resting-egg bank. Lecane hyaclista, Tricochera insignis and T. myersi, in addition to bdelloid rotifers, were common in Coutos and Seca lakes, and hatching rates were high (>50 daily hatchings, Table II). Hatching experiments with the dried macrophyte mats revealed that a substantial fraction of the zooplankton richness in the temporary lakes hatched from this plant substrate (Fig. 2). In Coutos Lake, 20 zooplankton species (33% of hatchlings) emerged exclusively from dried macrophyte mats, including rotifers (genera Keratella, Plygura, Tricochera and other Bdelloidea), the limnetic cladoceran Moina minuta, benthic cladocerans including Alona dentifera, Alona yara, Alonella clathratula, Graptoleberis occidentalis and Celsinotum candango, the anostracan Dendrocephalus sp. and the conchostracan Eulimnadia brasiliensis. In Seca Pond, 14 species hatched exclusively from macrophyte mats (26% of total hatchings), including Dendrocephalus sp. In Meio Lake, macrophyte fragments were sparsely present in the sediment, and only three species hatched from this plant substrate (Trichocerca sp., Alona ossiani and Chydorus pubescens). Hatching experiments with dried macrophyte mats indicated that this substrate is an important repository of invertebrate species for shallow lakes. Zooplankton richness was significantly higher in macrophyte mats on the 30th day of experiments than for the sediment samples over the same period in Coutos (t-test: \( df = 1, F = 5.26, P = 0.003 \)) and Seca lakes (t-test: \( df = 1, F = 3.05, P = 0.03 \)) (Fig. 3). Temporal response of zooplankton richness Zooplankton richness in all the lakes tended to increase over the incubation periods (Fig. 4). These patterns were significant from the 5th to the 30th day, in the permanent (ANOVA, \( df = 5, F = 5.6, P < 0.001 \)) and temporary lakes (ANOVA, \( df = 5, F = 4.6, P < 0.001 \)). In permanent lakes, zooplankton richness began to increase in 1 week (5th day), and maximum richness was reached in 4 weeks (by the 25th day). For temporary lakes, hatchings were delayed compared with permanent lakes. Hatching started within 2 weeks (from the 10th day of experiments), and maximum richness was reached in 5 weeks (by the 30th day). Zooplankton richness showed the same temporal pattern in the episodic Meio Lake, but very few species hatched (median 2.5 species), indicating a limited potential for the local resting-egg bank to restore zooplankton richness (Fig. 5). Resting-stage hatchings and zooplankton richness Hatching abundance had a significant effect on the overall species richness for permanent and temporary lakes (ANOVA, \( F = 18.52, P < 0.001 \)) (Fig. 6). In permanent lakes, hatching from the resting-stage bank restored richness within 2 weeks (median of 65.4 hatchlings), and thereafter decreased substantially until the 5th week (median 56.5 at the 30th day), confirming the rapid response of the regional egg bank to hatching stimulus. Therefore, for temporary lakes, hatching abundance increased substantially after 3 weeks (20th day) (median 854 hatchings), reaching the highest hatching abundance after 5 weeks (median 1089.7 hatchings). The strong influence of hatchings on zooplankton richness (\( R^2 = 0.90 \), residual \( df = 88 \)) is apparent in Fig. 7. In permanent lakes, zooplankton richness increased under a low hatching number (median 65.3 hatchings.d\(^{-1}\)), while for temporary lakes (except for Meio Lake, excluded from this analysis due to the very low richness), the increase of zooplankton richness seems to be associated with a very high number of hatchings (median 630.8 hatchings.d\(^{-1}\)). ![Bar chart showing the percentage of species hatched in lakes sediments and macrophyte mats](page_320_670_800_400.png) Fig. 2.
