4. Results and discussions

4.1. The dolines landscape from the Meledic Plateau salt karst system

An extensive salt karst system has developed in the Mânzălești salt formation. Except traditional local use (food preparation and dietary supplement for livestock), in the study area the salt has never been exploited by mining. As a consequence, the anthropomorphic effects on the geologic and geomorphologic environment are low. Thus the karstogenesis is driven only by natural processes and the evolution of the salt karst started most probably during Holocene. This karstified area has a great diversity of karst features.

![View of doline field in the Meledic Plateau salt karst system with wetlands in foreground: left aide - reed marsh; right side – a small pond with a littoral zone dominated by herbaceous flowering plant species (August 2015).](page_320_670_1808_1042.png)

Fig. 2. View of doline field in the Meledic Plateau salt karst system with wetlands in foreground: left aide - reed marsh; right side – a small pond with a littoral zone dominated by herbaceous flowering plant species (August 2015).

After field surveys and aerial photographs analysis two main types of karstic depressions have been identified in the area of Meledic Plateau: solution dolines and sinkholes or solution-collapse dolines. The sinkholes are mainly due to soil-cover and cap rock collapse. Their diameters vary between several meters up to more than 100 m, and the depths are even more than 50 m. They drain the rainwater and some of sinkholes, usually those ones with sub vertical and sculptured walls, are the entrances of salt caves.

In the study area, dolines are interstratal karst landforms [40] because subsurface solution has induced deformation and collapse of the overlying cover rocks. According to the genetic typology of dolines [14], they are

</page>

<page number="5">

cover dolines, not normal dolines, because the soluble rock is overlaid by a tick cap rock and soil. Thus, the rainwater infiltration and percolation are the main drivers of dissolution. The underground dissolution (subrosion) of rock salt has leaded to a slow lowering of the surface of land in flat, funnel and bowl shaped depressions. The evidence of subrosion is raveled as more or less rounded pinnacles in canyon valley slopes.

In terms of morphology most of salt dolines from Meledic Plateau are round or ovate and are dominantly funnel-shaped, but asymmetric types are also frequent. Their diameters vary between one meter up to several tens meters, but those with 1-5 m width prevail. The deep ranges from 1 to about 16 meters.

The dense net of dolines has generated an undulated surface and a field dolines landscape in area of the Meledic Plateau. The field dolines landscape is clearly perceivable especially on the north-western side, where there are step slopes. According to Belonni et al.[41], such a high density of dolines, reveals high hydraulic gradients. Although, at least in limestone karst systems, a normal doline is a dry doline because it cannot hold water as a result of concentrated drainage driven by infiltration and percolations [14], many dolines with impermeable bottom have retained rainwater in the area of the Meledic Plateau. Thus they have become lakes, ponds, marshes or humid terrains. All of them are freshwater wetlands that contribute significantly to local biodiversity.

In opposition to wet doline, the majority of normal dolines are vegetated by plant species that are typical for floristic composition of the local wildflower, hay meadows, and grazed grasslands. Moreover, some small doline are refuges for thermophile trees and shrubs such as Tillia cordata, Fraxinus excelsior, Quercus robur, Rosa canina, and Crategus monogyna. Because is difficult to mow the grass from small dolines, they are avoided by haymakers during hay harvest season and thus seedlings and sapling survives and can grow and develop into mature trees and bushes. Only on the edges of plateau where there are eroded soils and superficial landslides occur halophytes plant species.

However, due to dense net of dolines and spectacular assemblage of them it has developed a field dolines which is a specific feature within of the Meledic Plateua landscape (Fig. 2).

4.2. Wetlands typology from the Meledic Plateu karst system

All those dolines that are suitable to keep water because of insoluble residuum created by sub surface dissolution processes are potential wetlands. A number of 87 wetlands were identified in the study area. They are preponderantly scattered in the north-western quarter of the salt karst Meledic Plateau. The water is supplied to them by precipitation and by surface runoff. Wetlands from the Meledic Plateua have no channelized inflow or outflow. As a consequence, in the majority of these wetlands the water level is primarily under control of precipitation, local runoff and evapotranspiration. Because wetlands are so dynamic in water level, some of them, not enough large and deep, dry out toward the end of summer and develop gradually in a bare black mud flat surrounded by a belt of typical shallow-marsh plants like Juncus sp., Sparganium erectum, Alisma plantago-aquatica.

During the field survey of sampled wetlands a total of 53 vascular plant species were recorded. Eight were hydrophytes, including the carnivorous Utricularia vulgaris, and 45 were helophytes, including the marsh fern (Nephrodium thelypteris), whose occurrence in Romania is usually associated with the appearance of reed marshes and the plav [42] or plaur, as it is called in Romanian language [43, 44, 45]. Based on size and the species composition, diversity height, distribution and vegetation cover-water interspersion, were differentiated following types of wetlands: lakes, ponds, marshes, and wet meadows.

4.2.1. Lakes

Based on morphometric criteria (surface area and maximum deep) there are two big lakes. The largest lake is Lacul Meledic or Lacul Mare, as it is called by local people. Its area is 1.14 ha, and 5.4 m is quoted as the maximum deep [46], but during a sounding operation along a line transect in north area a deep of 6.9 m was reached. Emergent vegetation (reed and cattail) occurs in littoral zone from northern part of the lake. The surrounding morphology suggests that the lake depression originate from a collapse doline.

The other lake is named Castelu. It is much smaller than Lacul Mare but is located on the bottom of a large depression that is drained by few temporary valleys. The general shape of lake is elliptical and it has an area of 0.38

4.2.2. Ponds

The ponds from forest are small (50-70 m^2), without any macrophytes. Their water is brown in color (19 Forel-Ule Color Scale), with yellow-brown hue because of the leaf litter and various other organic debris that fall in ponds and on the surrounding ground.

The ponds spread out in the grasslands area of the plateau are more diverse in size and ecological successional stage. The following subtypes have been identified: ponds without emergent macrophytes and ponds with well-developed littoral vegetation. In the first category are included only two ponds, both with surface area around 150 m^2. Their shore is bordered by trees (Quercus robur, Tilia cordata) and bushes (Coryllus avellana, Crategus monogyna).

First type delineates the small ponds (< 25 m^2), with very shallow water (Fig. 3). The emergent vegetation consists of short grasses, sedges and herbaceous flowering plant species (Juncus sp., Carex sp., Agrostis stolonifera, Lythrum salicaria, Sparganium erectum, Rumex hydrolapathum, Rumex aquaticus, Alisma plantago-aquatica, Polygonum amphibium, Lysimachia vulgaris, Lysimachia nummularia. Among rooted floating species frequent is pond weed (Potamogeton natans). In some of ponds, duck weed (Lemna sp.) makes a dense mat on the water surface. Also the small ponds may dry out during the summer, especially when the water deep is less 1 m.

The ponds with reed bed are much larger than first type. They are permanently flooded although endure annual seasonal changes in the water level, mainly in response to local precipitation-evaporation balance. However, they display some concentric zonation of vegetation that depends on the contour of the ponds bottom and the maximum depth of water. Typically, from the shoreline toward the center of pond, the zones of vegetation are: wet-meadow zone, composed by sedges and herbaceous flowering species; shallow marsh zone, which is composed primarily by reed (Phragmites australis), and subsequently by broadleaf cattail (Typha latifolia), narrow leaf cattail (Typha angustifolia), bulrush (Schoenoplectus lacustris), marsh fern (Thelypteris palustris); deep marsh vegetation, composed by rooted floating-leaf plants (Potamogeton natans, Polygonum amphibium), unrooted floating plants (Ranunculus aquatilis, Lemna sp., Utricularia vulgaris), and submerged plants (Ceratophyllum submersum).

4.2.3. Marshes

In the area of the Meledic Plateau marshes are dolines with temporary, seasonal, semi-permanent and permanent water and that are completely or almost entirely covered by wetland vegetation. Based on dominant plant species there are reed marshes, cattail marshes, and mixed marshes, with distinct stands of reed and cattail, reed and grey willow (Salix cinerea), cattail and grey willow. Complex structures have some of those which include trees and shrubs in their area. Trees (Alnus glutinosa, Betula pendula) and grey willow bushes are located in the middle of the marsh. They make an island that is encircled by two or three vegetation belts: cattail belt, reed bed zone, and sedge and herbaceous flowering plants.

4.2.4. Wet meadows

Wet meadows occur on the top of the plateau, in large and shallow depressions. These depressions are sub circular, oval or hemispherical dolines that have a flat bottom (Fig. 4). These wetlands type lack the vegetative diversity in structure and layering. Dominant species are sedges, bulrush (Scirpus sp.), and other grasses that are able to grow on clay, moist and poorly oxygenated soils. Monospecific stands by narrow cattail are also present. During hay harvesting season, if the soil moisture level allows, the wet meadow may be mowed by the landowners.

4.3. Wetlands as habitats for wildlife

Fresh wetlands, as small discrete units scattered across the salt karst Meledic Plateau, actively engineer the landscape. They provide habitats for important invertebrates and vertebrates. During the field work it was noticed occurrence of odonates, two amphibians (Rana ridibunda, Rana dalmatina), and a reptile (Natrix natrix). There were not noticed any waterfowls, probably because wetland size is one of the limiting factors [47] in this area. Thus, although there is adequate wetland vegetation able to provide shelter and nesting habitats, ponds and marshes there are not enough large and do not have enough open water for landing, swimming, and feeding. Importantly, in terms of regional biodiversity, the wetlands from the Meledic Plateau are habitats for Large Copper (Lycaena dispar Haworth), one of the most endangered butterfly species in Europe that is classified as a priority for protection [26, 29]. In Romania Lycaena dispar is legally protected but is not listed in the national Red List of invertebrates as threatened species [25, 30].

This oligophagous butterfly species depends on several particular hygrophilous plant species in all stages of his life cycle. Thus, species of Rumex that are located in open and sunny habitats [48] are selected by female as host plant for oviposition and larval food plant after hatching [49, 50]. For nectaring, adults visit most frequently nine plant species [50, 51] and five of them occur in the study area: Lythrum salicaria, Cirsium arvense, Cirsium palustre, Mentha aquatica. In the study area, distribution of these plant species is especially correlated with the presence of small ponds.

Taking in account that in the designed area of the ROSCI0199 Platoul Meledic Natura 2000 site, the suitable habitats for large copper butterfly are surrounded by wild flower meadows, the main human threat is hay harvesting. Farmers still make hay traditionally, by hand, using scyntes, forks and rakes, or using handle mowing machine due to undulating topografic surface of plateau.

To prevent cutting the plants species that are vital for Lycaena dispar and also to protect them, local people need to be informed, educated about its biology and ecological requirements, and should be involved into conservation activities of the large copper butterfly. Regarding public awareness about this threatened butterfly, the first step is to establish adequate buffer zones around wetlands followed by the implementation of an appropriate long-term conservation management plan, both wetlands and hay meadows. Thus, to maintain larval habitats – the palatable Rumex species stands - is the fundamental goal according to the management activities which have been implemented in other countries [51, 52, 53]. However, the choosing of the appropriate conservation strategies requires a local study in order to investigate host plant preferences and habitat preferences in the Meledic Plateau area, even if the biology and ecology of this endangered butterfly has been extensively studied in other countries before [51, 48, 50, 52, 49].

5. Conclusions

Due to tectonic and sedimentological settings of the innermost tectonic unit of the Subcarpathian Nappe, in the area of the Slănic River basin, southern limit of Vrancea Hills, it has developed a salt karst area named the Meledic Plateau. Salt dissolution has created a great diversity of salt karst features, including dolines, that in this particular area are interstratal karst landforms, and key diagnostic karst landforms in general.

As a result of high density of dolines in conjunction with local landslides movements, the western half of the plateau has become a dolines field, with an undulating surface.

All those doline able to hold rain water, have turned into fresh water wetlands. These wetlands, which make a dense net in the Meledic Plateau, are discrete units and key features of the landscape. They are diverse in shape, size, floristic composition, and vegetation assemblages.

The wetlands landscape overlaps the salt karst landscape; their occurrence is strictly connected with natural karst processes, which enhance the natural value of the plateau. Therefore dolines from the Meledic Plateau are habitat for the hydrophilous butterfly Lycaena dispar, a species of European interest and the target species in declaring ROSCI0199 Platoul Meledic Natura 2000 site. Due to the traditional land use pattern, the main threat of Lycaena dispar in the area of Meledic Plateau is hay harvest. Thus, conservation strategies of Lycaena dispar should focus on the maintenance of its suitable habitat, including through the involvement of local people.

Zooplankton body size versus taxonomy in Mediterranean wetlands: implications for aquatic ecosystem evaluation Juan Diego Gilbert1,2,4, Inmaculada de Vicente3,5, Raquel Jiménez-Melero1,2,6, and Francisco Guerrero1,2,7 1Departamento de Biología Animal, Biología Vegetal y Ecología, Universidad de Jaén, Campus de Las Lagunillas, s/n. E–23071, Jaén, Spain 2Centro de Estudios Avanzados en Ciencias de la Tierra CEACTierra, Universidad de Jaén, Campus de Las Lagunillas, s/n. E–23071, Jaén, Spain 3Departamento de Ecología, Universidad de Granada, Campus de Fuentenueva, s/n. E–18071, Granada, Spain Abstract: Intrinsic ecological characteristics of Mediterranean wetlands make them excellent sites for studying biodiversity, but these wetlands have been studied much less frequently than temperate lakes. The invertebrates that inhabit them, and zooplankton specifically, play important roles in these wetlands. We compared the ability of taxon- and size-based analyses of the zooplankton community to predict the influence of environmental variables. We sampled environmental variables and zooplankton at 7 Mediterranean wetlands in the Iberian Peninsula (southern Spain) monthly along 1 hydroperiod cycle (2009–2010). We used 3 arrays for classifying the zooplankton community: 1) species occurring in >5% of the samples, 2) coarse-level taxa easily identified by a nonexpert (large branchiopods, small branchiopods, calanoid copepods, cyclopoid copepods, and harpacticoid copepods), and 3) 4 body-size classes (<1, 1–2.5, 2.5–10, and >10 mm in length). We used permutational analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) and canonical correspondence analysis (CCA) to test our hypotheses. Communities differed significantly among wetlands, and body size (55.8% of explained variance) was more useful than taxonomic composition (common taxa: 24.4%, coarse-level taxa: 26.5% of explained variance) for rapid assessment of the influence of the environmental variables on zooplankton community in temporary wetlands. Key words: zooplankton, Mediterranean wetlands, body size, eutrophication, wetland evaluation Wetlands are accepted globally as singular ecosystems (Mitsch and Gosselink 2000 and references therein). Nevertheless, small lentic ecosystems, and more specifically Mediterranean wetlands, have received much less attention than other aquatic ecosystems, such as large temperate lakes (Álvarez-Cobelas et al. 2005, Downing 2010). Mediterranean wetlands are unique because of their ecological characteristics. Most of them are very small with catchment area much larger than wetland surface area, and they experience a long vegetation period and strong seasonality in water supply (Álvarez-Cobelas et al. 2005). They are excellent repositories of biodiversity, frequently hold exclusive communities of aquatic organisms, and play an important role in the maintenance of regional biodiversity (Williams 1999, De Meester et al. 2005, Céréghino et al. 2008, Kagalou et al. 2010, Gilbert et al. 2014a, 2015a). They are recognized as essential hot spots of aquatic biodiversity, but the scarcity of research done in these ecosystems has made possible strongly detrimental human disturbance leading to the disappearance of many of them (Brinson and Malvárez 2002). A great fraction of Mediterranean wetlands are temporary and fishless (Conlon 2002). Thus, knowledge of the invertebrate communities that inhabit them is essential for modeling their trophic web structure (Wellborn et al. 1996, Quintana et al. 2006). Among invertebrates, the zooplankton assemblage is a good indicator for wetland assessment because zooplankton are easy to identify, play a key role in food webs, respond to environmental gradients (Jeppesen et al. 2000), and, in some cases, act as keystone species (Badosa et al. 2007). Aquatic assemblages can be analyzed on the basis of taxonomic identity or size of the individuals inhabiting them. The taxon-based approach is commonly used for analyzing the abundance or biomass of taxa in response to different experimental treatments or environmental variables (e.g., Quintana et al. 2006, Bagella et al. 2010). In contrast, the body-size approach is used to consider the distribution of biomass among size classes independently of taxonomic affiliation (e.g., Rojo and Rodríguez 1994, Blanco et al. 1998, Havens and Beaver 2011a, b). These approaches are complementary, but most studies of zooplankton assemblages, particularly in Mediterranean wetlands, have been based on the taxonomic approach. However, information about the size structure of zooplankton assemblages in wetlands is very useful for making management decisions because the body-size approach is simpler and less costly than the taxonomic approach (Havens and Beaver 2011a). The body-size approach has been used widely in oceanographic studies, in which investigators have used various optical techniques ranging from the more ancient Kontron, IBAS-I Image Analyzer (Rodríguez et al. 1987) or the semi-automatic image analyzer (AMS-VIDS 4; Guerrero and Rodríguez 1997) to more novel technologies, such as ZooScan (Gorsky et al. 2010), to obtain different biometric measures. We focused our study on the use of taxon- and size-based methods to explore whether taxonomic structure or body-size are good predictors of zooplankton responses to environmental influences in 7 Mediterranean wetlands located in the southern Iberian Peninsula. First, we analyzed zooplankton taxon abundance and size distribution. Second, we assessed the effect of environmental variables on zooplankton assemblages with the aid of permutational analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) and canonical correspondence analysis (CCA). METHODS Study site We worked in 7 wetlands (Fig. 1) in the Alto Guadalquivir region of the southeastern Iberian Peninsula. The study ![Geographical location of the study area in southern Spain and the 7 wetlands in the Alto Guadalquivir region.](page_1012_1342_1047_482.png) Figure 1. Geographical location of the study area in southern Spain and the 7 wetlands in the Alto Guadalquivir region. wetlands were classified based on the definition reported by Montes et al. (2004) and typology described by Rodríguez-Rodríguez and Benavente (2008) as playa-lake water bodies. The region has a Mediterranean climate, with 2 strongly marked seasons, a wet autumn–winter during which most of the annual rainfall occurs and a dry summer without precipitation (Álvarez-Cobelas et al. 2005). These climatic conditions are responsible for drastic water-level fluctuations, and most of the wetlands dry during the summer season. As a result of these water-level fluctuations, biotic and abiotic variables typically undergo dramatic temporal changes (Gilbert et al. 2014a, b, 2015a, b). We sampled wetlands periodically over 1 y. As is usual in Mediterranean regions, the wetlands were dry at the beginning of the hydrologic cycle in October and November 2009, except Castillo wetland, which filled in November. Therefore, the sampling period started in January 2010 except for Castillo (December 2009) and extended through December 2010. Zooplankton samples We collected zooplankton samples (plankton-net mesh size = 63 μm) monthly along 2 longitudinal transects, one from the shoreline to the open water and another along the shoreline. We combined the samples to obtain an integrated sample. We estimated the volume of filtered water as the distance of the haul multiplied by the mouth diameter of the net (27.5-cm mouth diameter). This sampling strategy allowed us to include all spatial and temporal heterogeneity characterizing the studied wetlands (Gilbert et al. 2015a). We preserved all samples in situ with 4% formalin (final concentration). In the laboratory, we counted crustacean zooplankton in the whole sample and identified individuals at the species level with the aid of keys published by Dussart (1967, 1969), Dussart and Defaye (1995), Einsle (1996), and Ranga-Reddy (1994) for copepods and Alonso (1996) for branchiopods. Later, we classified the zooplankton in 3 assemblages (Havens and Beaver 2011a) that corresponded to 3 matrices: 1) species matrix: species present in >5% of the total samples collected; 2) coarser-taxa matrix: taxa easily identified by a nonexpert after some training, including large branchiopods (LB; Anostraca, Conchostraca, Notostraca, Spinicaudata, and large Cladocera [Daphnia spp. and Simocephalus spp.]), small branchiopods (SB; small cladocerans), calanoid copepods (C), cyclopoid copepods (CY), and harpacticoid copepods (H); and 3) body-size matrix: 4 body-size classes that encompassed the observed range of sizes in the sampled zooplankton (S1: <1 mm, S2: 1–2.5 mm, S3: 2.5–10 mm, and S4: >10 mm). We estimated the abundance of each body-size class based on the average size of each taxon reported in the literature (Alonso 1996, Dussart 1967, 1969, Ranga-Reddy 1994, Dussart and Defaye 1995, Einsle 1996). Environmental variables We measured maximum depth (cm), Secchi disk depth (cm), temperature (°C), pH, and conductivity (μS/cm) monthly at the deepest point in each wetland. We measured temperature, conductivity, and pH in situ with a multiparameter YSI 556 MPS probe (Yellow Springs Instruments, Yellow Springs, Ohio). We measured turbidity (nephelometric turbidity units [NTU]) in situ with a Hanna HI93703 probe (Hanna Instruments, Woonsocket, Rhode Island) and fluorescence in situ with a field fluorometer (Aquafluor Handheld; Turner Design, San Jose, California) on an integrated sample from the 2 longitudinal transects (similar to the sampling design used for zooplankton samples). We estimated chlorophyll \( a \) (Chl \( a \)) concentration based on a fluorometry calibration curve (fluorescence = 16.584[Chl \( a \)] – 2.3616; \( R^2 = 0.998 \)) obtained in the laboratory based on Chl \( a \) standard solutions. We transported unfiltered integrated water samples to the laboratory within 3 h of collection and stored them in darkness and frozen at –20°C for <3 mo before analysis. In the laboratory, we digested unfiltered 50-mL aliquots with potassium persulfate for analysis of total P (TP) or sulfuric acid for analysis of total N (TN) (APHA 1995). We quantified TP and TN in the digested samples spectrophotometrically (HALO RB-10; Dynamica Scientific, Newport Pagnell, UK) by the molybdenum-blue method (Murphy and Riley 1962) or by ultraviolet spectrophotometric screening (APHA 1995), respectively. Detection limits were 1 μg P/L and 40 μg N/L for TP and TN, respectively. We measured the length of the aquatic phase or days of water inundation (DWI) as the presence of a taxon in relation to the day of the initial wetland inundation (the day on which a wetland basin was waterlogged) and wetland surface area (ha) as other explanatory variables. We estimated wetland surface area based on its length and width and formulae for the areas of simple shapes (ellipse or circle) fitted to the geometric form of the wetland on each sampling date. Statistical analysis We used PERMANOVA (PAST, version 3.06; Hammer et al. 2001) to conduct multivariate analysis of zooplankton species, coarser-taxa, and body-size assemblages. PERMANOVA was performed with 9999 permutations on Bray–Curtis distances among log(x + 1)-transformed abundances for each of the 3 matrices to test for differences in the assemblages among wetlands. PERMANOVA is not affected by unbalanced data sets (Alfonso et al. 2010). Significant differences were inferred at \( \alpha = 0.05 \). We used detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) to select the most appropriate direct statistical analysis to relate the 3 zooplankton matrices to environmental variables. The length of the DCA gradient was >3, indicating that a CCA was the most appropriate unimodal analysis (Iturron- dobeitia et al. 2004). CCA is a multivariate statistical ordination method that finds the maximum correlation between environmental and biological data sets (ter Braak 1987). Prior to analysis, we log(\( x + 1 \))-transformed data (except pH) from the zooplankton and environmental variable matrices to reduce the effect of different measurement scales of variables (Havens and Beaver 2011a). We removed species that were present in <5% of the samples from the species matrix. This step could be considered as a loss of information, but CCA is highly sensitive to low-abundance species (Zuur et al. 2010). We ran the CCAs with 499 Monte–Carlo permutations with significance set at \( p < 0.05 \). Multivariate analysis of ecological data was run with CANOCO (version 5; Microcomputer Software, Ithaca, New York). RESULTS Mean (±SE) values of the environmental variables in each wetland are presented in Table 1. Thirty-five zooplankton species were recorded during the sampling period. Of these species, 26 were present in >5% of the samples and constituted the species matrix. The most abundant common taxa were SB (35%) and CY (26%). The size classes S1 and S2 accounted for 38 and 35%, respectively, of the size-class matrix. Zooplankton assemblages described by all 3 matrices differed among wetlands (PERMANOVA, species matrix: Pseudo-\( F = 10.69, p < 0.01 \); coarse-taxa matrix: Pseudo-\( F = 6.40, p < 0.01 \); size-class matrix: Pseudo-\( F = 6.54, p < 0.01 \)). The CCA of the species matrix and environmental variables produced 3 significant axes (CCAs; Monte–Carlo tests, \( p < 0.05 \)). CCA1 (10.2% of explained variance) was correlated with turbidity, TP, and DWI; CCA2 (9%) was correlated with pH, area, maximum depth, TN, and Secchi-disk depth; and CCA3 (5.2%) was correlated with conductivity and Chl \( a \) (Table 2). Abundances of 13, 12, and 5 zooplankton species were correlated with CCA1, CCA2, and CCA3, respectively (Table 3). The CCA of the coarse-taxa matrix and environmental variable also produced 3 significant axes (Monte–Carlo tests, \( p < 0.05 \)). CCA1 (14.1%) was correlated with pH, Chl \( a \), area, maximum depth, Secchi-disk depth, and TN; CCA2 (10.0%) was correlated with conductivity and turbidity; and CCA3 (2.4%) was correlated with temperature, TP, and DWI (Table 2). Abundances of 3 (LC, C, and CY), 3 (LC, SC, and H), and 2 (LC and SC) coarse taxa were correlated with CCA1, CCA2, and CCA3, respectively (Table 3). The CCA of the body-size matrix and environmental variables yielded 3 significant axes (Monte–Carlo test, \( p < 0.05 \)). CCA1 (37.5%) was correlated with pH, maximum depth, Secchi-disk depth, TP, and TN; CCA2 (14.6%) was correlated with area and temperature; and CCA3 (3.7%) was correlated with turbidity, Chl \( a \), and DWI (Table 2). Abundances of size classes S1, S2, and S3 were correlated with CCA1; size class S4 was correlated with CCA2; and size class S1 was correlated with CCA3 (Table 3). DISCUSSION Taxon- and size-based analyses are 2 frequently used methods for assessing the effect of environmental variables on plankton community. Our results suggest that body size (55.8%) of explained variance is more informative than species (24.4%) or coarse taxa (26.5%) about the influence of the environmental variables on zooplankton community. Nevertheless, the combination of both approaches led us to a better understanding of the ecological functioning of aquatic systems (Strayer 1991, Rodríguez and Magnan 1993). Our results suggest that the zooplankton assemblages differ in species, coarse-level-taxa, and body-size composition among wetlands, and thus, reflect the extreme variability among Mediterranean wetlands and their key role for the maintenance of regional biodiversity (Williams 1997, Kagalou et al. 2010). Many investigators have found that zooplankton composition and body size are affected by factors, such as fish predation, food availability, temperature, and generation time (Brooks and Dodson 1965, Gillooly 2000, Hambright 2008, Fernández et al. 2009, Castellani et al. 2013, Lin et al. 2013, Quintana et al. 2015). All environmental variables in our study had a significant correlation with \( \geq 1 \) CCA of each analysis, a result indicating that all environmental variables in our study significantly affected the zooplankton assemblage. Maximum depth, Secchi-disk depth, TN, and DWI were more strongly correlated with the CCAs than other environmental variables (high Pearson \( r \) values; Table 2). The environmental variables that contributed to CCA1 of the CCAs based on coarse-taxa and size-class matrices were very similar to those that contributed to CCA2 of the CCA based on the species matrix. These axes might be linked to eutrophication level (see the opposite correlation between Secchi disk and TN in Table 2). The Chl \( a \) concentration supports this notion only for coarse taxonomic groups. However, the lack of a relationship between Chl \( a \) and eutrophication has been explained in these ecosystems as being a result of the presence of well-developed macrophyte beds, which negatively affect phytoplankton biomass and, consequently, Chl \( a \) concentration. Gilbert et al. (2015b) suggested competitive interactions between macrophytes and phytoplankton for inorganic nutrients and the release of allelopathic substances by macrophytes as main reasons for this negative relationship in these wetlands. They also pointed out a discrepancy between the trophic levels estimated based on the chlorophyll trophic state index (Carlson 1977) and the bioproduction number (BPN; Håkanson 1984), which is related to N and organic matter concentration in wetland sediments. The greater importance of TN than TP in our analyses is consistent with previous reports by Badosa et al. (2008), who found that N acts as a limiting nutrient and is more appropriate than P as an indicator of eutrophication in shallow Mediterranean wetlands. Eutrophication is a key process in wetlands and determines biological composition and community structure

(Maier 1996). Our results indicate that 12 species, 3 coarse taxa (LC, C, and CY), and 3 size classes (S1, S2, and S3) are affected by eutrophication. Eight of the 12 species were negatively and 4 were positively correlated with factors indicative of eutrophication (Table 3). These results are consistent with the biology of these species described by Margalef (1953), Armengol (1978), and Alonso (1996) for the Iberian Peninsula. The positive relationship of LC and CY with factors related to eutrophication also has been reported in the literature. Vijverberg and Boersma (1997) indicated that LC (Daphnia) have a better response to the increase in detritus and filaments of Cyanobacteria than do SC, but are more vulnerable to fish predation. Our study wetlands are fishless ecosystems, which may reinforce the tendency for LC to increase as eutrophication increases. The tendency of CY to increase with eutrophication also is well known (Marques and Boavida 1997, Parra et al. 2009). Last, a shift in the body-size distribution toward smaller individuals as eutrophication progresses is in accordance with the general pattern of reduced size in stressed communities described by Kerr (1974). The 2\textsuperscript{nd} interesting idea that can be extracted from environmental variables associated with CCA1 obtained with species matrix and CCA3 obtained with coarse-taxa and size-class matrices is related primarily to DWI and secondarily to light limitation associated with turbidity and P concentration in shallow ecosystems. Thus, these axes, which are associated with 13 species, 2 coarse-level taxa (LC and SC) and 1 size class (S1), are indirectly related to the eutrophication process. DWI or length of the aquatic phase is one of the most important variables that influence the biota of temporary ponds (Williams 1997). Our results suggest that it is a key variable for zooplankton assemblage composition (correlation with CCA1; Table 2), but is less important for coarse-taxa or size-class composition. Rewetting induces sediment resuspension, but the initial turbidity decreases with time since initiation of inundation (Scheffer 1998). Sediment desiccation drastically affects nutrient cycling in Mediterranean wetlands. Rewetting of dry surface sediment increases P concentration in the water column, thereby affecting the trophic state of the system (Gilbert et al. 2014b). The correlation between CCA1 and the 13 zooplankton species is in accord with the pattern of occurrence of those species in the water column from the start of the inundation period. The relationship with LC is explained by the prevalence of this group in temporary waters (Williams 1997). In contrast, SC and C have longer generation times (Allan 1976), and their occurrence in wetlands is later in the period of inundation. The relationship obtained with S1 is related to the idea that invertebrates of temporary ponds exhibit traits of r-selected species (sensu MacArthur and Wilson 1967), especially rapid growth, short life span, and small size (Williams 1997). The combined use of taxon- and body-size approaches allowed us to identify successional phases, according to the Intermediate Disturbance Hypothesis (Connell 1978). High diversity of species and body-size classes is achieved after inundation. Water inputs cause an input of nutrients to the ecosystem (Brucet et al. 2006), thereby increasing resource availability to a large number of species (Denslow 1985). As soon as water input ceases, resource scarcity begins and the assemblage moves to a competitive equilibrium characterized by low taxonomic and body-size diversity. Only CCA3 obtained with the species matrix, CCA2 obtained with the coarse-taxa and size-class matrices, the cyclopoid species *Acanthocyclops kieferi*, the Harpacticoida taxa group, and the largest body-size class (>10 mm) appear to be excluded from the influence of eutrophication. *Acanthocyclops kieferi* had low abundance and was present in Table 3. The individuals in the S4 body-size class belong to the Anostraca, which are regarded as ‘nexus species’ and transient in assemblage development (Angeler et al. 2008). In conclusion, our results suggest that body size might be better than taxonomic composition for rapid assessment of the influence of the environmental variables on zooplankton assemblages in temporary wetlands. We do not recommend a general move away from taxonomic studies because they provide fundamental information, e.g., for colonization processes or the appearance of new species. However, future investigators should test our conclusion in other aquatic systems, such as permanent or temperate wetlands. Moreover, our conclusions should be tested in relation to climate change, which could modify the size structure of the zooplankton favoring the small-sized species (Molinero et al. 2006). In this future scenario, temporary wetlands would suffer a drastic reduction in hydroperiod length, and therefore, pioneer species of the annual zooplankton succession could be favored over those that appear at the end of the hydrological cycle. This idea has been studied in relation to other alterations of wetlands, such as agricultural effects (Ruhí et al. 2009, Gilbert et al. 2017). Last, the 3 approaches have ecological and practical considerations for limnological monitoring programs. The species identification requires laborious analytical procedures and human and financial resources (Carignan and Villard 2002), whereas coarse-taxonomic and body-size approaches could be cost-effective tools for monitoring Mediterranean wetlands. This idea complements the approach taken by other authors (Rodríguez and Magnan 1993, Boix et al. 2004, Brucet et al. 2006) who recommend use of simultaneous methods in future limnological studies. Our approach provides a wider interpretation of the concept of diversity proposed by Margalef (1980, 1991), who pointed out the importance of the body size and taxonomic diversity and their relationships with some ecological factors (Rodríguez 2005, Quintana et al. 2006). Zooplankton body size versus taxonomy in Mediterranean wetlands: implications for aquatic ecosystem evaluation Juan Diego Gilbert1,2,4, Inmaculada de Vicente3,5, Raquel Jiménez-Melero1,2,6, and Francisco Guerrero1,2,7 1Departamento de Biología Animal, Biología Vegetal y Ecología, Universidad de Jaén, Campus de Las Lagunillas, s/n. E–23071, Jaén, Spain 2Centro de Estudios Avanzados en Ciencias de la Tierra CEACTierra, Universidad de Jaén, Campus de Las Lagunillas, s/n. E–23071, Jaén, Spain 3Departamento de Ecología, Universidad de Granada, Campus de Fuentenueva, s/n. E–18071, Granada, Spain Abstract: Intrinsic ecological characteristics of Mediterranean wetlands make them excellent sites for studying biodiversity, but these wetlands have been studied much less frequently than temperate lakes. The invertebrates that inhabit them, and zooplankton specifically, play important roles in these wetlands. We compared the ability of taxon- and size-based analyses of the zooplankton community to predict the influence of environmental variables. We sampled environmental variables and zooplankton at 7 Mediterranean wetlands in the Iberian Peninsula (southern Spain) monthly along 1 hydroperiod cycle (2009–2010). We used 3 arrays for classifying the zooplankton community: 1) species occurring in >5% of the samples, 2) coarse-level taxa easily identified by a nonexpert (large branchiopods, small branchiopods, calanoid copepods, cyclopoid copepods, and harpacticoid copepods), and 3) 4 body-size classes (<1, 1–2.5, 2.5–10, and >10 mm in length). We used permutational analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) and canonical correspondence analysis (CCA) to test our hypotheses. Communities differed significantly among wetlands, and body size (55.8% of explained variance) was more useful than taxonomic composition (common taxa: 24.4%, coarse-level taxa: 26.5% of explained variance) for rapid assessment of the influence of the environmental variables on zooplankton community in temporary wetlands. Key words: zooplankton, Mediterranean wetlands, body size, eutrophication, wetland evaluation Wetlands are accepted globally as singular ecosystems (Mitsch and Gosselink 2000 and references therein). Nevertheless, small lentic ecosystems, and more specifically Mediterranean wetlands, have received much less attention than other aquatic ecosystems, such as large temperate lakes (Álvarez-Cobelas et al. 2005, Downing 2010). Mediterranean wetlands are unique because of their ecological characteristics. Most of them are very small with catchment area much larger than wetland surface area, and they experience a long vegetation period and strong seasonality in water supply (Álvarez-Cobelas et al. 2005). They are excellent repositories of biodiversity, frequently hold exclusive communities of aquatic organisms, and play an important role in the maintenance of regional biodiversity (Williams 1999, De Meester et al. 2005, Céréghino et al. 2008, Kagalou et al. 2010, Gilbert et al. 2014a, 2015a). They are recognized as essential hot spots of aquatic biodiversity, but the scarcity of research done in these ecosystems has made possible strongly detrimental human disturbance leading to the disappearance of many of them (Brinson and Malvárez 2002). A great fraction of Mediterranean wetlands are temporary and fishless (Conlon 2002). Thus, knowledge of the invertebrate communities that inhabit them is essential for modeling their trophic web structure (Wellborn et al. 1996, Quintana et al. 2006). Among invertebrates, the zooplankton assemblage is a good indicator for wetland assessment because zooplankton are easy to identify, play a key role in food webs, respond to environmental gradients (Jeppesen et al. 2000), and, in some cases, act as keystone species (Badosa et al. 2007). Aquatic assemblages can be analyzed on the basis of taxonomic identity or size of the individuals inhabiting them. The taxon-based approach is commonly used for analyzing the abundance or biomass of taxa in response to different experimental treatments or environmental variables (e.g., Quintana et al. 2006, Bagella et al. 2010). In contrast, the body-size approach is used to consider the distribution of biomass among size classes independently of taxonomic affiliation (e.g., Rojo and Rodríguez 1994, Blanco et al. 1998, Havens and Beaver 2011a, b). These approaches are complementary, but most studies of zooplankton assemblages, particularly in Mediterranean wetlands, have been based on the taxonomic approach. However, information about the size structure of zooplankton assemblages in wetlands is very useful for making management decisions because the body-size approach is simpler and less costly than the taxonomic approach (Havens and Beaver 2011a). The body-size approach has been used widely in oceanographic studies, in which investigators have used various optical techniques ranging from the more ancient Kontron, IBAS-I Image Analyzer (Rodríguez et al. 1987) or the semi-automatic image analyzer (AMS-VIDS 4; Guerrero and Rodríguez 1997) to more novel technologies, such as ZooScan (Gorsky et al. 2010), to obtain different biometric measures. We focused our study on the use of taxon- and size-based methods to explore whether taxonomic structure or body-size are good predictors of zooplankton responses to environmental influences in 7 Mediterranean wetlands located in the southern Iberian Peninsula. First, we analyzed zooplankton taxon abundance and size distribution. Second, we assessed the effect of environmental variables on zooplankton assemblages with the aid of permutational analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) and canonical correspondence analysis (CCA). METHODS Study site We worked in 7 wetlands (Fig. 1) in the Alto Guadalquivir region of the southeastern Iberian Peninsula. The study ![Geographical location of the study area in southern Spain and the 7 wetlands in the Alto Guadalquivir region.](page_1012_1342_1047_482.png) Figure 1. Geographical location of the study area in southern Spain and the 7 wetlands in the Alto Guadalquivir region. wetlands were classified based on the definition reported by Montes et al. (2004) and typology described by Rodríguez-Rodríguez and Benavente (2008) as playa-lake water bodies. The region has a Mediterranean climate, with 2 strongly marked seasons, a wet autumn–winter during which most of the annual rainfall occurs and a dry summer without precipitation (Álvarez-Cobelas et al. 2005). These climatic conditions are responsible for drastic water-level fluctuations, and most of the wetlands dry during the summer season. As a result of these water-level fluctuations, biotic and abiotic variables typically undergo dramatic temporal changes (Gilbert et al. 2014a, b, 2015a, b). We sampled wetlands periodically over 1 y. As is usual in Mediterranean regions, the wetlands were dry at the beginning of the hydrologic cycle in October and November 2009, except Castillo wetland, which filled in November. Therefore, the sampling period started in January 2010 except for Castillo (December 2009) and extended through December 2010. Zooplankton samples We collected zooplankton samples (plankton-net mesh size = 63 μm) monthly along 2 longitudinal transects, one from the shoreline to the open water and another along the shoreline. We combined the samples to obtain an integrated sample. We estimated the volume of filtered water as the distance of the haul multiplied by the mouth diameter of the net (27.5-cm mouth diameter). This sampling strategy allowed us to include all spatial and temporal heterogeneity characterizing the studied wetlands (Gilbert et al. 2015a). We preserved all samples in situ with 4% formalin (final concentration). In the laboratory, we counted crustacean zooplankton in the whole sample and identified individuals at the species level with the aid of keys published by Dussart (1967, 1969), Dussart and Defaye (1995), Einsle (1996), and Ranga-Reddy (1994) for copepods and Alonso (1996) for branchiopods. Later, we classified the zooplankton in 3 assemblages (Havens and Beaver 2011a) that corresponded to 3 matrices: 1) species matrix: species present in >5% of the total samples collected; 2) coarser-taxa matrix: taxa easily identified by a nonexpert after some training, including large branchiopods (LB; Anostraca, Conchostraca, Notostraca, Spinicaudata, and large Cladocera [Daphnia spp. and Simocephalus spp.]), small branchiopods (SB; small cladocerans), calanoid copepods (C), cyclopoid copepods (CY), and harpacticoid copepods (H); and 3) body-size matrix: 4 body-size classes that encompassed the observed range of sizes in the sampled zooplankton (S1: <1 mm, S2: 1–2.5 mm, S3: 2.5–10 mm, and S4: >10 mm). We estimated the abundance of each body-size class based on the average size of each taxon reported in the literature (Alonso 1996, Dussart 1967, 1969, Ranga-Reddy 1994, Dussart and Defaye 1995, Einsle 1996). Environmental variables We measured maximum depth (cm), Secchi disk depth (cm), temperature (°C), pH, and conductivity (μS/cm) monthly at the deepest point in each wetland. We measured temperature, conductivity, and pH in situ with a multiparameter YSI 556 MPS probe (Yellow Springs Instruments, Yellow Springs, Ohio). We measured turbidity (nephelometric turbidity units [NTU]) in situ with a Hanna HI93703 probe (Hanna Instruments, Woonsocket, Rhode Island) and fluorescence in situ with a field fluorometer (Aquafluor Handheld; Turner Design, San Jose, California) on an integrated sample from the 2 longitudinal transects (similar to the sampling design used for zooplankton samples). We estimated chlorophyll \( a \) (Chl \( a \)) concentration based on a fluorometry calibration curve (fluorescence = 16.584[Chl \( a \)] – 2.3616; \( R^2 = 0.998 \)) obtained in the laboratory based on Chl \( a \) standard solutions. We transported unfiltered integrated water samples to the laboratory within 3 h of collection and stored them in darkness and frozen at –20°C for <3 mo before analysis. In the laboratory, we digested unfiltered 50-mL aliquots with potassium persulfate for analysis of total P (TP) or sulfuric acid for analysis of total N (TN) (APHA 1995). We quantified TP and TN in the digested samples spectrophotometrically (HALO RB-10; Dynamica Scientific, Newport Pagnell, UK) by the molybdenum-blue method (Murphy and Riley 1962) or by ultraviolet spectrophotometric screening (APHA 1995), respectively. Detection limits were 1 μg P/L and 40 μg N/L for TP and TN, respectively. We measured the length of the aquatic phase or days of water inundation (DWI) as the presence of a taxon in relation to the day of the initial wetland inundation (the day on which a wetland basin was waterlogged) and wetland surface area (ha) as other explanatory variables. We estimated wetland surface area based on its length and width and formulae for the areas of simple shapes (ellipse or circle) fitted to the geometric form of the wetland on each sampling date. Statistical analysis We used PERMANOVA (PAST, version 3.06; Hammer et al. 2001) to conduct multivariate analysis of zooplankton species, coarser-taxa, and body-size assemblages. PERMANOVA was performed with 9999 permutations on Bray–Curtis distances among log(x + 1)-transformed abundances for each of the 3 matrices to test for differences in the assemblages among wetlands. PERMANOVA is not affected by unbalanced data sets (Alfonso et al. 2010). Significant differences were inferred at \( \alpha = 0.05 \). We used detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) to select the most appropriate direct statistical analysis to relate the 3 zooplankton matrices to environmental variables. The length of the DCA gradient was >3, indicating that a CCA was the most appropriate unimodal analysis (Iturron- dobeitia et al. 2004). CCA is a multivariate statistical ordination method that finds the maximum correlation between environmental and biological data sets (ter Braak 1987). Prior to analysis, we log(\( x + 1 \))-transformed data (except pH) from the zooplankton and environmental variable matrices to reduce the effect of different measurement scales of variables (Havens and Beaver 2011a). We removed species that were present in <5% of the samples from the species matrix. This step could be considered as a loss of information, but CCA is highly sensitive to low-abundance species (Zuur et al. 2010). We ran the CCAs with 499 Monte–Carlo permutations with significance set at \( p < 0.05 \). Multivariate analysis of ecological data was run with CANOCO (version 5; Microcomputer Software, Ithaca, New York). RESULTS Mean (±SE) values of the environmental variables in each wetland are presented in Table 1. Thirty-five zooplankton species were recorded during the sampling period. Of these species, 26 were present in >5% of the samples and constituted the species matrix. The most abundant common taxa were SB (35%) and CY (26%). The size classes S1 and S2 accounted for 38 and 35%, respectively, of the size-class matrix. Zooplankton assemblages described by all 3 matrices differed among wetlands (PERMANOVA, species matrix: Pseudo-\( F = 10.69, p < 0.01 \); coarse-taxa matrix: Pseudo-\( F = 6.40, p < 0.01 \); size-class matrix: Pseudo-\( F = 6.54, p < 0.01 \)). The CCA of the species matrix and environmental variables produced 3 significant axes (CCAs; Monte–Carlo tests, \( p < 0.05 \)). CCA1 (10.2% of explained variance) was correlated with turbidity, TP, and DWI; CCA2 (9%) was correlated with pH, area, maximum depth, TN, and Secchi-disk depth; and CCA3 (5.2%) was correlated with conductivity and Chl \( a \) (Table 2). Abundances of 13, 12, and 5 zooplankton species were correlated with CCA1, CCA2, and CCA3, respectively (Table 3). The CCA of the coarse-taxa matrix and environmental variable also produced 3 significant axes (Monte–Carlo tests, \( p < 0.05 \)). CCA1 (14.1%) was correlated with pH, Chl \( a \), area, maximum depth, Secchi-disk depth, and TN; CCA2 (10.0%) was correlated with conductivity and turbidity; and CCA3 (2.4%) was correlated with temperature, TP, and DWI (Table 2). Abundances of 3 (LC, C, and CY), 3 (LC, SC, and H), and 2 (LC and SC) coarse taxa were correlated with CCA1, CCA2, and CCA3, respectively (Table 3). The CCA of the body-size matrix and environmental variables yielded 3 significant axes (Monte–Carlo test, \( p < 0.05 \)). CCA1 (37.5%) was correlated with pH, maximum depth, Secchi-disk depth, TP, and TN; CCA2 (14.6%) was correlated with area and temperature; and CCA3 (3.7%) was correlated with turbidity, Chl \( a \), and DWI (Table 2). Abundances of size classes S1, S2, and S3 were correlated with CCA1; size class S4 was correlated with CCA2; and size class S1 was correlated with CCA3 (Table 3). DISCUSSION Taxon- and size-based analyses are 2 frequently used methods for assessing the effect of environmental variables on plankton community. Our results suggest that body size (55.8%) of explained variance is more informative than species (24.4%) or coarse taxa (26.5%) about the influence of the environmental variables on zooplankton community. Nevertheless, the combination of both approaches led us to a better understanding of the ecological functioning of aquatic systems (Strayer 1991, Rodríguez and Magnan 1993). Our results suggest that the zooplankton assemblages differ in species, coarse-level-taxa, and body-size composition among wetlands, and thus, reflect the extreme variability among Mediterranean wetlands and their key role for the maintenance of regional biodiversity (Williams 1997, Kagalou et al. 2010). Many investigators have found that zooplankton composition and body size are affected by factors, such as fish predation, food availability, temperature, and generation time (Brooks and Dodson 1965, Gillooly 2000, Hambright 2008, Fernández et al. 2009, Castellani et al. 2013, Lin et al. 2013, Quintana et al. 2015). All environmental variables in our study had a significant correlation with \( \geq 1 \) CCA of each analysis, a result indicating that all environmental variables in our study significantly affected the zooplankton assemblage. Maximum depth, Secchi-disk depth, TN, and DWI were more strongly correlated with the CCAs than other environmental variables (high Pearson \( r \) values; Table 2). The environmental variables that contributed to CCA1 of the CCAs based on coarse-taxa and size-class matrices were very similar to those that contributed to CCA2 of the CCA based on the species matrix. These axes might be linked to eutrophication level (see the opposite correlation between Secchi disk and TN in Table 2). The Chl \( a \) concentration supports this notion only for coarse taxonomic groups. However, the lack of a relationship between Chl \( a \) and eutrophication has been explained in these ecosystems as being a result of the presence of well-developed macrophyte beds, which negatively affect phytoplankton biomass and, consequently, Chl \( a \) concentration. Gilbert et al. (2015b) suggested competitive interactions between macrophytes and phytoplankton for inorganic nutrients and the release of allelopathic substances by macrophytes as main reasons for this negative relationship in these wetlands. They also pointed out a discrepancy between the trophic levels estimated based on the chlorophyll trophic state index (Carlson 1977) and the bioproduction number (BPN; Håkanson 1984), which is related to N and organic matter concentration in wetland sediments. The greater importance of TN than TP in our analyses is consistent with previous reports by Badosa et al. (2008), who found that N acts as a limiting nutrient and is more appropriate than P as an indicator of eutrophication in shallow Mediterranean wetlands. Eutrophication is a key process in wetlands and determines biological composition and community structure

(Maier 1996). Our results indicate that 12 species, 3 coarse taxa (LC, C, and CY), and 3 size classes (S1, S2, and S3) are affected by eutrophication. Eight of the 12 species were negatively and 4 were positively correlated with factors indicative of eutrophication (Table 3). These results are consistent with the biology of these species described by Margalef (1953), Armengol (1978), and Alonso (1996) for the Iberian Peninsula. The positive relationship of LC and CY with factors related to eutrophication also has been reported in the literature. Vijverberg and Boersma (1997) indicated that LC (Daphnia) have a better response to the increase in detritus and filaments of Cyanobacteria than do SC, but are more vulnerable to fish predation. Our study wetlands are fishless ecosystems, which may reinforce the tendency for LC to increase as eutrophication increases. The tendency of CY to increase with eutrophication also is well known (Marques and Boavida 1997, Parra et al. 2009). Last, a shift in the body-size distribution toward smaller individuals as eutrophication progresses is in accordance with the general pattern of reduced size in stressed communities described by Kerr (1974). The 2\textsuperscript{nd} interesting idea that can be extracted from environmental variables associated with CCA1 obtained with species matrix and CCA3 obtained with coarse-taxa and size-class matrices is related primarily to DWI and secondarily to light limitation associated with turbidity and P concentration in shallow ecosystems. Thus, these axes, which are associated with 13 species, 2 coarse-level taxa (LC and SC) and 1 size class (S1), are indirectly related to the eutrophication process. DWI or length of the aquatic phase is one of the most important variables that influence the biota of temporary ponds (Williams 1997). Our results suggest that it is a key variable for zooplankton assemblage composition (correlation with CCA1; Table 2), but is less important for coarse-taxa or size-class composition. Rewetting induces sediment resuspension, but the initial turbidity decreases with time since initiation of inundation (Scheffer 1998). Sediment desiccation drastically affects nutrient cycling in Mediterranean wetlands. Rewetting of dry surface sediment increases P concentration in the water column, thereby affecting the trophic state of the system (Gilbert et al. 2014b). The correlation between CCA1 and the 13 zooplankton species is in accord with the pattern of occurrence of those species in the water column from the start of the inundation period. The relationship with LC is explained by the prevalence of this group in temporary waters (Williams 1997). In contrast, SC and C have longer generation times (Allan 1976), and their occurrence in wetlands is later in the period of inundation. The relationship obtained with S1 is related to the idea that invertebrates of temporary ponds exhibit traits of r-selected species (sensu MacArthur and Wilson 1967), especially rapid growth, short life span, and small size (Williams 1997). The combined use of taxon- and body-size approaches allowed us to identify successional phases, according to the Intermediate Disturbance Hypothesis (Connell 1978). High diversity of species and body-size classes is achieved after inundation. Water inputs cause an input of nutrients to the ecosystem (Brucet et al. 2006), thereby increasing resource availability to a large number of species (Denslow 1985). As soon as water input ceases, resource scarcity begins and the assemblage moves to a competitive equilibrium characterized by low taxonomic and body-size diversity. The individuals in the S4 body-size class belong to the Anostraca, which are regarded as ‘nexus species’ and transient in assemblage development (Angeler et al. 2008). In conclusion, our results suggest that body size might be better than taxonomic composition for rapid assessment of the influence of the environmental variables on zooplankton assemblages in temporary wetlands. We do not recommend a general move away from taxonomic studies because they provide fundamental information, e.g., for colonization processes or the appearance of new species. However, future investigators should test our conclusion in other aquatic systems, such as permanent or temperate wetlands. Moreover, our conclusions should be tested in relation to climate change, which could modify the size structure of the zooplankton favoring the small-sized species (Molinero et al. 2006). In this future scenario, temporary wetlands would suffer a drastic reduction in hydroperiod length, and therefore, pioneer species of the annual zooplankton succession could be favored over those that appear at the end of the hydrological cycle. This idea has been studied in relation to other alterations of wetlands, such as agricultural effects (Ruhí et al. 2009, Gilbert et al. 2017). Last, the 3 approaches have ecological and practical considerations for limnological monitoring programs. The species identification requires laborious analytical procedures and human and financial resources (Carignan and Villard 2002), whereas coarse-taxonomic and body-size approaches could be cost-effective tools for monitoring Mediterranean wetlands. This idea complements the approach taken by other authors (Rodríguez and Magnan 1993, Boix et al. 2004, Brucet et al. 2006) who recommend use of simultaneous methods in future limnological studies. Our approach provides a wider interpretation of the concept of diversity proposed by Margalef (1980, 1991), who pointed out the importance of the body size and taxonomic diversity and their relationships with some ecological factors (Rodríguez 2005, Quintana et al. 2006).
